docs.title: About this book
docs.text: This course provides a foundation for quantum computing, Post-Quantum Cryptography and quantum machine learning. It covers the fundamental concepts of quantum mechanics, quantum algorithms, and their applications in various areas, including cryptography, cybersecurity, machine learning, finance, the energy sector, etc. Students will gain a theoretical understanding of quantum computing and practical skills in implementing quantum algorithms for various tasks.

docs.title: 41.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Describe Braket's managed-service model and how it differs from vendor SDKs.
  2. Build and run circuits with the Braket SDK on simulators and QPUs.
  3. Compare the hardware vendors available through Braket.
  4. Compute the cost of a Braket experiment and design within a budget.
  5. Use Hybrid Jobs for variational algorithms.

docs.title: 41.2 The Managed-Service Model
docs.text:
Braket is not a competing SDK so much as a procurement and orchestration layer. Its value proposition is one account, one API and one bill for hardware from several independent companies.

Vendor SDK (Qiskit, Cirq) Amazon Braket Hardware access one vendor many vendors Account one per vendor one AWS account Billing free tier / research grants pay per task and per shot Simulators local local and managed (up to 34 qubits, GPU) Storage your machine S3, automatic Orchestration write your own Hybrid Jobs (managed containers)

When Braket is the right choice: benchmarking across hardware modalities, running production workloads with SLAs, or needing large managed simulators without owning a cluster.

When it is not: learning (IBM's free tier is better), or research needing pulse-level control (vendor SDKs expose more).

docs.title: Installation and a first circuit
docs.text:
pip install amazon-braket-sdk
aws configure                    # set credentials and region

from braket.circuits import Circuit
from braket.devices import LocalSimulator

circ = Circuit().h(0).cnot(0, 1)
circ.probability()

device = LocalSimulator()
result = device.run(circ, shots=1000).result()
print(result.measurement_counts)
# Counter({'00': 508, '11': 492})

The chaining style is distinctive: Circuit().h(0).cnot(0,1).rx(2, 0.5). Every gate method returns the circuit, so operations chain fluently.

docs.title: Gate reference
docs.text:
c = Circuit()
c.i(0); c.x(0); c.y(0); c.z(0)
c.h(0); c.s(0); c.si(0); c.t(0); c.ti(0); c.v(0); c.vi(0)   # v = sqrt(X)
c.rx(0, theta); c.ry(0, theta); c.rz(0, theta); c.phaseshift(0, phi)

c.cnot(0, 1); c.cz(0, 1); c.swap(0, 1); c.iswap(0, 1)
c.xx(0, 1, angle); c.yy(0, 1, angle); c.zz(0, 1, angle)     # Ising gates -- ion-native
c.ccnot(0, 1, 2); c.cswap(0, 1, 2)

Note xx, yy, zz. These Mølmer–Sørensen-type gates are native to trapped-ion hardware, so on IonQ they compile to a single physical operation, whereas a CNOT decomposes into several. Using the native gate set is often worth 2–3× in fidelity.

QuEra Aquila is different in kind. It is an analog Hamiltonian simulator, not a gate device. You specify a time-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonian — atom positions, laser detuning and Rabi frequency — and it evolves the system. Excellent for many-body physics; it cannot run gate circuits at all.

docs.title: 41.5 Cost Model
docs.text:
This is the practical constraint students must learn to plan around.

Component Price (indicative, US, 2024) Per task (a job submission) $0.30 Per shot — IonQ $0.03 Per shot — Rigetti / IQM $0.00035 SV1 simulator $0.075 per minute DM1 simulator $0.075 per minute TN1 simulator $0.275 per minute Hybrid Jobs (classical container) standard EC2 rates

The per-task charge is the trap. Submitting 1000 separate one-shot tasks costs \(1000\times\$0.30 = \$300\) in task fees alone. Always batch shots into a single task.

IonQ is ~85× more expensive per shot than Rigetti — reflecting slower gates and higher fidelity. Budget accordingly: use Rigetti for exploration and IonQ for final high-fidelity runs.

docs.title: 41.6 Hybrid Jobs
docs.text:
For variational algorithms, round-tripping between your laptop and AWS for every iteration is slow and expensive in task fees. Hybrid Jobs run your classical optimisation loop in an AWS container next to the QPU, with priority queue access.

from braket.jobs import hybrid_job
from braket.jobs.metrics import log_metric

@hybrid_job(device="arn:aws:braket:us-east-1::device/qpu/ionq/Aria-1")
def run_vqe(n_iterations=100):
    from braket.aws import AwsDevice
    device = AwsDevice(get_job_device_arn())
    params = initial_params
    for i in range(n_iterations):
        energy = evaluate(device, params)
        params = update(params, energy)
        log_metric(metric_name="energy", value=energy, iteration_number=i)
    return params

job = run_vqe(n_iterations=50)
print(job.arn, job.state())

Three concrete benefits.

  1. Priority queueing. The QPU is reserved for the job's duration, so iterations do not sit behind other users' tasks — this alone can turn a 12-hour run into 20 minutes.
  2. Lower latency. The classical loop runs in the same AWS region as the QPU.
  3. Checkpointing and metrics. Progress survives interruptions and is visible in CloudWatch.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Cost of a QSVM experiment
docs.text:
A QSVM needs a 50×50 kernel matrix at 1000 shots per entry. Compute the cost on (a) IonQ, (b) Rigetti, (c) SV1, assuming one task per kernel entry.

Solution.

Number of kernel entries. Symmetric, diagonal known:

\[ \frac{50\times49}{2} = \mathbf{1225\ \text{entries}} \]

(a) IonQ.

\[ \text{task fees} = 1225\times\$0.30 = \$367.50 \] \[ \text{shot fees} = 1225\times1000\times\$0.03 = \$36{,}750 \] \[ \boxed{\text{Total} = \$37{,}117.50} \]

(b) Rigetti.

\[ \text{task fees} = 1225\times\$0.30 = \$367.50 \] \[ \text{shot fees} = 1225\times1000\times\$0.00035 = \$428.75 \] \[ \boxed{\text{Total} = \$796.25} \]

(c) SV1 (noiseless simulator). At roughly 0.5 s per 1000-shot circuit:

\[ \text{time} = \frac{1225\times0.5}{60} = 10.2\ \text{minutes} \] \[ \boxed{\text{Total} = 10.2\times\$0.075 = \$0.77} \]

Comparison.

Platform Cost Ratio to SV1 SV1 simulator $0.77 1× Rigetti QPU $796 1030× IonQ QPU $37 118 48 000×

Three lessons.

  1. Develop on simulators. A $0.77 run tells you whether the algorithm works before you spend $37 000 finding out that it does not.
  2. Batch tasks. If the SDK allows submitting a batch of circuits as one task, the $367.50 in task fees collapses to $0.30. Use AwsQuantumTaskBatch.
  3. The \(O(M^2)\) wall is financial as well as computational (L27). Doubling to 100 training samples quadruples the cost: IonQ would run to about $150 000.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Native gates and fidelity on IonQ
docs.text:
A circuit needs 20 CNOTs. Compare running it as CNOTs versus rewriting with native \(XX\) (MS) gates on IonQ, given CNOT decomposes to 1 MS + 4 single-qubit gates, with \(\epsilon_{\text{MS}} = 0.4\%\) and \(\epsilon_{1q} = 0.03\%\).

Solution.

As CNOTs. Each CNOT compiles to 1 MS gate plus 4 single-qubit gates:

\[ 20\ \text{CNOTs} \Rightarrow 20\ \text{MS} + 80\ \text{single-qubit} \] \[ F = (1-0.004)^{20}\times(1-0.0003)^{80} = 0.996^{20}\times0.9997^{80} \] \[ = 0.9231 \times 0.9763 = \mathbf{0.9013} \]

Rewritten with native \(XX\) gates. If the algorithm's two-qubit interactions are naturally Ising-type (as in QAOA's \(Z_iZ_j\) terms, or Trotterised spin Hamiltonians), each maps to one MS gate with no surrounding single-qubit gates:

\[ 20\ \text{MS gates only} \] \[ F = 0.996^{20} = \mathbf{0.9231} \]

Improvement.

\[ \frac{1 - 0.9013}{1 - 0.9231} = \frac{0.0987}{0.0769} = \mathbf{1.28\times}\ \text{less error} \]

Where the gain is much larger. On superconducting hardware the same 20 two-qubit gates would also need SWAPs if the interactions are non-local. For a dense interaction graph on 8 qubits, routing typically triples the two-qubit count:

\[ F_{\text{supercond}} \approx (1-0.008)^{60} = \mathbf{0.618} \]

versus IonQ's \(0.923\) — a 5× smaller error on IonQ despite its 1000× slower gates.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{All-to-all connectivity plus native Ising gates is why trapped ions win on connectivity-heavy circuits.}\ } \]

Design rule. Express the algorithm in the hardware's native gate set. In Braket:

circ = Circuit().zz(0, 1, angle)     # native on IonQ -- 1 physical gate
# rather than
circ = Circuit().cnot(0,1).rz(1, angle).cnot(0,1)   # 2 MS + overhead

docs.title: Problem 3 — Designing within a budget
docs.text:
You have $500 of AWS credit and must demonstrate QAOA on a 6-node Max-Cut problem. Design the full experiment.

Solution.

Phase 1 — Simulator development (budget: $5).

from braket.devices import LocalSimulator      # FREE
  • Implement QAOA for \(p = 1, 2, 3\) on 6 qubits (\(2^6 = 64\) amplitudes — instant).
  • Grid-search \((\gamma,\beta)\) over \(20\times20\) points for each \(p\).
  • Brute-force the exact optimum for comparison (only \(2^6 = 64\) bitstrings).
  • Cost: $0 (local simulator).

Phase 2 — Noise study on DM1 (budget: $20).

dm1 = AwsDevice("arn:aws:braket:::device/quantum-simulator/amazon/dm1")
  • 6 qubits is within DM1's 17-qubit limit.
  • Sweep the two-qubit error rate from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-2}\) to predict which \(p\) survives on hardware.
  • ~20 configurations × 30 s = 10 minutes → $0.75.
  • Expected finding: \(p=1\) survives, \(p=3\) is destroyed by noise.

Phase 3 — Rigetti hardware run (budget: $50).

  • Circuit: \(p=1\), 6 qubits, \(|E|\) = say 9 edges → 18 CNOTs + 6 \(R_x\).
  • Batch all parameter settings into one task using AwsQuantumTaskBatch.
  • 10 parameter points × 2000 shots:
\[ \text{cost} = \underbrace{\$0.30}_{\text{one batched task}} + 10\times2000\times\$0.00035 = \$0.30 + \$7.00 = \$7.30 \]

Phase 4 — IonQ confirmation run (budget: $400).

  • Run only the single best parameter setting found in Phase 3.
  • Higher fidelity and all-to-all connectivity → no SWAPs.
\[ \text{shots affordable} = \frac{\$400 - \$0.30}{\$0.03} = \mathbf{13{,}323\ \text{shots}} \]

Use 10 000 shots, leaving margin.

\[ \text{cost} = \$0.30 + 10{,}000\times\$0.03 = \$300.30 \]

Total budget.

Phase Platform Cost 1. Development LocalSimulator $0.00 2. Noise study DM1 $0.75 3. Exploration Rigetti $7.30 4. Final result IonQ $300.30 Total $308.35 Remaining $191.65 for reruns

The strategy in one sentence. Spend compute where it is free, spend cheap hardware where you need to explore, and spend expensive hardware once, on the single configuration you have already validated.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Comparing three hardware modalities
docs.text:
Design a benchmark comparing IonQ, Rigetti and IQM on the same circuit, and predict the results.

Solution.

The benchmark circuit: GHZ state on \(n\) qubits, for \(n = 2,\dots,8\), measuring the fidelity of the \(\Pr[00\cdots0] + \Pr[11\cdots1]\) signal.

Why GHZ? It requires long-range entanglement — every qubit correlated with every other — which is exactly the regime where connectivity matters. It is also easy to verify: an ideal GHZ gives \(\Pr[0^n] = \Pr[1^n] = 0.5\) and zero probability for everything else.

def ghz(n):
    c = Circuit().h(0)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        c.cnot(i, i + 1)          # chain construction (topology-friendly)
    return c

devices = {
    "IonQ":    "arn:aws:braket:us-east-1::device/qpu/ionq/Aria-1",
    "Rigetti": "arn:aws:braket:us-west-1::device/qpu/rigetti/Ankaa-3",
    "IQM":     "arn:aws:braket:eu-north-1::device/qpu/iqm/Garnet",
}

for name, arn in devices.items():
    for n in range(2, 9):
        task = AwsDevice(arn).run(ghz(n).probability(), shots=1000)
        # record P(0^n) + P(1^n)

Predicted results.

\(n\) IonQ (all-to-all) Rigetti (lattice) IQM (square) 2 0.98 0.97 0.96 4 0.94 0.88 0.86 6 0.89 0.74 0.70 8 0.83 0.58 0.52

Reasoning behind the prediction.

  • IonQ uses a chain of MS gates with no SWAPs (all-to-all), so gate count is \(n-1\), giving \(F \approx 0.996^{n-1}\times(\text{single-qubit and readout errors})\).
  • Rigetti / IQM need the chain to lie along a physical path. On a lattice a linear chain usually fits without SWAPs too — so the gap is driven mainly by their higher two-qubit error (\(\sim0.8\)–\(1.5\%\) versus IonQ's \(0.4\%\)) and higher readout error.
  • The gap widens with \(n\) because errors compound multiplicatively.

A second, harder benchmark to add. Replace GHZ with a fully connected QAOA circuit (interactions between all pairs). Then Rigetti and IQM require \(O(n^2)\) SWAPs while IonQ requires none, and the gap should widen dramatically — predicted \(F_{n=8}\): IonQ 0.70, Rigetti 0.15.

What to report. Fidelity versus two-qubit gate count and versus wall-clock time, on the same axes. IonQ wins on fidelity; Rigetti wins on speed and cost by ~85×. There is no single "best" device — only best for a given circuit shape and budget.

docs.title: Problem 5 — When to use Braket versus a vendor SDK
docs.text:
Recommend Braket or a vendor SDK for each scenario.

(a) An undergraduate course lab. (b) A benchmarking paper comparing four hardware platforms. (c) Production VQE for a pharmaceutical company. (d) Research needing pulse-level control on IBM hardware. (e) A 30-qubit noiseless simulation without owning a cluster.

Solution.

(a) Course lab → Qiskit (vendor SDK). IBM's free tier gives students hardware access at no cost and no credit card. Braket requires an AWS account with billing enabled — an administrative barrier, and a genuine financial risk if a student submits 1000 unbatched tasks by accident. Never expose students to per-shot billing in a first course.

(b) Benchmarking paper → Braket. This is Braket's purpose. One SDK, one billing account, and — importantly for reproducibility — one uniform circuit representation across all four devices, eliminating the confound of different compilers. Writing the study in four vendor SDKs would introduce compiler differences that contaminate the hardware comparison.

(c) Production VQE → Braket, using Hybrid Jobs. Priority queue access is decisive: a 500-iteration VQE submitted as ordinary tasks could take days sitting behind other users. Hybrid Jobs reserve the device. AWS also provides the SLAs, IAM access control, audit logging and S3 data governance that a regulated pharmaceutical company requires.

(d) Pulse-level control on IBM → Qiskit. Braket exposes only the gate layer. Qiskit Pulse gives access to the underlying microwave waveforms — essential for gate calibration, custom pulse shaping and dynamical-decoupling research. Braket is not the wrong tool so much as the wrong layer.

(e) 30-qubit noiseless simulation → Braket SV1. 30 qubits needs 17 GB and substantial CPU. SV1 handles up to 34 qubits on managed parallel hardware at $0.075/minute — perhaps $5 for a substantial study, versus buying or renting a large-memory server. (Alternative: lightning.gpu on a rented EC2 instance, which may be cheaper for very long runs but requires you to manage the instance.)

The summary rule.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Vendor SDK for \emph{depth} (one platform, deeply); Braket for \emph{breadth} (many platforms, uniformly).}\ } \]

docs.title: 41.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Braket is a managed service, not a competing SDK: one AWS account and one API for IonQ (trapped ion, all-to-all), Rigetti and IQM (superconducting), and QuEra (neutral-atom analog).
  • Circuits use a fluent chaining style; native xx/yy/zz Ising gates compile to a single physical operation on trapped-ion hardware.
  • Simulators: LocalSimulator (free, ~25 qubits), SV1 (34 qubits), DM1 (17, noisy), TN1 (50, shallow).
  • Cost model: $0.30 per task plus per-shot fees — $0.03 on IonQ versus $0.00035 on Rigetti (85× cheaper). Always batch shots into one task; unbatched submission is the most common and most expensive mistake.
  • Hybrid Jobs run the classical optimisation loop next to the QPU with priority queueing — essential for variational algorithms.
  • The professional workflow: develop free on a local simulator → study noise on DM1 → explore cheaply on Rigetti → confirm once, at high shot count, on IonQ.
  • Vendor SDK for depth; Braket for breadth.

Next lesson: L42 — Microsoft Q# and the Quantum Development Kit.

Practise now: unit4-platforms-lab.html → Cost Calculator: enter circuit count, shots and device, and see the task and shot fees broken down, with batching savings highlighted.

docs.title: Lesson 45: Comparative Study, Benchmarking and Capstone Project
45.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Compare all major frameworks against a structured feature matrix.
  2. Define and compute the standard hardware benchmarks: quantum volume, CLOPS, EPLG, algorithmic qubits.
  3. Design a fair cross-platform comparison and avoid the standard pitfalls.
  4. Use OpenQASM 3 for portability between frameworks.
  5. Plan and execute the capstone project for this course.

The pragmatic conclusions.

\[ \text{Learn} \Rightarrow \text{Qiskit}; \quad \text{QML} \Rightarrow \text{PennyLane}; \quad \text{Compile} \Rightarrow \text{pytket}; \quad \text{Estimate} \Rightarrow \text{Q\#}; \quad \text{Benchmark} \Rightarrow \text{Braket} \]

docs.title: Quantum Volume (IBM, 2019)
docs.text:
Definition. The largest \(2^{n}\) such that the device can run a random square circuit on \(n\) qubits with depth \(n\) and achieve a heavy-output probability above \(2/3\) with \(97.5\%\) confidence.

\[ V_Q = 2^{n_{\max}} \]

A "square" circuit has depth equal to width, so QV probes qubit count, gate fidelity, connectivity and compiler quality together in a single number.

Device Quantum Volume \(n_{\max}\) IBM Falcon r5 128 7 Quantinuum H2 \(2^{20} \approx 10^{6}\) 20 IonQ Forte \(2^{22}\) (claimed) 22

Note what QV is not. Quantinuum's H2 has ~56 qubits but a QV of \(2^{20}\), while IBM's Condor has 1121 qubits and a far lower QV. Qubit count alone is nearly meaningless; QV captures fidelity and connectivity too. It saturates for large devices, though, which is why newer metrics were introduced.

docs.title: CLOPS — Circuit Layer Operations Per Second
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{CLOPS} = \frac{M \times K \times S \times D}{\text{total time}} \]

with \(M\) templates, \(K\) parameter updates, \(S\) shots, \(D\) layers. CLOPS measures speed, which QV ignores entirely — critical for variational algorithms that run thousands of circuits.

Typical: IBM Eagle ≈ 2 000–5 000 CLOPS; trapped-ion devices are orders of magnitude lower because of slow gates.

docs.title: EPLG — Error Per Layered Gate
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{EPLG} = 1 - \big(1 - \mathrm{LF}\big)^{1/(\text{number of two-qubit layers})} \]

derived from layer fidelity on a chain of \(n\) qubits. IBM introduced EPLG because QV saturates: EPLG scales to 100+ qubits and isolates the two-qubit error that actually limits circuits.

docs.title: Algorithmic Qubits (IonQ)
docs.text:
\[ \#AQ = \text{the largest } n \text{ such that a suite of standard algorithms succeeds on } n \text{ qubits} \]

Uses real algorithms (Bernstein–Vazirani, QFT, Grover, phase estimation, VQE, QAOA) rather than random circuits. More application-relevant than QV, but vendor-defined — treat cross-vendor comparisons with care.

docs.title: Choosing a benchmark
docs.text: Question Metric Can it run deep circuits? Quantum Volume, EPLG Can it run many circuits quickly? CLOPS Will my algorithm work? Algorithmic Qubits, or just run it How good are the two-qubit gates? EPLG, gate error from calibration How many qubits? qubit count — the least informative metric

docs.title: The five pitfalls
docs.text: Pitfall Why it invalidates the comparison Fix Different compilers you are benchmarking compilers, not hardware compile all with the same tool (e.g. TKET) Different shot counts statistical error differs fix shots across devices Hardware-native problems favours whichever device matches the problem graph use both native and random topologies Anecdotal timing ignores queue, compile and readout time report end-to-end wall clock One problem size proves nothing about scaling vary \(n\) and report the trend

docs.title: A defensible protocol
docs.text:
1. Choose a benchmark SUITE (QASMBench, MQT Bench, or a task-relevant set)
2. Compile EVERY circuit with the SAME compiler (pytket) to each device's native gate set
3. Fix shots (e.g. 4096) across all devices
4. Run each configuration >= 3 times on different days (hardware drifts daily)
5. Report:
     - success metric with error bars
     - two-qubit gate count after compilation
     - end-to-end wall-clock time
     - cost
6. Publish the code and the raw data

Step 4 is the one most often skipped. Superconducting device calibration changes daily; a single-day measurement can differ by 20–30 % from the weekly mean.

docs.title: 45.5 Portability via OpenQASM 3
docs.text:
# Qiskit -> QASM
from qiskit import qasm3
qasm_str = qasm3.dumps(qiskit_circuit)

# QASM -> Cirq
from cirq.contrib.qasm_import import circuit_from_qasm
cirq_circuit = circuit_from_qasm(qasm_str)

# QASM -> pytket
from pytket.qasm import circuit_from_qasm_str
tk = circuit_from_qasm_str(qasm_str)

# Braket accepts QASM directly
from braket.ir.openqasm import Program
device.run(Program(source=qasm_str), shots=1000)

Portability caveats to check every time.

  1. Endianness. Qiskit is little-endian; Cirq and Q# are big-endian. Always test with an asymmetric state (L37, L39).
  2. Gate-set coverage. Exotic gates may not round-trip; decompose to a common set first.
  3. Classical control. QASM 3 supports it; QASM 2 does not.
  4. Custom gates. Definitions may be inlined or lost.

Always verify a round trip on a small circuit before trusting a large one.

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Implement a quantum algorithm from Units I–III on at least two platforms, benchmark it honestly, and report your findings.

Deliverables.

  1. Code — reproducible, on two or more frameworks, in a public repository.
  2. Report (8–12 pages) — algorithm, implementation, results, honest analysis.
  3. Presentation (15 minutes) with a live demonstration.

docs.title: Suggested projects
docs.text: # Project Units drawn on Difficulty 1 Grover's search with a real predicate (e.g. Sudoku) I, II medium 2 Shor factoring 15, 21, 35 with full continued fractions II medium 3 QAOA on Max-Cut, hardware vs simulator III medium 4 VQE for \(\mathrm{H}_2\) / LiH bond dissociation curve III hard 5 QSVM vs classical SVM on a real dataset III medium 6 Quantum teleportation and superdense coding on hardware I easy 7 3-qubit error-correcting code with injected errors I medium 8 Barren-plateau study: gradient variance vs \(n\) III medium 9 Cross-platform benchmark of one algorithm on 3 devices IV medium 10 Resource estimation for a chosen algorithm in Q# IV hard

docs.title: Marking rubric
docs.text:
Criterion Marks Correct implementation (verified against theory) 25 Multi-platform implementation and comparison 15 Quality of analysis (error budget, statistics, scaling) 20 Honest assessment of limitations and classical baselines 15 Report clarity and structure 15 Presentation and demonstration 10 Total 100

Note the 15 marks for honesty. A project reporting "our QSVM achieved 91 % accuracy versus scikit-learn's 97 %, and here is why" scores higher than one claiming quantum advantage without a classical baseline. Every quantum result must be reported alongside the best classical alternative. This is the single most important professional habit this course can instil.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Computing quantum volume
docs.text:
A device passes the QV test at \(n=6\) but fails at \(n=7\). State its quantum volume. If gate errors improve 2×, estimate the new QV.

Solution.

\[ V_Q = 2^{6} = \mathbf{64} \]

Estimating the improvement. A QV circuit on \(n\) qubits has depth \(n\) and roughly \(n^2/2\) two-qubit gates (each layer pairs \(n/2\) qubits, over \(n\) layers):

\[ N_{2q} \approx \frac{n^{2}}{2} \]

The heavy-output test needs circuit fidelity roughly above \(2/3\):

\[ (1-\epsilon)^{n^{2}/2} \gtrsim \tfrac23 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{n^{2}}{2}\,\epsilon \lesssim \ln\tfrac32 = 0.405 \] \[ n_{\max} \approx \sqrt{\frac{0.81}{\epsilon}} \]

Calibrating from the observed data. \(n_{\max} = 6\) gives

\[ \epsilon \approx \frac{0.81}{36} = 0.0225 \]

After a 2× improvement, \(\epsilon' = 0.01125\):

\[ n'_{\max} \approx \sqrt{\frac{0.81}{0.01125}} = \sqrt{72} = 8.49 \ \Rightarrow\ n'_{\max} = \mathbf{8} \] \[ V_Q' = 2^{8} = \mathbf{256} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Halving the error rate quadruples the quantum volume.}\ } \]

Why the leverage is so high. \(n_{\max}\propto\epsilon^{-1/2}\) while \(V_Q = 2^{n_{\max}}\), so \(V_Q\) grows exponentially in \(\epsilon^{-1/2}\). This is why vendors invest so heavily in gate fidelity rather than qubit count — and why a 1000-qubit device with mediocre gates has a lower QV than a 20-qubit device with excellent ones.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Designing a fair three-platform comparison
docs.text:
Compare Grover's algorithm on IBM, IonQ and a simulator. Specify the protocol completely and predict the results.

Solution.

Algorithm. Grover on \(n = 3,4,5\) qubits, single marked item, \(k = \lfloor\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{2^n}\rfloor\) iterations.

Metric. \(\Pr[\text{marked}]\), compared against the theoretical \(\sin^2\big((2k+1)\theta\big)\) (L22).

The protocol, with each choice justified.

Step Choice Rationale Circuit construction Qiskit one source of truth Compilation pytket for all three removes the compiler as a confound Shots 4096 everywhere equal statistical error Repetitions 3 runs on 3 different days captures calibration drift Devices ibm_brisbane, IonQ Aria-1, Aer simulator two modalities plus the ideal reference Reporting mean ± std dev, plus CNOT count, wall clock and cost complete picture

Predicted results.

\(n\) \(k\) Theory Simulator IonQ IBM 3 2 0.945 0.945 0.89 ± 0.02 0.72 ± 0.05 4 3 0.961 0.961 0.81 ± 0.03 0.48 ± 0.07 5 4 0.999 0.999 0.68 ± 0.04 0.22 ± 0.08

Reasoning behind the prediction.

  • The simulator matches theory exactly — this is the correctness check. If it does not, the implementation is wrong, and no hardware result means anything.
  • IonQ degrades gracefully. The multi-controlled \(Z\) in the oracle and diffuser needs all-to-all connectivity; IonQ has it, so no SWAPs. Its 0.4 % two-qubit error compounds slowly.
  • IBM degrades sharply. Heavy-hex connectivity forces SWAPs for the multi-controlled gates. For \(n=5\) the \(C^4Z\) decomposition plus routing can exceed 60 CNOTs; at \(\epsilon = 8\times10^{-3}\) that gives \(F\approx0.62\), and the signal degrades further from readout error.
  • Error bars widen with \(n\) because deeper circuits are more sensitive to daily calibration drift.

What to report alongside.

Device \(n=5\) CNOTs Wall clock (incl. queue) Cost Simulator — 2 s $0 IonQ 44 25 min $369 IBM 68 3 h (queue) $0 (free tier)

The honest conclusion. "IonQ's all-to-all connectivity gives markedly better Grover fidelity at every size, at ~85× the cost per shot and comparable wall-clock time once queueing is included. Neither device is close to the noiseless result at \(n=5\). Classical search over \(2^5 = 32\) items is instantaneous."

docs.title: Problem 3 — Benchmarking a variational algorithm
docs.text:
Design a benchmark of a 6-qubit VQE across simulator, IBM and IonQ. What must be reported?

Solution.

System. \(\mathrm{H}_2\) in the STO-3G basis, mapped by Jordan–Wigner to 4 qubits (or 6 with a larger active space). Exact ground-state energy known classically — essential, because it gives ground truth.

Protocol.

  1. Classical reference. Compute the FCI (full configuration interaction) energy exactly. This is the target.
  2. Simulator, noiseless. Run VQE with the UCCSD ansatz. This validates the implementation. If it does not converge to the FCI energy, stop and debug — do not proceed to hardware.
  3. Simulator with a device noise model (AerSimulator.from_backend). Predicts the hardware result before spending money.
  4. Hardware, parameters fixed. Do not optimise on hardware. Take the optimal \(\vec\theta\) from step 2 and simply evaluate the energy. This isolates hardware noise from optimiser behaviour and is far cheaper.
  5. Hardware with error mitigation (readout + ZNE, L38).

What must be reported.

Quantity Why Absolute energy error vs FCI (in Hartree) the only meaningful accuracy measure Chemical accuracy achieved? (\(<1.6\ \mathrm{mHa}\)) the field's standard threshold Circuit depth and CNOT count after compilation explains the error Shots used and total wall clock the real cost Energy with and without mitigation quantifies mitigation's value The classical cost of the same calculation the honest baseline

Predicted results.

Configuration Energy error (Ha) Chemical accuracy? Exact (FCI) 0 — Simulator, noiseless \(10^{-8}\) ✓ Simulator + noise model 0.031 ✗ IBM raw 0.048 ✗ IBM + readout mitigation 0.021 ✗ IBM + readout + ZNE 0.009 ✗ IonQ + mitigation 0.004 ✗ (close)

The essential final line of the report. "Classical FCI solves this system exactly in \(<1\) millisecond on a laptop. The quantum computation took 4 hours and 12 million shots to reach 0.004 Ha — 2.5× worse than chemical accuracy. This experiment validates the implementation and quantifies current hardware limitations; it does not demonstrate any advantage."

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A VQE paper without the classical baseline and the mitigation ablation is not a scientific result.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 4 — Interpreting vendor benchmark claims
docs.text:
Three vendors publish these claims. Assess each critically.

(a) "Our device has 1121 qubits — the world's largest." (b) "We achieved quantum volume \(2^{20}\)." (c) "Our processor performed a calculation in 200 seconds that would take a supercomputer 10 000 years."

Solution.

(a) 1121 qubits (IBM Condor).

Assessment: nearly meaningless on its own. Qubit count says nothing about whether useful circuits can run. The questions to ask:

  • What is the two-qubit gate error? (If \(10^{-2}\), a 100-CNOT circuit has \(F = 0.37\).)
  • What is the quantum volume? (Condor's is far below Quantinuum's 56-qubit H2.)
  • What is the connectivity? (Heavy-hex, degree ~2.5 — SWAP-heavy.)
  • Has any algorithm been run on all 1121 qubits? (No.)

Verdict: an important engineering milestone for fabrication and control, not a computational capability claim. IBM itself de-emphasised raw qubit count in favour of EPLG for exactly this reason.

(b) Quantum volume \(2^{20}\) (Quantinuum H2).

Assessment: a strong and meaningful claim. QV is a well-defined, published protocol that simultaneously tests fidelity, connectivity and compilation. \(2^{20}\) means random square circuits on 20 qubits at depth 20 succeed — genuinely hard.

Still worth checking:

  • Was the protocol followed exactly (heavy-output > 2/3 at 97.5 % confidence)?
  • Was the compilation heavily specialised for the QV circuits? (QV permits arbitrary compilation, which is a known and much-debated loophole — the metric rewards compiler effort as well as hardware.)
  • What is the CLOPS? Trapped ions have excellent QV but slow gates; for variational algorithms needing \(10^{6}\) circuits, speed may matter more than depth.

Verdict: credible and informative, with the compilation caveat noted.

(c) "200 seconds versus 10 000 years" (Google Sycamore, 2019).

Assessment: the most contested claim in the field, and instructive precisely for that reason.

  • The task was random circuit sampling — deliberately constructed to be hard classically and with no known application. It is a proof of principle, not a useful computation.
  • The classical estimate was contested immediately. IBM argued that using disk storage rather than RAM reduces it to ~2.5 days. Later tensor-network improvements (Pan, Chen, Zhang 2021) reproduced the samples in hours on a GPU cluster.
  • The comparison target moved. As classical algorithms improved, the claimed advantage shrank by many orders of magnitude — which is the normal and healthy scientific process.
  • The physics result stands. Sycamore did perform a coherent 53-qubit computation with a measured fidelity of \(0.2\%\) — a genuine and impressive experimental achievement.

Verdict: a real experimental milestone, overstated as a computational claim. The lesson for students: any "quantum supremacy" claim is a claim about the current best classical algorithm, and classical algorithms improve.

The three questions to ask of any quantum advantage claim.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{(1) Is the task useful? (2) What is the \emph{best} classical algorithm? (3) Does the advantage \emph{scale}?}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 5 — A complete capstone project plan
docs.text:
Plan Project 3 (QAOA Max-Cut, hardware vs simulator) in full: timeline, milestones, deliverables and the risks.

Solution.

Objective. Implement QAOA for Max-Cut on Erdős–Rényi graphs of 4–8 nodes; compare \(p=1,2,3\) on a simulator, a noisy simulator and real hardware; benchmark against Goemans–Williamson.

Week-by-week plan.

Week Task Deliverable 1 Literature: Farhi et al. 2014; GW 1995; Bravyi et al. 2020 annotated bibliography 2 Implement QAOA in Qiskit; brute-force optimum for verification working code, \(n\le8\) 3 Classical parameter optimisation on the simulator; grid + COBYLA optimal \((\gamma,\beta)\) tables 4 Implement classical baselines: GW SDP, greedy, random baseline results 5 Port to PennyLane; verify identical results second implementation ✓ 6 Noisy simulation with FakeSherbrooke; predict hardware noise study 7 Compile with pytket; measure CNOT reduction compilation study 8 Run on IBM hardware (\(p=1,2\); \(p=3\) if depth allows) raw hardware data 9 Apply error mitigation; ablate its components mitigated results 10 Analysis, plots, error budget figures 11 Write the report draft 12 Revise; prepare presentation final submission

Key figures the report must contain.

  1. Approximation ratio versus \(p\), for simulator / noisy simulator / hardware / GW.
  2. Approximation ratio versus graph size \(n\).
  3. \(\langle C\rangle\) heat map over \((\gamma,\beta)\) — the QAOA energy landscape.
  4. CNOT count before and after pytket compilation.
  5. Error budget: how much of the gap from ideal is due to CNOT error, readout error and depth.

Predicted headline results.

Method Approximation ratio Random assignment 0.50 Greedy ~0.65 QAOA \(p=1\), simulator ~0.75 QAOA \(p=3\), simulator ~0.88 Goemans–Williamson ~0.92 QAOA \(p=1\), hardware ~0.68 QAOA \(p=3\), hardware ~0.55 (noise dominates)

The central finding to expect and to state plainly. Increasing \(p\) improves the simulated result monotonically but degrades the hardware result beyond \(p\approx2\), because the added depth costs more in noise than it gains in expressivity. There is an optimal \(p\) for a given noise level — a genuinely interesting and reportable result.

Risks and mitigations.

Risk Mitigation Hardware queue delays start hardware runs in week 8, not week 11; use FakeBackend meanwhile Optimisation fails to converge use parameter transfer from small instances (L34, Problem 5) Results too noisy to interpret reduce to \(n=4\), \(p=1\) — a clean result beats an ambitious mess Scope creep fix \(n\le8\) and \(p\le3\) in week 1 and do not expand

The report's concluding paragraph, drafted in advance.

"QAOA was implemented on two frameworks and validated against brute-force optima. On a noiseless simulator the approximation ratio improves monotonically with \(p\), reaching 0.88 at \(p=3\) — still below the classical Goemans–Williamson guarantee of 0.878 on these instances. On hardware, performance peaks at \(p=2\) and degrades thereafter as circuit depth outpaces coherence. Error mitigation recovered approximately 40 % of the noise-induced gap. No quantum advantage was observed or expected at this scale; the contribution of this work is a quantified characterisation of where hardware noise overtakes algorithmic improvement."

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{This is what a good capstone report looks like: rigorous, quantitative and honest.}\ } \]

docs.title: 45.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. A device passes QV at \(n=8\). What is \(V_Q\), and what error rate does the estimate imply? [Ans: 256; \(\epsilon\approx0.0127\)]
  2. Name three flaws in "our quantum computer solved it in 1 second".
  3. Which metric best predicts VQE performance: QV, CLOPS or qubit count? Justify.
  4. Convert a Qiskit circuit to QASM 3 and import it into pytket.
  5. Why must all devices in a benchmark use the same compiler?
  6. Design a fair comparison of two error-mitigation techniques.
  7. What are the three questions to ask of any quantum advantage claim?

docs.title: Framework selection
docs.text: \[ \text{Learn} \Rightarrow \text{Qiskit}; \quad \text{QML} \Rightarrow \text{PennyLane}; \quad \text{Compile} \Rightarrow \text{pytket}; \quad \text{Estimate} \Rightarrow \text{Q\#}; \quad \text{Benchmark} \Rightarrow \text{Braket} \]

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
• Quantum Volume tests depth, fidelity and connectivity jointly; \(n_{\max}\propto\epsilon^{-1/2}\), so halving the error quadruples \(V_Q\).
  • CLOPS measures speed (critical for variational algorithms); EPLG scales beyond QV's saturation; Algorithmic Qubits is application-oriented but vendor-defined.
  • Qubit count is the least informative metric.

docs.title: Fair comparison
docs.text: Same compiler, same shots, multiple days, multiple sizes, end-to-end timing, published data.

docs.title: What you have learned in DSE304
docs.text: Unit Capability I Manipulate qubits, gates and entanglement; compute measurement statistics; explain interference, no-cloning, teleportation and error correction II Derive and analyse Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani, Simon, QFT, phase estimation, Shor, Grover and HHL; assess the quantum threat to cryptography and the post-quantum response III Encode data, build quantum kernels and variational models, compute gradients, diagnose barren plateaus, and formulate optimisation problems for QAOA and annealing IV Use the major frameworks, transpile and mitigate errors, estimate fault-tolerant resources, and benchmark honestly

docs.title: The disposition this course has tried to instil
docs.text:
Quantum computing is a real and important field with a small number of proven advantages (Shor, Grover, quantum simulation), a large number of proposed ones that remain unproven, and a substantial gap between current hardware and useful application.

The most valuable professional skill is not writing a quantum circuit. It is telling the difference between a demonstration and an advantage — and reporting that difference honestly.

Always report the classical baseline.

docs.title: 39.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Build circuits in Cirq using qubits, moments and operations.
  2. Explain Cirq's explicit hardware model and how it differs from Qiskit's.
  3. Use cirq.Simulator for statevector and sampled simulation.
  4. Work with device constraints, native gate sets and Google's Sycamore architecture.
  5. Choose between Cirq and Qiskit for a given task.

docs.title: 39.2 Cirq's Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Google built Cirq around one principle: the programmer should see the hardware. Where Qiskit abstracts the device away and lets the transpiler sort it out, Cirq makes qubit identity, gate scheduling and device constraints explicit in the source code.

Concept Qiskit Cirq Qubit index into a register (0, 1, …) a named object (LineQubit(0), GridQubit(1,2)) Circuit ordered list of instructions ordered list of Moments Timing implicit; transpiler schedules explicit in the moment structure Device applied at transpile time a first-class object that validates as you build Philosophy abstract away the hardware expose the hardware

docs.title: Qubit types
docs.text:
import cirq

q0, q1, q2 = cirq.LineQubit.range(3)         # a 1-D chain: q(0), q(1), q(2)
g = cirq.GridQubit(2, 3)                     # 2-D grid position (row 2, col 3)
n = cirq.NamedQubit('alice')                 # arbitrary label

grid = cirq.GridQubit.rect(3, 3)             # a 3x3 grid of 9 qubits

Why named qubits matter. GridQubit(1,2) and GridQubit(1,3) are adjacent by construction, so Cirq can validate connectivity as you write the circuit rather than discovering the problem at transpile time.

docs.title: Moments — the key abstraction
docs.text:
A Moment is a set of operations that execute simultaneously on disjoint qubits. A circuit is an ordered list of moments.

circuit = cirq.Circuit([
    cirq.Moment([cirq.H(q0), cirq.H(q1)]),        # both Hadamards run in parallel
    cirq.Moment([cirq.CNOT(q0, q1)]),
    cirq.Moment([cirq.measure(q0, q1, key='m')]),
])
print(circuit)

0: ───H───@───M('m')───
          │   │
1: ───H───X───M────────

Moment count = circuit depth, directly and visibly. In Qiskit you call .depth() and hope the transpiler did what you wanted; in Cirq the depth is the structure of your source code.

docs.title: Insert strategies
docs.text:
When you append without specifying moments, Cirq chooses how to pack the operations:

circuit = cirq.Circuit()
circuit.append([cirq.H(q0), cirq.H(q1)], strategy=cirq.InsertStrategy.EARLIEST)
Strategy Behaviour EARLIEST pack into the earliest moment with free qubits (default, minimises depth) NEW every operation gets its own moment (maximum depth) INLINE insert into the previous moment if possible NEW_THEN_INLINE new moment first, then inline the rest

docs.title: 39.4 Gates
docs.text:
# single-qubit
cirq.X(q0), cirq.Y(q0), cirq.Z(q0), cirq.H(q0), cirq.S(q0), cirq.T(q0)
cirq.rx(theta)(q0), cirq.ry(theta)(q0), cirq.rz(theta)(q0)

# powers -- Cirq's distinctive feature
cirq.X**0.5      # sqrt(X)
cirq.Z**0.25     # T gate
cirq.X**t        # continuously parameterised

# two-qubit
cirq.CNOT(q0, q1), cirq.CZ(q0, q1), cirq.SWAP(q0, q1)
cirq.ISWAP(q0, q1)
cirq.CZ**0.5

# three-qubit
cirq.TOFFOLI(q0, q1, q2), cirq.FREDKIN(q0, q1, q2)

# Google hardware-native
cirq.FSimGate(theta, phi)(q0, q1)
cirq.SQRT_ISWAP(q0, q1)

The ** operator is Cirq's signature. Any gate can be raised to a real power: \(G^{t} = \exp(i\pi t\,\log G/(i\pi))\). This makes continuously parameterised gates natural — \(X^{0.5}\) is the "half-NOT", and \(Z^{0.25} = T\).

docs.title: Statevector
docs.text:
sim = cirq.Simulator()

circuit = cirq.Circuit([cirq.H(q0), cirq.CNOT(q0, q1)])
result = sim.simulate(circuit)

print(result.final_state_vector)
# [0.70710677+0.j  0.+0.j  0.+0.j  0.70710677+0.j]

print(cirq.dirac_notation(result.final_state_vector))
# 0.71|00⟩ + 0.71|11⟩

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
circuit.append(cirq.measure(q0, q1, key='result'))
samples = sim.run(circuit, repetitions=1000)

print(samples.histogram(key='result'))
# Counter({0: 508, 3: 492})       -- integers, not bitstrings!

Cirq reports outcomes as integers, not bitstrings: 0 = 00, 3 = 11. Convert with format(k, '02b'). Cirq is big-endian — the first qubit in the measure call is the most significant bit — which is the opposite of Qiskit and matches this course's textbook convention.

docs.title: Step-by-step simulation
docs.text:
for i, step in enumerate(sim.simulate_moment_steps(circuit)):
    print(f"moment {i}: {cirq.dirac_notation(step.state_vector())}")

Excellent for teaching — it prints the state after every moment, letting students watch superposition and entanglement appear.

docs.title: Density matrix and noise
docs.text:
noisy = circuit.with_noise(cirq.depolarize(p=0.01))
dm_sim = cirq.DensityMatrixSimulator()
result = dm_sim.simulate(noisy)
print(result.final_density_matrix)

Cirq's noise channels: cirq.depolarize, cirq.amplitude_damp, cirq.phase_damp, cirq.bit_flip, cirq.phase_flip, cirq.asymmetric_depolarize.

docs.title: Parameter sweeps — a Cirq strength
docs.text:
import sympy

theta = sympy.Symbol('theta')
circuit = cirq.Circuit([cirq.ry(theta)(q0), cirq.measure(q0, key='m')])

sweep = cirq.Linspace(key='theta', start=0, stop=np.pi, length=20)
results = sim.run_sweep(circuit, params=sweep, repetitions=1000)

for r in results:
    print(r.params['theta'], r.histogram(key='m'))

One symbolic circuit, many parameter values, one call. This is how variational algorithms are written in Cirq, and it is cleaner than Qiskit's assign_parameters loop.

docs.title: Validation as you build
docs.text:
import cirq_google

device = cirq_google.Sycamore
print(device.metadata.qubit_set)          # which GridQubits exist
print(device.metadata.gateset)            # which gates are native

# Cirq REFUSES an invalid circuit immediately:
q_a = cirq.GridQubit(3, 3)
q_b = cirq.GridQubit(6, 6)                # far apart -- not connected
bad = cirq.Circuit([cirq.CZ(q_a, q_b)])
device.validate_circuit(bad)
# ValueError: Qubits (3,3) and (6,6) are not adjacent

Compare with Qiskit, which accepts the circuit and silently inserts a long chain of SWAPs. Cirq's approach forces the programmer to confront the topology — more work, but no surprises.

docs.title: Sycamore's native gates
docs.text:
Gate Form Notes SYC \(\mathrm{FSim}(\pi/2, \pi/6)\) the native two-qubit gate SQRT_ISWAP \(\mathrm{FSim}(\pi/4, 0)\) the newer calibrated gate PhasedXZGate arbitrary single-qubit one physical pulse Z virtual free — implemented by shifting the phase reference

Virtual Z gates are a genuinely important optimisation. A \(Z\) rotation on superconducting hardware needs no pulse at all — it is a bookkeeping change to the phase of subsequent pulses. So \(R_z\) gates are error-free and take zero time, which is why the standard basis is \(\{R_z, \sqrt X, \text{CZ}\}\): put all the angles into free \(R_z\)s.

docs.title: Transpiling for a device
docs.text:
converted = cirq.optimize_for_target_gateset(
    circuit, gateset=cirq_google.SycamoreTargetGateset())

router = cirq.RouteCQC(device.metadata.nx_graph)
routed = router(circuit)

docs.title: Problem 1 — Building the same Bell state in Cirq and Qiskit
docs.text:
Write the Bell-state circuit in both frameworks and compare the outputs, being explicit about endianness.

Solution.

Cirq.

import cirq

q0, q1 = cirq.LineQubit.range(2)
circuit = cirq.Circuit([cirq.H(q0), cirq.CNOT(q0, q1),
                        cirq.measure(q0, q1, key='m')])

result = cirq.Simulator().run(circuit, repetitions=1000)
print(result.histogram(key='m'))
# Counter({0: 508, 3: 492})

Qiskit.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer.primitives import SamplerV2 as Sampler

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
print(Sampler().run([qc], shots=1000).result()[0].data.c.get_counts())
# {'00': 495, '11': 505}

Comparison.

Cirq Qiskit Output format Counter({0: 508, 3: 492}) {'00': 495, '11': 505} Encoding integers bitstrings Endianness big-endian (first measured qubit = MSB) little-endian (qubit 0 = LSB)

Converting Cirq's integers. 0 → '00', 3 → '11':

counts = {format(k, '02b'): v for k, v in result.histogram(key='m').items()}
# {'00': 508, '11': 492}

For the Bell state the two agree because 00 and 11 are palindromes. They will disagree on any asymmetric state.

Asymmetric test. Apply \(X\) to qubit 0 only:

Framework Reported Meaning Cirq 2 = '10' \(q_0 = 1\), \(q_1 = 0\) ✓ (big-endian) Qiskit '01' \(q_0 = 1\), \(q_1 = 0\) ✓ (little-endian)

Both are correct; they simply print the bits in opposite orders. Always run this test when porting code between frameworks.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Moments and circuit depth
docs.text:
Build a 4-qubit circuit applying \(H\) to all qubits, then CNOTs (0,1) and (2,3), then CNOT(1,2). Count moments under the EARLIEST and NEW strategies.

Solution.

import cirq
qs = cirq.LineQubit.range(4)

circuit = cirq.Circuit([
    cirq.H.on_each(*qs),
    cirq.CNOT(qs[0], qs[1]), cirq.CNOT(qs[2], qs[3]),
    cirq.CNOT(qs[1], qs[2]),
])
print(circuit)
print("moments (depth):", len(circuit))

Output.

0: ───H───@───────
          │
1: ───H───X───@───
              │
2: ───H───@───X───
          │
3: ───H───X───────

moments (depth): 3

Moment analysis (EARLIEST, the default).

Moment Operations Qubits used 0 \(H, H, H, H\) all 4 — fully parallel 1 CNOT(0,1), CNOT(2,3) 0,1,2,3 — disjoint, so parallel 2 CNOT(1,2) 1,2 — must wait for moment 1 \[ \text{depth} = \mathbf{3} \]

Under NEW. Every operation gets its own moment:

\[ 4\ (\text{Hadamards}) + 3\ (\text{CNOTs}) = \mathbf{7\ \text{moments}} \]

Why this matters physically. Depth 3 versus depth 7 means the circuit occupies the hardware for 3 gate-times instead of 7. With \(T_2 = 100\ \mu\)s and \(t_{\text{CX}} = 300\) ns, decoherence per circuit falls proportionally:

\[ F_{\text{depth }3} \approx e^{-3\times0.3/100} = 0.991, \qquad F_{\text{depth }7} \approx e^{-7\times0.3/100} = 0.979 \]

Cirq makes this trade-off visible in the source code; in Qiskit it is buried in the transpiler's scheduling pass.

docs.title: Problem 3 — QAOA in Cirq with a parameter sweep
docs.text:
Implement \(p=1\) QAOA for a 3-vertex path graph (edges 0-1, 1-2) in Cirq, sweeping \((\gamma,\beta)\) to find the optimum.

Solution.

import cirq, sympy, numpy as np

qs = cirq.LineQubit.range(3)
edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2)]
gamma, beta = sympy.Symbol('g'), sympy.Symbol('b')

circuit = cirq.Circuit()
circuit.append(cirq.H.on_each(*qs))                       # |+++>

# cost unitary: exp(-i gamma Z_i Z_j / 2) per edge
for i, j in edges:
    circuit.append([cirq.CNOT(qs[i], qs[j]),
                    cirq.rz(gamma)(qs[j]),
                    cirq.CNOT(qs[i], qs[j])])

# mixer
circuit.append(cirq.rx(2 * beta).on_each(*qs))
circuit.append(cirq.measure(*qs, key='m'))

def cut_value(bits):
    return sum(1 for i, j in edges if bits[i] != bits[j])

sim = cirq.Simulator()
sweep = (cirq.Linspace('g', 0, np.pi, 15) *
         cirq.Linspace('b', 0, np.pi/2, 15))
results = sim.run_sweep(circuit, params=sweep, repetitions=1000)

best = max(results, key=lambda r: np.mean([cut_value(row) for row in r.measurements['m']]))
print("best params:", best.params)
print("mean cut   :", np.mean([cut_value(r) for r in best.measurements['m']]))

Expected output.

best params: {'g': 1.795, 'b': 0.673}
mean cut   : 1.87

Analysis.

  • Maximum cut. The path \(0-1-2\) is bipartite: colour \(\{0,2\}\) one way and \(\{1\}\) the other, so \(C_{\max} = \mathbf{2}\) (both edges cut).
  • Random baseline. Each edge is cut with probability \(\frac12\), so \(\langle C\rangle_{\text{random}} = \mathbf{1.0}\).
  • QAOA \(p=1\) result: \(\langle C\rangle = 1.87\).
\[ \text{approximation ratio} = \frac{1.87}{2} = \mathbf{0.935} \]

Very good for \(p=1\) — better than the 0.6924 worst-case guarantee (L34), because the path graph is easy: it is bipartite, tree-like, and has no odd cycles to frustrate the optimisation.

The Cirq advantage on display. run_sweep with the product of two Linspace objects evaluates \(15\times15 = 225\) parameter combinations in one call, with the symbolic circuit compiled once. The equivalent Qiskit code requires an explicit loop over assign_parameters.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Device validation and routing cost
docs.text:
A circuit needs CZ between GridQubit(0,0) and GridQubit(2,2) on Sycamore. Show that validation fails, compute the routing cost, and give two fixes.

Solution.

Validation.

q_a, q_b = cirq.GridQubit(0, 0), cirq.GridQubit(2, 2)
circuit = cirq.Circuit([cirq.CZ(q_a, q_b)])
cirq_google.Sycamore.validate_circuit(circuit)
# ValueError: Qubit pair ((0,0), (2,2)) is not valid on this device

Distance. Sycamore's grid allows only horizontal and vertical neighbours, so the Manhattan distance applies:

\[ d = |2-0| + |2-0| = \mathbf{4\ \text{hops}} \]

Routing cost. Bringing the qubits adjacent needs \(d - 1 = 3\) SWAPs:

\[ 3\ \text{SWAPs}\times3\ \text{CZ-equivalents} + 1\ \text{CZ} = \mathbf{10\ \text{two-qubit gates}} \]

Fidelity at Sycamore's two-qubit error of \(\approx 6\times10^{-3}\):

\[ F = (1 - 0.006)^{10} = 0.994^{10} = \mathbf{0.9416} \]

One logical gate costs 5.8 % of the circuit fidelity.

Fix 1 — automatic routing.

router = cirq.RouteCQC(cirq_google.Sycamore.metadata.nx_graph)
routed = router(circuit)
print(len([op for m in routed for op in m if len(op.qubits) == 2]))   # ~10

Correct but expensive — it just does the SWAP insertion for you.

Fix 2 — redesign the qubit assignment. Choose logical-to-physical mappings so that interacting qubits are physically adjacent:

q_a, q_b = cirq.GridQubit(0, 0), cirq.GridQubit(0, 1)     # adjacent!
# cost: 1 CZ, fidelity 0.994
\[ \text{Fidelity improves from } 0.942 \text{ to } 0.994 \text{ — a } \mathbf{9.7\times} \text{ reduction in error.} \]

The design principle. For an algorithm with a known interaction graph — QAOA on a lattice, a 1-D chemistry chain, a surface code — map the problem graph onto the hardware graph by hand. Automatic routing is a fallback, not a strategy. This is exactly the discipline Cirq's validate-as-you-build design is meant to enforce.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Choosing between Cirq and Qiskit
docs.text:
Recommend Cirq or Qiskit for each project, with reasoning.

(a) A first-year course introducing quantum computing. (b) Research on gate calibration for a 2-D superconducting array. (c) Running a VQE on IBM hardware. (d) Simulating a 1-D spin chain with nearest-neighbour gates. (e) Benchmarking a circuit across five hardware vendors.

Solution.

(a) Course introduction → Qiskit. Far more textbooks, tutorials, videos and Stack Overflow answers exist. IBM's free hardware access is generous and requires no institutional agreement. The Qiskit Textbook is a complete course resource. Cirq's explicit device model, though pedagogically honest, adds friction for beginners who should first grasp gates and measurement.

(b) Gate calibration research on a 2-D array → Cirq. GridQubit matches the physical layout exactly; FSimGate(theta, phi) parameterises the actual physical interaction, so calibration means fitting \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) per qubit pair — which Cirq expresses natively. cirq.experiments contains ready-made cross-entropy benchmarking and Floquet calibration routines. This is Cirq's home territory.

(c) VQE on IBM hardware → Qiskit. Only Qiskit talks to IBM Runtime. EstimatorV2 with resilience_level=2 gives zero-noise extrapolation and readout mitigation as configuration options rather than code you must write. Qiskit Nature supplies the chemistry Hamiltonians. Using Cirq here would mean exporting to OpenQASM and re-importing — possible, but pointless friction.

(d) 1-D spin chain → Cirq. LineQubit is the physical model. Moments make the Trotter-step structure explicit: each moment is one layer of the Trotter decomposition, so circuit depth equals the number of Trotter steps by construction. cirq.Linspace sweeps the evolution time in one call.

(e) Cross-vendor benchmarking → neither; use Amazon Braket. Braket provides one SDK and one account for IonQ, Rigetti, IQM and QuEra. Writing this in Cirq or Qiskit means maintaining separate provider integrations. (Braket does accept Cirq circuits via a plugin, so a reasonable hybrid is: write in Cirq, submit via Braket.)

Summary table.

Criterion Cirq Qiskit Learning resources good excellent Hardware transparency excellent good Hardware access Google (restricted) IBM (open) Parameter sweeps excellent (run_sweep) good Error mitigation built in manual excellent (Runtime) Chemistry / ML libraries OpenFermion, TFQ Qiskit Nature, ML, Optimization Endianness big-endian (textbook) little-endian

They interoperate. cirq.qasm(circuit) and qiskit.qasm3.loads(...) move circuits between frameworks, so the professional answer is to use each where it is strongest.

docs.title: 39.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Write a Cirq circuit for a 3-qubit GHZ state and print its Dirac notation.
  2. What does Cirq's histogram return for the state \(|101\rangle\) on 3 qubits? [Ans: {5: N}]
  3. Build a circuit with depth 2 using 4 qubits and 2 CNOTs.
  4. Compute the Manhattan routing cost for GridQubit(1,1) to GridQubit(4,3). [Ans: 5 hops, 4 SWAPs, 13 two-qubit gates]
  5. Express \(T\) using Cirq's power notation. [Ans: cirq.Z**0.25]
