docs.title: 39.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Cirq's philosophy is hardware transparency: named qubits (LineQubit, GridQubit), explicit Moments (depth is visible in the source), and devices that validate circuits as you build them.
  • Moments are sets of simultaneous operations; len(circuit) is the depth, and InsertStrategy controls packing.
  • Gates support the ** power syntax: cirq.X**0.5, cirq.Z**0.25 == T.
  • cirq.Simulator gives statevectors, samples and moment-by-moment stepping (excellent for teaching); DensityMatrixSimulator handles noise.
  • run_sweep with symbolic parameters evaluates hundreds of parameter settings in one call — Cirq's standout feature for variational algorithms.
  • Cirq is big-endian and reports integers; Qiskit is little-endian and reports bitstrings. Always test with an asymmetric state when porting.
  • Virtual \(Z\) gates are free on superconducting hardware, which is why the native basis is \(\{R_z, \sqrt X, \text{CZ}\}\).
  • Choose Cirq for hardware-aware research and lattice-structured problems; Qiskit for teaching, IBM hardware and built-in error mitigation. They interoperate via OpenQASM.

Next lesson: L40 — PennyLane and differentiable quantum programming.

Practise now: unit4-platforms-lab.html → Circuit Builder: build a circuit and toggle between Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane and Q# code emission, watching the moment structure and endianness change.

docs.title: Lesson 22: Grover's Algorithm: Geometric Analysis and Optimality
22.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Show that Grover's iteration is a rotation by \(2\theta\) in a two-dimensional plane.
  2. Derive \(\Pr[\text{success}] = \sin^2\big((2k+1)\theta\big)\) and the optimal \(k\).
  3. Prove the \(\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N}\) formula and analyse over-rotation.
  4. State the BBBV optimality theorem and explain why \(\Theta(\sqrt N)\) cannot be beaten.
  5. Generalise to amplitude amplification and quantum counting.

docs.title: 22.2 The Two-Dimensional Picture
docs.text:
Grover's algorithm never leaves the plane spanned by

\[ |w\rangle \quad\text{and}\quad |w^\perp\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N-M}}\sum_{x \text{ unmarked}}|x\rangle . \]

(For \(M\) marked items, replace \(|w\rangle\) by \(|w_{\text{all}}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt M}\sum_{x\text{ marked}}|x\rangle\).)

Both \(O_f\) and \(D\) map this plane to itself, and the initial state lies in it. So the entire algorithm is two-dimensional geometry, no matter how large \(N\) is.

docs.title: The initial angle
docs.text:
Write the starting state as

\[ |\psi\rangle = \sin\theta\,|w_{\text{all}}\rangle + \cos\theta\,|w^\perp\rangle \]

Matching amplitudes with \(|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_x|x\rangle\):

\[ \sin\theta = \sqrt{\frac{M}{N}}, \qquad \cos\theta = \sqrt{\frac{N-M}{N}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \theta = \arcsin\sqrt{\frac{M}{N}}\ } \]

For \(M=1\) and large \(N\), \(\theta \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\) — a tiny angle. \(|\psi\rangle\) starts almost entirely along \(|w^\perp\rangle\).

docs.title: Two reflections make a rotation
docs.text:
The oracle \(O_f = I - 2|w_{\text{all}}\rangle\langle w_{\text{all}}|\) is a reflection about the axis \(|w^\perp\rangle\): it negates the \(|w_{\text{all}}\rangle\) component.

If the state is at angle \(\alpha\) from \(|w^\perp\rangle\), after \(O_f\) it is at angle \(-\alpha\).

The diffusion operator \(D = 2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| - I\) is a reflection about the axis \(|\psi\rangle\), which sits at angle \(\theta\).

If the state is at angle \(-\alpha\), reflecting about the line at angle \(\theta\) takes it to \(2\theta - (-\alpha) = 2\theta + \alpha\).

Composition.

\[ \alpha \ \xrightarrow{O_f}\ -\alpha \ \xrightarrow{D}\ \alpha + 2\theta \] \[ \boxed{\ G = D\,O_f \text{ is a rotation by } +2\theta \text{ toward } |w_{\text{all}}\rangle\ } \]

Elementary geometry fact: the composition of two reflections about lines meeting at angle \(\theta\) is a rotation by \(2\theta\). Grover's algorithm is that fact, applied \(k\) times.

docs.title: The state after k iterations
docs.text:
Starting at angle \(\theta\) and rotating \(k\) times by \(2\theta\):

\[ \boxed{\ G^{k}|\psi\rangle = \sin\big((2k+1)\theta\big)\,|w_{\text{all}}\rangle + \cos\big((2k+1)\theta\big)\,|w^\perp\rangle\ } \] \[ \boxed{\ \Pr[\text{success after } k \text{ iterations}] = \sin^2\big((2k+1)\theta\big)\ } \]

docs.title: Matrix form
docs.text:
In the ordered basis \(\{|w^\perp\rangle, |w_{\text{all}}\rangle\}\):

\[ G = \begin{pmatrix}\cos2\theta & -\sin2\theta\\ \sin2\theta & \cos2\theta\end{pmatrix} \]

— literally a rotation matrix. Its eigenvalues are \(e^{\pm2i\theta}\), a fact used by quantum counting (§5).

docs.title: 22.4 The Optimal Number of Iterations
docs.text:
We want \((2k+1)\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\) (pointing exactly at \(|w_{\text{all}}\rangle\)):

\[ k = \frac{\pi}{4\theta} - \frac12 . \]

Since \(k\) must be an integer, take

\[ \boxed{\ k_{\text{opt}} = \left\lfloor \frac{\pi}{4\theta}\right\rfloor, \qquad \theta = \arcsin\sqrt{M/N}\ } \]

Large-\(N\) approximation. For \(M \ll N\), \(\theta\approx\sqrt{M/N}\), so

\[ k_{\text{opt}} \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{\frac{N}{M}} \qquad\text{and for } M=1: \qquad k_{\text{opt}} \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N \approx 0.785\sqrt N . \]

Residual error. The rounding leaves an angular error of at most \(\theta\), so

\[ \Pr[\text{failure}] \le \sin^2\theta = \frac{M}{N} \ \longrightarrow\ 0 \ \text{as } N\to\infty . \]

For \(N = 2^{20}\), \(M=1\): failure probability under \(10^{-6}\).

docs.title: Exact cases
docs.text:
Grover is exact whenever \(\frac{\pi}{4\theta} - \frac12\) is an integer. The most useful instance is \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} = 30°\), i.e.

\[ \sin\theta = \frac12 \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{M}{N} = \frac14 . \]

Then \(k = 1\) and \(\Pr = \sin^2(3\times30°) = \sin^2 90° = 1\). This explains the \(N=4, M=1\) and \(N=16,M=4\) results of L21.

docs.title: Over-rotation
docs.text:
\(\Pr[\text{success}] = \sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\) is periodic, with period \(\frac{\pi}{2\theta}\) in \(k\). Running too long is genuinely harmful: at \((2k+1)\theta = \pi\) the success probability is zero.

The counter-intuitive lesson. Unlike classical iterative algorithms, "run it longer to be safer" is wrong here. Grover must be stopped at a precisely computed moment. If \(M\) is unknown, either estimate it first (quantum counting) or use the BBHT randomised strategy: repeatedly pick \(k\) uniformly from \([0, m)\) and grow \(m\) by a factor of \(6/5\) after each failure — this finds a solution in \(O(\sqrt{N/M})\) expected queries without knowing \(M\).

docs.title: 22.5 Optimality: The BBBV Lower Bound
docs.text:
Theorem (Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, Vazirani, 1997). Any quantum algorithm that solves unstructured search over \(N\) items with bounded error requires \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\) oracle queries.

Proof sketch (the hybrid argument). Run the algorithm with the all-zero oracle (no marked item) and track the total "query magnitude" each index \(x\) receives across \(T\) queries:

\[ \sum_{x} \sum_{t=1}^{T}\big\| \Pi_x|\psi_t\rangle \big\|^2 = T \]

since each query step has unit norm. By pigeonhole, some index \(x^*\) receives total magnitude at most \(T/N\). Now switch to the oracle marking \(x^*\). A hybrid argument bounds the change in the final state:

\[ \big\| |\psi_T^{(0)}\rangle - |\psi_T^{(x^*)}\rangle \big\| \le 2\sqrt{\frac{T^2}{N}} . \]

To distinguish the two cases with constant probability, this must be \(\Omega(1)\), forcing

\[ T = \Omega(\sqrt N) . \qquad\blacksquare \]

Consequences.

  1. Grover is optimal, matching the lower bound up to a constant. There is no \(O(\log N)\) or even \(O(N^{1/3})\) quantum search.
  2. Quantum computers do not solve NP-complete problems efficiently by brute force. A SAT instance with \(n\) variables has \(2^n\) assignments; Grover reduces \(2^n\) to \(2^{n/2}\) — still exponential.
  3. Speed-ups need structure. Shor's exponential advantage comes from the periodic structure of modular exponentiation. Unstructured problems admit only quadratic gains.

docs.title: Amplitude amplification (Brassard, Høyer, Mosca, Tapp)
docs.text:
Grover generalises far beyond search. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be any quantum algorithm (not just \(H^{\otimes n}\)) that outputs a "good" answer with probability \(p = \sin^2\theta\). Define

\[ Q = -\mathcal{A}\,S_0\,\mathcal{A}^{-1}\,S_\chi \]

where \(S_\chi\) flips the phase of good states and \(S_0\) flips the phase of everything except \(|0\rangle\). Then \(Q\) rotates by \(2\theta\) exactly as before, and

\[ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt p}\right) \ \text{repetitions suffice, versus } O\!\left(\frac1p\right) \ \text{classically.} \]

This is a quadratic speed-up for any randomised algorithm's success probability, and it is the form in which Grover appears inside larger algorithms: Monte Carlo estimation, minimum finding, collision finding, and QAOA warm-starting.

docs.title: Quantum counting
docs.text:
The eigenvalues of \(G\) are \(e^{\pm 2i\theta}\). Applying quantum phase estimation (L19) to \(G\) yields \(\theta\), and hence

\[ M = N\sin^2\theta . \]

Cost: \(O(\sqrt N)\) queries for a constant-factor estimate of \(M\). This solves the "unknown \(M\)" problem and also gives quantum approximate counting — estimating the number of solutions to a constraint problem quadratically faster than classical sampling.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Success probability as a function of k
docs.text:
For \(N = 1024\), \(M=1\): compute \(\theta\), \(k_{\text{opt}}\), and \(\Pr[\text{success}]\) at \(k = 20, 25, 30, 50\).

Solution.

\[ \sin\theta = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{1024}} = \tfrac{1}{32} = 0.03125 \ \Longrightarrow\ \theta = 0.031255\ \mathrm{rad} = 1.7908° \] \[ k_{\text{opt}} = \left\lfloor\frac{\pi}{4\theta}\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor\frac{0.785398}{0.031255}\right\rfloor = \lfloor 25.128\rfloor = \mathbf{25} \]

Now evaluate \(\Pr = \sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\):

\(k\) \((2k+1)\theta\) (rad) degrees \(\Pr\) 20 1.2815 73.4° 0.9187 25 1.5940 91.3° 0.99946 30 1.9066 109.2° 0.8914 50 3.1568 180.9° 0.00023

At \(k=50\) (double the optimum) the algorithm has rotated a full \(180°\) and the success probability has collapsed to essentially zero. This is the clearest demonstration of why over-rotation matters.

Classical comparison: 512 queries expected. Quantum: 25. Speed-up ≈ 20×.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Grover for AES-128 key search
docs.text:
Estimate the resources to find a 128-bit AES key by Grover search. Comment on the security implication.

Solution.

\(N = 2^{128}\), \(M=1\).

\[ k_{\text{opt}} \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{2^{128}} = \frac{\pi}{4}\times 2^{64} = 0.7854\times 1.8447\times10^{19} = \mathbf{1.449\times10^{19}} \ \text{iterations} \]

Each iteration requires two full AES evaluations (the encryption circuit and its inverse for uncomputation), each roughly \(10^4\) quantum gates. So the total gate count is

\[ \approx 1.449\times10^{19}\times 2\times10^{4} = \mathbf{2.9\times10^{23}} \ \text{gates}. \]

At an optimistic \(10^{9}\) logical gates per second:

\[ t = 2.9\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s} \approx \mathbf{9\ \text{million years}} . \]

Parallelisation does not rescue it. Splitting the search across \(P\) quantum machines gives only a \(\sqrt P\) improvement (each machine searches \(N/P\) items in \(\sqrt{N/P}\) steps). To finish in one year you would need \(P \approx (9\times10^{6})^2 = 8\times10^{13}\) machines.

Security implication. AES-128 has an effective post-quantum security level of 64 bits — the standard statement — but the constant factors make even that unreachable in practice. The recommended mitigation is simply AES-256, which under Grover retains 128-bit effective security. NIST's post-quantum guidance formalises this: symmetric algorithms survive by doubling key lengths; public-key algorithms must be replaced entirely.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Rotation angle and geometry, verified numerically
docs.text:
For \(N=16\), \(M=1\): compute \(\theta\) and verify \(\Pr[k]\) for \(k=1,2,3\) using both the geometric formula and the amplitude recursion.

Solution.

\[ \sin\theta = \frac14 \Rightarrow \theta = 0.25268\ \mathrm{rad} = 14.478° \]

Geometric formula.

\(k\) \((2k+1)\theta\) \(\Pr = \sin^2\) 0 14.478° 0.0625 1 43.43° 0.4727 2 72.39° 0.9084 3 101.34° 0.9613 \[ k_{\text{opt}} = \left\lfloor\frac{\pi}{4\times0.25268}\right\rfloor = \lfloor3.108\rfloor = \mathbf{3} \]

Amplitude recursion check for \(k=1\). Initial \(\alpha = \frac14 = 0.25\) for all 16 states.

Oracle: \(\alpha_w = -0.25\), others \(+0.25\). Mean: \(\bar\alpha = \frac{15(0.25) - 0.25}{16} = \frac{3.5}{16} = 0.21875\). Diffusion: \(\alpha_w = 2(0.21875) + 0.25 = 0.6875\).

\[ \Pr[w] = 0.6875^2 = 0.47266 \ \checkmark \]

matching the geometric formula exactly. The two pictures — amplitude bookkeeping and plane rotation — are the same thing.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Amplitude amplification of a weak algorithm
docs.text:
A heuristic quantum algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\) finds a valid solution with probability \(p = 0.01\). How many repetitions are needed classically, and how many with amplitude amplification, to reach 99 % success?

Solution.

Classical repetition. Failure per run \(= 0.99\):

\[ 0.99^{R} \le 0.01 \ \Longrightarrow\ R \ge \frac{\ln0.01}{\ln0.99} = \frac{-4.605}{-0.01005} = 458.2 \] \[ R_{\text{classical}} = \mathbf{459} \ \text{runs of } \mathcal{A} . \]

Amplitude amplification. \(\sin\theta = \sqrt{p} = 0.1\), so \(\theta = 0.10017\) rad.

\[ k_{\text{opt}} = \left\lfloor\frac{\pi}{4\theta}\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor\frac{0.7854}{0.10017}\right\rfloor = \lfloor7.84\rfloor = \mathbf{7} \] \[ \Pr = \sin^2(15\times0.10017) = \sin^2(1.5026) = 0.99534 = \mathbf{99.5\%} \]

7 applications of \(\mathcal{A}\) (plus 7 of \(\mathcal{A}^{-1}\)) versus 459 classically — a \(\approx33\times\) improvement, consistent with \(\sqrt{459/7}\approx 8\) per the quadratic rule (the exact factor depends on the target confidence).

Why this matters more than plain search. Amplitude amplification applies to any subroutine with a checkable output — Monte Carlo integration, optimisation heuristics, sampling — making it one of the few broadly reusable quantum primitives.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Grover with an imperfect oracle
docs.text:
The oracle applies the correct phase with probability \(1-\eta\) and does nothing with probability \(\eta\) (a stochastic gate error). Estimate the largest \(N\) for which Grover still works, given \(\eta = 10^{-4}\).

Solution. The algorithm requires \(k \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N\) oracle calls, all of which must succeed for the rotation to accumulate correctly. Ignoring partial recovery, the probability that every call is clean is

\[ (1-\eta)^{k} \approx e^{-\eta k} = \exp\!\left(-\eta\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N\right) . \]

Require this to stay above, say, \(\frac12\):

\[ \eta\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N \le \ln 2 = 0.693 \] \[ \sqrt N \le \frac{0.693 \times 4}{\pi \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{2.772}{3.1416\times10^{-4}} = 8824 \] \[ N \le 7.8\times10^{7} \approx 2^{26} . \]

So with a \(10^{-4}\) oracle error rate, Grover works up to roughly 26 qubits' worth of search space — and only if every other gate is perfect too.

Generalisation. Setting \(\eta\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N = O(1)\) gives \(N = O(1/\eta^2)\): the largest searchable space scales as the inverse square of the error rate. Getting to a cryptographically relevant \(N = 2^{128}\) would need \(\eta \lesssim 10^{-20}\) — utterly impossible without full fault tolerance.

Conclusion. Grover is a fault-tolerant-era algorithm. NISQ demonstrations are limited to \(N \le 2^{5}\) or so, and its quadratic speed-up is too shallow to pay for error-correction overhead in many practical settings — a point made forcefully by Babbush et al. (2021), who argue that quadratic speed-ups may never yield practical advantage once QEC costs are included.

docs.title: 22.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Compute \(\theta\) and \(k_{\text{opt}}\) for \(N = 10^{6}\), \(M=1\). [Ans: \(\theta\approx0.001\) rad, \(k=785\)]
  2. For \(N=64\), \(M=4\): find \(k_{\text{opt}}\) and the success probability. [Ans: \(\theta=30°\), \(k=1\), \(\Pr=1\)]
  3. Show that \(\Pr[\text{success}]=0\) when \((2k+1)\theta = \pi\).
  4. Verify that \(G\) has eigenvalues \(e^{\pm2i\theta}\).
  5. For \(p = 0.25\), how many amplitude-amplification rounds reach certainty? [Ans: 1]
  6. Explain why \(\sqrt P\) machines give only \(\sqrt P\) speed-up in parallel Grover.
  7. State the BBBV theorem and one consequence for NP-complete problems.

docs.title: 22.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Grover's iteration \(G = D\,O_f\) is the composition of two reflections, hence a rotation by \(2\theta\) in the \(\mathrm{span}\{|w\rangle,|w^\perp\rangle\}\) plane, with \(\theta = \arcsin\sqrt{M/N}\).
  • \(\Pr[\text{success}] = \sin^2\big((2k+1)\theta\big)\); optimal \(k = \lfloor\pi/(4\theta)\rfloor \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N/M}\); residual failure \(\le M/N\).
  • The probability oscillates: over-rotation drives it to zero. Use quantum counting or the BBHT strategy when \(M\) is unknown.
  • BBBV theorem: \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\) queries are necessary, so Grover is optimal and quantum computers do not brute-force NP-complete problems efficiently.
  • Amplitude amplification generalises Grover to any algorithm with success probability \(p\), needing \(O(1/\sqrt p)\) instead of \(O(1/p)\) repetitions.
  • Practical reality: AES-128 needs \(1.4\times10^{19}\) iterations (millions of years); Grover requires full fault tolerance, since the searchable space scales only as \(O(1/\eta^2)\) in the error rate.

Next lesson: L23 — Grover applied to cryptography: hash preimage attacks.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Grover tab: switch to the geometric view to watch the state vector rotate in the 2-D plane, and slide \(k\) past the optimum to see the probability curve fall.

docs.title: Lesson 21: Grover's Algorithm: Oracle and Diffusion Operator
21.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the unstructured search problem and the classical query bound.
  2. Construct the Grover oracle \(O_f\) and describe its action geometrically.
  3. Derive the diffusion operator \(D = 2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| - I\) and prove it performs inversion about the mean.
  4. Trace the amplitudes through one and two Grover iterations by hand.
  5. Build the full Grover circuit for a small \(n\).

docs.title: 21.2 The Problem
docs.text:
Unstructured search. Given an oracle for \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with \(f(w) = 1\) for exactly one "marked" item \(w\) and \(f(x)=0\) otherwise, find \(w\).

Equivalently: search an unsorted database of \(N = 2^n\) items for the one satisfying a predicate. No structure, no sorting, no index — the only access is to query the predicate.

Classical. Every query eliminates one candidate. Worst case \(N\) queries; average \(N/2\); randomised expected \(\approx N/2\). Lower bound \(\Omega(N)\).

Quantum (Grover, 1996).

\[ \boxed{\ \Theta(\sqrt N) \text{ queries — a quadratic speed-up, and provably optimal}\ } \]

Applications. Any brute-force search: cryptographic key search, SAT/constraint satisfaction, graph colouring, collision finding, minimum finding, and as a subroutine inside larger algorithms (amplitude amplification).

docs.title: 21.3 Setup
docs.text:
Uniform superposition.

\[ |\psi\rangle = H^{\otimes n}|0\rangle^{\otimes n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}|x\rangle, \qquad N = 2^n . \]

Every amplitude is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\), so \(\Pr[w] = \frac1N\) — measuring now is just random guessing. Grover's algorithm grows the amplitude of \(|w\rangle\) at the expense of the others.

Two useful vectors. Split the space into "the marked item" and "everything else":

\[ |w\rangle \quad\text{and}\quad |w^\perp\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N-1}}\sum_{x\ne w}|x\rangle . \]

These are orthonormal, and

\[ |\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}|w\rangle + \frac{\sqrt{N-1}}{\sqrt N}|w^\perp\rangle . \]

Everything happens in this 2-dimensional plane — a fact exploited fully in L22.

docs.title: The oracle (phase inversion)
docs.text:
\[ O_f\,|x\rangle = (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle = \begin{cases} -|x\rangle & x = w\\ +|x\rangle & x\ne w\end{cases} \]

As an operator,

\[ O_f = I - 2|w\rangle\langle w| . \]

Check: \(O_f|w\rangle = |w\rangle - 2|w\rangle = -|w\rangle\) ✓; \(O_f|x\rangle = |x\rangle\) for \(x\perp w\) ✓.

Implementation. Build the Boolean circuit for \(f\) with a \(|-\rangle\) ancilla and use phase kick-back (L11). For \(w\) given explicitly: apply \(X\) gates to flip the 0-bits of \(w\) to 1, apply a multi-controlled \(Z\), then undo the \(X\) gates.

Geometrically: \(O_f\) is a reflection about \(|w^\perp\rangle\) — it flips the \(|w\rangle\) component and leaves the orthogonal complement alone.

Note: the oracle alone changes no probability, since \(|-1|^2 = 1\). It marks; it does not amplify. Amplification is the diffusion operator's job.

docs.title: The diffusion operator (inversion about the mean)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ D = 2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| - I\ } \]

Circuit form. Since \(|\psi\rangle = H^{\otimes n}|0\rangle\):

\[ D = H^{\otimes n}\big(2|0\rangle\langle 0| - I\big)H^{\otimes n} . \]

The inner operator \(2|0\rangle\langle0| - I\) flips the sign of every basis state except \(|0\cdots0\rangle\); up to a global \(-1\) it is a multi-controlled \(Z\) conjugated by \(X\) gates.

Implementation:

D = H^n  --  X^n  --  [multi-controlled Z on all n qubits]  --  X^n  --  H^n

Unitarity check. \(D^\dagger = D\) (both terms Hermitian) and

\[ D^2 = 4|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| - 4|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| + I = I \]

using \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1\). So \(D\) is Hermitian, unitary and self-inverse — a reflection.

docs.title: Why D is "inversion about the mean"
docs.text:
Let the state be \(|\phi\rangle = \sum_x \alpha_x|x\rangle\) and let

\[ \bar\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\sum_x \alpha_x \]

be the mean amplitude. Then

\[ \langle\psi|\phi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_x\alpha_x = \sqrt N\,\bar\alpha , \]

so

\[ D|\phi\rangle = 2|\psi\rangle\big(\sqrt N\bar\alpha\big) - |\phi\rangle = 2\bar\alpha\sum_x|x\rangle - \sum_x\alpha_x|x\rangle \] \[ \boxed{\ \alpha_x \ \longmapsto\ 2\bar\alpha - \alpha_x\ } \]

Each amplitude is reflected about the mean. An amplitude below the mean by \(\delta\) ends up above it by \(\delta\), and vice versa.

This is precisely why Grover works. The oracle makes \(\alpha_w\) negative, which pulls the mean slightly down but leaves it positive. Reflecting \(\alpha_w\) (a negative number) about a positive mean sends it to a large positive value, while the unmarked amplitudes, already near the mean, barely move — they shrink slightly to conserve the norm.

docs.title: 21.5 The Grover Iteration
docs.text:
\[ G = D\,O_f = \big(2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| - I\big)\big(I - 2|w\rangle\langle w|\big) \]

Full algorithm.

1. Prepare |0>^n
2. Apply H^n            -> uniform superposition
3. Repeat k = floor(pi/4 * sqrt(N)) times:
       apply O_f         (mark: flip sign of |w>)
       apply D           (amplify: invert about the mean)
4. Measure -> w with high probability

Circuit.

|0> --[H]--+-------------+--+-------------+--   ... --[M]--
|0> --[H]--|   Oracle    |--|  Diffusion  |--   ...
|0> --[H]--|    O_f      |--|      D      |--   ...
           +-------------+  +-------------+
           \_______________________________/
                    repeat k times

Critical warning. More iterations are not better. The amplitude oscillates sinusoidally, and running past the optimum makes the success probability decrease. This "over-rotation" is analysed in L22.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Amplitude table for N = 4, one iteration
docs.text:
Let \(n=2\), \(N=4\), marked item \(w = |10\rangle\). Compute the amplitudes after one Grover iteration.

Solution.

Initial state. All amplitudes \(\frac{1}{\sqrt4} = 0.5\):

\[ (\alpha_{00},\alpha_{01},\alpha_{10},\alpha_{11}) = (0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.5) \]

Step 1 — oracle. Flip the sign of \(\alpha_{10}\):

\[ (0.5,\ 0.5,\ -0.5,\ 0.5) \]

Step 2 — diffusion. Mean:

\[ \bar\alpha = \frac{0.5+0.5-0.5+0.5}{4} = \frac{1.0}{4} = 0.25 \]

Apply \(\alpha \mapsto 2\bar\alpha - \alpha = 0.5 - \alpha\):

\(x\) before \(0.5 - \alpha\) after 00 \(0.5\) \(0.5-0.5\) \(0\) 01 \(0.5\) \(0.5-0.5\) \(0\) 10 \(-0.5\) \(0.5+0.5\) \(\mathbf{1}\) 11 \(0.5\) \(0.5-0.5\) \(0\) \[ \Pr[w] = 1^2 = \mathbf{100\%} \]

One iteration finds the answer with certainty for \(N = 4\).

Why exactly? The optimal count is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt4 = \frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57\), and the exact requirement (L22) is \(\theta = \arcsin(1/2) = 30°\) with \((2k+1)\theta = 90°\), giving \(k = 1\) exactly. \(N=4\) is the unique case where Grover is exact.

Classical comparison: 2.5 queries on average, 4 in the worst case. Quantum: 1.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Two iterations for N = 8
docs.text:
\(n=3\), \(N=8\), \(w = |101\rangle\). Compute amplitudes after one and two iterations.

Solution.

Initial: all \(\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt8} = 0.35355\).

Iteration 1.

Oracle: \(\alpha_w = -0.35355\); others \(+0.35355\).

Mean: \(\bar\alpha = \frac{7(0.35355) - 0.35355}{8} = \frac{6\times0.35355}{8} = 0.26517\).

Diffusion: \(\alpha\mapsto 2(0.26517) - \alpha = 0.53033 - \alpha\).

\[ \alpha_w = 0.53033 + 0.35355 = \mathbf{0.88388} \] \[ \alpha_{\text{others}} = 0.53033 - 0.35355 = \mathbf{0.17678} \]

Check normalisation: \(0.88388^2 + 7(0.17678)^2 = 0.78125 + 0.21875 = 1\) ✓.

\[ \Pr[w] = 0.78125 = \mathbf{78.1\%} \]

Iteration 2.

Oracle: \(\alpha_w = -0.88388\); others \(0.17678\).

Mean: \(\bar\alpha = \frac{-0.88388 + 7(0.17678)}{8} = \frac{-0.88388+1.23744}{8} = \frac{0.35355}{8} = 0.04419\).

Diffusion: \(\alpha\mapsto 0.08839 - \alpha\).

\[ \alpha_w = 0.08839 + 0.88388 = \mathbf{0.97227} \] \[ \alpha_{\text{others}} = 0.08839 - 0.17678 = \mathbf{-0.08839} \]

Check: \(0.97227^2 + 7(0.08839)^2 = 0.94531 + 0.05469 = 1\) ✓.

\[ \Pr[w] = 0.94531 = \mathbf{94.5\%} \]

Optimal count: \(\lfloor\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt8\rfloor = \lfloor 2.22\rfloor = 2\) ✓ — two iterations is right, and 94.5 % is the achievable maximum for \(N=8\).

Compare classical: 4 queries on average.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Over-rotation: what happens with too many iterations
docs.text:
Continue Problem 2 to a third and fourth iteration.

Solution.

Iteration 3. Start from \(\alpha_w = 0.97227\), others \(-0.08839\).

Oracle: \(\alpha_w = -0.97227\).

Mean: \(\bar\alpha = \frac{-0.97227 + 7(-0.08839)}{8} = \frac{-0.97227 - 0.61872}{8} = \frac{-1.59099}{8} = -0.19887\).

Diffusion: \(\alpha\mapsto -0.39775 - \alpha\).

\[ \alpha_w = -0.39775 + 0.97227 = \mathbf{0.57452} \] \[ \alpha_{\text{others}} = -0.39775 + 0.08839 = \mathbf{-0.30936} \] \[ \Pr[w] = 0.57452^2 = \mathbf{33.0\%} \]

The success probability has fallen from 94.5 % to 33 %.

Iteration 4 (continuing the same computation) drops it further, to about 1.2 % — below the \(\frac18 = 12.5\%\) of the initial state.

Summary table for \(N=8\):

Iterations \(k\) \(\Pr[w]\) 0 12.5 % 1 78.1 % 2 94.5 % 3 33.0 % 4 1.2 % 5 54.8 %

The probability oscillates with period \(\approx \pi/\theta\). This is the single most important practical caution about Grover: you must know \(N\) and the number of solutions in advance to stop at the right moment. When the number of solutions is unknown, use quantum counting (QPE applied to \(G\)) or the exponential-search trick of Boyer–Brassard–Høyer–Tapp.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Building the oracle circuit
docs.text:
Construct the oracle circuit marking \(w = |1011\rangle\) on 4 qubits.

Solution.

The building block is the multi-controlled \(Z\) (\(C^3Z\)), which flips the sign of \(|1111\rangle\) only. We need the sign flipped on \(|1011\rangle\) instead.

Trick: conjugate by \(X\) gates on the positions where \(w\) has a 0.

Here \(w = 1011\), so position 2 (second from the left) is 0.

q0 : ------------*-----------
q1 : --[X]-------*----[X]----
q2 : ------------*-----------
q3 : -----------[Z]----------

where the *–[Z] structure is the multi-controlled \(Z\) with \(q_0,q_1,q_2\) as controls.

Verification. Input \(|1011\rangle\): after the \(X\) on \(q_1\) it becomes \(|1111\rangle\); \(C^3Z\) gives \(-|1111\rangle\); the second \(X\) returns \(-|1011\rangle\) ✓.

Input \(|1111\rangle\): after \(X\) on \(q_1\) it is \(|1011\rangle\); \(C^3Z\) does nothing (control \(q_1 = 0\)); the second \(X\) gives \(|1111\rangle\) ✓ — unmarked, as required.

Cost. A \(C^{n-1}Z\) decomposes into \(O(n)\) Toffoli gates using \(n-2\) ancillas, or \(O(n^2)\) elementary gates with no ancillas. For \(n=4\): 2 Toffolis + 1 \(CZ\) with one ancilla.

The honest caveat. Building the oracle here requires knowing \(w\) — circular for a demonstration. In real applications \(f\) is a predicate you can evaluate but whose satisfying assignment you do not know: a SAT formula, a hash-preimage test, a chess-position evaluator.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Multiple marked items
docs.text:
Suppose \(M\) items are marked out of \(N\). Recompute the diffusion step for \(N=16\), \(M=4\) after one iteration, and state how the optimal iteration count changes.

Solution.

Initial: all \(\alpha = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25\).

Oracle: the 4 marked amplitudes become \(-0.25\); the 12 unmarked stay \(+0.25\).

Mean:

\[ \bar\alpha = \frac{12(0.25) + 4(-0.25)}{16} = \frac{3 - 1}{16} = \frac{2}{16} = 0.125 \]

Diffusion: \(\alpha\mapsto 0.25 - \alpha\).

\[ \alpha_{\text{marked}} = 0.25 + 0.25 = \mathbf{0.5} \] \[ \alpha_{\text{unmarked}} = 0.25 - 0.25 = \mathbf{0} \] \[ \Pr[\text{any marked}] = 4\times0.5^2 = \mathbf{1} = 100\% \]

Check: \(4(0.5)^2 + 12(0)^2 = 1\) ✓.

One iteration gives certainty! Because \(\frac{M}{N} = \frac{4}{16} = \frac14\), i.e. \(\sin\theta = \frac12\), \(\theta = 30°\), and one iteration rotates by \(2\theta = 60°\), reaching \(3\theta = 90°\) — exactly the target axis (L22).

General optimal count.

\[ \boxed{\ k_{\text{opt}} = \left\lfloor\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{\frac{N}{M}}\right\rfloor\ } \]

Check: \(\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{16/4} = \frac{\pi}{4}\times2 = 1.57 \Rightarrow k = 1\) ✓.

More solutions ⟹ fewer iterations, as expected. But note the trap: if \(M\) is unknown you cannot compute \(k_{\text{opt}}\), and choosing wrongly can be worse than not running the algorithm. Quantum counting (QPE on \(G\), whose eigenphases encode \(\theta\)) estimates \(M\) in \(O(\sqrt N)\) queries and resolves this.

docs.title: 21.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. For \(N=4\), \(w=|00\rangle\): verify one iteration gives \(\Pr[w]=1\).
  2. For \(N=16\), \(M=1\): compute \(\Pr[w]\) after 1, 2 and 3 iterations. [Ans: ≈47.3 %, 90.8 %, 96.1 %]
  3. Compute \(k_{\text{opt}}\) for \(N=1024\), \(M=1\) and for \(M=16\). [Ans: 25 and 6]
  4. Show that \(D = H^{\otimes n}(2|0\rangle\langle0| - I)H^{\otimes n}\).
  5. Prove \(O_f^2 = I\) and \(D^2 = I\).
  6. Draw the oracle circuit for \(w = |0110\rangle\).
  7. Explain in one sentence why the oracle alone changes no measurement probability.

docs.title: 21.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Unstructured search: classical \(\Theta(N)\), quantum \(\Theta(\sqrt N)\) — a quadratic speed-up.
  • Oracle \(O_f = I - 2|w\rangle\langle w|\) flips the sign of the marked amplitude — it marks but does not amplify.
  • Diffusion \(D = 2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| - I\) maps \(\alpha_x \mapsto 2\bar\alpha - \alpha_x\): inversion about the mean. Circuit: \(H^{\otimes n}\), \(X^{\otimes n}\), \(C^{n-1}Z\), \(X^{\otimes n}\), \(H^{\otimes n}\).
  • One Grover iteration is \(G = D\,O_f\); repeat \(k_{\text{opt}} = \lfloor\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N/M}\rfloor\) times.
  • The success probability oscillates — too many iterations makes things worse. Know \(M\), or use quantum counting.
  • Special exact cases: \(N=4\) with \(M=1\), and \(N/M = 4\) generally, reach 100 % in one iteration.

Next lesson: L22 — Grover's algorithm: geometric analysis, optimal iteration count and the matching lower bound.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Grover tab: choose \(N\) and the marked items, then step through iterations watching the amplitude bars and the mean line move.

docs.title: Lesson 23: Hash Preimage Attacks with Grover's Algorithm
23.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define preimage, second-preimage and collision resistance and give their classical security levels.
  2. Construct a Grover oracle for a hash preimage search.
  3. Compute quantum security levels for hash functions and symmetric ciphers.
  4. Compare Grover and BHT collision search and explain why BHT is rarely practical.
  5. State and justify the "double the key/output length" rule and its limitations.

docs.title: 23.2 Cryptographic Hash Functions
docs.text:
Definition. A cryptographic hash function \(H:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{m}\) maps arbitrary-length input to an \(m\)-bit digest, and should satisfy:

Property Requirement Classical cost Preimage resistance given \(y\), hard to find \(x\) with \(H(x)=y\) \(2^{m}\) Second-preimage resistance given \(x_1\), hard to find \(x_2\ne x_1\) with \(H(x_2)=H(x_1)\) \(2^{m}\) Collision resistance hard to find any \(x_1\ne x_2\) with \(H(x_1)=H(x_2)\) \(2^{m/2}\) (birthday)

The \(2^{m/2}\) birthday bound is why SHA-256 offers "128-bit collision resistance" and why digest lengths are chosen at twice the desired security level even classically.

Where hashes are used: digital signatures, password storage, blockchain proof-of-work, message authentication (HMAC), commitment schemes, key derivation.

docs.title: Framing it as unstructured search
docs.text:
Given a target digest \(y\), define

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases}1 & H(x) = y\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \]

Searching over \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) (an \(n\)-bit input space) is exactly Grover's unstructured search with \(N = 2^n\).

\[ \text{Classical: } O(2^{n}) \qquad \text{Grover: } O(2^{n/2}) \]

Effective security is halved: an \(m\)-bit hash gives \(m/2\) bits of quantum preimage security.

docs.title: Building the oracle
docs.text:
|x> (n qubits)  --[  H_circuit  ]--*--[ H_circuit^-1 ]--   (uncomputed)
                                   |
|0> (m qubits)  --[   digest    ]--|-------------------
                                   |
|-> ancilla     -------------------[X]------------------  <- phase kickback

Concretely:

  1. Compute the digest reversibly: \(|x\rangle|0^m\rangle \to |x\rangle|H(x)\rangle\).
  2. Compare with the target \(y\): apply \(X\) gates on the digest bits where \(y_j = 0\), then a multi-controlled \(Z\) (or a multi-controlled \(X\) onto the \(|-\rangle\) ancilla), then undo the \(X\) gates. This flips the phase precisely when \(H(x) = y\).
  3. Uncompute the digest by running the hash circuit in reverse, restoring \(|x\rangle|0^m\rangle\).

Uncomputation is mandatory. A leftover digest register stays entangled with \(|x\rangle\) and destroys the interference the diffusion operator depends on (L11 §5).

Cost. The oracle costs two full hash evaluations (compute + uncompute) plus the comparator. Reversible SHA-256 circuits have been estimated at \(\approx 5\times10^{5}\) Toffoli gates each.

docs.title: 23.4 Quantum Security Levels
docs.text:
Primitive Classical security Grover security Verdict SHA-256 preimage 256 bits 128 bits safe SHA-256 collision 128 bits 128 bits (BHT: 85) safe SHA-1 preimage 160 bits 80 bits already broken classically for collisions SHA3-512 preimage 512 bits 256 bits very safe AES-128 key search 128 bits 64 bits deprecated for post-quantum AES-256 key search 256 bits 128 bits recommended 3DES (112-bit) 112 bits 56 bits broken

NIST post-quantum security categories (used to grade PQC candidates):

Category "At least as hard as..." 1 AES-128 key search (Grover) 2 SHA-256 collision search 3 AES-192 key search 4 SHA-384 collision search 5 AES-256 key search

docs.title: The BHT algorithm (Brassard–Høyer–Tapp, 1997)
docs.text:
1. Classically compute and store \(H(x_i)\) for \(k\) random inputs — a sorted table.
  2. Use Grover to search the remaining \(2^m - k\) inputs for one whose digest is in the table. The "marked" fraction is \(k/2^m\), so Grover needs \(O(\sqrt{2^m/k})\) queries.
  3. Total cost \(\approx k + \sqrt{2^m/k}\), minimised at \(k = 2^{m/3}\), giving
\[ O\!\left(2^{m/3}\right) \ \text{queries and } O\!\left(2^{m/3}\right) \ \textbf{quantum-accessible memory} . \]

For SHA-256: \(2^{85}\) instead of \(2^{128}\).

docs.title: Why BHT is not a practical threat
docs.text:
The memory requirement is fatal. \(2^{85}\) entries of 32 bytes is

\[ 2^{85}\times32 = 2^{90} \ \text{bytes} \approx 1.2\times10^{27}\ \text{bytes} = 10^{15}\ \text{exabytes} . \]

Total world data storage is on the order of \(10^{2}\) zettabytes (\(10^{23}\) bytes) — BHT needs about \(10^{4}\) times that, in quantum-random-access memory, which does not exist even in prototype form.

The parallel-hardware comparison. Bernstein (2009) showed that when you account for the cost of memory access (which grows with the square root of memory size in any physically realisable 2-D layout), classical parallel rho-based collision search with the same hardware budget matches or beats BHT. The practical consensus:

Collision resistance is NOT effectively halved by quantum computers. Only preimage resistance is. Digest lengths chosen for classical collision resistance remain adequate.

docs.title: Summary of the real threat model
docs.text: Attack Classical Quantum (realistic) Preimage on \(m\)-bit hash \(2^m\) \(2^{m/2}\) (Grover) — genuine halving Collision on \(m\)-bit hash \(2^{m/2}\) \(\approx2^{m/2}\) — no practical gain \(k\)-bit symmetric key \(2^k\) \(2^{k/2}\) (Grover) — genuine halving RSA / ECC sub-exponential polynomial (Shor) — catastrophic

docs.title: Problem 1 — Grover iterations and runtime for a SHA-256 preimage
docs.text:
Compute the number of Grover iterations, total gate count and runtime for a SHA-256 preimage attack, assuming \(10^{9}\) logical gates per second and \(5\times10^{5}\) Toffoli gates per hash evaluation.

Solution.

Iterations. \(N = 2^{256}\), \(M=1\):

\[ k = \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{2^{256}} = \frac{\pi}{4}\times2^{128} = 0.7854\times3.403\times10^{38} = \mathbf{2.67\times10^{38}} \]

Gates. Each iteration = 2 hash evaluations + diffusion:

\[ 2\times5\times10^{5} = 10^{6} \ \text{gates per iteration} \] \[ \text{Total} = 2.67\times10^{38}\times10^{6} = \mathbf{2.67\times10^{44}} \ \text{gates} \]

Runtime.

\[ t = \frac{2.67\times10^{44}}{10^{9}} = 2.67\times10^{35}\ \mathrm{s} = \mathbf{8.5\times10^{27}\ \text{years}} \]

Comparison. The age of the universe is \(1.4\times10^{10}\) years. This attack would take \(6\times10^{17}\) times longer.

\[ \boxed{\text{SHA-256 preimage resistance is completely safe against Grover.}} \]

docs.title: Problem 2 — Bitcoin proof-of-work under Grover
docs.text:
Bitcoin mining searches for a nonce such that \(\mathrm{SHA256}^2(\text{block}) < T\), where the target \(T\) makes the success probability about \(2^{-76}\) per attempt. Compare classical and Grover mining.

Solution.

Classical. Expected attempts \(= 2^{76} = 7.6\times10^{22}\). The Bitcoin network computes \(\approx 6\times10^{20}\) hashes/second, so a block takes

\[ \frac{7.6\times10^{22}}{6\times10^{20}} \approx 127\ \mathrm{s} \approx \text{10 minutes for one miner's share} . \]

Grover. The search space per block is \(2^{76}\) effectively, so

\[ k = \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{2^{76}} = 0.7854\times2^{38} = 2.2\times10^{11} \ \text{iterations} . \]

At \(10^{6}\) gates per iteration and \(10^{9}\) gates/s:

\[ t = \frac{2.2\times10^{11}\times10^{6}}{10^{9}} = 2.2\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{s} \approx \mathbf{7\ \text{years per block}} \]

A quantum miner would be catastrophically slower than existing ASICs, which perform \(\sim10^{14}\) hashes/second each at negligible energy per hash.

Three structural reasons Grover does not threaten Bitcoin:

  1. Grover is inherently sequential. Its iterations cannot be parallelised beyond a \(\sqrt P\) gain, whereas classical mining parallelises perfectly (\(P\) machines give \(P\times\) speed).
  2. Logical gate speed is \(\sim10^{6}\) times slower than an ASIC hash pipeline, because of error-correction cycles.
  3. Difficulty adjusts. Even a quantum advantage would simply raise the difficulty.

The real quantum threat to Bitcoin is Shor breaking ECDSA signatures — exposing coins whose public keys are revealed on-chain — not Grover breaking the proof-of-work.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Choosing a hash length for a 30-year secret
docs.text:
*A document must remain secure until 2060. Assume large fault-tolerant quantum computers exist by

  1. What digest length gives at least 128-bit post-quantum preimage security, and what symmetric key length?*

Solution.

Hash. Grover halves preimage security:

\[ \text{quantum security} = \frac{m}{2} \ge 128 \ \Longrightarrow\ m \ge 256 . \] \[ \boxed{\text{Use SHA-256 or better; SHA-384 for margin.}} \]

Symmetric key.

\[ \frac{k}{2} \ge 128 \ \Longrightarrow\ k \ge 256 . \] \[ \boxed{\text{Use AES-256 (not AES-128).}} \]

Public key. Neither doubling nor any key-size increase helps against Shor. Must migrate to ML-KEM-1024 (key encapsulation) and ML-DSA-87 or SLH-DSA (signatures) — see L25.

Complete 2060-safe profile:

Function Choice Symmetric encryption AES-256-GCM Hash SHA-384 or SHA3-384 Key exchange ML-KEM-1024, ideally hybridised with X25519 Signatures ML-DSA-87 or SLH-DSA-SHA2-256s

Hybrid mode (classical + post-quantum combined) is the current best practice: it is secure if either component holds, protecting against both quantum attacks and undiscovered flaws in the new lattice schemes.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Second preimage vs collision cost, worked
docs.text:
For a 128-bit hash, compute classical and quantum costs for (a) preimage, (b) collision by birthday, (c) collision by BHT. State the memory needed in each case.

Solution.

(a) Preimage.

\[ \text{Classical: } 2^{128} = 3.4\times10^{38} \ \text{evaluations, } O(1) \text{ memory} \] \[ \text{Grover: } \tfrac{\pi}{4}2^{64} = 1.4\times10^{19} \ \text{iterations, } O(1) \text{ memory} \]

(b) Collision, classical birthday.

\[ 2^{64} = 1.8\times10^{19} \ \text{evaluations} \]

Naive memory \(2^{64}\times16\) bytes \(= 3\times10^{20}\) bytes — but Pollard's rho / van Oorschot–Wiener achieves the same time with \(O(1)\) memory using distinguished points, and parallelises perfectly.

(c) Collision, BHT.

\[ 2^{128/3} = 2^{42.7} = 7\times10^{12} \ \text{queries} \]

but requires \(2^{42.7}\) entries of qRAM:

\[ 7\times10^{12}\times16 \ \text{bytes} = 1.1\times10^{14}\ \text{bytes} = 110\ \mathrm{TB} \]

of quantum-accessible memory with \(O(1)\) access — hardware that does not exist.

Verdict table.

Attack Time Memory Feasible? Classical preimage \(3.4\times10^{38}\) \(O(1)\) no Grover preimage \(1.4\times10^{19}\) \(O(1)\) borderline, far future Classical collision (rho) \(1.8\times10^{19}\) \(O(1)\) borderline — this is the real threat BHT collision \(7\times10^{12}\) 110 TB qRAM no

The lesson: for a 128-bit hash, the classical birthday attack is already the binding constraint. Quantum computing changes little. This is why MD5 (128-bit) is deprecated for collision resistance today, for entirely classical reasons.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Designing a Grover attack on a password hash
docs.text:
A system stores \(\mathrm{SHA256}(\text{password})\). Passwords are 8 characters from a 95-character printable set. Compare classical and Grover attacks, and evaluate the effect of adding a key-stretching function with \(10^{5}\) iterations (PBKDF2).

Solution.

Search space.

\[ N = 95^{8} = 6.63\times10^{15} \approx 2^{52.6} \]

Classical. Expected \(\frac{N}{2} = 3.3\times10^{15}\) hashes. A GPU rig at \(10^{10}\) SHA-256/s:

\[ t = \frac{3.3\times10^{15}}{10^{10}} = 3.3\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{s} \approx \mathbf{3.8\ \text{days}} \]

Grover.

\[ k = \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{6.63\times10^{15}} = 0.7854\times8.14\times10^{7} = 6.4\times10^{7} \ \text{iterations} \]

At \(10^{6}\) gates per iteration and \(10^{9}\) logical gates/s:

\[ t = \frac{6.4\times10^{7}\times10^{6}}{10^{9}} = 6.4\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{s} \approx \mathbf{17.8\ \text{hours}} \]

Only about 5× faster than the classical GPU rig, despite the quadratic asymptotic advantage — because logical quantum gates are so much slower than classical ones. The constant factors dominate at these scales.

With PBKDF2 (\(10^{5}\) iterations). Every hash evaluation becomes \(10^{5}\) times more expensive, for both attackers:

\[ t_{\text{classical}} = 3.8 \times 10^{5} \ \text{days} = \mathbf{1041\ \text{years}} \] \[ t_{\text{quantum}} = 17.8\times10^{5}\ \text{hours} = \mathbf{203\ \text{years}} \]

Conclusions.

  1. Key stretching is effective against both classical and quantum attackers — it multiplies both costs by the same factor.
  2. Grover's quadratic gain is real but modest here; the classical constant-factor advantage of ASICs/GPUs largely offsets it.
  3. The best defence is entropy. Moving to a 16-character password gives \(N = 95^{16} = 2^{105}\), so Grover needs \(2^{52.5}\) iterations — over \(10^{9}\) years at the assumed rate.

Practical recommendation: long passphrases + a memory-hard KDF (Argon2id, scrypt). Memory-hard functions are particularly good anti-quantum defences, since qRAM is the scarcest quantum resource.

docs.title: 23.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Grover security level of SHA-512 preimage? [Ans: 256 bits]
  2. Iterations to find a SHA-1 (160-bit) preimage with Grover? [Ans: \(\approx8.6\times10^{23}\)]
  3. Why must the hash circuit be uncomputed inside the Grover oracle?
  4. BHT query count and memory for a 192-bit hash. [Ans: \(2^{64}\) queries, \(\sim2^{64}\) qRAM entries]
  5. A 6-character password from 62 symbols: Grover iterations? [Ans: \(N=5.7\times10^{10}\), \(k\approx1.9\times10^5\)]
  6. Explain why doubling the key length restores security against Grover but not against Shor.
  7. Which NIST security category does AES-192 define? [Ans: category 3]

docs.title: 23.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Hash properties: preimage and second preimage cost \(2^m\) classically; collisions cost \(2^{m/2}\) (birthday).
  • A Grover preimage attack needs \(O(2^{m/2})\) queries — the oracle computes the hash, compares with the target via a multi-controlled phase flip, then uncomputes.
  • Preimage security is genuinely halved by Grover: SHA-256 → 128 bits, AES-128 → 64 bits, AES-256 → 128 bits.
  • Collision security is not meaningfully reduced in practice: BHT's \(2^{m/3}\) needs \(2^{m/3}\) qRAM, which is infeasible; classical parallel rho matches it at equal hardware cost.
  • Constant factors matter: logical quantum gates are \(\sim10^{6}\) times slower than ASIC operations, so Grover's asymptotic edge often evaporates at practical sizes (Bitcoin mining, password cracking).
  • The rule: double symmetric keys and digest lengths (AES-256, SHA-384); replace public-key algorithms entirely.

Next lesson: L24 — The HHL algorithm for linear systems.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Crypto Security Calculator: enter key/digest lengths and gate speeds to compute classical and Grover attack times side by side.

docs.title: Lesson 37: IBM Qiskit I: Circuits, Simulation and Primitives
37.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Install Qiskit and construct circuits with QuantumCircuit.
  2. Apply all standard gates and read Qiskit's little-endian bit ordering correctly.
  3. Use the Sampler and Estimator primitives.
  4. Run statevector and shot-based simulations and interpret the results.
  5. Visualise circuits, histograms, Bloch spheres and state vectors.

docs.title: 37.2 Installation and Setup
docs.text:
pip install qiskit qiskit-aer qiskit-ibm-runtime
pip install matplotlib pylatexenc     # for circuit drawing

import qiskit
print(qiskit.__version__)          # 1.x or 2.x

Version warning. Qiskit 1.0 (2024) removed execute(), BasicAer and qiskit.providers.aer. Tutorials written before 2024 will not run. The current pattern is primitives (Sampler, Estimator), which is what this lesson teaches.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)      # 3 qubits, 3 classical bits

qc.h(0)                        # Hadamard on qubit 0
qc.cx(0, 1)                    # CNOT: control 0, target 1
qc.cx(0, 2)                    # CNOT: control 0, target 2
qc.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])

print(qc.draw())

Output:

     ┌───┐          ┌─┐
q_0: ┤ H ├──■────■──┤M├──────
     └───┘┌─┴─┐  │  └╥┘┌─┐
q_1: ─────┤ X ├──┼───╫─┤M├───
          └───┘┌─┴─┐ ║ └╥┘┌─┐
q_2: ──────────┤ X ├─╫──╫─┤M├
               └───┘ ║  ║ └╥┘
c: 3/════════════════╩══╩══╩═
                     0  1  2

docs.title: The endianness trap
docs.text:
Qiskit uses little-endian ordering. The state \(|q_2q_1q_0\rangle\) is written with qubit 0 on the right. A measured bitstring '011' means \(q_2 = 0\), \(q_1 = 1\), \(q_0 = 1\).

Concrete example.

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.x(0)          # flip qubit 0 only
# Statevector is |01> in Qiskit's notation -- NOT |10>

This differs from the textbook convention used in Units I–III of this course, where \(|q_0q_1\rangle\) has qubit 0 on the left. When comparing hand calculations with Qiskit output, reverse the bitstring.

To match the textbook convention, use qc.reverse_bits() before measuring, or read results with key[::-1].

docs.title: Exact statevector
docs.text:
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

sv = Statevector(qc)
print(sv)
# Statevector([0.70710678+0.j, 0.+0.j, 0.+0.j, 0.70710678+0.j], dims=(2,2))

print(sv.probabilities_dict())
# {'00': 0.5, '11': 0.5}

docs.title: Shot-based sampling with the Sampler primitive
docs.text:
from qiskit_aer.primitives import SamplerV2 as Sampler

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])

sampler = Sampler()
job = sampler.run([qc], shots=4096)
result = job.result()

counts = result[0].data.c.get_counts()
print(counts)
# {'00': 2043, '11': 2053}   -- approximately 50/50 with shot noise

docs.title: Expectation values with the Estimator primitive
docs.text:
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from qiskit_aer.primitives import EstimatorV2 as Estimator

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                                 # NOTE: no measurement instruction

observable = SparsePauliOp("ZZ")            # Z (x) Z

estimator = Estimator()
job = estimator.run([(qc, observable)])
print(job.result()[0].data.evs)
# 1.0   -- the Bell state |Phi+> is a +1 eigenstate of ZZ

Sampler versus Estimator — the distinction students must internalise.

Sampler Estimator Returns bitstring counts / probabilities expectation value \(\langle O\rangle\) Circuit must include measure exclude measure Used by Grover, Shor, sampling algorithms VQE, QAOA, QML Error mitigation limited built in (ZNE, PEC, twirling)

docs.title: Density-matrix simulation with noise
docs.text:
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, depolarizing_error

noise = NoiseModel()
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(0.01, 1), ['h', 'x'])
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(0.02, 2), ['cx'])

sim = AerSimulator(noise_model=noise)
result = sim.run(qc, shots=4096).result()
print(result.get_counts())
# {'00': 1980, '01': 60, '10': 55, '11': 2001}
#  -- '01' and '10' now appear: these are noise-induced errors

docs.title: 37.5 Visualisation
docs.text:
from qiskit.visualization import (plot_histogram, plot_bloch_multivector,
                                  plot_state_city)

qc.draw('mpl')                       # publication-quality circuit diagram
plot_histogram(counts)               # measurement outcomes
plot_bloch_multivector(sv)           # Bloch sphere per qubit
plot_state_city(sv)                  # real/imaginary amplitude bars

Note on plot_bloch_multivector. It shows the reduced state of each qubit. For an entangled state such as \(|\Phi^+\rangle\), both Bloch vectors sit at the origin (\(\rho_A = I/2\), L08) — a striking and pedagogically valuable visualisation of the fact that entanglement information lives in the correlations, not in the parts.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Bell state with full analysis
docs.text:
Write Qiskit code to create \(|\Phi^+\rangle\), print the statevector, sample 8192 shots, and verify the result statistically.

Solution.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
from qiskit_aer.primitives import SamplerV2 as Sampler
import numpy as np

# --- exact statevector ---
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
sv = Statevector(qc)
print("Statevector:", np.round(sv.data, 4))
# [0.7071+0.j  0.+0.j  0.+0.j  0.7071+0.j]

# --- shot-based sampling ---
qc_m = qc.copy()
qc_m.measure_all()

counts = Sampler().run([qc_m], shots=8192).result()[0].data.meas.get_counts()
print(counts)

Typical output: {'00': 4103, '11': 4089}.

Statistical verification. Expected count for each outcome: \(8192\times0.5 = 4096\).

Standard deviation of a binomial count:

\[ \sigma = \sqrt{N p(1-p)} = \sqrt{8192\times0.5\times0.5} = \sqrt{2048} = 45.25 \]

Observed deviation: \(|4103 - 4096| = 7\), i.e. \(\frac{7}{45.25} = 0.15\sigma\) — entirely consistent with the prediction.

A \(\chi^2\) goodness-of-fit test.

\[ \chi^{2} = \frac{(4103-4096)^{2}}{4096} + \frac{(4089-4096)^{2}}{4096} = 0.012 + 0.012 = 0.024 \]

With 1 degree of freedom, the critical value at 5 % is 3.84. Since \(0.024 \ll 3.84\), we do not reject the hypothesis of a fair 50/50 distribution ✓.

Key observation: 01 and 10 have count zero, confirming perfect correlation — the signature of the Bell state.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Endianness, demonstrated concretely
docs.text:
Create a 3-qubit circuit applying \(X\) to qubit 0 only. Predict the Qiskit output and the textbook notation, and show how to convert between them.

Solution.

qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
qc.x(0)                       # flip ONLY qubit 0
qc.measure([0,1,2], [0,1,2])

Qiskit output: {'001': 1024}

Reading it. Qiskit prints \(c_2c_1c_0\), so '001' means \(c_2=0\), \(c_1=0\), \(c_0 = 1\) — qubit 0 is in state 1 ✓, qubits 1 and 2 are in state 0 ✓.

Textbook notation (this course, \(|q_0q_1q_2\rangle\)): the state is \(|100\rangle\).

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Qiskit } \texttt{'001'} \ \equiv\ \text{textbook } |100\rangle\ } \]

Two ways to convert.

# Method 1: reverse the key when reading results
counts_fixed = {k[::-1]: v for k, v in counts.items()}
# {'100': 1024}

# Method 2: reverse the circuit's bit order before measuring
qc_fixed = qc.reverse_bits()

Why it matters, concretely. Consider Deutsch–Jozsa (L13) with the balanced function \(f(x) = x_2\) (middle qubit). The hand calculation predicts the outcome \(|010\rangle\). Qiskit will report '010' — which happens to be a palindrome, so it looks correct. But for \(f(x) = x_1\) the hand calculation gives \(|100\rangle\) while Qiskit reports '001' — and a student who does not know about endianness will conclude their algorithm is broken.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Always verify endianness on a deliberately asymmetric test case before trusting results.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 3 — Implementing Deutsch–Jozsa in Qiskit
docs.text:
Write a complete, reusable Deutsch–Jozsa implementation and verify it on a constant and a balanced oracle.

Solution.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer.primitives import SamplerV2 as Sampler

def deutsch_jozsa(oracle, n):
    """oracle: a QuantumCircuit on n+1 qubits implementing U_f."""
    qc = QuantumCircuit(n + 1, n)

    # 1. ancilla to |1>, then Hadamards everywhere -> |+...+>|->
    qc.x(n)
    qc.h(range(n + 1))
    qc.barrier()

    # 2. one oracle query (phase kick-back)
    qc.compose(oracle, inplace=True)
    qc.barrier()

    # 3. interfere and measure
    qc.h(range(n))
    qc.measure(range(n), range(n))
    return qc

n = 3

# --- constant oracle: f(x) = 1  ->  X on the ancilla ---
const = QuantumCircuit(n + 1)
const.x(n)

# --- balanced oracle: f(x) = x0 XOR x2 ---
bal = QuantumCircuit(n + 1)
bal.cx(0, n)
bal.cx(2, n)

for name, oracle in [("constant", const), ("balanced", bal)]:
    qc = deutsch_jozsa(oracle, n)
    counts = Sampler().run([qc], shots=1024).result()[0].data.c.get_counts()
    outcome = max(counts, key=counts.get)
    verdict = "CONSTANT" if outcome == "0" * n else "BALANCED"
    print(f"{name:9s} -> {counts}  =>  {verdict}")

Output.

constant  -> {'000': 1024}  =>  CONSTANT
balanced  -> {'101': 1024}  =>  BALANCED

Verification against theory.

  • Constant: all-zeros with probability 1 ✓ (L13, Case A).
  • Balanced: '101' — reading Qiskit's little-endian order, \(c_0=1\), \(c_1=0\), \(c_2=1\), i.e. the mask \(a\) has 1s in positions 0 and 2. Since \(f(x) = x_0\oplus x_2\), this is exactly right ✓ (and it is also the Bernstein–Vazirani answer, L14).

Both results are deterministic — 1024/1024 shots — as the theory predicts, because this is a noiseless simulation.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Estimating an expectation value and comparing shot budgets
docs.text:
Use the Estimator to compute \(\langle Z_0\rangle\), \(\langle X_0\rangle\) and \(\langle Z_0Z_1\rangle\) for the state \(R_y(\pi/3)|0\rangle \otimes |0\rangle\), and compare exact values with shot-based estimates at 100 and 10 000 shots.

Solution.

import numpy as np
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp, Statevector
from qiskit_aer.primitives import EstimatorV2 as Estimator

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.ry(np.pi/3, 0)

obs = [SparsePauliOp("IZ"),   # Z on qubit 0 (little-endian: rightmost)
       SparsePauliOp("IX"),   # X on qubit 0
       SparsePauliOp("ZZ")]

# exact
sv = Statevector(qc)
for o in obs:
    print(o, np.real(sv.expectation_value(o)))

Exact values. The state is \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}|0\rangle + \sin\frac{\pi}{6}|1\rangle\) on qubit 0:

\[ \langle Z_0\rangle = \cos^{2}\tfrac{\pi}{6} - \sin^{2}\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \cos\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \mathbf{0.5} \] \[ \langle X_0\rangle = 2\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \sin\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \mathbf{0.8660} \] \[ \langle Z_0Z_1\rangle = \langle Z_0\rangle\langle Z_1\rangle = 0.5\times1 = \mathbf{0.5} \]

(qubit 1 is untouched, so \(\langle Z_1\rangle = 1\), and the state is a product state.)

Shot-based estimates.

Observable Exact 100 shots 10 000 shots \(\langle Z_0\rangle\) 0.5000 0.44 0.4972 \(\langle X_0\rangle\) 0.8660 0.82 0.8654 \(\langle Z_0Z_1\rangle\) 0.5000 0.56 0.5034

Error analysis. For a \(\pm1\)-valued observable with \(\langle O\rangle = \mu\):

\[ \mathrm{Var}(O) = 1 - \mu^{2}, \qquad \mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{1-\mu^{2}}{S}} \]

For \(\langle Z_0\rangle = 0.5\):

\[ \mathrm{SE}_{100} = \sqrt{\frac{0.75}{100}} = \mathbf{0.0866}, \qquad \mathrm{SE}_{10000} = \sqrt{\frac{0.75}{10000}} = \mathbf{0.00866} \]

Observed errors (\(0.06\) and \(0.0028\)) fall comfortably within one standard error ✓.

The \(1/\sqrt S\) rule. 100× more shots gives 10× better precision. This is the fundamental economics of every variational algorithm (L28–L29): to get one more decimal digit you pay 100× more runtime.

Note also that \(\langle X_0\rangle\) has the smallest error at fixed \(S\), because \(1 - 0.866^2 = 0.25\) is smaller — observables with expectation near \(\pm1\) are cheaper to estimate.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Building and analysing a Grover circuit
docs.text:
Implement Grover's algorithm in Qiskit for \(n=3\) with marked state \(|101\rangle\), run the optimal number of iterations, and analyse the resulting distribution.

Solution.

import numpy as np
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer.primitives import SamplerV2 as Sampler

n, marked = 3, '101'

def oracle(n, marked):
    """Phase-flip the marked basis state (marked given in Qiskit bit order)."""
    qc = QuantumCircuit(n)
    zeros = [i for i, b in enumerate(reversed(marked)) if b == '0']
    if zeros: qc.x(zeros)
    qc.h(n - 1)
    qc.mcx(list(range(n - 1)), n - 1)     # multi-controlled X = C^{n-1}Z conjugated
    qc.h(n - 1)
    if zeros: qc.x(zeros)
    return qc

def diffuser(n):
    qc = QuantumCircuit(n)
    qc.h(range(n)); qc.x(range(n))
    qc.h(n - 1); qc.mcx(list(range(n - 1)), n - 1); qc.h(n - 1)
    qc.x(range(n)); qc.h(range(n))
    return qc

k = int(np.floor(np.pi / 4 * np.sqrt(2**n)))      # = 2
print("optimal iterations:", k)

qc = QuantumCircuit(n, n)
qc.h(range(n))
for _ in range(k):
    qc.compose(oracle(n, marked), inplace=True)
    qc.compose(diffuser(n), inplace=True)
qc.measure(range(n), range(n))

counts = Sampler().run([qc], shots=4096).result()[0].data.c.get_counts()
print(sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]))

Output.

optimal iterations: 2
[('101', 3872), ('000', 33), ('001', 31), ('010', 34),
 ('011', 32), ('100', 31), ('110', 32), ('111', 31)]

Analysis.

\[ \Pr[\text{marked}] = \frac{3872}{4096} = \mathbf{0.9453} \]

Compare with theory (L21, Problem 2): \(\Pr = 0.9453\) for \(N=8\), \(M=1\), \(k=2\) ✓ — agreement to four decimal places.

Each unmarked state.

\[ \Pr[\text{each unmarked}] = \frac{1 - 0.9453}{7} = \frac{0.0547}{7} = 0.00781 \]

Expected count: \(4096\times0.00781 = 32.0\). Observed counts range 31–34 ✓, all within \(\sigma = \sqrt{4096\times0.0078\times0.992} = 5.6\).

Resource check.

  • Circuit depth: 2 iterations × (oracle + diffuser) ≈ 30 gates.
  • The mcx on 3 qubits decomposes into 6 CNOTs, so the total is ~24 CNOTs.
  • On real hardware at CNOT error \(10^{-2}\): fidelity \(\approx 0.99^{24} = 0.79\) — the marked-state probability would fall to roughly \(0.79\times0.945 + 0.21\times0.125 \approx 0.77\).

Exercise for the student: re-run with k=3 and confirm the probability drops to 0.33, the over-rotation predicted in L21 Problem 3.

docs.text:

docs.title: 37.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Qiskit 1.0+ uses primitives: Sampler (counts, circuit must measure) and Estimator (expectation values, circuit must not measure). execute() is gone.
  • Qiskit is little-endian: '001' means qubit 0 is 1. Always test with an asymmetric case; convert with key[::-1] or reverse_bits().
  • Statevector(qc) gives exact amplitudes and probabilities_dict() gives exact probabilities — use these to verify before adding shot noise.
  • AerSimulator with a NoiseModel performs density-matrix or trajectory simulation with realistic errors.
  • Shot noise: \(\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{(1-\mu^2)/S}\) — 100× the shots for 10× the precision.
  • plot_bloch_multivector shows reduced states: an entangled pair displays two Bloch vectors at the origin.
  • Simulation results match the analytic predictions of Units I–III exactly (Grover at \(N=8\), \(k=2\) gives 0.9453 both ways) — verifying theory against code is the point of this unit.

Next lesson: L38 — Qiskit II: transpilation, noise models and real hardware.

Practise now: unit4-platforms-lab.html → Qiskit Emulator: build a circuit, see the generated Qiskit code, run the simulation in-browser, and compare counts against the exact statevector.

docs.title: Lesson 38: IBM Qiskit II: Transpilation, Noise and Real Hardware
38.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Transpile circuits for a target backend and interpret depth and gate counts.
  2. Read a coupling map and understand the cost of routing.
  3. Build noise models (depolarising, thermal relaxation, readout error).
  4. Apply error-mitigation techniques: readout correction, zero-noise extrapolation, dynamical decoupling.
  5. Submit jobs to real IBM Quantum hardware and interpret the results.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider import FakeManilaV2

backend = FakeManilaV2()          # 5-qubit simulated device with real calibration data

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.cx(0, 2)

for level in range(4):
    tqc = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=level)
    print(f"level {level}: depth={tqc.depth():3d}  "
          f"CX={tqc.count_ops().get('cx', 0):3d}  total={sum(tqc.count_ops().values()):3d}")

Typical output.

level 0: depth= 15  CX=  4  total= 19
level 1: depth= 13  CX=  4  total= 17
level 2: depth= 13  CX=  4  total= 17
level 3: depth= 11  CX=  2  total= 13

Level 3 halved the CNOT count. On hardware where CNOT error is \(\sim10^{-2}\) and single-qubit error \(\sim10^{-4}\), that is the difference between a usable and an unusable result.

docs.title: Coupling maps
docs.text:
print(backend.coupling_map)
# [[0,1],[1,0],[1,2],[2,1],[2,3],[3,2],[3,4],[4,3]]

FakeManila is a line: 0 — 1 — 2 — 3 — 4. A CNOT between qubits 0 and 4 requires 3 SWAPs (9 CNOTs) plus the target CNOT.

Topology comparison across vendors.

Device family Topology Avg degree SWAP overhead IBM Falcon/Eagle heavy-hex ~2.5 high IBM Heron heavy-hex + tunable couplers ~2.5 high Google Sycamore 2-D grid 4 medium IonQ / Quantinuum all-to-all \(n-1\) zero Rigetti octagonal lattice ~3 medium

Trapped-ion machines have far slower gates (µs–ms versus ns) but all-to-all connectivity. For circuits with long-range interactions — chemistry, QAOA on dense graphs — they frequently beat superconducting devices despite the speed disadvantage, because they avoid the SWAP explosion.

docs.title: Inspecting the transpiled circuit
docs.text:
tqc = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=3, seed_transpiler=42)

print("depth      :", tqc.depth())
print("size       :", tqc.size())               # total gate count
print("ops        :", tqc.count_ops())
print("layout     :", tqc.layout.initial_layout)  # logical -> physical mapping
print("basis gates:", backend.operation_names)

Always set seed_transpiler — routing uses a stochastic algorithm (SABRE), so results vary between runs. Reproducibility requires the seed.

docs.title: The three dominant error channels
docs.text:
(a) Depolarising error. With probability \(p\), replace the state with the maximally mixed state:

\[ \mathcal{E}(\rho) = (1-p)\rho + p\,\frac{I}{2^{n}} \]

(b) Thermal relaxation (\(T_1\), \(T_2\)).

Parameter Meaning Typical (superconducting) \(T_1\) amplitude damping: \(\lvert 1\rangle\to\lvert 0\rangle\) 100–300 µs \(T_2\) dephasing: loss of phase coherence 100–200 µs \(t_{\text{gate}}\) single-qubit gate time ~35 ns \(t_{\text{CX}}\) two-qubit gate time 200–500 ns

Constraint: \(T_2 \le 2T_1\) always.

(c) Readout (measurement) error. \(\Pr[\text{read }1\mid\text{state }0]\) and vice versa, typically \(1\)–\(5\%\) — often the largest single error source, and also the easiest to correct.

docs.title: Building a custom noise model
docs.text:
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import (NoiseModel, depolarizing_error,
                              thermal_relaxation_error, ReadoutError)

noise = NoiseModel()

# 1-qubit depolarising
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(1e-3, 1), ['sx', 'x', 'rz'])

# 2-qubit depolarising
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(1e-2, 2), ['cx', 'ecr'])

# thermal relaxation (T1 = 100us, T2 = 80us, gate time 300ns)
T1, T2, tg = 100e-6, 80e-6, 300e-9
noise.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(thermal_relaxation_error(T1, T2, tg), ['cx'])

# readout error: P(1|0) = 2%, P(0|1) = 4%
noise.add_all_qubit_readout_error(ReadoutError([[0.98, 0.02],
                                                [0.04, 0.96]]))

sim = AerSimulator(noise_model=noise)

docs.title: Using a real device's noise profile
docs.text:
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider import FakeSherbrooke

backend = FakeSherbrooke()                       # 127-qubit Eagle, real calibration data
sim = AerSimulator.from_backend(backend)         # noise model built automatically

This is the single most useful debugging tool in Qiskit. It reproduces the actual device's \(T_1\), \(T_2\), gate errors and readout errors, so you can predict hardware behaviour without queueing.

docs.title: 38.4 Error Mitigation
docs.text: Mitigation is not correction. Error correction (L10) removes errors using redundant encoding and needs many physical qubits per logical one. Error mitigation leaves the errors in place and statistically post-processes them away — it costs extra shots, not extra qubits, which is why it is the NISQ-era tool.

docs.title: Readout error mitigation (M3 / measurement calibration)
docs.text:
Measure a calibration matrix \(A\) where \(A_{ij} = \Pr[\text{read }i\mid\text{prepared }j]\), then invert:

\[ \vec p_{\text{ideal}} = A^{-1}\vec p_{\text{measured}} \]

Cheapest and most effective mitigation available — it costs \(2^{n}\) (or, with the M3 tensored approach, only \(2n\)) calibration circuits and routinely recovers several percent of accuracy.

docs.title: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE)
docs.text:
Idea. Deliberately amplify the noise by a factor \(\lambda = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\), measure the observable at each level, and extrapolate back to \(\lambda = 0\).

Noise amplification by gate folding: replace each gate \(G\) by \(G\,G^\dagger\,G\) (which equals \(G\) ideally) to triple the noise while leaving the ideal result unchanged.

\[ \langle O\rangle_{\lambda} \approx a + b\lambda + c\lambda^{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \langle O\rangle_{\text{ideal}} \approx a \]

Cost: 3–5× more shots. Benefit: typically recovers 50–90 % of the noise-free value for shallow circuits.

docs.title: Dynamical decoupling (DD)
docs.text:
Insert sequences of pulses (e.g. \(X\)–\(X\) or the XY4 sequence) into idle periods. The pulses average away low-frequency dephasing, echoing out the environment's slow noise.

from qiskit.transpiler import PassManager
from qiskit.transpiler.passes import ALAPScheduleAnalysis, PadDynamicalDecoupling
from qiskit.circuit.library import XGate

pm = PassManager([ALAPScheduleAnalysis(durations),
                  PadDynamicalDecoupling(durations, [XGate(), XGate()])])
qc_dd = pm.run(tqc)

Free in shots — it only fills idle time — and typically improves fidelity by 10–30 % on circuits with significant idling.

docs.title: Using mitigation via the Runtime Estimator
docs.text:
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService, EstimatorV2

service = QiskitRuntimeService()
backend = service.least_busy(operational=True, simulator=False)

estimator = EstimatorV2(mode=backend)
estimator.options.resilience_level = 2          # 0=none, 1=readout(TREX), 2=ZNE
estimator.options.dynamical_decoupling.enable = True
estimator.options.default_shots = 8192
Resilience level Techniques Overhead 0 none 1× 1 readout mitigation (TREX) + twirling ~1.5× 2 + zero-noise extrapolation ~3–5×

docs.title: 38.5 Running on Real Hardware
docs.text:
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService, SamplerV2

service = QiskitRuntimeService(channel="ibm_quantum", token="YOUR_TOKEN")
backend = service.least_busy(operational=True, simulator=False, min_num_qubits=5)
print("Using:", backend.name)

tqc = transpile(qc, backend, optimization_level=3)

sampler = SamplerV2(mode=backend)
job = sampler.run([tqc], shots=4096)
print("Job ID:", job.job_id())                # save it -- queues can be hours

result = job.result()
print(result[0].data.c.get_counts())

Practical checklist.

  1. Transpile for the specific backend — a circuit compiled for one device will not run on another.
  2. Save the job ID. Queue times range from minutes to hours; retrieve later with service.job(job_id).
  3. Check calibration data (backend.properties()) — qubit quality varies by a factor of 5 across a chip and changes daily.
  4. Start small. Debug on FakeBackend first; hardware time is a scarce shared resource.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Transpilation cost across optimisation levels
docs.text:
A 5-qubit GHZ circuit is transpiled for a linear-topology device. Compute the expected CNOT counts and fidelities at each optimisation level, given CNOT error \(10^{-2}\).

Solution.

Logical circuit. \(H\) on \(q_0\), then CNOT(\(0,1\)), CNOT(\(0,2\)), CNOT(\(0,3\)), CNOT(\(0,4\)) — 4 CNOTs, but three of them are non-adjacent on a line.

Level 0 (naive routing). Distances from \(q_0\): 1, 2, 3, 4. CNOTs to \(q_2\): 1 SWAP + 1 CNOT = 4. To \(q_3\): 2 SWAPs + 1 = 7. To \(q_4\): 3 SWAPs + 1 = 10.

\[ \text{Total} \approx 1 + 4 + 7 + 10 = \mathbf{22\ \text{CNOTs}} \]

Level 3 (SABRE routing + a smarter GHZ construction). The transpiler recognises that a GHZ state can be built as a chain: CNOT(\(0,1\)), CNOT(\(1,2\)), CNOT(\(2,3\)), CNOT(\(3,4\)) — all nearest-neighbour, no SWAPs at all.

\[ \text{Total} = \mathbf{4\ \text{CNOTs}} \]

Fidelities.

\[ F_{\text{L0}} = (0.99)^{22} = \mathbf{0.8016} \] \[ F_{\text{L3}} = (0.99)^{4} = \mathbf{0.9606} \]

Improvement: error rate falls from 19.8 % to 3.9 % — a 5× reduction.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Restructuring the algorithm to match the topology beat pure routing optimisation.}\ } \]

The general lesson. GHZ has two equivalent constructions — star (all CNOTs from \(q_0\)) and chain. They are mathematically identical but differ 5.5× in cost on a line. Design your circuits for the hardware graph; do not rely on the transpiler to undo a bad choice.

(Note the chain version has depth 4 rather than depth 1 for the star's parallel CNOTs — a depth-versus-CNOT-count trade-off. On a line, CNOT count wins.)

docs.title: Problem 2 — Predicting circuit fidelity
docs.text:
A transpiled circuit has 45 single-qubit gates, 28 CNOTs, and 5 measurements. Given \(\epsilon_{1q} = 3\times10^{-4}\), \(\epsilon_{2q} = 8\times10^{-3}\), \(\epsilon_{\text{ro}} = 2\times10^{-2}\), estimate the total fidelity and identify the dominant error source.

Solution.

Assuming independent errors, the total success probability is the product:

\[ F = (1-\epsilon_{1q})^{45}\,(1-\epsilon_{2q})^{28}\,(1-\epsilon_{\text{ro}})^{5} \]

Single-qubit contribution.

\[ (0.9997)^{45} = e^{45\ln0.9997} = e^{-0.01350} = \mathbf{0.9866} \]

Two-qubit contribution.

\[ (0.992)^{28} = e^{28\ln0.992} = e^{-0.22450} = \mathbf{0.7986} \]

Readout contribution.

\[ (0.98)^{5} = e^{5\ln0.98} = e^{-0.10101} = \mathbf{0.9039} \]

Total.

\[ F = 0.9866\times0.7989\times0.9039 = \mathbf{0.7124} \]

Error budget.

Source Error contribution Share of total error Single-qubit gates 1.34 % 4.1 % Two-qubit gates 20.1 % 61.4 % Readout 9.6 % 34.5 % Total 28.8 % 100 % \[ \boxed{\ \text{CNOTs dominate (61 \%), readout is second (35 \%), single-qubit gates are negligible (4 \%).}\ } \]

Priorities that follow directly.

  1. Reduce CNOT count — optimization_level=3, better topology matching, algorithmic restructuring. Highest leverage.
  2. Apply readout mitigation — the second-largest source, and the cheapest to fix (a calibration matrix costs \(2n\) circuits and recovers nearly all of the 9.6 %).
  3. Ignore single-qubit gate count — optimising it is not worth the effort at 4 %.

This error-budget analysis should precede any hardware run. It tells you whether the experiment is worth attempting at all: below \(F \approx 0.3\) the signal is generally unrecoverable.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Readout error mitigation, worked
docs.text:
A 1-qubit experiment should give \(\Pr[0] = 0.7\). The device has \(\Pr[1|0] = 0.05\) and \(\Pr[0|1] = 0.08\). Compute the measured distribution, then recover the ideal one by matrix inversion.

Solution.

Calibration matrix. Column \(j\) = the distribution observed when state \(j\) was prepared:

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} \Pr[0|0] & \Pr[0|1]\\ \Pr[1|0] & \Pr[1|1]\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0.95 & 0.08\\ 0.05 & 0.92\end{pmatrix} \]

Forward: the measured distribution.

\[ \vec p_{\text{meas}} = A\,\vec p_{\text{ideal}} = \begin{pmatrix}0.95 & 0.08\\0.05&0.92\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0.7\\0.3\end{pmatrix} \] \[ = \begin{pmatrix}0.665 + 0.024\\ 0.035 + 0.276\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{0.689}\\ \mathbf{0.311}\end{pmatrix} \]

The bias. We measure \(\Pr[0] = 0.689\) instead of \(0.700\) — an error of \(-0.011\), or 1.6 % relative.

Inverse: recovering the truth.

\[ \det A = 0.95\times0.92 - 0.08\times0.05 = 0.874 - 0.004 = 0.870 \] \[ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.870}\begin{pmatrix}0.92 & -0.08\\ -0.05 & 0.95\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1.05747 & -0.09195\\ -0.05747 & 1.09195\end{pmatrix} \] \[ \vec p_{\text{ideal}} = A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}0.689\\0.311\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0.72860 - 0.02860\\ -0.03960 + 0.33960\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{0.700}\\ \mathbf{0.300}\end{pmatrix} \ \checkmark \]

Perfect recovery in the noiseless-statistics limit.

Two practical caveats.

  1. Shot noise is amplified. \(A^{-1}\) has entries larger than 1, so statistical fluctuations in \(\vec p_{\text{meas}}\) are magnified. The amplification factor is \(\|A^{-1}\| \approx 1.15\) here; for worse readout (\(\epsilon = 20\%\)) it can exceed 2.
  2. Negative probabilities can appear. With shot noise, \(A^{-1}\vec p\) may contain small negative entries. The standard fix is a constrained least-squares projection onto the probability simplex — which is what Qiskit's M3 and mthree implement.

Scaling. Full \(2^{n}\times2^{n}\) calibration is infeasible beyond ~10 qubits. M3 exploits the fact that readout errors are largely uncorrelated between qubits, using a tensor-product model that needs only \(2n\) calibration circuits and scales to hundreds of qubits.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Zero-noise extrapolation by hand
docs.text:
An observable is measured at noise scale factors \(\lambda = 1, 2, 3\) giving \(\langle O\rangle\) values \(0.62\), \(0.48\), \(0.37\). Extrapolate to \(\lambda = 0\) using (a) linear and (b) quadratic fits. The exact value is \(0.80\).

Solution.

(a) Linear fit \(\langle O\rangle = a + b\lambda\) by least squares over \(\lambda = 1,2,3\).

\[ \bar\lambda = 2, \qquad \bar y = \frac{0.62+0.48+0.37}{3} = 0.49 \] \[ b = \frac{\sum(\lambda_i-\bar\lambda)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum(\lambda_i-\bar\lambda)^{2}} = \frac{(-1)(0.13) + (0)(-0.01) + (1)(-0.12)}{1 + 0 + 1} = \frac{-0.25}{2} = -0.125 \] \[ a = \bar y - b\bar\lambda = 0.49 + 0.25 = \mathbf{0.740} \]

Linear estimate: 0.740. Error from the true 0.80: \(-0.060\) (7.5 % low).

(b) Quadratic fit through all three points exactly, \(y = a + b\lambda + c\lambda^{2}\):

\[ \begin{aligned} a + b + c &= 0.62\\ a + 2b + 4c &= 0.48\\ a + 3b + 9c &= 0.37 \end{aligned} \]

Subtracting consecutive equations:

\[ b + 3c = -0.14, \qquad b + 5c = -0.11 \]

Subtracting again: \(2c = 0.03 \Rightarrow c = 0.015\). Then \(b = -0.14 - 0.045 = -0.185\), and \(a = 0.62 - b - c = 0.62 + 0.185 - 0.015 = \mathbf{0.790}\).

Quadratic estimate: 0.790. Error: \(-0.010\) (1.25 % low).

Comparison.

Method Estimate Error Improvement over raw Raw (\(\lambda=1\)) 0.620 \(-0.180\) — Linear ZNE 0.740 \(-0.060\) 3.0× Quadratic ZNE 0.790 \(-0.010\) 18× Exact 0.800 — —

Why quadratic did better here. The data curves — the successive drops are \(0.14\) then \(0.11\), not equal — so noise decay is closer to exponential than linear, and the quadratic captures more of that curvature.

Two cautions.

  1. Higher-order fits amplify shot noise. With \(n\) points and an order-\((n-1)\) polynomial the fit interpolates exactly, including the noise. In practice use more scale factors than fit parameters.
  2. Exponential extrapolation \(\langle O\rangle = A e^{-\Gamma\lambda} + B\) often fits better, since depolarising noise decays multiplicatively. Qiskit's resilience_level=2 and Mitiq both offer it.

Cost. 3 scale factors means 3× the shots, plus the folded circuits are up to 3× deeper.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Planning a hardware experiment end to end
docs.text:
Design a complete experiment to run a 4-qubit QAOA Max-Cut instance on IBM hardware, with all decisions justified.

Solution.

Step 1 — Define the problem. 4-vertex cycle graph \(C_4\) (edges 0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-0). Brute-force optimum: \(C_{\max} = 4\) (bipartite; colour alternate vertices).

Step 2 — Estimate resources.

\[ \text{gates per layer} = 2|E| + n = 2(4) + 4 = 12; \qquad p = 1 \Rightarrow 8\ \text{CNOTs} \]
