Primitive Hard problem Quantum attack Status RSA integer factoring Shor — polynomial broken Diffie–Hellman discrete log mod \(p\) Shor — polynomial broken ECDSA / ECDH elliptic-curve discrete log Shor — polynomial (fewer qubits than RSA!) broken DSA discrete log Shor broken AES-128 key search Grover — \(2^{64}\) weakened AES-256 key search Grover — \(2^{128}\) safe SHA-256/384 preimage Grover — \(2^{128}/2^{192}\) safe Lattice problems SVP/CVP/LWE none known believed safe Hash-based signatures hash security only Grover only safe (most conservative) Code-based (McEliece) syndrome decoding none known believed safe

The asymmetry. Symmetric cryptography survives by doubling parameters. All deployed public-key cryptography must be replaced.

Elliptic curves fall first. Breaking a 256-bit ECC key needs about 2330 logical qubits, versus ~4100 for RSA-2048 — because the group order is much smaller. Ironically, the "stronger" modern choice is the easier quantum target.

docs.title: 25.3 The NIST Standards (August 2024)
docs.text:
After an eight-year competition (2016–2024), NIST published:

FIPS Name Original Purpose Basis 203 ML-KEM CRYSTALS-Kyber key encapsulation Module-LWE (lattices) 204 ML-DSA CRYSTALS-Dilithium signatures (primary) Module-LWE/SIS 205 SLH-DSA SPHINCS+ signatures (backup) hash functions only (2025) FN-DSA Falcon signatures (compact) NTRU lattices

Also standardised for stateful use: XMSS and LMS (RFC 8391/8554) for firmware signing.

HQC (code-based) was selected in March 2025 as a backup KEM with a different mathematical foundation from lattices — insurance against a lattice breakthrough.

docs.title: Lattices
docs.text:
Definition. Given linearly independent \(\vec b_1,\dots,\vec b_n\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the lattice they generate is

\[ \mathcal{L} = \left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i\vec b_i \ :\ z_i\in\mathbb{Z}\right\} \]

— a regular grid of points, infinite in extent but discrete.

Hard problems.

Problem Statement Best known SVP (shortest vector) find the shortest non-zero \(\vec v\in\mathcal L\) \(2^{\Theta(n)}\) classically and quantumly CVP (closest vector) given \(\vec t\notin\mathcal L\), find the nearest lattice point \(2^{\Theta(n)}\) SIS (short integer solution) find short \(\vec z\) with \(A\vec z\equiv 0 \bmod q\) \(2^{\Theta(n)}\)

Why lattices resist quantum attack. Shor's algorithm solves the abelian Hidden Subgroup Problem. Lattice problems reduce to the dihedral HSP, which is non-abelian. The best known quantum algorithm (Kuperberg's sieve) runs in \(2^{O(\sqrt n)}\) — sub-exponential but still exponential, and it does not translate into a practical attack on the parameters in use.

Lattices also enjoy worst-case to average-case reductions (Ajtai 1996; Regev 2005): breaking a random instance is as hard as solving the worst case, an unusually strong security guarantee that RSA does not have.

docs.title: Learning With Errors (LWE)
docs.text:
Definition (Search-LWE). Fix a secret \(\vec s\in\mathbb{Z}_q^{n}\). Given many samples

\[ \big(\vec a_i,\ b_i = \langle\vec a_i,\vec s\rangle + e_i \bmod q\big) \]

with \(\vec a_i\) uniform and \(e_i\) small "noise" drawn from a narrow distribution, recover \(\vec s\).

Without the noise this is just a linear system, solved instantly by Gaussian elimination. The small errors make it hard — Gaussian elimination amplifies them catastrophically.

Definition (Decision-LWE). Distinguish LWE samples from uniform random pairs. Regev proved this is as hard as Search-LWE, and (quantumly) as hard as worst-case lattice problems.

docs.title: Module-LWE
docs.text:
Plain LWE needs large matrices — public keys of megabytes. Ring-LWE replaces \(\mathbb{Z}_q\) with the polynomial ring \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^{n}+1)\), so a whole \(n\times n\) structured matrix is described by \(n\) coefficients and multiplication uses an NTT in \(O(n\log n)\).

Module-LWE interpolates: work with \(k\times k\) matrices over the ring, giving a security/size dial. Kyber uses \(n = 256\) with \(k \in \{2,3,4\}\). Module structure hedges against attacks that might exploit the full algebraic structure of Ring-LWE.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Ring \(R_q = \mathbb{Z}_{3329}[X]/(X^{256}+1)\); \(q = 3329\), \(n = 256\).

Variant \(k\) NIST level Public key Ciphertext Secret key ML-KEM-512 2 1 (≈AES-128) 800 B 768 B 1632 B ML-KEM-768 3 3 (≈AES-192) 1184 B 1088 B 2400 B ML-KEM-1024 4 5 (≈AES-256) 1568 B 1568 B 3168 B

ML-KEM-768 is the recommended default (used by Chrome, Signal, Cloudflare).

docs.title: The scheme (structure)
docs.text:
Key generation.

  1. Sample a uniform matrix \(\mathbf{A}\in R_q^{k\times k}\) (expanded from a 32-byte seed \(\rho\) — the key stores the seed, not the matrix).
  2. Sample a small secret \(\mathbf{s}\in R_q^{k}\) and small error \(\mathbf{e}\in R_q^{k}\) from a centred binomial distribution.
  3. Compute \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}\).
  4. Public key: \((\rho, \mathbf{t})\). Secret key: \(\mathbf{s}\).

Recovering \(\mathbf{s}\) from \((\mathbf{A},\mathbf{t})\) is exactly Module-LWE.

Encapsulation (sender produces a shared secret + ciphertext).

  1. Sample small \(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{e}_1, e_2\).
  2. \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{e}_1\)
  3. \(v = \mathbf{t}^{T}\mathbf{r} + e_2 + \mathrm{Encode}(m)\), where \(m\) is a random 32-byte message
  4. Ciphertext: \((\mathbf{u}, v)\), compressed. Shared secret: \(K = \mathrm{KDF}(m, H(c))\).

Decapsulation.

  1. Compute \(v - \mathbf{s}^{T}\mathbf{u}\) and decode to recover \(m'\).
  2. Re-encrypt \(m'\) and check the ciphertext matches (the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform), giving CCA security; on mismatch, return a pseudorandom key rather than failing — this prevents chosen- ciphertext attacks.
  3. \(K = \mathrm{KDF}(m', H(c))\).

Why decryption works.

\[ v - \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{u} = \big(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e}\big)^T\mathbf{r} + e_2 + \mathrm{Encode}(m) - \mathbf{s}^T\big(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{e}_1\big) \] \[ = \mathrm{Encode}(m) + \underbrace{\mathbf{e}^T\mathbf{r} + e_2 - \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{e}_1}_{\text{small}} \]

The big terms \(\mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{r}\) cancel exactly. The residual is a sum of products of small values, which stays below \(q/4\); \(\mathrm{Encode}\) maps each message bit to \(0\) or \(\lceil q/2\rceil\), so rounding recovers \(m\) correctly with failure probability \(< 2^{-138}\).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: ML-KEM is faster than RSA-2048 and comparable to X25519 — key generation and encapsulation take tens of microseconds. The cost is size: a 1184-byte public key versus 32 bytes for X25519, which matters for constrained IoT devices and can push TLS handshakes past one MTU.

docs.title: ML-DSA (Dilithium) — the default
docs.text:
Based on Module-LWE and Module-SIS, using the Fiat–Shamir with aborts paradigm: generate a commitment from a masked secret, derive a challenge by hashing, respond, and reject-and-retry if the response would leak information about the secret. Rejection sampling makes the signature distribution independent of the key.

Variant NIST level Public key Signature ML-DSA-44 2 1312 B 2420 B ML-DSA-65 3 1952 B 3309 B ML-DSA-87 5 2592 B 4627 B

docs.title: SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) — the conservative choice
docs.text:
Security rests on hash functions alone — no number theory, no lattices. Built from:

  • WOTS+ one-time signatures (a Winternitz hash chain),
  • Merkle trees authenticating many one-time keys,
  • a hypertree of Merkle trees, plus FORS (a few-time signature) at the leaves,
  • a randomised index so the same leaf is rarely reused, making it stateless.
Property Value Public key 32–64 B (tiny) Signature 7 856 – 49 856 B (huge) Signing speed slow (milliseconds) Assumption only that SHA-2/SHAKE is secure

Use it for firmware signing and root certificates — anything long-lived where you cannot risk a lattice break and where signature size does not matter.

docs.title: FN-DSA (Falcon) — compact
docs.text:
NTRU lattices with Gaussian sampling over the ring.

Variant Public key Signature Falcon-512 897 B 666 B Falcon-1024 1793 B 1280 B

Smallest post-quantum signatures, ideal for certificate chains. The drawback is implementation difficulty: it needs constant-time floating-point Gaussian sampling, notoriously easy to get wrong and vulnerable to side-channel attacks.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Scheme PK Sig Sign speed Verify speed Assumption RSA-2048 256 B 256 B slow fast factoring (broken) Ed25519 32 B 64 B fast fast ECDLP (broken) ML-DSA-65 1952 B 3309 B fast fast Module-LWE/SIS Falcon-512 897 B 666 B medium fast NTRU SLH-DSA-128s 32 B 7856 B very slow medium hashes only

docs.title: 25.7 Migration Strategy
docs.text:
1. Inventory. Find every use of RSA/ECC — TLS, VPNs, code signing, PKI, SSH, database encryption, embedded firmware. This is usually the hardest and longest step.

2. Prioritise by data lifetime. "Harvest now, decrypt later" means confidentiality of long-lived data is the urgent case. Medical records, state secrets and genomic data need PQC today. Ephemeral session data is less urgent.

3. Deploy hybrid modes first. Combine classical and post-quantum:

\[ K = \mathrm{KDF}\big(K_{\text{X25519}} \,\|\, K_{\text{ML-KEM}}\big) \]

Secure if either component holds. Already deployed as X25519MLKEM768 in Chrome, Firefox, Cloudflare, AWS and Signal's PQXDH.

4. Build crypto-agility. Design systems so algorithms can be swapped without redesign — the lesson of the slow SHA-1 and TLS 1.0 migrations.

5. Watch the timeline. NIST's guidance: deprecate RSA/ECC by 2030, disallow by 2035.

docs.title: Problem 1 — A toy LWE instance
docs.text:
Let \(q = 17\), \(n = 3\), secret \(\vec s = (2, 5, 3)\). Given the samples below, verify each and explain why recovering \(\vec s\) is hard at scale.

\(i\) \(\vec a_i\) \(b_i\) \(e_i\) 1 \((1,3,2)\) \(\mathbf{7}\) \(+1\) 2 \((4,1,6)\) \(\mathbf{15}\) \(+1\) 3 \((2,2,1)\) \(\mathbf{0}\) \(0\)

Solution.

Sample 1. \(\langle\vec a_1,\vec s\rangle = 1(2) + 3(5) + 2(3) = 2+15+6 = 23 \equiv 6 \pmod{17}\). With \(e_1 = +1\): \(b_1 = 7\) ✓

Sample 2. \(4(2)+1(5)+6(3) = 8+5+18 = 31 \equiv 14 \pmod{17}\). With \(e_2 = +1\): \(b_2 = 15\) ✓

Sample 3. \(2(2)+2(5)+1(3) = 4+10+3 = 17 \equiv 0 \pmod{17}\). With \(e_3=0\): \(b_3 = 0\) ✓

Why it is hard. Without noise, three equations in three unknowns over \(\mathbb{Z}_{17}\) are solved by Gaussian elimination in a few operations. With noise, the system is inconsistent: no exact solution exists, and Gaussian elimination's row operations combine and amplify the errors, so the "solution" is garbage.

Brute force over all \(\vec s\) costs \(q^{n} = 17^{3} = 4913\) here — trivial. But Kyber uses \(q = 3329\) and \(n\cdot k = 256\times3 = 768\) dimensions:

\[ 3329^{768} \approx 10^{2712} \]

Lattice reduction (BKZ) does far better than brute force, but still requires \(2^{\Theta(n)}\) time, and the parameters are set so this exceeds \(2^{128}\) even for the best known classical and quantum lattice sieves.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Kyber decryption correctness
docs.text:
Show that Kyber decryption recovers the message, and estimate the error budget.

Solution.

The computation.

\[ v - \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{u} = \big(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{r} + e_2 + \mathrm{Encode}(m)\big) - \mathbf{s}^T\big(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{e}_1\big) \]

Substitute \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e}\), so \(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{e}^T\mathbf{r}\):

\[ = \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{e}^T\mathbf{r} + e_2 + \mathrm{Encode}(m) - \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{e}_1 \] \[ \boxed{\ = \mathrm{Encode}(m) + \underbrace{\big(\mathbf{e}^T\mathbf{r} + e_2 - \mathbf{s}^T\mathbf{e}_1\big)}_{\text{total noise } \delta}\ } \]

Error budget. \(\mathrm{Encode}\) maps bit 0 to \(0\) and bit 1 to \(\lceil q/2\rceil = 1665\). Decoding rounds to whichever is nearer, so it succeeds iff

\[ |\delta| < \frac{q}{4} = \frac{3329}{4} = 832 . \]

Magnitude of \(\delta\). Each of \(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{e},\mathbf{r},\mathbf{e}_1\) has coefficients from a centred binomial \(\mathrm{CBD}(\eta)\) with \(\eta = 2\), so entries lie in \([-2,2]\) with standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{\eta/2} = 1\). The dominant terms are inner products of \(256k\) such values, so by the central limit theorem \(\delta\) is approximately Gaussian with

\[ \sigma_\delta \approx \sqrt{2\cdot 256k}\ \cdot O(1) \approx 40 \ \text{for } k=3 . \]

Then

\[ \Pr[|\delta| \ge 832] \approx 2\,\Phi(-832/40) = 2\Phi(-20.8) \]

— astronomically small. The published figure for ML-KEM-768, accounting exactly for compression noise, is

\[ \Pr[\text{decryption failure}] < 2^{-164} . \]

Why the failure rate must be tiny. Decryption failures leak information about the secret key (the failing ciphertexts correlate with \(\mathbf{s}\)). An adversary who can collect failures mounts a key-recovery attack. So the bound must be far below any practical query budget.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Bandwidth cost of migration
docs.text:
A TLS 1.3 handshake currently uses X25519 (32 B key share each way) and Ed25519 certificates (32 B key + 64 B signature). Compute the handshake size increase when moving to X25519+ML-KEM-768 hybrid with ML-DSA-65 certificates. Assume a chain of 3 certificates.

Solution.

Current (classical).

Item Size Client key share (X25519) 32 B Server key share (X25519) 32 B 3 × cert public key (Ed25519) 96 B 3 × cert signature (Ed25519) 192 B Handshake signature 64 B Total crypto material 416 B

Post-quantum hybrid.

Item Size Client key share (X25519 + ML-KEM-768 PK) \(32 + 1184 = 1216\) B Server key share (X25519 + ML-KEM ciphertext) \(32 + 1088 = 1120\) B 3 × cert public key (ML-DSA-65) \(3\times1952 = 5856\) B 3 × cert signature (ML-DSA-65) \(3\times3309 = 9927\) B Handshake signature 3309 B Total 21 428 B \[ \text{Increase factor} = \frac{21428}{416} \approx \mathbf{51\times} \]

Practical consequences.

  1. TCP slow start. The initial congestion window is typically 10 packets ≈ 14 KB. A 21 KB handshake needs an extra round trip — measurably slower page loads.
  2. QUIC amplification limit. A server may send at most 3× the bytes received before address validation, which post-quantum certificate chains can exceed.
  3. Mitigations in progress: using Falcon for certificates (666 B signatures) cuts the total to about 6 KB; certificate compression (RFC 8879); abridged certificate chains that omit intermediates the client already has; KEMTLS, which replaces handshake signatures with KEM operations entirely.

This is why key-exchange migration (ML-KEM) is proceeding faster than certificate migration (ML-DSA): the key-exchange overhead is tolerable today, the certificate overhead is not.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Choosing algorithms for three scenarios
docs.text:
Recommend a post-quantum algorithm for each, with justification.

(a) Firmware signing for a 20-year industrial controller. (b) TLS key exchange for a high-traffic CDN. (c) Signatures in a blockchain where every signature is stored forever. (d) A constrained IoT sensor with 32 KB RAM.

Solution.

(a) Firmware, 20-year lifetime → SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) or LMS/XMSS. Reasoning: the device must remain verifiable for 20 years, during which a lattice cryptanalysis breakthrough is a real risk. SLH-DSA's security rests on hash functions only — the most conservative assumption available, and the one property Grover merely halves. Firmware is signed rarely (slow signing is fine) and the 8–50 KB signature is negligible next to a firmware image. If state can be managed reliably, stateful LMS gives smaller signatures.

(b) CDN TLS key exchange → X25519MLKEM768 hybrid. Reasoning: exactly what Cloudflare and Google deployed. ML-KEM-768 gives NIST level 3; the hybrid retains X25519 so a flaw in either scheme is not fatal. Performance is excellent (faster than RSA-2048); the 1.2 KB overhead per handshake is acceptable. Do not use pure ML-KEM yet — hybrid is current best practice.

(c) Blockchain, signatures stored forever → Falcon (FN-DSA-512). Reasoning: on-chain storage is the scarcest resource and is paid for by every node forever. Falcon's 666-byte signature is by far the smallest post-quantum option — 5× smaller than ML-DSA-44 and 12× smaller than SLH-DSA. The implementation risk (constant-time Gaussian sampling) is manageable because blockchain clients use a small number of audited libraries. Verification is fast, which matters when every node verifies every signature.

(d) Constrained IoT, 32 KB RAM → ML-KEM-512 + ML-DSA-44, or pre-shared symmetric keys. Reasoning: ML-KEM-512 needs about 3 KB of working memory and is implementable on Cortex-M4. SLH-DSA is ruled out by signature size and signing time; Falcon is ruled out by the floating-point requirement. Best of all, if the deployment allows it: avoid public-key cryptography entirely and use pre-shared AES-256 keys, which are quantum-safe with no bandwidth cost.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Quantifying the harvest-now-decrypt-later risk
docs.text:
Data must remain confidential for \(Y\) years. Migration to PQC takes \(M\) years. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives in \(Q\) years. State Mosca's inequality and apply it to (a) medical records (\(Y = 50\), \(M = 5\), \(Q = 15\)) and (b) a news website's session cookies (\(Y = 0.01\), \(M = 1\), \(Q = 15\)).

Solution.

Mosca's theorem. You have a problem if

\[ \boxed{\ Y + M \ >\ Q\ } \]

— i.e. if data encrypted today is still sensitive when the quantum computer arrives, given that migration itself takes time.

(a) Medical records.

\[ Y + M = 50 + 5 = 55 \quad > \quad Q = 15 \] \[ \text{Deficit} = 55 - 15 = \mathbf{40\ \text{years}} \]

Severe problem. Records encrypted today with RSA/ECC and captured by an adversary will be readable roughly 15 years from now, while still being sensitive for another 35 years. Action: migrate immediately, and re-encrypt archived data with PQC or with symmetric-only schemes.

(b) Session cookies.

\[ Y + M = 0.01 + 1 = 1.01 \quad < \quad Q = 15 \]

No problem for confidentiality. By the time a quantum computer exists, every cookie encrypted today is long expired.

But note the different risk for authentication. Signatures and certificates must be quantum-safe at the moment of use, not retroactively — an adversary cannot forge a past signature after the fact, but from year 15 onward they can forge new ones. So the deadline for signature migration is \(Q\) itself, not \(Q - Y\). Both deadlines matter; they are simply different.

General decision rule.

Data type \(Y\) Urgency State secrets, genomic data 50–100 critical — migrate now Medical, legal, financial records 10–50 high Corporate IP 5–20 high Personal email 5–10 medium Session tokens, ephemeral traffic < 1 low (but signatures still need migrating by \(Q\))

docs.title: 25.9 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Verify an LWE sample: \(q=13\), \(\vec s = (3,1)\), \(\vec a = (2,4)\), \(e = -1\). Find \(b\). [Ans: \(b = 9\)]
  2. Compare ML-KEM-768 and RSA-3072 public-key sizes. [Ans: 1184 B vs 384 B — about 3× larger]
  3. Why can Shor's algorithm not be applied to lattice problems?
  4. Which NIST security level does ML-DSA-65 target? [Ans: level 3]
  5. Compute the handshake overhead using Falcon-512 instead of ML-DSA-65 in Problem 3.
  6. Apply Mosca's inequality with \(Y=10\), \(M=3\), \(Q=20\). [Ans: \(13 < 20\) — no immediate problem, but little margin]
  7. Why does Kyber use Module-LWE rather than plain Ring-LWE?

docs.title: 25.10 Summary
docs.text:
• Shor breaks all deployed public-key cryptography (RSA, DH, ECDSA); Grover only halves symmetric and hash security, fixed by doubling parameters.
  • NIST standards (Aug 2024): ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (204), SLH-DSA (205); FN-DSA and HQC follow.
  • Lattice problems (SVP, CVP, LWE, Module-LWE) resist quantum attack because they reduce to the non-abelian dihedral HSP, and they enjoy worst-case-to-average-case reductions.
  • ML-KEM (Kyber): \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e}\) hides \(\mathbf{s}\); decryption works because the large terms cancel and the residual noise stays below \(q/4\); failure probability \(<2^{-164}\), which matters because failures leak key information.
  • Signatures: ML-DSA (default), FN-DSA/Falcon (smallest), SLH-DSA/SPHINCS+ (most conservative, hash-only).
  • Migration: inventory → prioritise by data lifetime → hybrid modes (X25519MLKEM768) → crypto-agility. NIST: deprecate RSA/ECC by 2030, disallow by 2035.
  • Mosca's inequality \(Y + M > Q\) tells you whether to act now.

Unit II is now complete. You can construct oracles, derive Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani and Simon, build the QFT and phase estimation, assemble Shor's algorithm end to end, analyse Grover geometrically, and explain both the quantum threat to cryptography and the standardised response.

Next lesson: L26 — Introduction to quantum machine learning and data encoding (Unit III begins).

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → PQC Explorer: build a toy LWE instance, watch encryption and decryption succeed while the noise stays inside the decoding radius, and use the Mosca calculator on your own data-lifetime assumptions.

docs.title: Lesson 35: Quantum Annealing and the Adiabatic Model
35.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the adiabatic theorem and the runtime condition involving the spectral gap.
  2. Describe adiabatic quantum computation (AQC) and its equivalence to the circuit model.
  3. Distinguish AQC from quantum annealing as implemented by D-Wave.
  4. Analyse quantum tunnelling versus classical thermal hopping.
  5. Assess the experimental evidence for and against a quantum-annealing speed-up.

docs.title: 35.2 The Adiabatic Theorem
docs.text:
Statement. If a system starts in the ground state of \(H(0)\) and the Hamiltonian is varied slowly enough, the system remains in the instantaneous ground state of \(H(t)\) throughout.

The quantitative condition. Let \(s = t/T \in[0,1]\) and let

\[ \Delta(s) = E_1(s) - E_0(s) \]

be the spectral gap between the ground and first excited states. The evolution stays adiabatic provided

\[ \boxed{\ T \ \gg\ \frac{\displaystyle\max_{s}\left|\left\langle E_1(s)\left|\frac{dH}{ds}\right|E_0(s)\right\rangle\right|} {\displaystyle\min_{s}\Delta(s)^{2}}\ } \]

Read the exponent carefully. Runtime scales as \(1/\Delta_{\min}^{2}\). Halving the minimum gap quadruples the required time.

The Landau–Zener formula makes this precise for a two-level crossing: the probability of an unwanted transition out of the ground state is

\[ P_{\text{excite}} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{2\pi\Delta_{\min}^{2}}{4\hbar\,|d(E_1-E_0)/dt|}\right) . \]

docs.title: The construction
docs.text:
\[ H(s) = (1-s)\,H_B \;+\; s\,H_C, \qquad s: 0 \to 1 \] Component Role \(H_B = -\sum_i X_i\) initial Hamiltonian; ground state is \(\lvert +\rangle^{\otimes n}\) — easy to prepare \(H_C\) problem Hamiltonian; its ground state is the answer

Procedure. Prepare \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\), ramp \(s\) from 0 to 1 over time \(T\), then measure in the computational basis.

docs.title: Equivalence to the circuit model
docs.text:
Theorem (Aharonov, van Dam, Kempe, Landau, Lloyd, Regev, 2004). AQC and the circuit model are polynomially equivalent. Anything computable in the circuit model is computable adiabatically with only polynomial overhead, and vice versa.

So AQC is universal — it is not a weaker model. But this equivalence requires arbitrary \(k\)-local Hamiltonians, whereas real annealers implement only the restricted 2-local stoquastic Ising form.

docs.title: The gap problem
docs.text:
The runtime is governed entirely by \(\Delta_{\min}\), and this is where hardness reappears:

\(\Delta_{\min}\) scaling Runtime Verdict \(\Omega(1/\mathrm{poly}(n))\) polynomial efficient \(\Theta(2^{-cn})\) exponential no advantage

For NP-hard problems the gap is generically exponentially small, so AQC gives no free lunch — exactly as expected, since AQC is equivalent to the circuit model and BQP is not known to contain NP.

The gap is also hard to predict. Computing \(\Delta_{\min}\) for a given instance is itself an exponentially hard eigenvalue problem, so you cannot know in advance how slowly to anneal.

docs.title: What D-Wave actually implements
docs.text:
\[ H(s) = -\frac{A(s)}{2}\sum_i \sigma^x_i \;+\; \frac{B(s)}{2}\left(\sum_ih_i\sigma^z_i + \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma^z_i\sigma^z_j\right) \]

with \(A(0)\gg B(0)\) and \(A(1)\ll B(1)\): the transverse field is ramped down while the problem Hamiltonian is ramped up.

docs.title: Five ways it differs from ideal AQC
docs.text:
Ideal AQC D-Wave quantum annealing Closed system, zero temperature Open system at ~15 mK, coupled to a thermal bath Arbitrary \(k\)-local \(H\) 2-local Ising only, stoquastic (no sign problem) Full connectivity sparse Pegasus/Zephyr graph — needs minor embedding Coherent throughout coherence \(\sim\) ns; the anneal lasts \(\mu\)s ⟹ mostly incoherent Provably universal not universal — stoquastic 2-local is not known to be universal

Stoquasticity matters. A Hamiltonian is stoquastic if all off-diagonal elements are non-positive in the computational basis. Such Hamiltonians have no sign problem, and Quantum Monte Carlo can simulate them efficiently in many regimes — which is a direct obstacle to claiming exponential advantage.

docs.title: Hardware scale
docs.text:
Generation Qubits Topology Degree D-Wave 2000Q (2017) 2048 Chimera 6 Advantage (2020) 5640 Pegasus 15 Advantage2 (2024) 4400+ Zephyr 20

Minor embedding maps a dense logical problem onto this sparse graph by representing one logical qubit as a chain of ferromagnetically coupled physical qubits. Embedding a complete graph \(K_n\) into Pegasus needs \(O(n^2)\) physical qubits, so 5640 physical qubits support only about \(\mathbf{180}\) fully connected logical variables. Chain breaks (when a chain's qubits disagree) are a major error source.

docs.title: 35.5 Tunnelling versus Thermal Hopping
docs.text:
This is the physical intuition for why quantum annealing might help.

Classical simulated annealing must climb over an energy barrier. The escape rate follows the Arrhenius law:

\[ P_{\text{thermal}} \sim \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{\text{barrier}}}{k_BT}\right) \]

— it depends on the barrier height only.

Quantum annealing can tunnel through the barrier. The WKB tunnelling amplitude is

\[ P_{\text{tunnel}} \sim \exp\!\left(-\frac{w\sqrt{E_{\text{barrier}}}}{\Gamma}\right) \]

— it depends on both the height and the width \(w\).

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Quantum annealing should win for barriers that are \emph{tall but thin}.}\ } \]

Where it should lose: wide, shallow barriers, and rugged "golf-course" landscapes with no structure at all.

Experimental confirmation. Boixo et al. (2016) constructed a synthetic problem with deliberately tall, thin barriers and measured a \(10^{8}\times\) speed-up of D-Wave over simulated annealing on a single core. But Denchev et al. and subsequent work showed that Quantum Monte Carlo — a classical algorithm that also tunnels — matched the annealer's scaling. The advantage was over simulated annealing specifically, not over the best classical method.

docs.title: Claims and rebuttals
docs.text:
Claim Rebuttal \(10^{8}\times\) over simulated annealing (Google, 2016) matched by Quantum Monte Carlo, a classical algorithm Speed-up on 3-D spin glasses matched by specialised classical solvers (Selby's algorithm) Practical advantage on real applications no peer-reviewed demonstration on an industrial problem to date Quantum effects are present in the device ✓ this is well established — entanglement and tunnelling have been directly measured

The consensus position (2024): D-Wave devices are genuinely quantum — entanglement during the anneal has been experimentally verified — but no scaling advantage over the best classical algorithms has been demonstrated on any problem of practical interest. The 2023–24 results on quantum simulation of spin dynamics (as opposed to optimisation) are more promising and are where the strongest current claims lie.

docs.title: Where annealing is nonetheless useful
docs.text:
• Sampling rather than optimisation (Boltzmann sampling for QBMs, L33).
  • Quantum simulation of the transverse-field Ising model itself — a physics goal, not an optimisation one.
  • Hybrid solvers (D-Wave's own LeapHybrid) that use the QPU as one heuristic among several inside a classical framework; these are competitive, but the classical parts do most of the work.

docs.title: QAOA versus quantum annealing
docs.text:
QAOA (gate model) Quantum annealing Hardware universal gate device special-purpose annealer Qubits available ~100–1000 ~5000 Connectivity limited, but SWAPs allow any graph sparse, needs embedding Error correction possible in principle none Parameters \(2p\), classically optimised annealing schedule only Theoretical guarantee exact as \(p\to\infty\) exact as \(T\to\infty\) Universality universal not universal (stoquastic 2-local)

They are the same idea — QAOA is Trotterised annealing (L34 §3.1) — implemented on different hardware. Annealers have more qubits; gate devices have more control and a path to error correction.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Annealing time from the spectral gap
docs.text:
A problem has \(\Delta_{\min} = 0.01\) energy units and \(\max\|dH/ds\| = 10\). Estimate the required annealing time. Repeat for \(\Delta_{\min} = 0.001\).

Solution.

\[ T \gg \frac{\max\|dH/ds\|}{\Delta_{\min}^{2}} \]

Case 1: \(\Delta_{\min} = 0.01\).

\[ T \gg \frac{10}{(0.01)^{2}} = \frac{10}{10^{-4}} = \mathbf{10^{5}}\ \text{time units} \]

Case 2: \(\Delta_{\min} = 0.001\).

\[ T \gg \frac{10}{10^{-6}} = \mathbf{10^{7}}\ \text{time units} \]

A 10× smaller gap requires a 100× longer anneal — the quadratic dependence in action.

Why this is the central difficulty. For NP-hard problems the gap typically closes as \(\Delta_{\min}\sim 2^{-cn}\), so

\[ T \sim 2^{2cn} \]

— exponential, and worse than the classical brute-force \(2^{n}\) unless \(c < \frac12\). Quantum annealing does not evade NP-hardness.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Tunnelling versus thermal escape, quantified
docs.text:
A barrier has height \(E_b = 10\) (in units of \(k_BT\)) and width \(w\). Compare thermal and tunnelling escape rates for \(w = 1\) and \(w = 10\), with transverse field \(\Gamma = 2\).

Solution.

Thermal rate (independent of width):

\[ P_{\text{thermal}} \sim e^{-E_b/k_BT} = e^{-10} = \mathbf{4.54\times10^{-5}} \]

Tunnelling rate.

\[ P_{\text{tunnel}} \sim \exp\!\left(-\frac{w\sqrt{E_b}}{\Gamma}\right) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{w\sqrt{10}}{2}\right) = \exp(-1.5811\,w) \]

For \(w = 1\) (thin barrier):

\[ P_{\text{tunnel}} = e^{-1.5811} = \mathbf{0.2058} \] \[ \frac{P_{\text{tunnel}}}{P_{\text{thermal}}} = \frac{0.2058}{4.54\times10^{-5}} = \mathbf{4534\times} \]

Quantum annealing is ~4500× faster. ✓

For \(w = 10\) (wide barrier):

\[ P_{\text{tunnel}} = e^{-15.811} = \mathbf{1.36\times10^{-7}} \] \[ \frac{P_{\text{tunnel}}}{P_{\text{thermal}}} = \frac{1.36\times10^{-7}}{4.54\times10^{-5}} = \mathbf{0.0030} \]

Quantum annealing is ~330× slower. ✗

Summary table.

Barrier \(P_{\text{thermal}}\) \(P_{\text{tunnel}}\) Winner Tall, thin (\(w=1\)) \(4.5\times10^{-5}\) \(0.21\) quantum, 4500× Tall, wide (\(w=10\)) \(4.5\times10^{-5}\) \(1.4\times10^{-7}\) classical, 330× \[ \boxed{\ \text{Quantum annealing helps only on landscapes with tall, thin barriers.}\ } \]

Whether real-world optimisation landscapes have this character is an empirical question with no general answer — which is precisely why the advantage claims have been so contested.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Minor embedding cost
docs.text:
A dense QUBO with 100 fully connected variables is to be run on a Pegasus-topology annealer with 5640 qubits and degree 15. Estimate the physical qubits needed. Will it fit?

Solution.

Embedding a complete graph \(K_n\) into Chimera requires \(\approx n^2/4\) physical qubits; Pegasus improves this to roughly

\[ \text{physical qubits} \approx \frac{n^{2}}{7} \ \text{(empirical for Pegasus)} \]

For \(n = 100\):

\[ \frac{100^{2}}{7} = \frac{10{,}000}{7} \approx \mathbf{1430\ \text{physical qubits}} \]

Fits comfortably within 5640 ✓.

Chain length.

\[ \bar\ell = \frac{1430}{100} \approx \mathbf{14\ \text{physical qubits per logical variable}} \]

Consequences of long chains.

  1. Chain breaks. Each chain must remain ferromagnetically aligned. If the chain coupling \(J_{\text{chain}}\) is too weak the chain breaks; if too strong it dominates the problem energy scale and washes out the actual \(h_i, J_{ij}\) values. With \(\ell = 14\), chain-break rates of 10–30 % are typical.
  2. Reduced precision. The device has finite analogue precision (~4–5 bits) on \(h\) and \(J\). Strong chain couplings consume much of that dynamic range, leaving the problem couplings poorly resolved.
  3. Effective problem-size limit.
\[ n_{\max} \approx \sqrt{7\times5640} \approx \mathbf{199\ \text{fully connected variables}} \]

The practical conclusion. A 5640-qubit annealer solves dense problems of only ~180–200 variables — a size that classical solvers handle exactly in seconds (Gurobi routinely solves dense QUBOs of several hundred variables). Sparse problems that map natively fare much better, which is why published annealing successes are almost always on problems whose graph matches the hardware.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Reading an annealing experiment critically
docs.text:
A paper reports that a D-Wave annealer solved a 500-variable problem in 20 µs while "a classical computer took 30 minutes". List five questions you must ask before accepting a claim of quantum advantage.

Solution.

1. What was the classical baseline? If it was simulated annealing with default parameters, the comparison is weak. The correct baselines are the best available classical algorithms: Gurobi/CPLEX, Selby's algorithm for Chimera-structured problems, parallel tempering, or Quantum Monte Carlo. Many claimed advantages evaporate against these.

2. Was the total time measured, or only the anneal time? 20 µs is the anneal time. Real wall-clock time includes programming the QPU (~10 ms), readout (~100 µs per sample), thermalisation between samples, and the classical minor-embedding computation (which can take minutes and is often excluded). Honest end-to-end timing typically adds three to four orders of magnitude.

3. How many samples were needed, and was the optimum verified? An annealer returns a distribution. If 10 000 anneals were needed to see the optimum once, the true cost is \(10^{4}\times20\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 0.2\) s, not 20 µs. And was the returned solution verified optimal, or just the best seen?

4. Was the problem native to the hardware graph? If the problem was generated to match Chimera/Pegasus connectivity, it is not representative — and such instances are precisely the ones specialised classical solvers (Selby) handle easily. Genuine applications rarely have hardware-matched topology.

5. What is the scaling, not the single data point? A single problem size proves nothing. The question is how time-to-solution grows with \(n\) for quantum versus classical. Advantage means a better exponent or a better polynomial degree, not a better constant on one instance. Nearly every retracted advantage claim failed on this point.

A sixth question worth adding: was the comparison run on comparable hardware budgets? A $15M annealer versus one laptop core is not a fair fight; the honest comparison is against a classical cluster of equivalent cost.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Designing an annealing application end to end
docs.text:
Design a quantum-annealing solution for portfolio optimisation: select \(k\) assets from \(N\) to maximise expected return subject to a risk constraint. Specify the QUBO, embedding and honest expectations.

Solution.

Classical formulation (Markowitz).

\[ \max_{\vec x\in\{0,1\}^{N}} \ \ \vec\mu^{T}\vec x \;-\; q\,\vec x^{T}\Sigma\vec x \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \sum_i x_i = k \]

where \(\vec\mu\) is expected returns, \(\Sigma\) the covariance matrix, and \(q\) the risk-aversion parameter.

QUBO formulation. Move the constraint into a penalty:

\[ \min_{\vec x}\ \ -\vec\mu^{T}\vec x + q\,\vec x^{T}\Sigma\vec x + \lambda\Big(\sum_ix_i - k\Big)^{2} \] \[ Q_{ii} = -\mu_i + q\Sigma_{ii} + \lambda(1 - 2k), \qquad Q_{ij} = 2q\Sigma_{ij} + 2\lambda \ (i<j) \]

(using \(x_i^2 = x_i\) to fold the diagonal of the penalty into the linear term).

Choosing \(\lambda\). It must exceed the maximum objective swing from adding or removing one asset: \(\lambda > \max_i|\mu_i| + 2q\max_i\sum_j|\Sigma_{ij}|\).

Embedding. \(\Sigma\) is dense — every pair of assets is correlated — so this is a complete graph \(K_N\). From Problem 3, \(N \approx 180\) is the ceiling.

Honest expectations.

Aspect Reality Problem size ≤ 180 assets on current hardware Classical baseline Gurobi solves 180-asset QUBOs to proven optimality in seconds Quantum result a heuristic solution, no optimality certificate Wall-clock seconds including embedding and sampling — comparable, not faster Solution quality typically within 1–5 % of optimal, sometimes exactly optimal Verdict no advantage today

Where annealing could add value nonetheless.

  1. Solution diversity. Annealers naturally return many near-optimal portfolios, which is genuinely useful for scenario analysis — an exact solver returns one.
  2. Real-time re-optimisation. Once embedded, re-running with updated \(\vec\mu\) is fast, since the expensive embedding is reusable.
  3. As one heuristic among several inside a hybrid solver, contributing diversity to a portfolio of methods.

The recommendation to give a client. Use classical solvers for production. Use the annealer for research, benchmarking and building institutional readiness — so that if hardware improves by the one to two orders of magnitude needed, the pipeline already exists. Do not claim, or accept a claim of, current advantage.

docs.title: 35.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Compute \(T\) for \(\Delta_{\min}=0.05\) and \(\max\|dH/ds\| = 4\). [Ans: \(T\gg1600\)]
  2. Compare tunnelling and thermal rates for \(E_b = 20\), \(w = 2\), \(\Gamma = 3\). [Ans: tunnel \(e^{-2.98}=0.051\) vs thermal \(e^{-20}=2\times10^{-9}\) — quantum wins]
  3. How many logical variables fit fully connected in 2048 Chimera qubits? [Ans: \(\approx\sqrt{4\times2048}\approx 90\)]
  4. Why does a stoquastic Hamiltonian limit the claim of exponential advantage?
  5. State the adiabatic theorem and explain the \(1/\Delta^2\) scaling.
  6. Give three differences between ideal AQC and D-Wave annealing.
  7. Explain why QAOA and quantum annealing are the same algorithm on different hardware.

docs.title: 35.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Adiabatic theorem: stay in the ground state if \(T \gg \max\|dH/ds\|/\Delta_{\min}^{2}\) — runtime scales as the inverse square of the spectral gap.
  • AQC with \(H(s) = (1-s)H_B + sH_C\) is polynomially equivalent to the circuit model, so it is universal — but for NP-hard problems the gap is generically exponentially small.
  • D-Wave quantum annealing differs from ideal AQC in five ways: open system, 2-local stoquastic only, sparse connectivity needing minor embedding, largely incoherent, and not known to be universal.
  • Tunnelling beats thermal hopping for tall, thin barriers (\(e^{-w\sqrt{E_b}/\Gamma}\) versus \(e^{-E_b/k_BT}\)) and loses for wide ones — whether real landscapes are favourable is an open empirical question.
  • Evidence: quantum effects in the hardware are confirmed; no scaling advantage over the best classical algorithms has been demonstrated on a problem of practical interest. Claimed speed-ups have repeatedly been matched by Quantum Monte Carlo or specialised solvers.
  • Minor embedding limits dense problems to ~180 fully connected variables on a 5640-qubit machine — a size classical solvers handle exactly in seconds.
  • QAOA is Trotterised annealing. Annealers offer more qubits; gate devices offer control, universality and a path to error correction.

Unit III is now complete. You can encode classical data, build quantum kernels and variational classifiers, compute gradients by parameter shift, recognise and mitigate barren plateaus, and formulate and solve combinatorial problems by QAOA and annealing — with a calibrated sense of what is demonstrated and what is aspiration.

Next lesson: L36 — The quantum software landscape (Unit IV begins).

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → Annealing Lab: draw an energy landscape, set the temperature and transverse field, and race a simulated-annealing walker against a tunnelling one.

docs.title: 33.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Recall the classical Boltzmann machine / RBM, its energy function and its training rule.
  2. Explain why classical training is hard (the intractable partition function) and how contrastive divergence works around it.
  3. Define the quantum Boltzmann machine with a transverse-field Hamiltonian.
  4. Derive the QBM gradient and explain the non-commutativity obstacle.
  5. Describe how quantum annealers are used to sample Boltzmann distributions, and assess the results honestly.

docs.title: Energy-based models
docs.text:
A Boltzmann machine is a generative model: a stochastic network of binary units \(\vec v\) (visible) and \(\vec h\) (hidden) with energy

\[ E(\vec v,\vec h) = -\sum_i a_iv_i - \sum_j b_jh_j - \sum_{i,j} w_{ij}v_ih_j \]

and probability given by the Boltzmann (Gibbs) distribution

\[ P(\vec v,\vec h) = \frac{e^{-E(\vec v,\vec h)}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_{\vec v,\vec h} e^{-E(\vec v,\vec h)} . \]

\(Z\) is the partition function. Low-energy configurations are more probable, so training amounts to shaping the energy landscape so that the data sits in the valleys.

docs.title: Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM)
docs.text:
Removing visible–visible and hidden–hidden connections leaves a bipartite graph, which makes the conditionals factorise:

\[ P(h_j = 1\mid\vec v) = \sigma\!\left(b_j + \sum_i w_{ij}v_i\right), \qquad P(v_i = 1\mid\vec h) = \sigma\!\left(a_i + \sum_j w_{ij}h_j\right) \]

with \(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\). This enables block Gibbs sampling: update all hidden units in parallel, then all visible units.

docs.title: The training rule
docs.text:
Maximise the log-likelihood \(\mathcal{L} = \sum_{\text{data}}\log P(\vec v)\). The gradient is

\[ \boxed{\ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial w_{ij}} = \underbrace{\big\langle v_ih_j\big\rangle_{\text{data}}}_{\text{positive phase}} - \underbrace{\big\langle v_ih_j\big\rangle_{\text{model}}}_{\text{negative phase}}\ } \]

The positive phase is easy — clamp \(\vec v\) to a data point and sample \(\vec h\).

The negative phase is hard — it requires sampling from the model's own equilibrium distribution, which needs \(Z\), a sum over \(2^{n}\) configurations.

docs.title: Contrastive divergence (Hinton, 2002)
docs.text:
Instead of running the Gibbs chain to equilibrium, run it for \(k\) steps (usually \(k=1\)) starting from the data:

v0 = data point
h0 ~ P(h | v0)
v1 ~ P(v | h0)
h1 ~ P(h | v1)
grad w_ij  ~=  v0_i h0_j  -  v1_i h1_j

CD-1 is a biased approximation of the true gradient — it does not follow the gradient of any objective function exactly — yet it works remarkably well in practice, and it is what made deep belief networks feasible in 2006.

This is exactly the gap a quantum computer might fill. If a quantum device could sample the true Boltzmann distribution efficiently, the negative phase would be exact, removing CD's bias.

docs.title: The Hamiltonian
docs.text:
Replace the classical energy function with a quantum Hamiltonian. Amin et al. (PRX, 2018):

\[ \boxed{\ H = -\sum_i \Gamma_i\,\sigma^{x}_{i} \;-\; \sum_i b_i\,\sigma^{z}_{i} \;-\; \sum_{i<j} w_{ij}\,\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\ } \] Term Role \(\sigma^z_i\), \(\sigma^z_i\sigma^z_j\) classical Ising energy — recovers the classical BM exactly \(\sigma^x_i\) (transverse field) purely quantum — does not commute with \(\sigma^z\)

docs.title: The quantum Gibbs state
docs.text:
\[ \rho = \frac{e^{-H}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \mathrm{Tr}\big(e^{-H}\big) \]

(Setting \(\beta = 1\) by absorbing temperature into \(H\).) Measuring the visible qubits in the \(Z\) basis gives

\[ P(\vec v) = \mathrm{Tr}\big(\Lambda_{\vec v}\,\rho\big), \qquad \Lambda_{\vec v} = |\vec v\rangle\langle\vec v|\otimes I_{\text{hidden}} . \]

docs.title: Why the transverse field matters
docs.text:
If \(\Gamma_i = 0\), \(H\) is diagonal in the computational basis, \(\rho\) is a classical Gibbs distribution, and the QBM is a classical BM. Nothing is gained.

If \(\Gamma_i \ne 0\), then \([\sigma^x, \sigma^z] \ne 0\): the eigenstates of \(H\) are superpositions of computational basis states, and \(\rho\) has off-diagonal coherences. The model can then represent distributions no classical BM with the same connectivity can — this is the claimed expressivity advantage.

docs.title: The non-commutativity obstacle
docs.text:
The classical derivation used

\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\mathrm{Tr}\,e^{-H} = -\left\langle \frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta}\right\rangle . \]

This step requires \(\left[H, \frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta}\right] = 0\). For the \(b_i\) and \(w_{ij}\) parameters (which multiply \(\sigma^z\) terms) this fails once \(\Gamma\ne0\), and for \(\Gamma_i\) itself it fails too. The correct expression involves the Kubo–Mori integral

\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\,\mathrm{Tr}\big(e^{-H}\big) = -\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{Tr}\left(e^{-sH}\,\frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta}\,e^{-(1-s)H}\right)ds \]

which is not a simple expectation value and cannot be estimated by ordinary sampling.

Amin et al.'s workaround. Instead of maximising the log-likelihood, maximise a variational lower bound obtained from the Golden–Thompson inequality \(\mathrm{Tr}\,e^{A+B} \le \mathrm{Tr}\big(e^{A}e^{B}\big)\). The bound is differentiable by sampling, giving a trainable — if slightly weaker — objective.

docs.title: The bound-based training rule
docs.text:
For visible-only (or bound-restricted) parameters, the gradient recovers the familiar form:

\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{bound}}}{\partial w_{ij}} = \big\langle \sigma^z_i\sigma^z_j\big\rangle_{\text{data-clamped}} - \big\langle \sigma^z_i\sigma^z_j\big\rangle_{\text{model}} \]

— structurally identical to the classical rule, but with expectations taken in the quantum Gibbs state.

docs.title: 33.4 Sampling: Where the Quantum Computer Enters
docs.text:
Three routes to sampling from \(\rho = e^{-H}/Z\):

Method Idea Status Quantum annealing (D-Wave) anneal slowly; the device equilibrates with its cryogenic environment and returns approximately Boltzmann samples used in practice; effective temperature is uncontrolled Gibbs state preparation algorithms based on quantum phase estimation or quantum Metropolis fault-tolerant era only Variational (VarQITE) imaginary-time evolution with a parameterised circuit NISQ-compatible, approximate

docs.title: The D-Wave route in practice
docs.text:
D-Wave hardware natively implements

\[ H(s) = A(s)\left(-\sum_i\sigma^x_i\right) + B(s)\left(\sum_i h_i\sigma^z_i + \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma^z_i\sigma^z_j\right) \]

which is exactly the QBM Hamiltonian form. Stopping the anneal early (a "reverse anneal" or a paused anneal) leaves a residual transverse field \(\Gamma \propto A(s)\), sampling from a quantum Boltzmann distribution.

Three practical problems.

  1. Unknown effective temperature. The device does not thermalise at the nominal fridge temperature; \(\beta_{\text{eff}}\) must be estimated per problem and drifts.
  2. Limited connectivity. The Chimera/Pegasus/Zephyr graphs are sparse. Dense \(w_{ij}\) requires minor embedding, in which one logical qubit becomes a chain of physical qubits — inflating qubit count and introducing chain-break errors.
  3. Not truly thermal. Real annealers exhibit freeze-out: the distribution stops evolving partway through the anneal, so the samples come from an intermediate, non-equilibrium distribution.

docs.title: Reported results, honestly
docs.text:
• Amin et al. (2018) trained small QBMs (fewer than 10 visible units) and found that a non-zero transverse field gave better log-likelihood than the classical equivalent on synthetic data.
  • Benedetti et al. (2017) trained an RBM on Bars-and-Stripes using a D-Wave sampler and matched classical CD, having first calibrated \(\beta_{\text{eff}}\) from the data.
  • No demonstration to date beats classical CD on a real-world dataset. The consistent finding is parity, not advantage — with the quantum route far slower in wall-clock time.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Boltzmann probabilities and the partition function
docs.text:
A 2-visible-unit BM has \(E(v_1,v_2) = -a_1v_1 - a_2v_2 - w\,v_1v_2\) with \(a_1 = 0.5\), \(a_2 = -0.3\), \(w = 1.0\). Compute \(Z\) and all four probabilities.

Solution.

Energies.

\[ E(0,0) = 0 \] \[ E(1,0) = -0.5 \] \[ E(0,1) = +0.3 \] \[ E(1,1) = -0.5 + 0.3 - 1.0 = -1.2 \]

Boltzmann weights \(e^{-E}\).

\[ e^{0} = 1.0000 \] \[ e^{0.5} = 1.6487 \] \[ e^{-0.3} = 0.7408 \] \[ e^{1.2} = 3.3201 \]

Partition function.

\[ Z = 1.0000 + 1.6487 + 0.7408 + 3.3201 = \mathbf{6.7097} \]

Probabilities.

\((v_1,v_2)\) \(E\) \(e^{-E}\) \(P\) \((0,0)\) 0 1.0000 0.1490 \((1,0)\) \(-0.5\) 1.6487 0.2457 \((0,1)\) \(+0.3\) 0.7408 0.1104 \((1,1)\) \(\mathbf{-1.2}\) 3.3201 0.4948

Sum \(= 0.9999\) ✓.

Interpretation. The positive coupling \(w = 1\) makes \((1,1)\) by far the most likely — the units are correlated. Note that \(Z\) required summing \(2^{2} = 4\) terms; for 100 units it would be \(2^{100}\) terms, which is exactly why the negative phase is intractable.

docs.title: Problem 2 — One step of contrastive divergence
docs.text:
An RBM has 2 visible and 1 hidden unit, \(w_{11} = 1.0\), \(w_{21} = -0.5\), \(a_1 = a_2 = 0\), \(b_1 = 0.2\). Perform one CD-1 step for the data point \(\vec v = (1,0)\).

Solution.

Positive phase — sample \(h\) given \(\vec v_0 = (1,0)\).

\[ P(h_1 = 1\mid\vec v_0) = \sigma\big(b_1 + w_{11}v_1 + w_{21}v_2\big) = \sigma(0.2 + 1.0 - 0) = \sigma(1.2) \] \[ \sigma(1.2) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-1.2}} = \frac{1}{1+0.30119} = \mathbf{0.76852} \]

Say the sample gives \(h_0 = 1\).

Positive-phase statistics.

\[ \langle v_1h_1\rangle_{\text{data}} = 1\times1 = 1, \qquad \langle v_2h_1\rangle_{\text{data}} = 0\times1 = 0 \]

Negative phase — reconstruct \(\vec v_1\) given \(h_0 = 1\).

\[ P(v_1 = 1\mid h_0) = \sigma(a_1 + w_{11}h_1) = \sigma(1.0) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-1}} = \mathbf{0.73106} \] \[ P(v_2 = 1\mid h_0) = \sigma(a_2 + w_{21}h_1) = \sigma(-0.5) = \frac{1}{1+e^{0.5}} = \mathbf{0.37754} \]

Say the samples give \(\vec v_1 = (1, 0)\).

Re-sample \(h\) given \(\vec v_1\). Identical to the positive phase: \(P = 0.76852\); say \(h_1 = 1\).

Negative-phase statistics.

\[ \langle v_1h_1\rangle_{\text{model}} = 1, \qquad \langle v_2h_1\rangle_{\text{model}} = 0 \]

Gradients.

\[ \Delta w_{11} \propto 1 - 1 = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \Delta w_{21} \propto 0 - 0 = \mathbf{0} \]

Interpretation. The reconstruction exactly matched the data, so there is nothing to learn from this sample — the model already assigns it high probability. This is the essence of CD: the gradient measures the discrepancy between the data and the model's reconstruction of it. When they agree, learning stops.

(In practice one averages over a minibatch; single-sample gradients are extremely noisy, and the stochastic sampling means a different draw of \(\vec v_1\) would have produced a non-zero gradient.)

docs.title: Problem 3 — Transverse field and the ground state
docs.text:
A single-qubit QBM has \(H = -\Gamma\sigma^x - b\sigma^z\). Compute the eigenvalues, the ground state, and \(\langle\sigma^z\rangle\) in the Gibbs state, for \(\Gamma = 1\), \(b = 1\).

Solution.

\[ H = -\begin{pmatrix} b & \Gamma\\ \Gamma & -b\end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix} \]

Eigenvalues. \(\det(H - \lambda I) = 0\) gives \(\lambda^{2} - (\Gamma^{2}+b^{2}) = 0\):

\[ \lambda = \pm\sqrt{\Gamma^2 + b^2} = \pm\sqrt2 = \pm1.41421 \]

Ground state (\(\lambda_- = -\sqrt2\)). Solve \((H + \sqrt2 I)|\psi\rangle = 0\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix}-1+\sqrt2 & -1\\ -1 & 1+\sqrt2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\end{pmatrix} = 0 \]

From the first row: \(\beta = (\sqrt2 - 1)\alpha = 0.41421\alpha\). Normalising:

\[ |\psi_0\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+0.41421^{2}}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0.41421\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0.92388\\ 0.38268\end{pmatrix} \]

A superposition of \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) — impossible for a classical BM, whose states are always definite bit strings.

Gibbs state at \(\beta = 1\). In the eigenbasis, \(\rho = \frac{1}{Z}\mathrm{diag}(e^{\sqrt2}, e^{-\sqrt2})\):

\[ Z = e^{1.41421} + e^{-1.41421} = 4.11325 + 0.24316 = 4.35637 \] \[ p_- = \frac{4.11325}{4.35641} = 0.94419, \qquad p_+ = 0.05582 \]

Expectation of \(\sigma^z\). The excited state is orthogonal to \(|\psi_0\rangle\): \(|\psi_1\rangle = (-0.38268,\ 0.92388)^T\).

\[ \langle\psi_0|\sigma^z|\psi_0\rangle = 0.92388^2 - 0.38268^2 = 0.85355 - 0.14645 = 0.70711 \] \[ \langle\psi_1|\sigma^z|\psi_1\rangle = 0.14645 - 0.85355 = -0.70711 \] \[ \langle\sigma^z\rangle = 0.94419(0.70711) + 0.05582(-0.70711) = \mathbf{0.62819} \]

Compare the classical case (\(\Gamma = 0\)). Then \(\langle\sigma^z\rangle = \tanh(b) = \tanh(1) = 0.76159\).

\[ \boxed{\ \text{The transverse field \emph{reduces} the magnetisation from } 0.762 \text{ to } 0.628.\ } \]

This is quantum fluctuation: the \(\sigma^x\) term drives transitions between \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\), partially destroying the \(z\)-alignment. It is exactly the effect a QBM exploits — an extra, tunable source of "disorder" that has no classical analogue at the same temperature.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Partition-function cost and why sampling is needed
docs.text:
Compute the cost of evaluating \(Z\) exactly for a fully connected BM with 20, 50 and 100 units. At \(10^{9}\) terms/second, how long does each take?

Solution.

\(Z = \sum_{\text{configs}} e^{-E}\) has \(2^{n}\) terms.

\(n\) \(2^{n}\) Time at \(10^{9}\)/s 20 \(1.05\times10^{6}\) 1.0 ms 50 \(1.13\times10^{15}\) 13 days 100 \(1.27\times10^{30}\) \(1.27\times10^{21}\) s = \(4\times10^{13}\) years

At 100 units — a tiny model by modern standards — exact evaluation exceeds the age of the universe by a factor of 3000.

Why sampling solves it. Estimating \(\langle v_ih_j\rangle_{\text{model}}\) needs only samples from \(P\), not \(Z\) itself. MCMC (Gibbs sampling) generates such samples with each step costing \(O(n^2)\) — polynomial. The catch is mixing time: the chain may need exponentially many steps to reach equilibrium if the energy landscape has deep, separated valleys.

This is precisely the gap a quantum annealer targets. Instead of a random walk that must climb out of valleys, quantum tunnelling can pass through barriers, potentially mixing faster. Whether this yields a genuine speed-up on realistic landscapes remains the central open question of quantum annealing (L35).

docs.title: Problem 5 — Designing a QBM experiment on hardware
docs.text:
Design an experiment to test whether a QBM outperforms a classical RBM. Specify the dataset, architecture, hardware, controls and metrics — and predict the result.

Solution.

Dataset. Bars-and-Stripes on a \(4\times4\) grid: 16 visible units, 30 valid patterns out of \(2^{16} = 65536\). Small enough to compute the exact log-likelihood, which is essential for an honest comparison.

Architecture. 16 visible + 8 hidden units, fully connected between layers (RBM topology). Parameters: \(16\times8 + 16 + 8 = \mathbf{152}\).

Hardware. D-Wave Advantage. Minor embedding of a \(16\times8\) bipartite graph onto the Pegasus topology requires chains of ~4 physical qubits per logical qubit, so about 100 physical qubits.

The four arms of the experiment.

Arm Sampler Purpose A Classical CD-1 the standard baseline B Classical Gibbs, 1000 steps the "exact-sampling" ceiling C D-Wave, \(\Gamma = 0\) (full anneal) tests the sampler, not quantumness D D-Wave, \(\Gamma > 0\) (paused anneal) tests quantumness specifically

Arms C and D are the crucial pair. Comparing D against C isolates the effect of the transverse field, controlling for everything else about the hardware.

Critical calibration. Estimate \(\beta_{\text{eff}}\) for the annealer by fitting the observed energy histogram to a Boltzmann distribution. Without this, the comparison is meaningless — much of the early literature's apparent advantage came from an uncalibrated effective temperature.

Metrics.

  1. Exact log-likelihood on held-out data (computable at this size).
  2. KL divergence between the model and the true BAS distribution.
  3. Wall-clock time to reach a target log-likelihood — including embedding, programming and readout overhead, not just anneal time.
  4. Chain-break fraction — if above ~5 %, the embedding is unreliable and results are suspect.

Predicted outcome, stated in advance.

  • Arms A, B, C, D will reach comparable log-likelihoods, with B (exact Gibbs) marginally best.
  • Arm D may show a small improvement over C, consistent with Amin et al.'s finding that a transverse field helps modestly.
  • Arm A (classical CD-1) will win decisively on wall-clock time, by three to four orders of magnitude, because a D-Wave call carries ~10 ms of programming and readout overhead per sample batch while CD-1 runs in microseconds.

The honest conclusion to draw. QBMs are scientifically interesting — they demonstrate that a transverse field enriches the model class — but they are not yet practically competitive. The bottleneck is not the algorithm but the sampler: hardware overhead, uncontrolled effective temperature, limited connectivity and freeze-out. Designing the experiment with arms C and D, and calibrating \(\beta_{\text{eff}}\), is what separates a rigorous study from a press release.

docs.title: 33.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. For \(E(v) = -2v\), compute \(P(v=1)\) with one binary unit. [Ans: \(e^2/(1+e^2) = 0.881\)]
  2. Compute \(\sigma(0.5)\) and \(\sigma(-1.5)\). [Ans: 0.6225, 0.1824]
  3. Find the eigenvalues of \(H = -\Gamma\sigma^x - b\sigma^z\) for \(\Gamma = 0.5\), \(b = 2\). [Ans: \(\pm2.0616\)]
  4. Why does \([H,\partial H/\partial\theta]\ne0\) break the classical gradient derivation?
  5. How many terms in \(Z\) for a 30-unit BM? [Ans: \(1.07\times10^{9}\)]
  6. Compute \(\langle\sigma^z\rangle\) for a classical BM with \(b=0.8\), \(\Gamma=0\). [Ans: \(\tanh 0.8 = 0.6640\)]
  7. Name three practical problems with using a D-Wave device as a Boltzmann sampler.

docs.title: 33.7 Summary
docs.text:
• A Boltzmann machine is an energy-based generative model with \(P \propto e^{-E}\); training needs \(\langle\cdot\rangle_{\text{data}} - \langle\cdot\rangle_{\text{model}}\), and the model term is intractable because \(Z\) sums \(2^n\) configurations.
  • Contrastive divergence replaces equilibrium sampling with a \(k\)-step chain — biased, but effective.
  • A QBM adds a transverse field \(-\Gamma\sum_i\sigma^x_i\), making \(H\) non-diagonal so the Gibbs state \(\rho = e^{-H}/Z\) carries coherences no classical BM can represent.
  • Non-commutativity breaks the standard gradient derivation; Amin et al. train a variational lower bound derived from the Golden–Thompson inequality instead.
  • Quantum annealers natively realise the QBM Hamiltonian and can be used as Boltzmann samplers, but suffer from unknown \(\beta_{\text{eff}}\), sparse connectivity requiring minor embedding, and freeze-out.
  • Honest status: a transverse field demonstrably enriches the model class on small synthetic problems, but no result beats classical CD on real data, and hardware overhead costs 3–4 orders of magnitude in wall-clock time.

Next lesson: L34 — The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA).

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → Boltzmann Lab: set weights and biases, see the full energy table and Boltzmann distribution, sweep the transverse field \(\Gamma\) and watch \(\langle\sigma^z\rangle\) fall as quantum fluctuations grow.

docs.title: 30.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Recall the classical CNN structure and its two key inductive biases.
  2. Define the quantum convolution and quantum pooling layers.
  3. Explain how QCNN achieves \(O(\log n)\) depth and \(O(\log n)\) parameters.
  4. State why QCNNs provably avoid barren plateaus.
  5. Describe the MERA connection and the canonical application to quantum phase recognition.

docs.title: 30.2 Classical CNN Recap
docs.text:
A CNN alternates:

  • Convolution — apply the same small filter across all positions (translation invariance + weight sharing).
  • Pooling — downsample, reducing resolution while keeping the strongest features (hierarchical locality).
  • Fully connected layers at the end for classification.

The two inductive biases that make CNNs work:

  1. Locality — nearby pixels are more related than distant ones.
  2. Translation invariance — a feature means the same thing wherever it appears.

Weight sharing cuts the parameter count from \(O(n^2)\) (fully connected) to \(O(k)\) for a filter of size \(k\), independent of the input size.

docs.title: Convolution layer
docs.text:
Apply the same two-qubit unitary \(U(\vec\theta)\) to every neighbouring pair:

\[ \mathcal{C}(\vec\theta) = \bigotimes_{\text{pairs }(i,i+1)} U_{i,i+1}(\vec\theta) \]

Weight sharing is explicit: every pair uses the identical parameter vector \(\vec\theta\). A general two-qubit unitary needs 15 parameters (the dimension of \(SU(4)\)); simplified ansätze use 6.

Translation invariance follows immediately from using the same \(U\) everywhere — the quantum analogue of a shared convolutional filter.

docs.title: Pooling layer
docs.text:
Classical pooling discards information deterministically (max, average). Quantum pooling has two standard forms:

(a) Measurement-based pooling. Measure one qubit of each pair and apply a rotation to its partner conditioned on the outcome:

\[ \text{measure } q_{2i+1} \ \Rightarrow\ \text{apply } V(\vec\phi)^{m} \text{ to } q_{2i} \]

This is a genuine non-linearity — measurement is not a unitary operation — and it is the direct analogue of a CNN's activation function.

(b) Trace-out pooling. Simply stop using the qubit. Formally, take the partial trace. Simpler to implement but discards the information rather than using it.

Either way, the number of active qubits halves at each pooling layer.

docs.title: Fully connected layer
docs.text: Once \(O(1)\) qubits remain, apply a general unitary \(F(\vec\theta_{\mathrm{FC}})\) and measure.

docs.title: Logarithmic scaling
docs.text:
Quantity Value Layers \(\log_2 n\) (halving each time) Parameters \(O(\log n)\) — because of weight sharing Circuit depth \(O(\log n)\) Qubits \(n\)

For \(n = 1024\): only \(\log_2 1024 = 10\) layers, and a few dozen parameters total. Compare a hardware-efficient ansatz with \(L\) layers on 1024 qubits: \(2\times1024\times L\) parameters.

docs.title: No barren plateaus — and it is a theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Pesah, Cerezo, Wang, Volkoff, Sornborger, Coles, PRX 2021). For a QCNN with local measurements, the gradient variance is

\[ \mathrm{Var}\left[\partial_k L\right] \in \Omega\!\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\right) \]

— polynomially, not exponentially, small. QCNNs are trainable at scale.

Why. Three reinforcing reasons:

  1. Shallow depth. \(O(\log n)\) layers cannot form a 2-design over the full \(2^n\)-dimensional space.
  2. Local structure. Each gate acts on 2 qubits, and the measured observable is local, so the causal lightcone of any parameter contains only \(O(\mathrm{polylog}\,n)\) gates.
  3. Weight sharing. With \(O(\log n)\) independent parameters, each one influences many gates, so its gradient is a sum of contributions rather than a single vanishing term.
\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The QCNN is the flagship example that architectural structure defeats barren plateaus.}\ } \]

docs.title: The MERA connection
docs.text:
Read the QCNN backwards and it becomes the Multiscale Entanglement Renormalisation Ansatz (MERA), a tensor network used in condensed-matter physics to represent critical ground states.

MERA (physics) QCNN (ML) Disentanglers convolution layers Isometries (coarse-graining) pooling layers Renormalisation-group flow feature hierarchy Run bottom-up to generate a state Run top-down to classify a state

Why this matters. MERA is known to represent physically relevant states efficiently. Since QCNN is its inverse, the QCNN is guaranteed to be able to recognise exactly those states — a principled reason to expect it to work on quantum data.

docs.title: 30.5 The Canonical Application: Quantum Phase Recognition
docs.text:
The problem. Given a many-body ground state \(|\psi\rangle\), determine which phase of matter it belongs to (e.g. topological versus trivial). Classically this needs a hand-designed order parameter, which for topological phases is a non-local string operator that is often unknown.

The QCNN solution. Feed the state directly into the QCNN and train it to output the phase label. No order parameter is needed — the network learns one.

The Cong–Choi–Lukin result. On the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2\) symmetry-protected topological phase of a cluster-Ising chain, a QCNN trained on a handful of examples identified the phase boundary more accurately than the best known string order parameter, and generalised to system sizes it was never trained on.

This is the QQ quadrant done right. The data is already quantum (no encoding bottleneck), the classical alternative is genuinely hard (exponential tomography, or an unknown order parameter), and the architecture matches the physics. Of everything in Unit III, this is the most credible route to practical quantum advantage in machine learning.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Counting layers, parameters and depth
docs.text:
Design a QCNN for 16 qubits with 15-parameter convolution unitaries and 6-parameter pooling unitaries. Count layers, parameters and depth, and compare with a hardware-efficient ansatz.

Solution.

Layers. \(16 \to 8 \to 4 \to 2 \to 1\), i.e. \(\log_2 16 = \mathbf{4}\) conv–pool blocks.

Parameters. With weight sharing, each block has one shared conv unitary and one shared pool unitary:

\[ P = 4\times(15 + 6) + \underbrace{15}_{\text{final FC on 2 qubits}} = 84 + 15 = \mathbf{99} \]

(If parameters were also shared across blocks, this would fall to \(15 + 6 + 15 = 36\).)

Depth. Each conv layer applies gates to disjoint pairs in parallel — depth \(O(1)\) per layer (about 2 time steps for a \(SU(4)\) decomposition into 3 CNOTs). Pooling adds 1–2 more.

\[ \text{depth} \approx 4\times(2+2) \approx \mathbf{16} \]

Comparison with a hardware-efficient ansatz on 16 qubits with 8 layers:

QCNN Hardware-efficient Parameters 99 \(2\times16\times8 = 256\) Depth 16 \(\approx 8\times(1 + 16) = 136\) Barren plateau no (proved) yes Gradient shots at \(n=16\) \(\sim10^{3}\) \(\sim10^{5}\)

The QCNN is 2.6× fewer parameters, 8× shallower, and trainable.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Tracing a two-qubit convolution
docs.text:
A convolution unitary \(U(\theta) = \exp(-i\theta\,Z\otimes Z/2)\) acts on \(|{+}{+}\rangle\). Compute the output state and its entanglement, and interpret \(\theta\) as a filter strength.

Solution.

\(Z\otimes Z\) is diagonal with eigenvalues \(+1\) on \(|00\rangle,|11\rangle\) and \(-1\) on \(|01\rangle,|10\rangle\). Since \((Z\otimes Z)^2 = I\):

\[ U(\theta) = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,I - i\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,Z\otimes Z \]

Apply to \(|{+}{+}\rangle = \frac12(|00\rangle+|01\rangle+|10\rangle+|11\rangle)\):

\[ U|{+}{+}\rangle = \tfrac12\Big[e^{-i\theta/2}\big(|00\rangle+|11\rangle\big) + e^{+i\theta/2}\big(|01\rangle+|10\rangle\big)\Big] \]

Entanglement (concurrence, from L08). With \(a_{00}=a_{11}=\frac{e^{-i\theta/2}}{2}\) and \(a_{01}=a_{10}=\frac{e^{i\theta/2}}{2}\):

\[ C = 2\left|a_{00}a_{11} - a_{01}a_{10}\right| = 2\left|\frac{e^{-i\theta}}{4} - \frac{e^{i\theta}}{4}\right| = \frac{1}{2}\big|e^{-i\theta} - e^{i\theta}\big| = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2|\sin\theta| \] \[ \boxed{\ C = |\sin\theta|\ } \] \(\theta\) \(C\) Meaning \(0\) 0 identity — filter does nothing \(\pi/4\) 0.707 partial correlation detected \(\pi/2\) 1 maximally entangling — strongest filter \(\pi\) 0 back to a product state (up to phase)

Interpretation as a learned filter. \(\theta\) controls how strongly the layer correlates neighbouring qubits — exactly what a convolutional filter weight does classically. Training adjusts \(\theta\) to whatever correlation strength the data demands. At \(\theta = \pi/2\) the filter maximally couples the pair; at \(\theta=0\) it passes the input through unchanged (a "do nothing" filter, which the network can learn if the feature is irrelevant).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Gradient scaling: QCNN versus hardware-efficient
docs.text:
Estimate the shots needed for one gradient component at \(n = 8, 16, 32, 64\) for a QCNN (\(\mathrm{Var}\sim1/n^2\)) and a deep hardware-efficient ansatz (\(\mathrm{Var}\sim2^{-n}\)), at SNR 3.

Solution.

\[ S = \left(\frac{3}{\sigma}\right)^{2} = \frac{9}{\mathrm{Var}} \] \(n\) QCNN \(\mathrm{Var} = n^{-2}\) \(S_{\text{QCNN}}\) HEA \(\mathrm{Var}=2^{-n}\) \(S_{\text{HEA}}\) 8 \(1.56\times10^{-2}\) \(5.8\times10^{2}\) \(3.91\times10^{-3}\) \(2.3\times10^{3}\) 16 \(3.91\times10^{-3}\) \(2.3\times10^{3}\) \(1.53\times10^{-5}\) \(5.9\times10^{5}\) 32 \(9.77\times10^{-4}\) \(9.2\times10^{3}\) \(2.33\times10^{-10}\) \(3.9\times10^{10}\) 64 \(2.44\times10^{-4}\) \(3.7\times10^{4}\) \(5.42\times10^{-20}\) \(1.7\times10^{20}\)

At \(n = 64\), at 10 kHz:

\[ t_{\text{QCNN}} = \frac{3.7\times10^{4}}{10^{4}} = \mathbf{3.7\ \text{seconds}} \] \[ t_{\text{HEA}} = \frac{1.7\times10^{20}}{10^{4}} = 1.7\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s} = \mathbf{540\ \text{million years}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \text{Polynomial versus exponential — the difference between a usable and a useless architecture.}\ } \]

This single table is the strongest argument in the course for problem-structured ansätze.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Designing a QCNN for image classification
docs.text:
Adapt a QCNN to classify \(8\times8\) grayscale images (64 pixels) into 2 classes. Specify encoding, architecture and parameter count, and state the honest caveat.

Solution.

Encoding. Two options:

  • Amplitude encoding: 64 pixels into \(\log_2 64 = 6\) qubits. Compact, but the \(O(64)\) preparation depth is the bottleneck, and it destroys the 2-D spatial structure the QCNN is designed to exploit.
  • Angle encoding after PCA: reduce 64 pixels to 8 principal components, then angle-encode on 8 qubits with depth \(O(1)\). Recommended for NISQ.

Take the second: 8 qubits.

Architecture.

Layer 1: conv (shared 15-param SU(4) on pairs 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6-7)
         pool (6-param, measure odd qubits)         8 -> 4 qubits
Layer 2: conv (shared 15-param on pairs 0-1, 2-3)
         pool (6-param)                             4 -> 2 qubits
Layer 3: fully connected (15-param SU(4) on the remaining pair)
         measure <Z_0>                              -> class label

Parameters.

\[ P = \underbrace{2\times(15+6)}_{\text{two conv-pool blocks}} + \underbrace{15}_{\text{FC}} = \mathbf{57} \]

Depth. \(\approx 1\) (encoding) \(+ 2\times4 + 3 = \mathbf{12}\) gates deep — very NISQ-friendly.

Training. SPSA, 1024 shots, cross-entropy loss.

The honest caveat, which must be stated. For \(8\times8\) images:

  • A classical CNN with two conv layers achieves >99 % on MNIST-style data in seconds.
  • The PCA step already reduced 64 pixels to 8 numbers, and a logistic regression on those 8 components typically gets 90–95 %.
  • The QCNN's spatial inductive bias is largely wasted, because PCA destroyed the spatial structure it was designed for.

The right conclusion. A QCNN on classical image data is a good exercise in the architecture but not a competitive method. QCNNs earn their keep on quantum data — many-body states, quantum sensor readings, error-syndrome patterns — where the 1-D chain structure is physically meaningful and no classical alternative exists.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Quantum phase recognition, worked conceptually
docs.text:
Explain how a QCNN distinguishes an SPT phase from a trivial phase in a spin chain, and why this succeeds where a naive approach fails.

Solution.

The physics. The cluster-Ising Hamiltonian

\[ H = -J\sum_{i} Z_{i-1}X_{i}Z_{i+1} - h_1\sum_i X_i - h_2\sum_i X_iX_{i+1} \]

has an SPT phase (protected by \(\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2\) symmetry) for small \(h_1,h_2\) and a trivial paramagnetic phase for large \(h_1\).

Why naive approaches fail.

  1. Local order parameters are all zero. The SPT phase has no local order parameter — that is what "topological" means. Measuring \(\langle Z_i\rangle\), \(\langle X_i\rangle\) or any single-site observable gives the same answer in both phases.

  2. The correct order parameter is a non-local string:

    \[ S = \left\langle Z_1X_2X_3\cdots X_{n-1}Z_n\right\rangle \]

    — it must be guessed in advance, and for a general unknown phase nobody knows what it is. 3. Tomography is exponential. Reconstructing \(|\psi\rangle\) to test it classically needs \(O(4^n)\) measurements.

How the QCNN succeeds.

  1. Convolution layers detect local correlations such as \(Z_{i-1}X_iZ_{i+1}\) — the stabilisers of the cluster state. These are nonzero in the SPT phase.
  2. Pooling propagates the information upward. A correlation detected on qubits \((i-1,i,i+1)\) is compressed into the surviving qubit, so the next layer sees correlations over a doubled length scale.
  3. After \(\log_2 n\) layers, the single remaining qubit encodes a correlation spanning the whole chain — which is precisely a string order parameter, discovered rather than assumed.
  4. Training on a few labelled states adjusts the shared filters to whichever correlations distinguish the phases.

The renormalisation-group interpretation. Each conv–pool block is one step of RG coarse-graining: short-range fluctuations are removed and the long-distance universal behaviour — the phase — is retained. This is why the depth is \(\log n\) and why the network generalises to system sizes it never saw: the RG flow is scale-invariant.

Result (Cong–Choi–Lukin 2019). The QCNN located the phase boundary more sharply than the known string order parameter, and did so from a small number of training states.

docs.title: 30.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. How many conv–pool layers for 64 qubits? [Ans: 6]
  2. Parameter count for a 32-qubit QCNN with 15-param conv and 6-param pool, plus a 15-param FC. [Ans: \(5\times21+15 = 120\)]
  3. Compute the concurrence produced by \(\exp(-i\theta X\otimes X/2)\) on \(|00\rangle\). [Ans: \(|\sin\theta|\)]
  4. Why does weight sharing help avoid barren plateaus?
  5. Explain the MERA–QCNN correspondence in three sentences.
  6. Shots for one QCNN gradient component at \(n=128\) with \(\mathrm{Var}=n^{-2}\), SNR 3. [Ans: \(1.5\times10^{5}\)]
  7. Name two application domains where a QCNN is genuinely the right tool.

docs.title: 30.8 Summary
docs.text:
• A QCNN alternates convolution (shared two-qubit unitaries on neighbouring pairs — weight sharing and translation invariance) and pooling (measure-and-condition or trace-out, halving the qubit count), ending with a small fully connected block.
  • Scaling: \(\log_2 n\) layers, \(O(\log n)\) parameters, \(O(\log n)\) depth.
  • QCNNs provably avoid barren plateaus: \(\mathrm{Var}[\partial L] = \Omega(1/\mathrm{poly}(n))\), because of shallow depth, local lightcones and weight sharing. The gradient-cost table (Problem 3) shows polynomial versus exponential shot requirements.
  • The architecture is the inverse of MERA, which is why it efficiently represents and recognises physically relevant many-body states.
  • Killer application: quantum phase recognition — the network learns a non-local string order parameter that would otherwise have to be guessed, and generalises across system sizes via the RG interpretation.
  • On classical image data a QCNN is a useful exercise but not competitive; its real domain is quantum data.

Next lesson: L31 — Quantum linear regression.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → QCNN Builder: set the qubit count, watch the conv–pool tree contract, and compare gradient-variance curves for QCNN versus hardware-efficient ansätze.

docs.title: Lesson 32: Quantum k-Means Clustering and the Swap Test
32.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Recall Lloyd's algorithm for classical k-means and its complexity.
  2. Derive the swap test and use it to estimate state overlap.
  3. Convert an overlap into a Euclidean distance and know exactly when this is valid.
  4. Describe the quantum k-means (Lloyd–Mohseni–Rebentrost) algorithm and its claimed speed-up.
  5. Assess the caveats honestly and describe the NISQ-friendly variants.

docs.title: Lloyd's algorithm
docs.text:
1. Initialise k centroids (k-means++ recommended)
2. repeat until assignments stop changing:
     ASSIGN:  each point x_i -> nearest centroid c_j    (M*k distance computations)
     UPDATE:  c_j <- mean of the points assigned to it
3. return the centroids and the assignment

Objective (within-cluster sum of squares):

\[ J = \sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{\vec x_i \in C_j}\big\|\vec x_i - \vec c_j\big\|^{2} \]

Lloyd's algorithm monotonically decreases \(J\) and therefore converges — but only to a local minimum, which is why initialisation (k-means++) matters.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
\[ O\big(M\,k\,d\,T\big) \]

for \(M\) points, \(k\) clusters, \(d\) dimensions, \(T\) iterations. The bottleneck is the assignment step: \(Mk\) distance computations, each costing \(O(d)\).

docs.title: 32.3 The Swap Test
docs.text: The primitive that makes quantum distance estimation possible.

docs.title: Circuit
docs.text:
ancilla |0>  --[H]--------*--------[H]--[M]
                          |
reg A  |phi>  ------------x-----------
                          |
reg B  |psi>  ------------x-----------

   (the two x's joined by | form a controlled-SWAP = Fredkin gate)

docs.title: Derivation
docs.text:
Initial state. \(|0\rangle|\phi\rangle|\psi\rangle\).

After \(H\) on the ancilla.

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle + |1\rangle\big)|\phi\rangle|\psi\rangle \]

After the controlled-SWAP (swaps registers A and B only when the ancilla is \(|1\rangle\)):

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big(|0\rangle|\phi\rangle|\psi\rangle + |1\rangle|\psi\rangle|\phi\rangle\Big) \]

After the second \(H\). Substitute \(|0\rangle\to\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\) and \(|1\rangle\to\frac{|0\rangle-|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\):

\[ \frac12\Big[|0\rangle\big(|\phi\rangle|\psi\rangle + |\psi\rangle|\phi\rangle\big) + |1\rangle\big(|\phi\rangle|\psi\rangle - |\psi\rangle|\phi\rangle\big)\Big] \]

Probability of measuring \(0\). The \(|0\rangle\) branch has squared norm

\[ \frac14\Big(\langle\phi|\langle\psi| + \langle\psi|\langle\phi|\Big) \Big(|\phi\rangle|\psi\rangle + |\psi\rangle|\phi\rangle\Big) = \frac14\Big(1 + |\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^{2} + |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^{2} + 1\Big) \] \[ \boxed{\ \Pr[0] = \frac{1 + \big|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\big|^{2}}{2}\ } \] \[ \boxed{\ \big|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\big|^{2} = 2\Pr[0] - 1\ } \qquad\blacksquare \]

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
\(\lvert\langle\phi\rvert\psi\rangle\rvert^2\) \(\Pr[0]\) Meaning \(1\) \(1\) identical states — the ancilla never reads 1 \(0.5\) \(0.75\) partially overlapping \(0\) \(0.5\) orthogonal — ancilla is a fair coin

Resources. 1 ancilla + \(2n\) data qubits; \(n\) Fredkin gates (each ≈ 2 Toffolis, so ≈ 14 \(T\) gates).
