Shot cost. Estimating \(\Pr[0]\) to precision \(\epsilon\) needs \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots — and the error on \(|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2\) is twice that on \(\Pr[0]\).

docs.title: The Hadamard test — when you need the sign
docs.text:
The swap test returns only \(|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2\), losing the sign and phase. To get \(\mathrm{Re}\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\), use the Hadamard test: prepare \(|0\rangle|\phi\rangle\), apply \(H\), apply a controlled-\(U\) that maps \(|\phi\rangle\to|\psi\rangle\), apply \(H\), and measure:

\[ \Pr[0] = \frac{1 + \mathrm{Re}\langle\phi|\psi\rangle}{2} \]

Inserting an \(S^\dagger\) on the ancilla gives the imaginary part instead.

docs.title: The identity
docs.text:
For normalised states,

\[ \big\||\phi\rangle - |\psi\rangle\big\|^{2} = \langle\phi|\phi\rangle + \langle\psi|\psi\rangle - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\phi|\psi\rangle = 2 - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\phi|\psi\rangle \]

For real, non-negative amplitudes (the usual case in amplitude encoding of non-negative data), \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) is real and non-negative, so

\[ \boxed{\ d^{2} = 2 - 2\sqrt{2\Pr[0]-1}\ } \]

docs.title: The normalisation trap — and its fix
docs.text:
Amplitude encoding normalises, so \(|\phi\rangle\) carries only the direction of \(\vec x\). Two points at very different magnitudes but the same direction have overlap 1 and apparent distance 0, even though their Euclidean distance is large.

Fix: the norm-augmented encoding. Append the magnitude information explicitly. Define

\[ |\phi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt Z}\Big(\|\vec x\|\,|0\rangle|\hat x\rangle + \|\vec c\|\,|1\rangle|\hat c\rangle\Big), \qquad |\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\Big), \]

with \(Z = \|\vec x\|^{2}+\|\vec c\|^{2}\). Then

\[ \big|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\big|^{2} = \frac{\big\|\vec x - \vec c\big\|^{2}}{2Z} \]

giving the true Euclidean distance. This is the construction used in Lloyd, Mohseni and Rebentrost (2013), and it is why their algorithm needs one extra ancilla qubit.

Simpler alternative used in practice: standardise all data to unit norm before encoding, so that \(\|\vec x - \vec c\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos\vartheta\) is a legitimate distance on the unit sphere (a cosine distance). Valid when direction is what matters — text embeddings, spectra, normalised images.

docs.title: The algorithm
docs.text:
1. Encode all M data points and k centroids as quantum states  (amplitude encoding)
2. repeat until convergence:
     ASSIGN: for each point i and centroid j:
                 run the swap test  ->  estimate d(x_i, c_j)
                 assign i to argmin_j d
             (optionally: use Grover / minimum-finding to get sqrt(k) speed-up here)
     UPDATE: recompute centroids  (classically, or with a quantum mean-estimation subroutine)
3. return assignments

docs.title: The claimed complexity
docs.text:
Step Classical Quantum One distance \(O(d)\) \(O(\log d)\) (swap test on \(\log d\) qubits) Find the nearest of \(k\) \(O(k)\) \(O(\sqrt k)\) (Dürr–Høyer minimum finding) One assignment round \(O(Mkd)\) \(O(M\sqrt k\log d)\) \[ \boxed{\ \text{Total: } O(Mkd) \ \longrightarrow\ O\!\left(M\sqrt{k}\log d\right)\ } \]

— exponential in \(d\), quadratic in \(k\).

docs.title: The caveats — the same four, again
docs.text:
1. State preparation. Encoding \(M\) points of dimension \(d\) costs \(O(Md)\) unless qRAM exists — which already matches the classical read cost. This is the binding constraint.
  2. Precision. Each distance needs \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots. To distinguish two nearly-equidistant centroids you need small \(\epsilon\), and near cluster boundaries this becomes expensive.
  3. Re-preparation. Centroids change every iteration, so the states must be re-prepared each round — a cost the complexity table quietly omits.
  4. Dequantisation. Tang (2019) gave a classical algorithm with \(\mathrm{polylog}\) scaling under the same \(\ell^2\)-sampling access assumption. The exponential-in-\(d\) claim does not survive a fair comparison.

docs.title: What survives
docs.text:
Claim Verdict Exponential in \(d\) ✗ dequantised for low-rank data; state preparation dominates otherwise Quadratic in \(k\) (Grover minimum finding) ✓ genuine — Grover's speed-up is unconditional Useful on quantum-native data ✓ yes — no encoding bottleneck

Honest position for students: quantum k-means is an excellent vehicle for teaching the swap test, amplitude encoding and quantum subroutine composition. Its practical advantage on classical data is not established.

docs.title: NISQ-friendly variants
docs.text:
• q-means (Kerenidis et al., 2019): a robust version with proven convergence to a \(\delta\)-approximate solution, requiring only \(\epsilon\)-accurate distances.
  • Quantum-assisted clustering: use the quantum computer only for distance estimation on a subset (coresets), doing the rest classically.
  • QAOA-based clustering: formulate clustering as MaxCut on a similarity graph and solve with QAOA (L34) — currently the most practical NISQ route.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Swap test on two specific states
docs.text:
Compute \(\Pr[0]\) for the swap test on (a) \(|\phi\rangle = |0\rangle\), \(|\psi\rangle = |0\rangle\); (b) \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\); (c) \(|0\rangle\) and \(|+\rangle\); (d) \(|+\rangle\) and \(\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1,2)^T\).

Solution.

\[ \Pr[0] = \frac{1+|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^{2}}{2} \]

(a) \(\langle0|0\rangle = 1\): \(\Pr[0] = \frac{1+1}{2} = \mathbf{1}\). The ancilla never reads 1 — a single shot that returns 1 proves the states differ.

(b) \(\langle0|1\rangle = 0\): \(\Pr[0] = \frac{1+0}{2} = \mathbf{0.5}\). Maximally distinguishable, and the ancilla is a fair coin.

(c) \(\langle0|+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), so \(|\cdot|^2 = 0.5\):

\[ \Pr[0] = \frac{1+0.5}{2} = \mathbf{0.75} \]

(d) \(\langle +|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1+2}{\sqrt5} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} = 0.94868\):

\[ |\langle+|\psi\rangle|^{2} = \frac{9}{10} = 0.9, \qquad \Pr[0] = \frac{1.9}{2} = \mathbf{0.95} \]

Note the sensitivity. \(\Pr[0]\) ranges only over \([0.5, 1]\) — a compressed dynamic range. This is why the swap test needs many shots: distinguishing \(|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2 = 0.90\) from \(0.92\) means distinguishing \(\Pr[0] = 0.950\) from \(0.960\), a difference of only 0.01.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Estimating a distance with a shot budget
docs.text:
Two normalised data points give a swap test with \(\Pr[0] = 0.92\) over 4096 shots. Compute the overlap, the distance, and the uncertainty in the distance.

Solution.

Overlap.

\[ |\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^{2} = 2(0.92) - 1 = \mathbf{0.84} \] \[ |\langle\phi|\psi\rangle| = \sqrt{0.84} = 0.91652 \]

Distance (assuming real non-negative amplitudes):

\[ d^{2} = 2 - 2(0.91652) = 0.16696 \ \Longrightarrow\ d = \mathbf{0.4086} \]

Uncertainty propagation.

Shot noise on \(\Pr[0]\):

\[ \sigma_{p} = \sqrt{\frac{0.92\times0.08}{4096}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.0736}{4096}} = \sqrt{1.797\times10^{-5}} = 4.239\times10^{-3} \]

On the squared overlap \(F = 2p-1\):

\[ \sigma_F = 2\sigma_p = 8.478\times10^{-3} \]

On \(\sqrt F\): \(\sigma_{\sqrt F} = \frac{\sigma_F}{2\sqrt F} = \frac{8.478\times10^{-3}}{2(0.91652)} = 4.625\times10^{-3}\).

On \(d^2 = 2 - 2\sqrt F\): \(\sigma_{d^2} = 2\sigma_{\sqrt F} = 9.25\times10^{-3}\).

On \(d\): \(\sigma_d = \frac{\sigma_{d^2}}{2d} = \frac{9.25\times10^{-3}}{2(0.4086)} = \mathbf{1.13\times10^{-2}}\).

\[ \boxed{\ d = 0.409 \pm 0.011 \quad (2.8\%\ \text{relative})\ } \]

Design implication. To halve the uncertainty you need 4× the shots (\(1/\sqrt S\) scaling). And notice the error amplification: a 0.46 % relative error in \(\Pr[0]\) became a 2.8 % error in \(d\) — a factor of 6, because of the square-root and the compressed dynamic range.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Full quantum k-means iteration by hand
docs.text:
Cluster \(\vec x_1 = (1,0)\), \(\vec x_2 = (0,1)\), \(\vec x_3 = (1,1)\) into \(k=2\) clusters with initial centroids \(\vec c_1 = (1,0)\), \(\vec c_2 = (0,1)\). Use normalised (cosine) distance and give the swap test probability for each pair.

Solution.

Normalise everything (amplitude encoding requires it).

\[ |x_1\rangle = (1,0)^{T},\quad |x_2\rangle = (0,1)^{T},\quad |x_3\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)^{T} \] \[ |c_1\rangle = (1,0)^{T},\quad |c_2\rangle = (0,1)^{T} \]

Assignment step — all six overlaps.

Pair \(\langle x\rvert c\rangle\) \(\lvert\cdot\rvert^2\) \(\Pr[0]\) \(d^2 = 2-2\lvert\cdot\rvert\) \(x_1, c_1\) \(1\) 1.0 1.00 0 \(x_1, c_2\) \(0\) 0.0 0.50 2 \(x_2, c_1\) \(0\) 0.0 0.50 2 \(x_2, c_2\) \(1\) 1.0 1.00 0 \(x_3, c_1\) \(1/\sqrt2\) 0.5 0.75 0.586 \(x_3, c_2\) \(1/\sqrt2\) 0.5 0.75 0.586

Assignments.

  • \(x_1 \to C_1\) (distance 0 versus 2)
  • \(x_2 \to C_2\) (distance 0 versus 2)
  • \(x_3\) is exactly equidistant (\(0.586\) from both). Tie — break arbitrarily; say \(x_3\to C_1\).

Update step.

\[ \vec c_1 = \frac{\vec x_1 + \vec x_3}{2} = \frac{(1,0)+(1,1)}{2} = (1,\ 0.5) \] \[ \vec c_2 = \vec x_2 = (0,1) \]

Normalised for the next round:

\[ |c_1\rangle = \frac{(1, 0.5)}{\sqrt{1.25}} = (0.8944,\ 0.4472)^{T}, \qquad |c_2\rangle = (0,1)^{T} \]

Second assignment round — new overlaps with \(c_1\).

\[ \langle x_1|c_1\rangle = 0.8944 \Rightarrow \Pr[0] = \frac{1+0.8}{2} = 0.90 \] \[ \langle x_3|c_1\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(0.8944+0.4472) = 0.9487 \Rightarrow \Pr[0] = 0.95 \] \[ \langle x_2|c_1\rangle = 0.4472 \Rightarrow \Pr[0] = \frac{1+0.2}{2} = 0.60 \]

Assignments are unchanged (\(x_2\) still prefers \(c_2\) with \(\Pr[0] = 1\)), so the algorithm has converged in 2 iterations.

Shot cost. 6 swap tests per round × 2 rounds × 1024 shots = 12 288 shots — to cluster three 2-D points, a task a classical computer completes in nanoseconds. This concretely illustrates the constant-factor problem in quantum ML.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Grover speed-up in the assignment step
docs.text:
With \(k = 256\) clusters, compare classical linear scan and Dürr–Høyer quantum minimum finding for the nearest-centroid search, including the constant factor.

Solution.

Classical. Compare all \(k\) distances: \(k = \mathbf{256}\) distance evaluations.

Quantum (Dürr–Høyer). The algorithm repeatedly runs Grover search for an element smaller than a current threshold, halving the candidate set:

\[ \text{expected queries} \approx \frac{22.5\sqrt{k}}{2} + \ldots \approx 22.5\sqrt{k} \ \text{in the original bound, though } \approx 3\sqrt k \text{ is typical in practice.} \]

Using the practical estimate:

\[ 3\sqrt{256} = 3\times16 = \mathbf{48} \ \text{oracle calls} \]

Speed-up factor: \(256/48 \approx \mathbf{5.3\times}\).

But each "oracle call" is expensive. It requires a full coherent distance computation — a swap test embedded inside a Grover oracle, meaning the distance must be computed reversibly into a register rather than measured. With \(\epsilon\)-precision distances this costs \(O(1/\epsilon)\) repetitions (via amplitude estimation) per oracle call.

Revised comparison with \(\epsilon = 0.01\):

\[ \text{quantum} = 48 \times O(100) = 4800 \ \text{circuit executions} \] \[ \text{classical} = 256 \ \text{floating-point operations} \]

The classical version wins by a factor of \(\sim10^{6}\) in wall-clock time, because each classical "operation" is a nanosecond and each quantum circuit execution is a millisecond.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{The } \sqrt k \text{ speed-up is real asymptotically but does not pay for itself at } k = 256.\ } \]

Break-even requires \(k\) large enough that \(\sqrt k \cdot(\text{quantum constant}) < k\cdot(\text{classical constant})\), i.e. \(\sqrt k > 10^{6}\), so \(k > 10^{12}\) clusters — not a realistic clustering problem.

docs.title: Problem 5 — When quantum clustering genuinely helps
docs.text:
Identify a realistic scenario where quantum clustering is the right tool, and design the pipeline.

Solution.

Scenario: clustering quantum states from a quantum experiment.

A quantum simulator prepares ground states \(|\psi(\vec g)\rangle\) of a many-body Hamiltonian at many parameter settings \(\vec g\). The goal is to cluster the parameter settings by phase of matter, without knowing the phase diagram in advance.

Why classical methods fail.

  • Each state lives in \(\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}\); to cluster them classically you would first need tomography, costing \(O(4^{n})\) measurements per state. For \(n = 20\) that is \(10^{12}\) measurements per data point.
  • Classical shadows reduce this but still need \(O(\log)\)-many measurements per observable and require knowing which observables matter — precisely what is unknown.

Why quantum clustering works here.

  • No encoding bottleneck. The states are already quantum — the simulator hands them over directly. Amplitude encoding costs nothing.
  • The swap test is the natural similarity measure. \(|\langle\psi(\vec g)|\psi(\vec g')\rangle|^2\) is the fidelity, which is exactly the physically meaningful notion of "same phase": fidelity drops sharply across a phase boundary (the fidelity susceptibility diverges there).

Pipeline.

1. For each pair (g, g'), prepare |psi(g)> and |psi(g')> on 2n+1 qubits
2. Run the swap test -> fidelity F(g,g')
3. Build the similarity matrix S with S_ij = F(g_i, g_j)
4. Convert to a distance:  D_ij = sqrt(2 - 2*sqrt(S_ij))
5. Run classical spectral clustering or k-medoids on D
6. Cluster boundaries in parameter space = PHASE BOUNDARIES

Cost. \(\binom{P}{2}\) swap tests for \(P\) parameter settings, each \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots. For \(P = 50\) and \(\epsilon = 0.01\): \(1225\times10^{4} = 1.2\times10^{7}\) shots — about 20 minutes at 10 kHz. Entirely feasible.

Why this is the honest use case.

Requirement Satisfied? Data is quantum-native ✓ no state-preparation cost Classical alternative is exponentially hard ✓ tomography is \(O(4^n)\) Similarity measure is physically meaningful ✓ fidelity ↔ phase Output is small (a clustering) ✓ no exponential readout

This is the same lesson as L30's quantum phase recognition: the credible applications of QML are in the QQ quadrant, where the data is quantum, the classical alternative is exponentially expensive, and the answer is small. On classical tabular data, the constant factors and the encoding bottleneck defeat every proposed advantage.

docs.title: 32.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Swap test on \(|+\rangle\) and \(|-\rangle\): what is \(\Pr[0]\)? [Ans: 0.5]
  2. \(\Pr[0] = 0.85\): find the overlap and the distance. [Ans: \(F = 0.7\), \(d = 0.572\)]
  3. Derive \(\Pr[0] = \frac{1+|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2}{2}\) from scratch.
  4. Shots for \(\pm0.01\) accuracy in \(F\) when \(\Pr[0] = 0.9\)? [Ans: \(\approx3600\)]
  5. Why does amplitude encoding lose magnitude information, and how is it recovered?
  6. Compute the classical complexity of k-means with \(M=10^{6}\), \(k=100\), \(d=50\), \(T=20\). [Ans: \(10^{11}\) operations]
  7. Explain why quantum k-means on a CSV file gives no advantage.

docs.title: 32.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Lloyd's algorithm costs \(O(Mkd)\) per iteration; the assignment step dominates.
  • The swap test gives \(\Pr[0] = \frac{1 + |\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2}{2}\) using 1 ancilla, \(2n\) data qubits and \(n\) Fredkin gates. The Hadamard test recovers the sign/phase.
  • Distance from overlap: \(d^2 = 2 - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\). Amplitude encoding normalises, so magnitude must be restored via a norm-augmented encoding — or you must accept cosine distance.
  • Quantum k-means claims \(O(Mkd) \to O(M\sqrt k\log d)\), combining the \(\log d\) swap test with \(\sqrt k\) Dürr–Høyer minimum finding.
  • Caveats: state preparation costs \(O(Md)\) without qRAM; centroids must be re-prepared each round; precision costs \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\); and Tang dequantised the low-rank case. Only the \(\sqrt k\) factor is unconditionally real, and it does not pay for itself at realistic \(k\).
  • The honest application is quantum-native data: clustering many-body states by fidelity to map a phase diagram — where tomography is \(O(4^n)\) and fidelity is the physically correct similarity measure.

Next lesson: L33 — Quantum Boltzmann machines.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → Swap Test Lab: build two states, run the swap test with a chosen shot count, and see the estimated overlap converge to the exact value with error bars.

docs.title: Lesson 27: Quantum Kernel Methods and the Quantum Support Vector Machine
27.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Recall the SVM primal and dual problems and the kernel trick.
  2. Define the quantum kernel and describe the two circuits that estimate it.
  3. Assemble the complete QSVM pipeline and count its circuit executions.
  4. Analyse the \(O(M^2)\) kernel-matrix cost and the shot-noise requirement.
  5. State honestly where quantum kernels can and cannot give an advantage.

docs.title: The maximum-margin classifier
docs.text:
Given labelled data \(\{(\vec x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{M}\) with \(y_i\in\{-1,+1\}\), find the hyperplane \(\vec w\cdot\vec x + b = 0\) maximising the margin.

Primal (soft margin).

\[ \min_{\vec w, b, \xi} \ \frac12\|\vec w\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{M}\xi_i \] \[ \text{s.t. } y_i(\vec w\cdot\vec x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i, \quad \xi_i \ge 0 \]

Dual.

\[ \max_{\vec\alpha}\ \sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^{M}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_iy_j\, \underbrace{\vec x_i\cdot\vec x_j}_{\text{only via inner products}} \] \[ \text{s.t. } 0\le\alpha_i\le C, \quad \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0 \]

Crucially, the data enters only through inner products \(\vec x_i \cdot \vec x_j\).

docs.title: The kernel trick
docs.text:
Replace \(\vec x_i\cdot\vec x_j\) by \(k(\vec x_i,\vec x_j) = \langle\phi(\vec x_i),\phi(\vec x_j)\rangle\) for some feature map \(\phi\) into a (possibly infinite-dimensional) space. You never need to compute \(\phi\) explicitly — only the kernel values.

Prediction.

\[ f(\vec x) = \mathrm{sign}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_iy_i\,k(\vec x_i,\vec x) + b\right) \]

Mercer's condition. \(k\) is a valid kernel iff the Gram matrix \(K_{ij} = k(\vec x_i,\vec x_j)\) is symmetric positive semi-definite for every finite dataset.

Classical kernels.

Kernel Formula Linear \(\vec x\cdot\vec x'\) Polynomial \((\vec x\cdot\vec x' + c)^{d}\) RBF (Gaussian) \(\exp\big(-\gamma\Vert \vec x-\vec x'\Vert ^2\big)\) Sigmoid \(\tanh(\kappa\,\vec x\cdot\vec x' + c)\)

docs.title: 27.3 The Quantum Kernel
docs.text:
Definition. With a quantum feature map \(|\phi(\vec x)\rangle = U_{\phi}(\vec x)|0\rangle^{\otimes n}\),

\[ \boxed{\ k_Q(\vec x,\vec x') = \big|\langle\phi(\vec x)|\phi(\vec x')\rangle\big|^{2} = \big|\langle0|U_{\phi}^{\dagger}(\vec x)\,U_{\phi}(\vec x')|0\rangle\big|^{2}\ } \]

Valid kernel? Yes: \(K_{ij} = |\langle\phi_i|\phi_j\rangle|^2 = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_i\rho_j)\) with \(\rho_i = |\phi_i\rangle\langle\phi_i|\), which is a Gram matrix of density matrices under the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product and is therefore PSD ✓.

Properties. \(k_Q(\vec x,\vec x) = 1\); \(0\le k_Q\le 1\); symmetric.

The strategic idea. The feature space is \(\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\) — exponentially large in the qubit count. If \(U_\phi\) is chosen so that the induced kernel is hard to evaluate classically, the quantum computer provides a kernel no classical machine can compute. That is the QSVM advantage argument.

docs.title: Circuit 1 — the compute–uncompute (fidelity) method
docs.text:
|0>^n --[ U_phi(x') ]--[ U_phi(x)^dagger ]--[M]^n-->  count outcome 0^n
\[ \Pr[0^n] = \big|\langle0|U_\phi^\dagger(\vec x)U_\phi(\vec x')|0\rangle\big|^{2} = k_Q(\vec x,\vec x') \]

Estimate: run \(S\) shots, count how often all-zeros appears, divide by \(S\).

Property Value Qubits \(n\) Depth \(2\times\) depth of \(U_\phi\) Statistical error \(\sqrt{k(1-k)/S}\)

The standard method — implemented as FidelityQuantumKernel in Qiskit.

docs.title: Circuit 2 — the swap test
docs.text:
ancilla   |0> --[H]--------*--------[H]--[M]
                           |
register  |phi(x)>  -------x--------
                           |
register  |phi(x')> -------x--------      (controlled SWAP = Fredkin)
\[ \Pr[\text{ancilla}=0] = \frac{1 + |\langle\phi(\vec x)|\phi(\vec x')\rangle|^{2}}{2} = \frac{1 + k_Q}{2} \] \[ \Longrightarrow\quad k_Q = 2\Pr[0] - 1 \]

Derivation. After the first \(H\) and the controlled SWAP:

\[ \tfrac12\Big[|0\rangle\big(|\phi\rangle|\phi'\rangle + |\phi'\rangle|\phi\rangle\big) + |1\rangle\big(|\phi\rangle|\phi'\rangle - |\phi'\rangle|\phi\rangle\big)\Big] \]

The \(|0\rangle\) branch has squared norm \(\frac{1}{4}\cdot 2(1 + |\langle\phi|\phi'\rangle|^2)\), giving the stated probability. \(\blacksquare\)

Compute–uncompute Swap test Qubits \(n\) \(2n+1\) Depth \(2\times\) \(1\times\) + \(n\) Fredkins Readout \(n\)-bit all-zeros 1 ancilla bit Preferred on NISQ yes (fewer qubits) when depth is the constraint

docs.title: 27.4 The QSVM Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Choose feature map U_phi (e.g. ZZFeatureMap, reps=2)
2. Build the training kernel matrix:
       K_ij = k_Q(x_i, x_j)   for all i <= j   ->  M(M+1)/2 circuits
3. Feed K into a CLASSICAL SVM solver (e.g. libsvm) -> alpha, b
4. Build the test kernel:  K'_ij = k_Q(x_test_i, x_train_j)  ->  M_test * M circuits
5. Predict: f(x) = sign( sum_i alpha_i y_i K'(x, x_i) + b )

Only step 2 and step 4 are quantum. The optimisation itself is entirely classical and convex — QSVM has no barren-plateau problem and no local minima, which is a genuine advantage over variational methods (L28, L29).

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Stage Circuit evaluations Training kernel \(\frac{M(M+1)}{2}\times S\) shots Test kernel \(M_{\text{test}}\times M\times S\) shots

For \(M = 100\), \(S = 8192\): \(5050 \times 8192 \approx 4.1\times10^{7}\) shots. At \(10^{4}\) shots/second on cloud hardware, that is over an hour — and this is only 100 training points.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The } O(M^2) \textbf{ kernel-matrix cost is the practical ceiling on QSVM.}\ } \]

Classical SVMs also form \(O(M^2)\) kernel entries, but each costs nanoseconds rather than seconds.

docs.title: Shot noise and kernel-matrix integrity
docs.text:
Each \(K_{ij}\) carries statistical error \(\epsilon \approx \sqrt{k(1-k)/S}\). With \(S = 8192\) and \(k\approx0.5\), \(\epsilon \approx 0.0055\).

Two consequences.

  1. Noise can destroy positive semi-definiteness. A noisy \(K\) may have small negative eigenvalues, which breaks the convexity the SVM solver relies on. Fix: project onto the PSD cone by clipping negative eigenvalues to zero, or add \(\delta I\) to the diagonal.
  2. Precision requirement scales with \(M\). To keep the solution stable, \(\epsilon = O(1/M)\) is needed, so \(S = O(M^2)\) shots per entry, giving \(O(M^4)\) total shots. This is the strongest scaling objection to QSVM.

docs.title: 27.5 Does It Actually Help? An Honest Assessment
docs.text:
The positive result (Liu, Arunachalam, Temme, 2021). There exists a constructed classification problem, based on the discrete logarithm, for which a quantum kernel gives a provable exponential advantage over any classical learner. Existence is settled.

The negative results.

  • Product feature maps are classically simulable. The kernel factorises into \(\prod_j\cos^2\!\big(\frac{x_j-x_j'}{2}\big)\) (L26, Problem 2) — computable in \(O(d)\) classically. Entanglement in \(U_\phi\) is necessary.
  • Exponential concentration. For expressive random feature maps, \(k_Q(\vec x,\vec x')\) concentrates around a constant \(\sim2^{-n}\) for all \(\vec x\ne\vec x'\): the kernel matrix approaches the identity, and the model memorises the training set and generalises terribly. Distinguishing entries then requires \(S = O(2^{n})\) shots. This is the kernel-method analogue of barren plateaus.
  • Huang et al. (2021). Given the same data-access assumptions, classical ML models match quantum kernel methods on most practical datasets.

The design tension, stated plainly.

\[ \text{too simple} \Rightarrow \text{classically simulable}; \qquad \text{too expressive} \Rightarrow \text{kernel concentrates, no generalisation} \]

Useful quantum kernels must sit in a narrow band, and finding that band for real problems is an open research question. Present QSVM to students as scientifically interesting and pedagogically essential, not as a deployed technology.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Computing a quantum kernel by hand
docs.text:
Using single-qubit \(R_y\) angle encoding, compute \(k_Q(x,x')\) for \(x = 0\), \(x' = \pi/2\). Verify with the fidelity circuit.

Solution.

\[ |\phi(0)\rangle = R_y(0)|0\rangle = |0\rangle \] \[ |\phi(\pi/2)\rangle = R_y(\pi/2)|0\rangle = \cos\tfrac{\pi}{4}|0\rangle + \sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}|1\rangle = |+\rangle \] \[ \langle\phi(0)|\phi(\pi/2)\rangle = \langle0|+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \] \[ k_Q = \left|\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^{2} = \mathbf{0.5} \]

Check with the general formula \(k_Q = \cos^2\!\big(\frac{x-x'}{2}\big)\):

\[ \cos^2\!\left(\frac{0 - \pi/2}{2}\right) = \cos^2\!\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac12 \ \checkmark \]

Fidelity circuit. Apply \(R_y(\pi/2)\) then \(R_y(0)^\dagger = I\), giving \(|+\rangle\); measuring gives \(0\) with probability \(\frac12\) ✓.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Building and checking a 3×3 kernel matrix
docs.text:
Three 1-D data points \(x_1 = 0\), \(x_2 = \pi/2\), \(x_3 = \pi\) with \(R_y\) encoding. Build \(K\), check PSD, and comment on separability.

Solution.

Using \(k(x,x') = \cos^2\!\big(\frac{x-x'}{2}\big)\):

\[ k_{11}=k_{22}=k_{33}=1 \] \[ k_{12} = \cos^2(\pi/4) = 0.5, \qquad k_{23} = \cos^2(-\pi/4) = 0.5 \] \[ k_{13} = \cos^2(-\pi/2) = 0 \] \[ K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 1\end{pmatrix} \]

PSD check. Eigenvalues of this symmetric tridiagonal matrix: the pattern \(\mathrm{tridiag}(0.5,1,0.5)\) of size 3 has eigenvalues \(1 + 2(0.5)\cos\frac{k\pi}{4}\) for \(k = 1,2,3\):

\[ \lambda = 1 + \cos\tfrac{\pi}{4},\ 1 + \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2},\ 1+\cos\tfrac{3\pi}{4} = 1.7071,\ 1.0,\ 0.2929 \]

All positive ⟹ positive definite ✓, so \(K\) is a valid kernel matrix.

Separability comment. \(x_1\) and \(x_3\) are orthogonal (\(k_{13} = 0\)) — the encoding maps them to \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\), antipodal on the Bloch sphere. \(x_2\) sits exactly between them. So the encoding maps the interval \([0,\pi]\) onto a great arc of the Bloch sphere, preserving the geometry faithfully. This kernel is essentially a squared-cosine similarity — smooth, well-behaved, and entirely classical.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Shot budget and wall-clock time
docs.text:
A QSVM has 200 training and 50 test samples, 4096 shots per kernel entry, and the device runs 5000 shots/second. Compute the total shots and runtime.

Solution.

Training kernel (symmetric, diagonal known to be 1):

\[ \frac{M(M-1)}{2} = \frac{200\times199}{2} = 19{,}900 \ \text{entries} \] \[ 19{,}900\times4096 = 8.15\times10^{7}\ \text{shots} \]

Test kernel:

\[ 50\times200 = 10{,}000 \ \text{entries} \ \Longrightarrow\ 10{,}000\times4096 = 4.10\times10^{7}\ \text{shots} \]

Total:

\[ 8.15\times10^{7} + 4.10\times10^{7} = \mathbf{1.22\times10^{8}\ \text{shots}} \]

Runtime:

\[ t = \frac{1.22\times10^{8}}{5000} = 24{,}500\ \mathrm{s} = \mathbf{6.8\ \text{hours}} \]

Plus queueing. On shared cloud hardware, job latency typically dominates: 30 000 separate circuit jobs at even 1 second of overhead each adds another 8 hours.

Scaling. Doubling to 400 training samples quadruples the training kernel cost to 27 hours.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{QSVM is limited to a few hundred samples on current hardware.}\ } \]

Mitigations in use: kernel-matrix sparsification (compute only near-neighbour entries), Nyström low-rank approximation, and batched circuit submission.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Kernel concentration, quantified
docs.text:
For a random \(n\)-qubit feature map, \(\mathbb{E}[k_Q] \approx 2^{-n}\) for distinct points. How many shots are needed to distinguish \(k = 2^{-n}\) from \(k = 2\times2^{-n}\) at \(n = 20\)? Interpret.

Solution.

At \(n=20\): \(k_1 = 2^{-20} = 9.54\times10^{-7}\), \(k_2 = 1.91\times10^{-6}\).

Difference: \(\Delta = 9.54\times10^{-7}\).

For a Bernoulli estimate with tiny \(p\), \(\mathrm{SE} \approx \sqrt{p/S}\). To resolve \(\Delta\) at 2 standard errors:

\[ 2\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{S}} \le \Delta \ \Longrightarrow\ S \ge \frac{4k_1}{\Delta^{2}} = \frac{4\times9.54\times10^{-7}}{(9.54\times10^{-7})^{2}} \] \[ S \ge \frac{3.82\times10^{-6}}{9.10\times10^{-13}} = \mathbf{4.2\times10^{6}\ \text{shots per entry}} \]

Per kernel entry. For a 100-sample dataset that is \(4950\times4.2\times10^{6} = 2\times10^{10}\) shots — over 60 years at 10 kHz.

Interpretation: exponential concentration is fatal. The kernel matrix becomes \(K \approx I\), meaning:

  • Every point is "orthogonal" to every other in feature space.
  • The SVM can fit the training data perfectly (\(\alpha_i\) nonzero for all \(i\)) but has learned nothing generalisable — the model is pure memorisation.
  • Test predictions default to \(\mathrm{sign}(b)\), i.e. the majority class.

Design response. Restrict the feature map's expressivity: shallow circuits, limited entanglement, problem-informed structure. Concentration is the kernel-method form of the barren plateau (L29), and it comes from the same source — the exponential dimension of Hilbert space.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Comparing quantum and classical kernels on XOR
docs.text:
The XOR dataset: \((0,0)\to-1\), \((1,1)\to-1\), \((0,1)\to+1\), \((1,0)\to+1\). Show that (a) a linear kernel fails, (b) a product angle-encoding quantum kernel also fails, (c) a ZZ feature map succeeds.

Solution.

(a) Linear kernel. XOR is the textbook non-linearly-separable problem: no hyperplane \(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b\) separates \(\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\) from \(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}\). Attempting it gives the contradictory system

\[ b < 0,\quad w_1+w_2+b<0,\quad w_2+b>0,\quad w_1+b>0 . \]

Adding the last two: \(w_1+w_2+2b > 0\); the second gives \(w_1+w_2+b<0\), so \(b > 0\) — contradicting the first. Fails. ✗

(b) Product angle encoding. Scale inputs by \(\pi\) so \(0\to0\) and \(1\to\pi\). The kernel is

\[ k(\vec x,\vec x') = \prod_{j=1}^{2}\cos^{2}\!\left(\frac{\pi(x_j - x'_j)}{2}\right) = \prod_j \begin{cases}1 & x_j = x'_j\\ 0 & x_j\ne x'_j\end{cases} \]

So \(K = I\) — every distinct pair is orthogonal. The SVM memorises the four points but has no structure to generalise from; a fifth point would be classified arbitrarily.

More fundamentally, the feature map is a product, so the model is a sum of independent per-feature terms. XOR requires the interaction term \(x_1x_2\), which a product map cannot represent. ✗

(c) ZZ feature map. Add the entangling term

\[ U_{\phi}(\vec x) = \exp\Big(i\,\phi_{12}(\vec x)\,Z_1Z_2\Big)\,\exp\Big(i\sum_j x_jZ_j\Big)H^{\otimes2}, \qquad \phi_{12} = (\pi-x_1)(\pi-x_2) . \]

The \(Z_1Z_2\) term makes the state's phase depend on the product of the features. Concretely, the relative phase acquired distinguishes the "same" pairs \(\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\) from the "different" pairs \(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}\), exactly the XOR structure.

The resulting kernel matrix has the block structure

\[ K \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\\ \cdot & 1 & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot&\cdot&1&\cdot\\ \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&1\end{pmatrix} \ \text{with large within-class entries and small across-class entries,} \]

which is separable in feature space. Succeeds. ✓

The lesson, in one sentence. Entanglement in the feature map is what lets a quantum kernel represent feature interactions — precisely analogous to how the classical polynomial kernel \((\vec x\cdot\vec x'+1)^2\) solves XOR by introducing the \(x_1x_2\) monomial.

Honest footnote: the classical RBF or degree-2 polynomial kernel also solves XOR, instantly. The quantum kernel is not better here — it is a demonstration that entangling maps have the right kind of expressivity.

docs.title: 27.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Compute \(k_Q(0, \pi)\) for single-qubit \(R_y\) encoding. [Ans: 0]
  2. Show that \(K_{ij} = \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_i\rho_j)\) is always PSD.
  3. Total shots for \(M=50\) training, 4096 shots/entry? [Ans: \(\approx5.0\times10^{6}\)]
  4. Derive \(\Pr[\text{ancilla}=0] = \frac{1+|\langle\phi|\phi'\rangle|^2}{2}\) for the swap test.
  5. Why does a product feature map give no quantum advantage? Answer in two sentences.
  6. Given noisy \(K\) with eigenvalues \((2.1, 0.8, -0.03)\), describe two repairs.
  7. Compute the qubit and depth cost of the swap test versus compute–uncompute for \(n=8\).

docs.title: 27.8 Summary
docs.text:
• SVMs depend on data only through inner products, so any PSD kernel can be substituted (the kernel trick).
  • Quantum kernel: \(k_Q(\vec x,\vec x') = |\langle\phi(\vec x)|\phi(\vec x')\rangle|^2\), always a valid Mercer kernel, with an exponentially large feature space \(\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\).
  • Two estimation circuits: compute–uncompute (measure \(\Pr[0^n]\), \(n\) qubits, double depth) and the swap test (\(2n+1\) qubits, one ancilla bit).
  • QSVM = quantum kernel matrix + classical convex SVM solver. No barren plateaus, no local minima — a real structural advantage over variational models.
  • Cost is \(O(M^2)\) kernel entries and, for stability, \(O(M^4)\) total shots — limiting QSVM to a few hundred samples on current hardware.
  • Honest verdict: a provable exponential advantage exists for a constructed problem, but product maps are classically simulable and highly expressive maps suffer exponential kernel concentration (\(k\to2^{-n}\), \(K\to I\), no generalisation). Useful kernels live in a narrow band that is still being mapped.

Next lesson: L28 — The Variational Quantum Classifier.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → Kernel Lab: choose a feature map and dataset, build the kernel matrix, view its heat map and eigenvalues, and watch the decision boundary form.

docs.title: 31.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Derive the normal equations for ordinary least squares and state their complexity.
  2. Map linear regression onto HHL and identify each assumption.
  3. Describe the variational alternative and compare the two routes.
  4. Explain the role of ridge regularisation in controlling the condition number.
  5. Distinguish what can and cannot be extracted from the quantum solution.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Given design matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}\) (\(M\) samples, \(d\) features) and targets \(\vec y\in\mathbb{R}^{M}\), find \(\vec\beta\) minimising

\[ L(\vec\beta) = \|X\vec\beta - \vec y\|^{2} . \]

docs.title: The normal equations
docs.text:
Set the gradient to zero:

\[ \nabla_{\vec\beta}L = 2X^{T}\big(X\vec\beta - \vec y\big) = 0 \] \[ \boxed{\ X^{T}X\,\vec\beta = X^{T}\vec y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \vec\beta = \big(X^{T}X\big)^{-1}X^{T}\vec y\ } \]

The matrix \(A = X^TX\) is \(d\times d\), symmetric and positive semi-definite — exactly the form HHL requires, with no Hermitian dilation needed.

docs.title: Ridge regression
docs.text:
\[ L_{\text{ridge}}(\vec\beta) = \|X\vec\beta - \vec y\|^{2} + \lambda\|\vec\beta\|^{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \vec\beta = \big(X^{T}X + \lambda I\big)^{-1}X^{T}\vec y \]

Two roles for \(\lambda\):

  1. Statistical: shrinks coefficients, reducing variance and handling multicollinearity.
  2. Numerical: raises \(\lambda_{\min}\) from possibly 0 to at least \(\lambda\), so
\[ \kappa\big(X^TX+\lambda I\big) = \frac{\lambda_{\max}+\lambda}{\lambda_{\min}+\lambda} \ \le\ \frac{\lambda_{\max}+\lambda}{\lambda} . \]

For the quantum algorithm the second role is decisive. HHL's runtime scales with \(\kappa\), and without regularisation \(\kappa(X^TX) = \kappa(X)^2\) can be enormous. Ridge regularisation is not optional in quantum linear regression — it is what makes it run at all.

docs.title: Classical complexity
docs.text: Method Cost Normal equations (direct) \(O(Md^2 + d^3)\) QR / SVD \(O(Md^2)\), numerically stabler Conjugate gradient \(O(Md\sqrt\kappa)\) per solve Stochastic gradient descent \(O(Md)\) per epoch

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
1. Prepare  |b> proportional to X^T y                      (state preparation)
2. Apply HHL with A = X^T X + lambda I                     (QPE + rotation + post-select)
3. Obtain  |beta> proportional to A^{-1} |b>
4. Extract a SCALAR functional (never all d coefficients)

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
\[ O\!\left(\frac{\log d \cdot s^{2}\kappa^{2}}{\epsilon}\right) \]

versus the classical \(O(Md^2 + d^3)\) — exponentially better in \(d\), under the L24 caveats.

docs.title: What can be extracted
docs.text:
Quantity Method Cost Speed-up? Prediction \(\hat y_{\text{new}} = \vec x_{\text{new}}^{T}\vec\beta\) swap test between \(\lvert\beta\rangle\) and \(\lvert x_{\text{new}}\rangle\) \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots yes \(\lVert\vec\beta\rVert\) from the post-selection probability \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) yes Coefficient of determination \(R^2\) scalar functional \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) yes Which feature is largest measure and take the mode \(O(d)\) shots no All \(d\) coefficients full tomography \(O(d/\epsilon^2)\) no \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Quantum linear regression accelerates prediction, not interpretation.}\ } \]

For applications where the coefficients themselves are the deliverable — econometrics, clinical risk factors, regulated credit models — quantum linear regression offers nothing. This is worth stating clearly, because it is often obscured in popular accounts.

docs.title: The swap-test prediction circuit
docs.text:
To compute \(\hat y = \langle x_{\text{new}}|\beta\rangle\):

|0>       --[H]-----*-----[H]--[M]
                    |
|beta>    ----------x----------
                    |
|x_new>   ----------x----------
\[ \Pr[0] = \frac{1 + |\langle x_{\text{new}}|\beta\rangle|^{2}}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad |\hat y|^{2} \propto 2\Pr[0]-1 \]

(The sign requires a Hadamard test with an extra controlled phase, since the swap test returns only the squared magnitude.)

docs.title: 31.4 Route 2 — Variational Quantum Linear Regression
docs.text: For NISQ hardware, HHL is far too deep (it needs QPE). The variational alternative:

docs.title: Formulation
docs.text:
Parameterise the solution as a quantum state \(|\beta(\vec\theta)\rangle = V(\vec\theta)|0\rangle\) and minimise

\[ C(\vec\theta) = \big\| A|\beta(\vec\theta)\rangle - |b\rangle \big\|^{2} = \langle\beta|A^{\dagger}A|\beta\rangle - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\langle b|A|\beta\rangle + \langle b|b\rangle \]

Each term is an expectation value measurable by a Hadamard test. This is the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) of Bravo-Prieto et al. (2019).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: HHL route Variational route Circuit depth \(O(\kappa/\epsilon)\) — deep (QPE) \(O(\text{layers})\) — shallow Hardware era fault-tolerant NISQ Guarantee provable complexity heuristic, no guarantee Barren plateaus none yes — a real risk Optimisation none needed non-convex

docs.title: 31.5 A Fully Worked Numerical Example
docs.text:
Dataset (4 points, 1 feature + intercept).

\(i\) \(x_i\) \(y_i\) 1 1 2 2 2 3 3 3 5 4 4 6

Design matrix (with an intercept column):

\[ X = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \vec y = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\5\\6\end{pmatrix} \]

Compute \(A = X^TX\).

\[ X^{T}X = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 10\\ 10 & 30\end{pmatrix} \]

(top-left: \(4\) ones; top-right and bottom-left: \(1+2+3+4=10\); bottom-right: \(1+4+9+16=30\).)

Compute \(\vec b = X^{T}\vec y\).

\[ X^{T}\vec y = \begin{pmatrix}2+3+5+6\\ 1(2)+2(3)+3(5)+4(6)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}16\\ 2+6+15+24\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}16\\47\end{pmatrix} \]

Solve. \(\det A = 4(30) - 100 = 20\).

\[ A^{-1} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{pmatrix}30 & -10\\ -10 & 4\end{pmatrix} \] \[ \vec\beta = \frac{1}{20}\begin{pmatrix}30 & -10\\-10 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}16\\47\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{pmatrix}480 - 470\\ -160 + 188\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{pmatrix}10\\28\end{pmatrix} \] \[ \boxed{\ \vec\beta = \begin{pmatrix}0.5\\ 1.4\end{pmatrix} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat y = 0.5 + 1.4x\ } \]

Check. Predictions: \(1.9, 3.3, 4.7, 6.1\) against \(2,3,5,6\). Residuals \(0.1, -0.3, 0.3, -0.1\); sum \(= 0\) ✓ (a property of the least-squares fit with an intercept).

\[ \mathrm{RSS} = 0.01+0.09+0.09+0.01 = 0.20 \]

Condition number. Eigenvalues of \(A\): from \(\lambda^2 - 34\lambda + 20 = 0\),

\[ \lambda = \frac{34\pm\sqrt{1156-80}}{2} = \frac{34\pm32.80}{2} = 33.40,\ 0.599 \] \[ \kappa = \frac{33.40}{0.599} = \mathbf{55.8} \]

Quite ill-conditioned for a 2×2 problem — because the intercept column and the \(x\) column are strongly correlated (the \(x\) values are not centred). Centring \(x\) would make \(A\) diagonal and \(\kappa\) far smaller — an important practical preprocessing step for the quantum algorithm.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Effect of centring on the condition number
docs.text:
Re-do the example above with \(x\) centred (\(\tilde x_i = x_i - \bar x\)). Compute the new \(A\), \(\kappa\), and the coefficients.

Solution.

\(\bar x = 2.5\), so \(\tilde x = (-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)\).

\[ X^{T}X = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 0\\ 0 & \sum\tilde x_i^2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 0\\0 & 2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix} \]

Diagonal! Centring removed the correlation between the intercept and slope columns.

\[ \kappa = \frac{5}{4} = \mathbf{1.25} \]

Compare \(\kappa = 55.8\) uncentred — a 45× reduction.

\[ X^{T}\vec y = \begin{pmatrix}16\\ -1.5(2)-0.5(3)+0.5(5)+1.5(6)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}16\\ -3-1.5+2.5+9\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}16\\7\end{pmatrix} \] \[ \vec\beta = \begin{pmatrix}16/4\\ 7/5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\1.4\end{pmatrix} \]

So \(\hat y = 4 + 1.4\tilde x = 4 + 1.4(x - 2.5) = 0.5 + 1.4x\) ✓ — the same fitted line, as it must be.

Impact on HHL runtime. Original HHL scales as \(\kappa^2\):

\[ \frac{55.8^{2}}{1.25^{2}} = \frac{3114}{1.5625} \approx \mathbf{1993\times \text{speed-up}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Centre and standardise your features. It is free classically and worth } \sim2000\times \textbf{ quantumly.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 2 — Ridge regression and the condition number
docs.text:
A design matrix gives \(A = X^TX\) with eigenvalues \(\{100, 10, 0.01\}\). Compute \(\kappa\), then compute it after ridge regularisation with \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(\lambda = 1\). Discuss the bias–variance trade-off.

Solution.

Unregularised.

\[ \kappa = \frac{100}{0.01} = \mathbf{10{,}000} \]

Catastrophic: HHL would need \(\kappa^2 = 10^{8}\) times the base cost.

With \(\lambda = 0.1\). Eigenvalues become \(\{100.1, 10.1, 0.11\}\):

\[ \kappa = \frac{100.1}{0.11} = \mathbf{910} \]

An 11× reduction in \(\kappa\), so a \(121\times\) reduction in HHL runtime.

With \(\lambda = 1\). Eigenvalues \(\{101, 11, 1.01\}\):

\[ \kappa = \frac{101}{1.01} = \mathbf{100} \]

A 100× reduction in \(\kappa\), i.e. \(10^{4}\times\) in runtime.

Trade-off.

\(\lambda\) \(\kappa\) HHL cost (rel.) Statistical bias 0 10 000 \(1\) none (unbiased) 0.1 910 \(1.2\times10^{-2}\) small 1 100 \(10^{-4}\) moderate 10 ~10 \(10^{-6}\) large — underfits

The classical view: choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation to minimise test error, balancing bias against variance.

The quantum view adds a third term: runtime. The optimal \(\lambda\) for a quantum implementation is larger than the statistically optimal one, because the runtime benefit is quadratic in \(1/\kappa\) while the statistical cost grows only gradually. A principled choice minimises

\[ \text{test error}(\lambda) + \gamma\cdot\kappa(\lambda)^{2} \]

for a cost weight \(\gamma\) reflecting the price of quantum runtime.

This is a genuine and under-appreciated design insight: quantum algorithms change which hyperparameters are optimal.**

docs.title: Problem 3 — Prediction via swap test, with shot budget
docs.text:
After quantum linear regression, \(|\beta\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.25}}(0.5, 1.0)^T\) (normalised) and a new point is encoded as \(|x_{\text{new}}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T\). Compute \(\Pr[0]\) in the swap test and the shots needed for 1 % accuracy in \(\hat y\).

Solution.

Normalise \(|\beta\rangle\). \(\|(0.5,1.0)\| = \sqrt{0.25+1} = \sqrt{1.25} = 1.1180\), so

\[ |\beta\rangle = (0.4472,\ 0.8944)^{T} \]

Overlap.

\[ \langle x_{\text{new}}|\beta\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(0.4472 + 0.8944) = \frac{1.3416}{1.4142} = 0.94868 \] \[ |\langle x_{\text{new}}|\beta\rangle|^{2} = 0.9 \]

Swap-test probability.

\[ \Pr[0] = \frac{1 + 0.9}{2} = \mathbf{0.95} \]

Shot budget. We measure \(\Pr[0]\) and infer \(F = 2\Pr[0]-1\), so \(\delta F = 2\,\delta\Pr[0]\). We want 1 % relative accuracy in \(\hat y \propto \sqrt F\):

\[ \frac{\delta \hat y}{\hat y} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\delta F}{F} \le 0.01 \ \Longrightarrow\ \delta F \le 0.02 F = 0.018 \ \Longrightarrow\ \delta\Pr[0] \le 0.009 \] \[ \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{S}} \le 0.009, \quad p = 0.95 \] \[ S \ge \frac{0.95\times0.05}{0.009^{2}} = \frac{0.0475}{8.1\times10^{-5}} = \mathbf{587\ \text{shots}} \]

Round up to 1024. Note this is independent of \(d\) — predicting with a 10-feature or a 10 000-feature model costs the same number of shots. That is where the quantum advantage lives.

docs.title: Problem 4 — When is quantum linear regression worth it?
docs.text:
For each case, decide whether the quantum route helps, and justify.

(a) \(d = 10\), \(M = 1000\), need all coefficients. (b) \(d = 10^{6}\) sparse features, need predictions only, data from a quantum simulation. (c) \(d = 100\), \(\kappa = 10^{6}\). (d) \(d = 10^{4}\), dense \(X\), classical data in a CSV file.

Solution.

(a) No. \(d = 10\) is trivially small; classical solution takes microseconds. And needing all coefficients forces \(O(d)\) tomography, destroying any advantage even if \(d\) were large.

(b) Yes — the best case. Four boxes ticked:

  • sparse ⟹ Hamiltonian simulation is efficient ✓
  • predictions only ⟹ scalar readout via swap test ✓
  • quantum-generated data ⟹ no state-preparation bottleneck ✓
  • \(d = 10^{6}\) ⟹ classical \(O(d^3) = 10^{18}\) operations is infeasible, while \(\log_2 10^6 = 20\) qubits suffice ✓

(c) No. \(\kappa = 10^{6}\) makes HHL cost \(\kappa^2 = 10^{12}\) times the base — worse than classical, which is trivial at \(d = 100\) anyway. Fix first: centre, standardise, and apply ridge regularisation; if \(\kappa\) can be brought below \(\sim10^2\) the question becomes worth revisiting.

(d) No. Two independent killers:

  • Dense \(X\) ⟹ \(s = d = 10^4\), and the \(s^2\) factor gives \(10^{8}\) — Hamiltonian simulation is not efficient.
  • Data in a CSV ⟹ loading \(10^{4}\) values into amplitudes costs \(O(10^{4})\) gates, which already matches the classical read cost.

The checklist for HHL-based regression.

\[ \text{sparse } A \ \wedge\ \text{small } \kappa \ \wedge\ \text{quantum-native or structured input} \ \wedge\ \text{scalar output} \]

All four are required. Miss any one and the advantage disappears.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Variational quantum linear regression by hand
docs.text:
Solve \(A\vec\beta = \vec b\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), \(|b\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T\) using the VQLS cost with the single-parameter ansatz \(|\beta(\theta)\rangle = R_y(\theta)|0\rangle\). Find the optimal \(\theta\).

Solution.

Ansatz. \(|\beta(\theta)\rangle = \big(\cos\frac\theta2,\ \sin\frac\theta2\big)^{T}\).

Apply \(A\).

\[ A|\beta(\theta)\rangle = \begin{pmatrix}2\cos\frac\theta2\\ \sin\frac\theta2\end{pmatrix} \]

Cost function. VQLS uses the normalised overlap (so the solution is found up to scale):

\[ C(\theta) = 1 - \frac{\big|\langle b|A|\beta(\theta)\rangle\big|^{2}}{\big\|A|\beta(\theta)\rangle\big\|^{2}} \]

Numerator.

\[ \langle b|A|\beta\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(2\cos\tfrac\theta2 + \sin\tfrac\theta2\right) \]

Denominator.

\[ \big\|A|\beta\rangle\big\|^{2} = 4\cos^{2}\tfrac\theta2 + \sin^{2}\tfrac\theta2 \]

Write \(c = \cos\frac\theta2\), \(s = \sin\frac\theta2\):

\[ C(\theta) = 1 - \frac{\frac12(2c+s)^{2}}{4c^{2}+s^{2}} \]

Minimise. Equivalently maximise \(g = \frac{(2c+s)^2}{4c^2+s^2}\). By Cauchy–Schwarz, writing \(\vec u = (2c, s)\) and \(\vec v = (1,1)\):

\[ (2c+s)^{2} = (\vec u\cdot\vec v)^{2} \le \|\vec u\|^{2}\|\vec v\|^{2} = (4c^2+s^2)\cdot 2 \]

with equality iff \(\vec u \parallel \vec v\), i.e. \(2c = s\):

\[ \tan\frac{\theta}{2} = 2 \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{\theta}{2} = \arctan 2 = 1.10715 \ \Longrightarrow\ \boxed{\theta^{*} = 2.2143\ \text{rad} = 126.87°} \]

At the optimum \(g = 2\), so \(C = 1 - \frac12\cdot2 = \mathbf{0}\) — the ansatz represents the exact solution.

Verify against the exact solution.

\[ \vec\beta_{\text{exact}} = A^{-1}\vec b = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0.5\\1\end{pmatrix} \ \propto\ \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} \]

Normalised: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1,2)^T = (0.4472, 0.8944)^T\).

From the ansatz at \(\theta^{*}\): \(\cos(1.10715) = 0.4472\), \(\sin(1.10715) = 0.8944\) ✓

Perfect agreement. The variational method found the exact solution because the single-parameter \(R_y\) ansatz happens to cover all real 2-D states — for larger systems the ansatz is only an approximation, and this is precisely where barren plateaus and expressivity limits bite.

docs.title: 31.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Fit \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) to \((1,3),(2,5),(3,7)\). [Ans: \(\beta_0=1,\beta_1=2\), exact fit]
  2. Compute \(\kappa\) for \(X^TX = \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\). [Ans: 3]
  3. Ridge with \(\lambda=2\) on eigenvalues \(\{50,5,0.5\}\): new \(\kappa\)? [Ans: \(52/2.5 = 20.8\)]
  4. Swap test gives \(\Pr[0]=0.8\): what is \(|\langle x|\beta\rangle|^2\)? [Ans: 0.6]
  5. Why does centring features reduce the condition number?
  6. Shots for 2 % accuracy in \(\hat y\) when \(p = 0.9\)? [Ans: ≈ 141]
  7. Give the four conditions required for HHL regression to help.

docs.title: 31.8 Summary
docs.text:
• OLS: \(\vec\beta = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\vec y\); \(A = X^TX\) is symmetric PSD — HHL-ready without dilation.
  • Ridge regularisation raises \(\lambda_{\min}\), cutting \(\kappa\); for the quantum algorithm this is essential, not merely statistical.
  • HHL route: \(O(\log d\cdot s^2\kappa^2/\epsilon)\) versus classical \(O(Md^2+d^3)\) — exponential in \(d\), but only under all four L24 caveats.
  • Quantum linear regression accelerates prediction, not interpretation. Predictions cost \(O(1/\epsilon^2)\) shots independent of \(d\); extracting all \(d\) coefficients costs \(O(d)\) and kills the advantage.
  • Variational route (VQLS) trades provable guarantees for NISQ-compatible shallow circuits, inheriting barren plateaus and non-convexity.
  • Preprocessing pays off enormously: centring features made \(\kappa\) fall from 55.8 to 1.25 in the worked example — a \(\sim2000\times\) HHL speed-up for free.
  • Checklist: sparse \(A\) ∧ small \(\kappa\) ∧ quantum-native input ∧ scalar output. All four, or no advantage.

Next lesson: L32 — Quantum k-means clustering and the swap test.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → Regression Lab: enter data points, see \(X^TX\), its eigenvalues and \(\kappa\), watch centring and ridge change \(\kappa\) live, and compare the classical and HHL-simulated solutions.

docs.title: Lesson 6: Quantum Measurement and the Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
6.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State all four postulates of quantum mechanics in the form used in quantum computing.
  2. Apply the Born rule to compute measurement probabilities in any basis.
  3. Compute the post-measurement state using projectors.
  4. Compute expectation values \(\langle A\rangle\) and uncertainties \(\Delta A\).
  5. Explain measurement in a rotated basis as rotate → measure in \(Z\).
  6. State the uncertainty principle for two observables and apply it to the Paulis.

docs.title: Postulate 1 — State space
docs.text: The state of an isolated quantum system is a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a complex Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) associated with the system. For \(n\) qubits, \(\mathcal{H} = (\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n} = \mathbb{C}^{2^n}\).

docs.title: Postulate 2 — Evolution
docs.text:
The evolution of a closed quantum system is described by a unitary transformation:

\[ |\psi(t_2)\rangle = U(t_1,t_2)\,|\psi(t_1)\rangle . \]

In continuous time this is the Schrödinger equation

\[ i\hbar\frac{d}{dt}|\psi(t)\rangle = H|\psi(t)\rangle \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad U(t) = e^{-iHt/\hbar}, \]

for a time-independent Hamiltonian \(H\) (a Hermitian operator, the energy observable). In quantum computing we usually set \(\hbar = 1\) and specify gates directly as unitaries.

docs.title: Postulate 3 — Measurement
docs.text:
A quantum measurement is described by a collection \(\{M_m\}\) of measurement operators satisfying the completeness relation

\[ \sum_m M_m^\dagger M_m = I . \]

If the state before measurement is \(|\psi\rangle\), then

\[ \boxed{\ \Pr[m] = \langle\psi| M_m^\dagger M_m |\psi\rangle\ } \]

and the state immediately after obtaining outcome \(m\) is

\[ \boxed{\ |\psi'\rangle = \frac{M_m|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{\Pr[m]}}\ } \]

The denominator re-normalises the collapsed state. Completeness guarantees \(\sum_m \Pr[m] = 1\).

docs.title: Postulate 4 — Composite systems
docs.text: The state space of a composite system is the tensor product of the component state spaces. If system \(j\) is prepared in \(|\psi_j\rangle\), the joint state is \(|\psi_1\rangle\otimes|\psi_2\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|\psi_n\rangle\).

docs.title: 6.3 Projective Measurement
docs.text:
The special case used in nearly all of quantum computing.

Definition (Projective / von Neumann measurement). An observable is a Hermitian operator \(A\) with spectral decomposition

\[ A = \sum_m \lambda_m P_m, \qquad P_m = \sum_{k} |v_{m,k}\rangle\langle v_{m,k}| \]

where \(P_m\) projects onto the eigenspace of eigenvalue \(\lambda_m\). The projectors satisfy

\[ P_m^\dagger = P_m, \qquad P_m P_{m'} = \delta_{mm'}P_m, \qquad \sum_m P_m = I . \]

Born rule. Measuring \(A\) on \(|\psi\rangle\) yields outcome \(\lambda_m\) with probability

\[ \Pr[\lambda_m] = \langle\psi|P_m|\psi\rangle = \| P_m|\psi\rangle \|^2 , \]

and the post-measurement state is \(\dfrac{P_m|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{\Pr[\lambda_m]}}\).

docs.title: The computational-basis measurement
docs.text:
For a single qubit, measuring \(Z\) uses \(P_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|\) and \(P_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|\). For \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\):

\[ \Pr[0] = \langle\psi|0\rangle\langle 0|\psi\rangle = |\langle 0|\psi\rangle|^2 = |\alpha|^2, \qquad \Pr[1] = |\beta|^2 , \]

and the state collapses to \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\). This is the elementary rule stated in L01, now derived from the postulate.

For an \(n\)-qubit register \(|\psi\rangle = \sum_x \alpha_x|x\rangle\):

\[ \Pr[x] = |\alpha_x|^2 = |\langle x|\psi\rangle|^2 . \]

docs.title: Partial measurement
docs.text: Measuring only qubit 1 of a two-qubit state uses \(P_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|\otimes I\) and \(P_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|\otimes I\). The unmeasured qubit is left in the correspondingly conditioned state — this is exactly the mechanism behind teleportation (L10).

docs.title: Repeatability
docs.text:
Because \(P_m^2 = P_m\), measuring the same observable twice in a row gives the same answer with certainty:

\[ \Pr[\text{same}] = \frac{\|P_m P_m|\psi\rangle\|^2}{\|P_m|\psi\rangle\|^2} = \frac{\|P_m|\psi\rangle\|^2}{\|P_m|\psi\rangle\|^2} = 1 . \]

docs.title: 6.4 Measuring in a Rotated Basis
docs.text:
Real hardware measures only in the computational basis. To measure an arbitrary observable you must rotate first.

Recipe. To measure in the orthonormal basis \(\{|b_0\rangle,|b_1\rangle\}\), find the unitary \(V\) with \(V|b_0\rangle = |0\rangle\) and \(V|b_1\rangle = |1\rangle\), apply \(V\), then measure \(Z\).

Basis Rotation to apply before \(Z\)-measurement \(Z\): \(\lvert 0\rangle,\lvert 1\rangle\) none \(X\): \(\lvert +\rangle,\lvert -\rangle\) \(H\) \(Y\): \(\lvert {+}i\rangle,\lvert {-}i\rangle\) \(S^\dagger\) then \(H\)

Check for \(X\): \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\) and \(H|-\rangle = |1\rangle\) ✓.

This is why the Bloch coordinate \(x\) is measured by "apply \(H\), then count zeros and ones": every tomography routine in Qiskit or Cirq does exactly this.

docs.title: 6.5 Expectation Values and Uncertainty
docs.text:
Definition (Expectation value).

\[ \langle A\rangle_\psi = \langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle = \sum_m \lambda_m \Pr[\lambda_m] . \]

This is the average over many repetitions on identically prepared states — not the result of a single measurement. For \(A\) with eigenvalues \(\pm1\) (any Pauli),

\[ \langle A\rangle = (+1)\Pr[+1] + (-1)\Pr[-1] = \Pr[+1] - \Pr[-1] . \]

Definition (Standard deviation / uncertainty).

\[ \Delta A = \sqrt{\langle A^2\rangle - \langle A\rangle^2} . \]

Theorem (Robertson uncertainty relation). For observables \(A\) and \(B\),

\[ \Delta A \cdot \Delta B \ \ge\ \frac{1}{2}\big|\langle [A,B]\rangle\big|, \qquad [A,B] = AB - BA . \]

Consequence for the Paulis. \([X,Y] = 2iZ\), so

\[ \Delta X \cdot \Delta Y \ \ge\ \big|\langle Z\rangle\big| . \]

For \(|\psi\rangle = |0\rangle\): \(\langle Z\rangle = 1\), so \(\Delta X\,\Delta Y \ge 1\). Indeed \(\langle X\rangle = \langle Y\rangle = 0\) and \(X^2=Y^2=I\) give \(\Delta X = \Delta Y = 1\) — the bound is saturated. You cannot know \(X\) and \(Y\) simultaneously.

Commuting observables are compatible. If \([A,B]=0\) they share an eigenbasis and can be measured simultaneously with no uncertainty trade-off. E.g. \(Z\otimes I\) and \(I\otimes Z\) commute — you can measure both qubits at once.

docs.title: 6.6 What Measurement Costs You
docs.text:
Three hard limits that shape every algorithm in this course:

  1. Collapse. After measuring, the superposition is gone. You get one sample, not the amplitudes.
  2. Holevo's bound. \(n\) qubits can transmit at most \(n\) classical bits of accessible information.
  3. No-cloning (L09). You cannot copy the state to measure it in several bases.

Therefore any quantum algorithm must engineer interference so that the single measurement at the end is very likely to reveal the answer. Reading out "all \(2^n\) amplitudes" is impossible.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Born rule in two bases
docs.text:
For \(|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\big(|0\rangle + 2|1\rangle\big)\), compute (a) \(\Pr[0],\Pr[1]\) in the \(Z\) basis, (b) \(\Pr[+],\Pr[-]\) in the \(X\) basis, (c) the post-measurement state if the \(X\)-measurement gives \(-\).

Solution.

(a) \(\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\), \(\beta = \frac{2}{\sqrt5}\):

\[ \Pr[0] = \tfrac15 = 0.2, \qquad \Pr[1] = \tfrac45 = 0.8 . \]

(b) \(\langle +|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1+2) = \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\), \(\langle -|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(1-2) = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{10}}\).

\[ \Pr[+] = \tfrac{9}{10} = 0.9, \qquad \Pr[-] = \tfrac{1}{10} = 0.1 \qquad (\text{sum } = 1\ \checkmark) \]

(c) Post-measurement state after outcome \(-\):

\[ |\psi'\rangle = \frac{P_-|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{\Pr[-]}} = \frac{|-\rangle\langle-|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{1/10}} = \frac{(-1/\sqrt{10})\,|-\rangle}{1/\sqrt{10}} = -|-\rangle \simeq |-\rangle . \]

The \(-1\) is a global phase and is discarded. The state has collapsed to \(|-\rangle\); the original amplitudes are irretrievably lost.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Expectation value and uncertainty
docs.text:
For \(|\psi\rangle = \cos\frac{\pi}{6}|0\rangle + \sin\frac{\pi}{6}|1\rangle\), compute \(\langle Z\rangle\), \(\langle X\rangle\), \(\Delta Z\) and \(\Delta X\).

Solution. \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.8660\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac12\). So \(\alpha = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\beta = \frac12\), both real.

\[ \langle Z\rangle = |\alpha|^2 - |\beta|^2 = \tfrac34 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac12 \] \[ \langle X\rangle = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta) = 2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx 0.8660 \]

Since \(Z^2 = X^2 = I\), we have \(\langle Z^2\rangle = \langle X^2\rangle = 1\). Hence

\[ \Delta Z = \sqrt{1 - \tfrac14} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.8660 \] \[ \Delta X = \sqrt{1 - \tfrac34} = \frac12 = 0.5 \]

Check the uncertainty relation. \(\langle Y\rangle = 2\mathrm{Im}(\alpha^*\beta) = 0\), and \(\Delta Z\,\Delta X = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12 = 0.433 \ge \frac12|\langle[Z,X]\rangle| = \frac12|2i\langle Y\rangle| = 0\) ✓.

Note \(\langle X\rangle^2 + \langle Y\rangle^2 + \langle Z\rangle^2 = \frac34 + 0 + \frac14 = 1\) ✓ (pure state on the Bloch sphere).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Partial measurement of a two-qubit state
docs.text:
A register is in \(|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\big(|00\rangle + |01\rangle + 2|11\rangle\big)\). Measure only the first qubit in the \(Z\) basis. Find the outcome probabilities and both possible post-measurement states.

Solution. Check normalisation: \(\frac{1+1+4}{6} = 1\) ✓.

Projector for outcome 0 on qubit 1: \(P_0 = |0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I\). Applying it keeps only the terms whose first bit is 0:

\[ P_0|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\big(|00\rangle + |01\rangle\big) \] \[ \Pr[q_1 = 0] = \|P_0|\psi\rangle\|^2 = \frac{1+1}{6} = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3} \]

Post-measurement state:

\[ |\psi_0'\rangle = \frac{P_0|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{1/3}} = \sqrt3\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\big(|00\rangle+|01\rangle\big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|00\rangle + |01\rangle\big) = |0\rangle\otimes|+\rangle . \]

Similarly \(P_1|\psi\rangle = \frac{2}{\sqrt6}|11\rangle\):

\[ \Pr[q_1 = 1] = \frac46 = \frac23, \qquad |\psi_1'\rangle = \frac{(2/\sqrt6)|11\rangle}{\sqrt{2/3}} = |11\rangle . \]

Total: \(\frac13 + \frac23 = 1\) ✓.

Observation. Measuring qubit 1 changed the state of qubit 2 even though qubit 2 was not touched: it became \(|+\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\) depending on the outcome. This is the signature of entanglement, and it is the working principle of teleportation.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Designing a measurement in a rotated basis
docs.text:
Show how to measure the observable \(A = \frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}\) on hardware that only measures \(Z\). What are the possible outcomes?

Solution. First, note \(A^2 = \frac{(X+Z)^2}{2} = \frac{X^2 + XZ + ZX + Z^2}{2}\). Since \(X\) and \(Z\) anticommute, \(XZ + ZX = 0\), so \(A^2 = \frac{I+I}{2} = I\). Hence the eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(\pm 1\).

Observe that \(A = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix} = H\). The Hadamard gate is this observable. Its eigenvectors satisfy \(H|h_\pm\rangle = \pm|h_\pm\rangle\); the \(+1\) eigenvector lies along the Bloch axis \(\hat n = \frac{\hat x + \hat z}{\sqrt2}\).

Measurement recipe. We need a unitary \(V\) with \(VHV^\dagger = Z\). Since \(H\) is a \(\pi\) rotation about \(\frac{\hat x+\hat z}{\sqrt2}\), and we want to bring that axis onto \(\hat z\), use a rotation of \(-\pi/4\) about the \(y\)-axis:

\[ V = R_y(-\pi/4) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac{\pi}{8} & \sin\frac{\pi}{8}\\ -\sin\frac{\pi}{8} & \cos\frac{\pi}{8}\end{pmatrix} \]

Procedure: apply \(R_y(-\pi/4)\) to the qubit, then measure in the computational basis. Reading \(0\) means outcome \(+1\); reading \(1\) means outcome \(-1\).

Generalisation. To measure \(\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma\), rotate \(\hat n\) onto \(\hat z\) and measure \(Z\). Every "measure this observable" instruction reduces to rotate, then measure \(Z\).

docs.title: Problem 5 — Sampling error: how many shots?
docs.text:
A quantum circuit outputs \(|1\rangle\) with true probability \(p = 0.75\). You run it \(N\) times and estimate \(\hat p\). How many shots are needed so that the standard error is below 0.01?

Solution. Each shot is a Bernoulli trial. The estimator \(\hat p = \frac{\text{count of }1}{N}\) has

\[ \mathrm{Var}(\hat p) = \frac{p(1-p)}{N}, \qquad \mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N}} . \]

Require \(\mathrm{SE} \le 0.01\):

\[ \sqrt{\frac{0.75\times0.25}{N}} \le 0.01 \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{0.1875}{N} \le 10^{-4} \ \Longrightarrow\ N \ge 1875 . \]

So about 1900 shots.

The general lesson. Statistical error falls as \(1/\sqrt N\), so improving precision by a factor of 10 costs 100× more shots. This \(1/\sqrt N\) wall is why variational algorithms (Unit III) are expensive, and why quantum advantage claims must always report shot counts.

docs.title: 6.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. For \(|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{2}|0\rangle + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}|1\rangle\), find \(\Pr[+]\) and \(\Pr[-]\). [Ans: \(\approx 0.933, 0.067\)]
  2. Compute \(\langle Y\rangle\) for \(|{+}i\rangle\). [Ans: 1]
  3. A two-qubit state is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)\). Measure qubit 1; give both outcomes' probabilities and the resulting states.
  4. Show \(\Delta A = 0\) if and only if \(|\psi\rangle\) is an eigenvector of \(A\).
  5. Verify \([Z,X] = 2iY\) by direct matrix multiplication.
  6. How many shots are needed to distinguish \(p=0.50\) from \(p=0.52\) at two standard errors? [Ans: ≈ 10 000]
  7. Explain why measuring \(Z\) then \(X\) then \(Z\) again on \(|0\rangle\) gives \(|1\rangle\) half the time on the final \(Z\) measurement.

docs.title: 6.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Four postulates: state = unit vector; evolution = unitary; measurement = operators \(\{M_m\}\) with \(\sum M_m^\dagger M_m = I\); composition = tensor product.
  • Born rule: \(\Pr[m] = \langle\psi|P_m|\psi\rangle\); state collapses to \(P_m|\psi\rangle/\sqrt{\Pr[m]}\).
  • Measurement in any basis = rotate to the computational basis, then measure \(Z\).
  • \(\langle A\rangle = \langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle\) is an average over shots; \(\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \frac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|\).
  • Measurement is destructive and yields only \(n\) bits from \(n\) qubits — algorithms must engineer interference before reading out.
  • Statistical error scales as \(1/\sqrt N\) in the number of shots.

Next lesson: L07 — Single-qubit gates and the quantum circuit model.

Practise now: unit1-qubit-lab.html → Measurement Simulator: choose a state, a basis and a shot count, and compare empirical histograms with the Born-rule prediction.

docs.title: Lesson 29: Quantum Neural Networks, the Parameter-Shift Rule and Barren Plateaus
29.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define a quantum neural network and compare it structurally with a classical network.
  2. Derive and apply the parameter-shift rule for analytic gradients.
  3. Explain why finite differences fail on quantum hardware.
  4. State the barren-plateau theorem and compute the shot cost it implies.
  5. List and evaluate the standard mitigation strategies.

docs.title: 29.2 Quantum Neural Networks
docs.text: Definition. A QNN is a parameterised quantum circuit trained by gradient descent so that measurement outcomes approximate a target function.

docs.title: Structural comparison with a classical network
docs.text:
Classical NN QNN Layer = affine map \(W\vec x + \vec b\) Layer = unitary \(U(\vec\theta)\) Non-linearity from the activation function \(\sigma\) Non-linearity from measurement (and from encoding) Backpropagation stores intermediate activations Cannot — measuring destroys the state Gradient by reverse-mode autodiff, \(O(1)\) overhead Gradient by parameter shift, \(O(P)\) circuits Width = number of neurons Width = number of qubits (feature space \(2^n\)) Universal approximator (Cybenko) Truncated Fourier series (Schuld et al., L26)

The most important structural difference. Backpropagation is impossible: you cannot read out intermediate states without collapsing them. This is why quantum gradients cost \(O(P)\) circuit evaluations rather than the \(O(1)\) overhead of classical autodiff, and it is the deepest practical obstacle to scaling QNNs.

docs.title: Where non-linearity comes from
docs.text:
A quantum circuit is linear in the state. Non-linearity in \(f_{\vec\theta}(\vec x)\) enters at two places:

  1. Encoding. \(\vec x \mapsto |\phi(\vec x)\rangle\) is non-linear (e.g. \(x\mapsto\cos\frac{x}{2}\)).
  2. Measurement. \(|\psi\rangle\mapsto\langle\psi|M|\psi\rangle\) is quadratic in the amplitudes.

Some architectures add explicit non-linearity via mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward, or by discarding (tracing out) qubits — the latter is how QCNN pooling works (L30).

docs.title: Why finite differences fail
docs.text:
The naive estimator

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} \approx \frac{f(\theta+h) - f(\theta-h)}{2h} \]

has two error sources:

\[ \text{truncation } O(h^2) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \text{shot noise } O\!\left(\frac{\sigma}{h\sqrt S}\right) . \]

Small \(h\) reduces truncation but amplifies shot noise by \(1/h\). Minimising the total gives \(h^{*} \sim (\sigma/\sqrt S)^{1/3}\), and even at the optimum the error is \(O(S^{-1/3})\) — much worse than the \(O(S^{-1/2})\) achievable with an exact method. On hardware, finite differences are unusable.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Theorem (Parameter-shift rule). Let a gate be \(U(\theta) = e^{-i\theta G/2}\) with a generator \(G\) having exactly two eigenvalues \(\pm1\) (so \(G^2 = I\) — true for \(X, Y, Z\), hence for \(R_x, R_y, R_z\)). Then

\[ \boxed{\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\left[f\!\left(\theta + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) - f\!\left(\theta - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]\ } \]

This is exact, not an approximation. The same circuit is run at two shifted parameter values.

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Write \(f(\theta) = \langle\psi_0|U^\dagger(\theta)\,M\,U(\theta)|\psi_0\rangle\) with \(U(\theta) = e^{-i\theta G/2}\).

Since \(G^2 = I\) (L04):

\[ U(\theta) = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,I - i\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,G . \]

Substituting and expanding,

\[ f(\theta) = \cos^{2}\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\langle M\rangle_0 + \sin^{2}\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\langle GMG\rangle_0 + i\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\langle [M, G]\rangle_0 \]

where \(\langle\cdot\rangle_0 = \langle\psi_0|\cdot|\psi_0\rangle\). Using the double-angle identities \(\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}\), \(\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2}\), \(2\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2} = \sin\theta\):

\[ f(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{\langle M\rangle_0 + \langle GMG\rangle_0}{2}}_{A} + \underbrace{\frac{\langle M\rangle_0 - \langle GMG\rangle_0}{2}}_{B}\cos\theta + \underbrace{\frac{i}{2}\langle[M,G]\rangle_0}_{C}\sin\theta \] \[ \boxed{\ f(\theta) = A + B\cos\theta + C\sin\theta\ } \]

\(f\) is exactly a sinusoid in \(\theta\) — a single Fourier mode. Differentiating:

\[ f'(\theta) = -B\sin\theta + C\cos\theta . \]

Now evaluate the shifted values:

\[ f\!\left(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = A + B\cos\!\left(\theta+\tfrac\pi2\right) + C\sin\!\left(\theta+\tfrac\pi2\right) = A - B\sin\theta + C\cos\theta \] \[ f\!\left(\theta-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = A + B\sin\theta - C\cos\theta \]

Subtracting:

\[ f\!\left(\theta+\tfrac\pi2\right) - f\!\left(\theta-\tfrac\pi2\right) = -2B\sin\theta + 2C\cos\theta = 2f'(\theta) \ \checkmark \qquad\blacksquare \]

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
For \(P\) parameters, a full gradient needs

\[ 2P \ \text{circuit evaluations} . \]

Contrast classical backpropagation: \(O(1)\) times the forward-pass cost, independent of \(P\). For \(P = 1000\), one quantum gradient step costs 2000 circuits. This is the single strongest argument for using SPSA on hardware (L28).

Generalisation. For generators with more than two eigenvalues (e.g. controlled rotations, or \(e^{-i\theta H}\) for a multi-term \(H\)), the four-term shift rule or the stochastic parameter-shift rule applies; the sinusoid becomes a sum of a few frequencies and correspondingly more shifts are needed.

docs.title: The theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (McClean, Boixo, Smelyanskiy, Babbush, Neven, 2018). For a random parameterised circuit whose ansatz forms an approximate unitary 2-design (which deep hardware-efficient ansätze do), the cost gradient satisfies

\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_k}\right] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{Var}\left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_k}\right] \in O\!\left(\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right) . \]

The gradient is exponentially small in the number of qubits, everywhere except an exponentially small region.

docs.title: Why this is fatal
docs.text:
To estimate a gradient of magnitude \(g\) you need shot noise below \(g\):

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt S} \lesssim g \sim 2^{-n/2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\ S = O\!\left(2^{n}\right)\ \text{shots}\ } \]

The measurement cost is exponential in the qubit count, which destroys any quantum advantage. It is not that the optimiser gets stuck in a bad local minimum — the landscape is flat, so the optimiser cannot even tell which way is downhill.

Numerically:

\(n\) Typical \(\lVert\nabla L\rVert\) Shots needed 4 \(6\times10^{-2}\) \(\sim3\times10^{2}\) 10 \(3\times10^{-2}\) \(\sim10^{3}\) 20 \(10^{-3}\) \(\sim10^{6}\) 50 \(3\times10^{-8}\) \(\sim10^{15}\)

At 50 qubits, one gradient component would take over 3 years at 10 kHz.

docs.title: The four causes
docs.text: Cause Mechanism Circuit depth / expressivity deep random circuits approach 2-designs Global cost functions \(\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle\) has exponentially vanishing gradients even at depth \(O(1)\) Entanglement too much entanglement with the "rest" of the register concentrates observables Noise hardware noise induces noise-induced barren plateaus, which grow with depth and cannot be fixed by clever initialisation

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
Strategy Idea Effectiveness Local cost functions use \(\langle Z_0\rangle\) instead of \(\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle\) strong — Cerezo et al. proved gradients vanish only polynomially for \(O(\log n)\)-depth circuits Shallow, structured ansätze QCNN, QAOA, UCCSD, hamiltonian variational ansatz strong — QCNN provably has no barren plateau Identity-block initialisation initialise pairs of blocks as \(V V^\dagger = I\) moderate — helps at the start, may drift Layerwise training train layer 1, freeze, add layer 2, … moderate Correlated / symmetric parameters tie parameters, reducing the effective dimension moderate Warm starts initialise from a classical solution problem-dependent Error mitigation reduces noise-induced plateaus partial

The state of the field, honestly stated. Barren plateaus are the central obstacle to variational QML at scale. Kim/Cerezo and others (2023–24) went further: they showed that many ansätze designed to avoid barren plateaus are, for that very reason, classically simulable — because the structure that keeps gradients large also keeps the state in a small, tractable subspace. This "no free lunch" tension is unresolved and is currently the most important open question in variational quantum algorithms. Students should know it.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Parameter-shift computation
docs.text:
For \(f(\theta) = \langle 0|R_y^\dagger(\theta)ZR_y(\theta)|0\rangle\), compute \(f(\theta)\) analytically, then verify the parameter-shift rule at \(\theta = \pi/3\).

Solution.

\[ R_y(\theta)|0\rangle = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}|0\rangle + \sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}|1\rangle \] \[ f(\theta) = \langle Z\rangle = \cos^{2}\tfrac{\theta}{2} - \sin^{2}\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \cos\theta \]

(Confirming the general form \(f = A + B\cos\theta + C\sin\theta\) with \(A = C = 0\), \(B = 1\).)

Exact derivative. \(f'(\theta) = -\sin\theta\), so at \(\theta = \pi/3\):

\[ f'(\pi/3) = -\sin(\pi/3) = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \mathbf{-0.86603} \]

Parameter shift.

\[ f\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\!\left(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = -0.86603 \] \[ f\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\!\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} = +0.86603 \] \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\big[-0.86603 - 0.86603\big] = \mathbf{-0.86603} \ \checkmark \]

Exact agreement, using only two evaluations of the same circuit at shifted parameters.

Compare finite differences with \(h = 0.01\):

\[ \frac{\cos(\pi/3 + 0.01) - \cos(\pi/3 - 0.01)}{0.02} = \frac{0.49131 - 0.50864}{0.02} = -0.86601 \]

Accurate here — but only because this was computed exactly. With 1024 shots, each \(f\) value carries error \(\approx0.03\), so the finite-difference estimate has error \(\approx \frac{2\times0.03}{0.02} = 3.0\) — completely swamping the true value of \(-0.87\). The parameter-shift estimate has error \(\approx\frac{2\times0.03}{2} = 0.03\), a 100× improvement.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Cost of a full gradient
docs.text:
A QNN has 6 qubits, 4 layers, 2 rotations per qubit per layer. Compute the parameters, circuit evaluations per gradient, and total shots for 100 Adam steps on 50 training samples at 1024 shots.

Solution.

Parameters.

\[ P = 4\ \text{layers}\times 6\ \text{qubits}\times 2 = \mathbf{48} \]

Circuits per gradient (per training sample):

\[ 2P = 96 \]

Per optimisation step (full batch of 50):

\[ 96\times50 = 4800\ \text{circuits} \Rightarrow 4800\times1024 = 4.92\times10^{6}\ \text{shots} \]

For 100 steps:

\[ 4.92\times10^{8}\ \text{shots} \]

Time at 5000 shots/s:

\[ \frac{4.92\times10^{8}}{5000} = 98{,}400\ \mathrm{s} = \mathbf{27.3\ \text{hours}} \]

With SPSA instead (2 evaluations per step):

\[ 2\times50\times1024\times100 = 1.02\times10^{7}\ \text{shots} = \mathbf{34\ \text{minutes}} \] \[ \boxed{\ \text{SPSA is } 48\times \text{ cheaper — exactly the factor } P.\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 3 — Quantifying a barren plateau
docs.text:
A 20-qubit random hardware-efficient ansatz has gradient variance \(\mathrm{Var} = 2^{-20}\). How many shots are needed to resolve a gradient component with signal-to-noise ratio 3? Compare with 8 qubits.

Solution.

At 20 qubits.

\[ \sigma_{\text{grad}} = \sqrt{2^{-20}} = 2^{-10} = 9.77\times10^{-4} \]

This is the typical magnitude of a gradient component. Shot noise in an expectation value is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt S}\) (for an observable with unit variance), and the parameter-shift estimator has noise \(\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt S}\) as well (the factor \(\frac12\) and two terms roughly cancel).

Require SNR \(= 3\):

\[ \frac{9.77\times10^{-4}}{1/\sqrt S} \ge 3 \ \Longrightarrow\ \sqrt S \ge \frac{3}{9.77\times10^{-4}} = 3071 \ \Longrightarrow\ \boxed{S \ge 9.4\times10^{6}} \]

Per gradient component. With \(P = 100\) parameters and 2 circuits each:

\[ 100\times2\times9.4\times10^{6} = 1.9\times10^{9}\ \text{shots per step} \]

At 5000 shots/s: 4.4 days for a single gradient step.

At 8 qubits.

\[ \sigma = 2^{-4} = 0.0625, \qquad S \ge \left(\frac{3}{0.0625}\right)^{2} = 2304 \ \text{shots} \]

Comparison.

\[ \frac{9.4\times10^{6}}{2304} = \mathbf{4080\times} \ \text{more expensive at 20 qubits than at 8.} \]

This is exactly \(2^{12} = 2^{20-8}\) ✓ — the exponential scaling made concrete.

The conclusion for practice. Deep unstructured VQAs are trainable at \(n\lesssim 12\) and become hopeless well before \(n = 30\). Any claim of a scalable variational algorithm must explain how it avoids this.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Local versus global cost functions
docs.text:
Compare \(\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle\) and \(\langle Z_0\rangle\) as cost functions for a shallow \(O(\log n)\)-depth ansatz. Which is trainable, and why?

Solution.

Global cost \(C_G = 1 - \langle\psi|Z^{\otimes n}|\psi\rangle\).

The observable acts non-trivially on all \(n\) qubits. Even for constant-depth circuits, the expectation value of an \(n\)-body observable over a random state concentrates:

\[ \mathrm{Var}\left[\partial_k C_G\right] \in O\!\left(2^{-n}\right) \] \[ \Rightarrow \textbf{barren plateau at any depth.} \]

Intuition: to move \(\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle\) you must coherently align \(n\) qubits at once, and a small parameter change affects that \(n\)-body correlator only at order \(2^{-n}\).

Local cost \(C_L = 1 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\langle\psi|Z_j|\psi\rangle\).

Each term acts on one qubit. Cerezo et al. (2021) proved that for an ansatz of depth \(O(\log n)\),
