\[ \mathrm{Var}\left[\partial_k C_L\right] \in \Omega\!\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\right) \] \[ \Rightarrow \textbf{trainable — the gradient vanishes only polynomially.} \]

Intuition: by the lightcone argument, a single-qubit observable in a shallow circuit is affected only by gates inside its causal cone, which contains \(O(\mathrm{polylog}\,n)\) gates — an effectively small system, immune to \(2^{-n}\) concentration.

Numerical illustration at \(n = 20\), depth \(= \log_2 20 \approx 4\):

Cost \(\mathrm{Var}[\partial C]\) Shots for SNR 3 Global \(\sim 10^{-6}\) \(\sim10^{7}\) Local \(\sim 10^{-2}\) \(\sim10^{2}\)

A five-order-of-magnitude difference from changing one line of code.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Always use local cost functions.}\ } \]

If the problem genuinely demands a global quantity (e.g. state fidelity), use the "local-to-global" trick: train with the local cost first, then switch to the global one for fine-tuning once you are near the solution.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Diagnosing a stalled training run
docs.text:
A VQC with 12 qubits and 8 layers shows a loss that decreases from 0.50 to 0.497 in 500 iterations, then flatlines. Diagnose the cause and give a concrete remediation plan.

Solution.

Diagnosis: barren plateau, not a local minimum. Three pieces of evidence:

  1. Loss barely moved (0.003 over 500 steps) — a local minimum would show fast initial descent then flattening; a plateau is flat from the start.
  2. 12 qubits × 8 layers = 192 parameters with a random hardware-efficient ansatz — deep enough to approximate a 2-design.
  3. Loss ≈ 0.5 = the random-guessing value for balanced binary classification. The model has learned nothing at all.

Confirmatory test. Sample the gradient norm at 20 random parameter settings and check whether

\[ \mathrm{Var}[\partial_k L] \approx 2^{-12} = 2.4\times10^{-4} . \]

If yes, it is a barren plateau; if the variance is large but the optimiser is oscillating, it is a learning-rate or noise problem instead.

Remediation plan, in priority order.

  1. Switch to a local cost function — from \(\langle Z^{\otimes12}\rangle\) to \(\frac{1}{12}\sum_j\langle Z_j\rangle\) or just \(\langle Z_0\rangle\). Highest impact, one line of code.
  2. Cut the depth from 8 layers to 2–3, reducing \(P\) from 192 to ~60. Add depth back only if the model underfits.
  3. Adopt a structured ansatz — a QCNN (L30) on 12 qubits has provably non-vanishing gradients and uses \(O(\log n)\) depth.
  4. Identity-block initialisation — initialise so the circuit starts near identity, where the landscape is not yet flat.
  5. Layerwise training — train 2 layers to convergence, freeze them, add 2 more.
  6. Reduce qubit count — if only 6 features matter, use 6 qubits; the plateau scales as \(2^{-n}\), so halving \(n\) improves gradients by \(2^{6} = 64\times\).
  7. Increase shots — a last resort. This does not fix the plateau, only lets you see through it, and the cost is exponential.

Expected outcome. Steps 1–3 together typically restore training. If the loss still refuses to move below 0.5, the problem is not the plateau but the model class: check that the encoding gives the required Fourier frequencies (L26, Problem 4) and that a classical baseline can separate the data at all.

docs.title: 29.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Apply the parameter-shift rule to \(f(\theta)=\cos\theta\) at \(\theta = 0\). [Ans: 0]
  2. Prove \(f(\theta) = A + B\cos\theta + C\sin\theta\) for any single \(R_y(\theta)\) gate.
  3. Compute the circuits per gradient for \(P = 250\). [Ans: 500]
  4. At \(n=16\), what shots give SNR 2 if \(\sigma_{\text{grad}} = 2^{-8}\)? [Ans: \(\approx2.6\times10^{5}\)]
  5. Why is backpropagation impossible on a quantum computer?
  6. Name three causes of barren plateaus and one mitigation for each.
  7. Explain the trade-off between avoiding barren plateaus and retaining quantum advantage.

docs.title: 29.7 Summary
docs.text:
• A QNN is a PQC trained by gradient descent; non-linearity comes from the encoding and from measurement, not from the gates.
  • Backpropagation is impossible (measurement destroys intermediate states), so gradients cost \(O(P)\) circuits rather than \(O(1)\).
  • Parameter-shift rule: \(\partial_\theta f = \frac12\big[f(\theta+\frac\pi2) - f(\theta-\frac\pi2)\big]\) — exact, because \(f(\theta) = A + B\cos\theta + C\sin\theta\) for any \(R_x/R_y/R_z\) parameter. Requires \(2P\) circuits.
  • Finite differences fail on hardware: error \(O(S^{-1/3})\) versus \(O(S^{-1/2})\), and shot noise is amplified by \(1/h\).
  • Barren plateaus: for 2-design ansätze, \(\mathrm{Var}[\partial L] = O(2^{-n})\), requiring \(O(2^{n})\) shots. The landscape is flat, not merely rugged.
  • Causes: depth/expressivity, global cost functions, excess entanglement, hardware noise.
  • Mitigations: local costs (strongest — restores polynomial scaling for \(O(\log n)\) depth), structured ansätze (QCNN, QAOA), identity-block initialisation, layerwise training.
  • Open tension: ansätze that provably avoid barren plateaus tend to be classically simulable — currently the central unresolved question in variational quantum algorithms.

Next lesson: L30 — Quantum convolutional neural networks.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → Gradient Lab: compare parameter-shift and finite-difference estimates under shot noise, and plot gradient variance against qubit count to see the plateau appear.

docs.title: Lesson 11: Quantum Oracles and the Phase Kick-Back Algorithm
11.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Distinguish the bit oracle \(U_f\) from the phase oracle \(O_f\) and convert between them.
  2. Derive the phase kick-back identity and explain its mechanism.
  3. Explain the role of the ancilla prepared in \(|-\rangle\).
  4. State the query complexity model and why it is the right framework for proving speed-ups.
  5. Recognise phase kick-back as the shared engine of Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani, Simon, Grover and phase estimation.

docs.title: 11.2 The Query (Oracle) Model
docs.text:
Definition (Oracle). An oracle is a black-box unitary implementing an unknown function \(f\). The algorithm may apply the oracle but may not inspect its internals.

Definition (Query complexity). The query complexity of a problem is the minimum number of oracle calls needed to solve it, ignoring all other gate costs.

Why this model? Query complexity is the setting in which provable, unconditional separations between classical and quantum computing exist. Statements like "Deutsch–Jozsa needs 1 quantum query versus \(2^{n-1}+1\) classical queries" are theorems, not conjectures. By contrast, Shor's advantage over classical factoring is only a conjectured separation, since no super-polynomial classical lower bound for factoring is known.

docs.title: The bit oracle (XOR / standard oracle)
docs.text:
\[ U_f\,|x\rangle|y\rangle = |x\rangle\,|y\oplus f(x)\rangle \]

Introduced in L09. It writes the answer into an ancilla register by XOR, is self-inverse, and is built from Toffoli/CNOT gates. With \(y = 0\) it gives \(|x\rangle|f(x)\rangle\).

docs.title: The phase oracle
docs.text:
\[ O_f\,|x\rangle = (-1)^{f(x)}\,|x\rangle \]

The oracle marks solutions with a minus sign and leaves the basis labels untouched. There is no ancilla in the final state, which is exactly what interference needs.

Why the phase oracle is the useful one. After \(O_f\), the register is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle\) — a superposition whose phases encode the entire truth table of \(f\). Applying \(H^{\otimes n}\) converts those phases into amplitudes that interfere. By contrast, the bit oracle leaves the answer entangled with an ancilla, and that entanglement destroys interference (see §5).

docs.title: 11.4 Phase Kick-Back
docs.text:
Theorem (Phase kick-back). Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\) and let the ancilla be prepared in

\[ |-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big) . \]

Then

\[ \boxed{\ U_f\,\big(|x\rangle \otimes |-\rangle\big) = (-1)^{f(x)}\,|x\rangle\otimes|-\rangle\ } \]

Proof. Expand the ancilla and apply the definition of \(U_f\):

\[ U_f|x\rangle\frac{|0\rangle - |1\rangle}{\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big(|x\rangle|0\oplus f(x)\rangle - |x\rangle|1\oplus f(x)\rangle\Big) \] \[ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}|x\rangle\Big(|f(x)\rangle - |\overline{f(x)}\rangle\Big) \]

Now split into two cases.

Case \(f(x) = 0\):

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big) = |-\rangle = (+1)|-\rangle \]

Case \(f(x) = 1\):

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|1\rangle - |0\rangle\big) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle-|1\rangle\big) = (-1)|-\rangle \]

Both cases are summarised by the factor \((-1)^{f(x)}\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
Three observations, each essential:

  1. The ancilla is unchanged. It exits in \(|-\rangle\), exactly as it entered. It is a catalyst: used but not consumed, and never measured.
  2. The phase appears on the input register, even though \(U_f\) nominally writes to the ancilla. The phase has been "kicked back" from target to control — hence the name.
  3. By linearity it applies to superpositions:
\[ U_f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x |x\rangle\right)|-\rangle = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle\right)|-\rangle . \]

Conclusion. One call to the bit oracle \(U_f\), with the ancilla in \(|-\rangle\), implements the phase oracle \(O_f\) on the whole superposition. This converts the entire truth table of \(f\) into a pattern of \(\pm\) signs in a single query.

docs.title: Why |-⟩?
docs.text:
\(|-\rangle\) is the \(-1\) eigenvector of \(X\): \(X|-\rangle = -|-\rangle\). The oracle applies \(X^{f(x)}\) to the ancilla conditioned on \(x\), and applying \(X\) to its own eigenvector returns the eigenvalue as a phase.

General principle (this is the whole idea behind phase estimation, L19). If \(U|u\rangle = e^{i\theta}|u\rangle\) and we apply a controlled-\(U\) with the target in \(|u\rangle\):

\[ \mathrm{c}\text{-}U\,\big(|c\rangle|u\rangle\big) = e^{i\theta c}|c\rangle|u\rangle . \]

The eigenvalue phase is transferred to the control. Phase kick-back is the special case \(U = X\), \(\theta = \pi\).

docs.title: The universal algorithm template
docs.text:
Every algorithm in Unit II has this shape:

Step 1  Prepare  |0>^n  |1>
Step 2  Apply    H^(x)n on the input register,  H on the ancilla   -> ancilla is |->
Step 3  Query    U_f once (or a few times)  -> phases (-1)^{f(x)} appear
Step 4  Interfere: apply H^(x)n (or QFT, or Grover diffusion)
Step 5  Measure the input register

Steps 3–4 are the heart: write phases, then convert phases into amplitudes.

docs.title: 11.5 The Minimal Phase Kick-Back Circuit
docs.text:
For \(n = 1\) the oracle for \(f(x) = x\) is simply a CNOT (control = input, target = ancilla). The ancilla is prepared in \(|-\rangle\) by applying \(X\) then \(H\) to \(|0\rangle\):

q0 (input)   : --[H]--------*---[H]---[M]--
                            |
q1 (ancilla) : --[X]--[H]--[X]-------------
                 \____ ____/
                      v
                prepares |->

Trace.

\[ |0\rangle|0\rangle \xrightarrow{X \text{ on } q_1} |0\rangle|1\rangle \xrightarrow{H\otimes H} |+\rangle|-\rangle \] \[ \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CNOT}} \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big((-1)^{0}|0\rangle + (-1)^{1}|1\rangle\big)|-\rangle = |-\rangle|-\rangle \] \[ \xrightarrow{H \text{ on } q_0} |1\rangle|-\rangle \]

Measuring \(q_0\) gives 1 with certainty. The oracle "wrote" \(f(0)\oplus f(1) = 1\) into \(q_0\) using one query. This tiny circuit is already the Deutsch algorithm (L12).

docs.title: 11.6 Why the Ancilla Must Be |-⟩ (the Entanglement Trap)
docs.text:
Suppose a student prepares the ancilla in \(|0\rangle\) instead. Then

\[ U_f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x|x\rangle\right)|0\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x |x\rangle|f(x)\rangle . \]

The input register is now entangled with the ancilla. Its reduced state is the mixture

\[ \rho_{\text{in}} = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_x |x\rangle\langle x| = \frac{I}{2^n}, \]

which is maximally mixed — all coherence is gone. Applying \(H^{\otimes n}\) to a maximally mixed state does nothing useful, and the subsequent measurement is uniformly random.

The general rule. Any record of \(x\) left anywhere — in an ancilla, in a "garbage" register, in the environment — destroys the interference. This is why oracle implementations must uncompute their scratch qubits, and it is the same phenomenon as decoherence.

Preparing the ancilla in \(|-\rangle\) avoids this entirely: it factorises out of the state, so the input register stays pure and coherent.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Verifying kick-back for a constant function
docs.text:
Let \(f(x) = 1\) for all \(x \in \{0,1\}^2\). Compute \(U_f\left(\frac12\sum_x|x\rangle\right)|-\rangle\) and then apply \(H^{\otimes2}\) to the input register. What is measured?

Solution. By phase kick-back with \(f(x)=1\) for every \(x\):

\[ U_f\left(\frac12\sum_x|x\rangle\right)|-\rangle = \left(\frac12\sum_x (-1)^1|x\rangle\right)|-\rangle = -\left(\frac12\sum_x|x\rangle\right)|-\rangle \]

The result is \(-|{+}{+}\rangle|-\rangle\) — the state is unchanged up to a global phase. A constant function contributes the same phase to every branch, and a uniform phase is unobservable.

Apply \(H^{\otimes2}\):

\[ H^{\otimes 2}\left(-|{+}{+}\rangle\right) = -|00\rangle . \]

Measuring gives \(\mathbf{00}\) with probability 1.

Insight. A constant \(f\) returns the register to \(|00\rangle\). This will be exactly the decision rule of Deutsch–Jozsa: all zeros ⟹ constant.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Kick-back for a balanced function
docs.text:
Now let \(f(x_1x_2) = x_1\) (balanced: half the inputs give 0, half give 1). Repeat Problem 1.

Solution.

\[ \frac12\sum_x (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle = \frac12\Big[(-1)^0|00\rangle + (-1)^0|01\rangle + (-1)^1|10\rangle + (-1)^1|11\rangle\Big] \] \[ = \frac12\big(|00\rangle + |01\rangle - |10\rangle - |11\rangle\big) \]

Factorise:

\[ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big)\otimes\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle+|1\rangle\big) = |-\rangle\otimes|+\rangle \]

Apply \(H^{\otimes2}\): \(H|-\rangle = |1\rangle\) and \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\), so the state becomes

\[ |10\rangle . \]

Measuring gives \(\mathbf{10}\) with probability 1 — not \(00\).

Insight. Balanced \(f\) never returns \(00\). Comparing Problems 1 and 2 gives the complete Deutsch–Jozsa decision rule after one query, versus \(2^{n-1}+1 = 3\) classical queries for \(n=2\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Converting a bit oracle into a phase oracle by circuit
docs.text:
Show explicitly that the circuit "\(X\), \(H\) on the ancilla; \(U_f\); \(H\), \(X\) on the ancilla" implements the phase oracle \(O_f\) exactly, restoring the ancilla to \(|0\rangle\).

Solution. Start with \(|x\rangle|0\rangle\).

Step 1 — ancilla preparation. \(X\) then \(H\):

\[ |0\rangle \xrightarrow{X} |1\rangle \xrightarrow{H} |-\rangle \]

State: \(|x\rangle|-\rangle\).

Step 2 — oracle. Phase kick-back:

\[ U_f|x\rangle|-\rangle = (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle|-\rangle \]

Step 3 — ancilla restoration. \(H\) then \(X\):

\[ |-\rangle \xrightarrow{H} |1\rangle \xrightarrow{X} |0\rangle \]

Final state:

\[ (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle\otimes|0\rangle = \big(O_f|x\rangle\big)\otimes|0\rangle \ \checkmark \]

The ancilla is returned to \(|0\rangle\) and completely disentangled, so it can be reused. This "prepare–query–unprepare" sandwich is the standard idiom in Qiskit and Cirq for building a phase oracle from a Boolean circuit.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Generalised kick-back with a controlled-U
docs.text:
Let \(U|u\rangle = e^{2\pi i\theta}|u\rangle\). Compute the output of the circuit: \(H\) on the control, controlled-\(U\), \(H\) on the control, with the target held in \(|u\rangle\). Find \(\Pr[0]\).

Solution.

\[ |0\rangle|u\rangle \xrightarrow{H} \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle + |1\rangle\big)|u\rangle \]

Apply controlled-\(U\) (acts only on the \(|1\rangle\) branch):

\[ \to \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\theta}|1\rangle\big)|u\rangle \]

The eigenvalue phase has moved onto the control; the target is untouched. Apply \(H\):

\[ \to \frac{1}{2}\Big[(1 + e^{2\pi i\theta})|0\rangle + (1 - e^{2\pi i\theta})|1\rangle\Big]|u\rangle \] \[ \Pr[0] = \left|\frac{1+e^{2\pi i\theta}}{2}\right|^2 = \cos^2(\pi\theta), \qquad \Pr[1] = \sin^2(\pi\theta) \]

Check. At \(\theta = 1/2\) (i.e. \(U = X\), \(|u\rangle = |-\rangle\), eigenvalue \(-1\)): \(\Pr[0] = \cos^2(\pi/2) = 0\), so the measurement gives 1 with certainty — reproducing the minimal circuit of §4 ✓.

This is the Hadamard test, and it is precisely the building block of quantum phase estimation (L19), which in turn drives Shor's algorithm and HHL.

docs.title: Problem 5 — What goes wrong with the wrong ancilla
docs.text:
Repeat Problem 2 (\(f(x_1x_2) = x_1\)) but with the ancilla prepared in \(|0\rangle\). Compute the reduced state of the input register and the measurement statistics after \(H^{\otimes2}\).

Solution.

\[ U_f\left(\frac12\sum_x|x\rangle\right)|0\rangle = \frac12\Big[|00\rangle|0\rangle + |01\rangle|0\rangle + |10\rangle|1\rangle + |11\rangle|1\rangle\Big] \]

The input register is entangled with the ancilla. Trace out the ancilla:

\[ \rho_{\text{in}} = \frac14\Big[\big(|00\rangle+|01\rangle\big)\big(\langle00|+\langle01|\big) + \big(|10\rangle+|11\rangle\big)\big(\langle10|+\langle11|\big)\Big] \]

This is a mixture of \(|0\rangle|+\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle|+\rangle\) — the coherence between the \(x_1=0\) and \(x_1=1\) blocks has been destroyed.

Apply \(H^{\otimes2}\) to each branch:

  • \(|0\rangle|+\rangle \to |+\rangle|0\rangle \to\) measuring gives \(00\) or \(10\), each w.p. ½.
  • \(|1\rangle|+\rangle \to |-\rangle|0\rangle \to\) measuring gives \(00\) or \(10\), each w.p. ½.

Result: \(\Pr[00] = \Pr[10] = \frac12\).

Compare with Problem 2, where the answer was \(10\) with certainty. Seeing \(00\) would wrongly indicate "constant". The algorithm is broken.

Diagnosis. The ancilla acted as a which-path detector. Once the environment (here, the ancilla) records which branch was taken, interference is impossible — the same physics as the double-slit experiment losing its fringes when the slit is monitored.

docs.title: 11.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Verify phase kick-back explicitly for \(n=1\), \(f(0)=1\), \(f(1)=0\).
  2. Show \(O_f^2 = I\) for any Boolean \(f\).
  3. For \(f(x_1x_2) = x_1\oplus x_2\), compute \(\frac12\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle\) and apply \(H^{\otimes2}\). [Ans: \(|11\rangle\)]
  4. In Problem 4, what value of \(\theta\) makes \(\Pr[0] = \Pr[1] = \frac12\)? [Ans: \(\theta = 1/4\) or \(3/4\)]
  5. Explain why the ancilla in phase kick-back is never measured.
  6. If a circuit leaves a garbage qubit entangled with \(x\), describe two ways to fix it.
  7. Give the query complexity of determining \(f(0)\oplus f(1)\) classically and quantumly. [Ans: 2 and 1]

docs.title: 11.9 Summary
docs.text:
• The query model measures oracle calls; it is where provable quantum–classical separations live.
  • Bit oracle: \(U_f|x\rangle|y\rangle = |x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle\). Phase oracle: \(O_f|x\rangle = (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle\).
  • Phase kick-back: \(U_f|x\rangle|-\rangle = (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle|-\rangle\) — one bit-oracle query implements the phase oracle on an entire superposition, leaving the ancilla untouched.
  • The generalised version transfers an eigenvalue \(e^{i\theta}\) of \(U\) onto a control qubit; this is the Hadamard test and the seed of phase estimation.
  • The ancilla must be \(|-\rangle\): an ancilla in \(|0\rangle\) entangles with the input, destroys coherence, and randomises the output. Uncompute all garbage.
  • Universal template: superpose → kick back phases → interfere → measure.

Next lesson: L12 — The Deutsch algorithm.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Oracle Explorer: pick any \(f\), choose the ancilla state, and watch the phase pattern and final measurement histogram side by side.

docs.title: Lesson 9: Quantum Parallelism, Interference and the No-Cloning Theorem
9.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Construct the oracle unitary \(U_f\) for a classical Boolean function and explain why the extra register is needed.
  2. State what quantum parallelism does and, crucially, what it does not give you.
  3. Explain constructive and destructive interference of amplitudes and identify it in a circuit.
  4. Prove the no-cloning theorem and state the related no-deleting and no-broadcasting results.
  5. Describe the consequences of no-cloning for error correction, eavesdropping (BB84) and classical intuition.

docs.title: The reversibility problem
docs.text:
Consider \(f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^m\). Most such functions are not injective, so the map \(|x\rangle \mapsto |f(x)\rangle\) is not invertible and cannot be unitary. Example: \(f(x) = 0\) for all \(x\) would map every basis state onto one state — that collapses the space.

Solution: the standard oracle construction. Use two registers and record the answer with XOR:

\[ \boxed{\ U_f\,|x\rangle|y\rangle = |x\rangle\,|y \oplus f(x)\rangle\ } \]

where \(\oplus\) is bitwise XOR.

\(U_f\) is always unitary. It is a permutation of the computational basis, and it is its own inverse:

\[ U_f^2 |x\rangle|y\rangle = U_f|x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle = |x\rangle|y \oplus f(x)\oplus f(x)\rangle = |x\rangle|y\rangle \]

since \(a\oplus a = 0\). So \(U_f^2 = I\), i.e. \(U_f = U_f^{-1} = U_f^\dagger\). \(\blacksquare\)

Reading out \(f(x)\). Set \(y = 0\): \(U_f|x\rangle|0\rangle = |x\rangle|f(x)\rangle\).

Terminology. \(|x\rangle\) is the query/input register; \(|y\rangle\) is the ancilla/output register. In the query complexity model we count calls to \(U_f\), ignoring the cost of the internal gates — this is how all Unit II speed-ups are stated and proved.

Physical implementation. Any Boolean circuit made of AND, OR, NOT is converted into Toffoli and CNOT gates, with ancillas for intermediate results, which are then uncomputed (run the circuit backwards) to free them. Uncomputation is essential: leftover "garbage" ancillas remain entangled with the input and destroy the interference the algorithm depends on.

docs.title: 9.3 Quantum Parallelism
docs.text:
Prepare the input register in a uniform superposition and apply \(U_f\) once:

\[ |0\rangle^{\otimes n}|0\rangle \xrightarrow{H^{\otimes n}\otimes I} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{x=0}^{2^n-1}|x\rangle|0\rangle \] \[ \xrightarrow{\ U_f\ } \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{x=0}^{2^n-1}|x\rangle\,|f(x)\rangle \]

A single application of \(U_f\) has produced a state containing all \(2^n\) input–output pairs simultaneously. This is quantum parallelism.

docs.title: The catch — and it is a big one
docs.text:
Measuring this state gives one random pair \((x, f(x))\) — exactly what one classical evaluation of \(f\) at a random point would give. Quantum parallelism by itself provides zero advantage.

The central insight of the whole course. The exponentially many values of \(f\) are present in the amplitudes but are not accessible. A useful algorithm must apply further unitaries that make the amplitudes of undesired answers cancel and those of the desired answer add. That mechanism is interference, and it — not parallelism — is where the speed-up comes from.

Formally, this is why every algorithm in Unit II has the shape:

\[ \text{superpose} \ \to\ \text{query } U_f \ \to\ \textbf{interfere} \ \to\ \text{measure} \]

docs.title: 9.4 Interference
docs.text:
Because amplitudes are complex numbers, they can cancel. Probabilities never can.

Classical: \(\Pr[\text{outcome}] = \sum_{\text{paths}} \Pr[\text{path}] \ge 0\) — contributions only accumulate.

Quantum: \(\Pr[\text{outcome}] = \left|\sum_{\text{paths}} A_{\text{path}}\right|^2\) — amplitudes add first, and can cancel.

docs.title: The minimal example
docs.text:
Consider \(H\) applied twice to \(|0\rangle\).

\[ |0\rangle \xrightarrow{H} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|1\rangle \xrightarrow{H} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\tfrac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\right) + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\tfrac{|0\rangle-|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\right) \]

Collect terms:

\[ |0\rangle: \ \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1 \qquad \text{(constructive)} \] \[ |1\rangle: \ \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0 \qquad \text{(destructive)} \] \[ H^2|0\rangle = |0\rangle . \]

The two paths to \(|1\rangle\) cancel exactly. A classical random walk taking two fair coin flips would land on 1 with probability \(\frac12\); the quantum version lands on 0 with certainty.

docs.title: Amplitude bookkeeping
docs.text:
For a circuit \(U = U_T\cdots U_2U_1\), the amplitude to go from \(|i\rangle\) to \(|j\rangle\) is a sum over all computational paths:

\[ \langle j|U|i\rangle = \sum_{k_1,\dots,k_{T-1}} \langle j|U_T|k_{T-1}\rangle\cdots\langle k_1|U_1|i\rangle . \]

Designing a quantum algorithm = arranging the phases along these paths so that everything except the answer cancels. This is exactly what the Grover diffusion operator (L21) and the QFT (L18) do.

docs.title: 9.5 The No-Cloning Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Wootters–Zurek, Dieks, 1982). There is no unitary \(U\) such that for every state \(|\psi\rangle\),

\[ U\big(|\psi\rangle \otimes |s\rangle\big) = |\psi\rangle\otimes|\psi\rangle \]

for some fixed blank state \(|s\rangle\).

Proof. Suppose such a \(U\) existed. Take two arbitrary states \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\):

\[ U|\psi\rangle|s\rangle = |\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle, \qquad U|\phi\rangle|s\rangle = |\phi\rangle|\phi\rangle . \]

Take the inner product of the two left-hand sides. Since \(U\) is unitary it preserves inner products:

\[ \big(\langle\psi|\langle s|\big)U^\dagger U\big(|\phi\rangle|s\rangle\big) = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle\,\langle s|s\rangle = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle . \]

Now the right-hand sides:

\[ \big(\langle\psi|\langle\psi|\big)\big(|\phi\rangle|\phi\rangle\big) = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle^2 . \]

Equating, and writing \(z = \langle\psi|\phi\rangle\):

\[ z = z^2 \ \Longrightarrow\ z(z-1) = 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ z = 0 \text{ or } z = 1 . \]

So cloning is possible only if the two states are orthogonal (\(z=0\)) or identical (\(z=1\)). A universal cloner would have to work for all pairs, including those with \(0 < |z| < 1\). Contradiction. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: What no-cloning does and does not forbid
docs.text:
Allowed Forbidden Copying known states (just re-prepare them) Copying an unknown state Copying states from a known orthonormal set Copying non-orthogonal states Copying classical bits (they are orthogonal) Perfect universal cloning Approximate cloning (best fidelity \(5/6\) for qubits) Perfect cloning Moving a state (teleportation) Duplicating a state

Note that CNOT does copy basis states: \(\mathrm{CNOT}|x\rangle|0\rangle = |x\rangle|x\rangle\) for \(x\in\{0,1\}\). But applied to a superposition,

\[ \mathrm{CNOT}\big(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\big)|0\rangle = \alpha|00\rangle + \beta|11\rangle \ \ne\ \big(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\big)^{\otimes2} . \]

It produces entanglement, not a copy. This is the concrete way no-cloning shows up in practice.

docs.title: Companion theorems
docs.text:
• No-deleting theorem (Pati–Braunstein, 2000): given two copies of an unknown state, you cannot unitarily delete one.
  • No-broadcasting theorem: the mixed-state generalisation — a set of non-commuting density matrices cannot be broadcast.
  • No-hiding theorem: information lost from a system must be present somewhere in the environment — the basis of black-hole information arguments.

docs.title: 9.6 Consequences of No-Cloning
docs.text:
(a) Quantum error correction must be indirect. The classical repetition code copies a bit three times. That is illegal here. Instead, QEC encodes one logical qubit into an entangled state of several physical qubits and measures stabilisers — operators that reveal the error without revealing (and hence collapsing) the encoded state. Developed in L10.

(b) Quantum cryptography becomes possible. In BB84, Alice sends qubits in randomly chosen bases. Eve cannot copy them to measure later; any measurement she makes disturbs the state and introduces a detectable error rate (25 % if she measures every qubit in a random basis). Security rests on a law of physics, not on computational hardness.

(c) No superluminal signalling. If cloning were possible, Alice could make many copies of her half of a Bell pair and infer Bob's measurement basis instantly. No-cloning closes that loophole.

(d) Amplification is impossible. A weak quantum signal cannot be amplified without noise, which is why long-distance quantum communication needs quantum repeaters rather than amplifiers.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Building an oracle
docs.text:
Let \(f:\{0,1\}^2 \to \{0,1\}\) with \(f(x_1x_2) = x_1 \wedge x_2\). Write the action of \(U_f\) on all basis states, give a circuit, and compute \(U_f\) applied to a uniform superposition.

Solution.

Action \(U_f|x_1x_2\rangle|y\rangle = |x_1x_2\rangle|y\oplus (x_1\wedge x_2)\rangle\):

Input \(\lvert x_1x_2 y\rangle\) \(f(x)\) Output \(\lvert 000\rangle\) 0 \(\lvert 000\rangle\) \(\lvert 010\rangle\) 0 \(\lvert 010\rangle\) \(\lvert 100\rangle\) 0 \(\lvert 100\rangle\) \(\lvert 110\rangle\) 1 \(\lvert 111\rangle\) \(\lvert 111\rangle\) 1 \(\lvert 110\rangle\)

Circuit: a single Toffoli gate with controls \(x_1,x_2\) and target \(y\). (This is why Toffoli is the universal classical gate — AND is realised directly.)

Applying to the uniform superposition with \(y = 0\):

\[ U_f\left(\frac12\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^2}|x\rangle\right)|0\rangle = \frac12\big(|00\rangle|0\rangle + |01\rangle|0\rangle + |10\rangle|0\rangle + |11\rangle|1\rangle\big) . \]

All four input–output pairs, produced by one call to \(U_f\). But measuring returns a single random pair — parallelism without interference is worthless.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Interference in a two-path circuit
docs.text:
A qubit starts in \(|0\rangle\). Apply \(H\), then \(P(\phi) = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\phi})\), then \(H\). Find \(\Pr[0]\) as a function of \(\phi\), and evaluate at \(\phi = 0, \pi/2, \pi\).

Solution.

\[ |0\rangle \xrightarrow{H} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle) \xrightarrow{P(\phi)} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle + e^{i\phi}|1\rangle) \] \[ \xrightarrow{H} \tfrac{1}{2}\big[(|0\rangle+|1\rangle) + e^{i\phi}(|0\rangle - |1\rangle)\big] \] \[ = \frac{1+e^{i\phi}}{2}|0\rangle + \frac{1-e^{i\phi}}{2}|1\rangle \] \[ \Pr[0] = \left|\frac{1+e^{i\phi}}{2}\right|^2 = \frac{(1+\cos\phi)^2 + \sin^2\phi}{4} = \frac{2+2\cos\phi}{4} = \cos^2\frac{\phi}{2} \] \(\phi\) \(\Pr[0]\) Interference \(0\) \(1\) Fully constructive on \(\lvert 0\rangle\) \(\pi/2\) \(0.5\) Partial \(\pi\) \(0\) Fully destructive on \(\lvert 0\rangle\)

This is the quantum interferometer, and \(\Pr[0] = \cos^2(\phi/2)\) is the fringe pattern. A phase written in the middle of the circuit becomes a measurable probability at the end. Every algorithm in Unit II is an instance of this template: the oracle writes a phase, and the final Hadamards read it out.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Applying the no-cloning proof
docs.text:
Show explicitly that no unitary can clone both \(|0\rangle\) and \(|+\rangle\).

Solution. Assume \(U|0\rangle|0\rangle = |0\rangle|0\rangle\) and \(U|+\rangle|0\rangle = |+\rangle|+\rangle\).

Take inner products of the inputs:

\[ \big(\langle 0|\langle 0|\big)\big(|+\rangle|0\rangle\big) = \langle 0|+\rangle\langle0|0\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot 1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.7071 \]

Take inner products of the outputs:

\[ \big(\langle0|\langle0|\big)\big(|+\rangle|+\rangle\big) = \langle0|+\rangle^2 = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2 = \frac12 = 0.5 \]

Unitaries preserve inner products, so we would need \(0.7071 = 0.5\). Contradiction.

Alternative constructive argument. Suppose \(U\) clones the basis, i.e. \(U|x\rangle|0\rangle = |x\rangle|x\rangle\) for \(x \in \{0,1\}\). Then by linearity,

\[ U|+\rangle|0\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(U|0\rangle|0\rangle + U|1\rangle|0\rangle\big) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|00\rangle + |11\rangle\big) = |\Phi^+\rangle . \]

But a true clone would be

\[ |+\rangle|+\rangle = \tfrac12\big(|00\rangle+|01\rangle+|10\rangle+|11\rangle\big) . \]

Overlap: \(\langle\Phi^+|{+}{+}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac12(1 + 1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), not 1. Linearity itself forbids cloning — you get entanglement instead.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Eavesdropping in BB84
docs.text:
In BB84, Alice sends a qubit in a basis chosen at random from \(\{Z, X\}\). Eve intercepts, measures in a random basis, and re-sends the collapsed state. Bob measures in Alice's basis. What is the probability that Bob's bit differs from Alice's?

Solution. Condition on Eve's basis choice.

Case 1: Eve picks the same basis as Alice (probability \(\frac12\)). Her measurement returns Alice's bit and leaves the state unchanged. Bob then gets the correct bit with probability 1. Error probability = 0.

Case 2: Eve picks the wrong basis (probability \(\frac12\)). Say Alice sent \(|0\rangle\) and Eve measures in \(X\). She gets \(|+\rangle\) or \(|-\rangle\) with probability ½ each and re-sends it. Bob measures in \(Z\):

\[ \Pr[\text{Bob gets }1 \mid \text{state } |\pm\rangle] = \tfrac12 . \]

Error probability = ½.

Total:

\[ \Pr[\text{error}] = \tfrac12\cdot 0 + \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \boxed{\tfrac14 = 25\%} \]

Significance. Alice and Bob publicly compare a random sample of their bits. A 25 % mismatch rate where 0 % is expected exposes Eve immediately. Eve cannot avoid this by cloning the qubit and measuring later — no-cloning forbids it. The security is information-theoretic, not computational: a quantum computer does not help Eve.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Why parallelism alone fails
docs.text:
A student proposes: "Prepare \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x |x\rangle|f(x)\rangle\), then measure the second register; if I see \(f(x)=1\) the first register collapses to the superposition of all solutions, so I have solved SAT." Identify the flaw and quantify it.

Solution. The mechanics are correct. Measuring the second register and obtaining 1 leaves the first register in

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{x : f(x)=1}|x\rangle , \]

where \(M\) is the number of solutions. Two things then go wrong.

(1) The probability of seeing 1 is tiny.

\[ \Pr[f(x)=1] = \frac{M}{2^n} . \]

For a hard SAT instance with, say, a unique solution and \(n = 100\):

\[ \Pr = \frac{1}{2^{100}} \approx 7.9\times10^{-31} . \]

Expected number of repetitions before success: \(2^{100}\) — exactly the classical brute-force cost. No speed-up whatsoever.

(2) Even after a successful projection, measuring the first register returns one uniformly random solution — which is all you wanted, but you paid \(2^n\) attempts to get there.

What actually works. Grover's algorithm (L21–L22) does not measure the ancilla. It uses the oracle to write a phase on solutions and then applies the diffusion operator to grow their amplitudes gradually, reaching near-certainty after only

\[ \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2^n}{M}} \]

iterations — a quadratic improvement, and it comes entirely from interference.

Conclusion. Superposition is free; interference is the algorithm.

docs.title: 9.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Construct \(U_f\) for \(f(x) = x \oplus 1\) (NOT) on one qubit. Which gate is it? [Ans: CNOT then \(X\) on the target]
  2. Show \(U_f^\dagger = U_f\) for any Boolean \(f\).
  3. In the interferometer of Problem 2, what \(\phi\) gives \(\Pr[1] = 0.25\)? [Ans: \(\phi = \pi/3\)]
  4. Prove that cloning would allow superluminal signalling using a shared Bell pair.
  5. If Eve measures only 50 % of the qubits in BB84, what error rate do Alice and Bob observe? [Ans: 12.5 %]
  6. Explain why \(\mathrm{CNOT}|\psi\rangle|0\rangle\) is not a clone for a general \(|\psi\rangle\), using concurrence.
  7. Why must ancilla qubits be uncomputed before the final interference step?

docs.title: 9.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Classical \(f\) becomes the unitary oracle \(U_f|x\rangle|y\rangle = |x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle\); it is self-inverse and is built from Toffoli/CNOT gates.
  • Quantum parallelism evaluates \(f\) on all \(2^n\) inputs with one query — but measurement returns only one random pair, so it gives no advantage by itself.
  • Interference — amplitudes adding and cancelling — is the actual source of quantum speed-up. Template: superpose → query → interfere → measure.
  • No-cloning: unitarity and linearity forbid copying an unknown state; only orthogonal or identical states can be cloned.
  • Consequences: error correction must use stabiliser measurements rather than copies; BB84 gains physics-based security; no superluminal signalling; no noiseless amplification.

Next lesson: L10 — Quantum teleportation, superdense coding and error correction.

Practise now: unit1-qubit-lab.html → Interference Lab: sweep \(\phi\) in the Mach–Zehnder circuit of Problem 2 and watch the fringe pattern \(\cos^2(\phi/2)\) appear.

docs.title: 19.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the phase estimation problem and its input requirements.
  2. Derive the QPE circuit and show why the inverse QFT extracts the phase.
  3. Prove the exact case (\(\theta\) an \(n\)-bit binary fraction) gives the answer with probability 1.
  4. Apply the precision–probability theorem to choose the number of counting qubits.
  5. Recognise QPE as the central subroutine of Shor's algorithm, HHL and quantum chemistry.

docs.title: 19.2 The Problem
docs.text:
Given:

  • A unitary \(U\) (as a circuit, so that controlled-\(U^{2^k}\) can be applied).
  • An eigenstate \(|u\rangle\) with \(U|u\rangle = e^{2\pi i\theta}|u\rangle\), \(\theta\in[0,1)\).

Find: an estimate of \(\theta\) to \(n\) bits of precision.

Why \([0,1)\)? Every eigenvalue of a unitary has modulus 1, so it can be written \(e^{2\pi i\theta}\) with \(\theta \in [0,1)\). The problem is to extract that real number.

QPE is the most important subroutine in quantum computing. Shor's order finding is QPE applied to the modular-multiplication operator. HHL is QPE applied to \(e^{iAt}\). Quantum chemistry algorithms are QPE applied to \(e^{-iHt}\) to find ground-state energies. Learn it once, use it everywhere.

docs.title: 19.3 The Circuit
docs.text:
Two registers:

  • Counting register: \(t\) qubits, initialised to \(|0\rangle^{\otimes t}\). Larger \(t\) ⟶ more precision.
  • Eigenstate register: holds \(|u\rangle\).
              t counting qubits
  |0> --[H]--------------------*----------------.
  |0> --[H]-----------------*--|--- [ QFT^-1 ] --[M]--> estimate of theta
  |0> --[H]--------------*--|--|----------------'
                         |  |  |
  |u> -----------------[U^1][U^2][U^4]--- ... ---------  (unchanged)

The \(j\)-th counting qubit (from the bottom) controls \(U^{2^{j}}\).

docs.title: 19.4 Derivation
docs.text:
Step 1 — superpose the counting register.

\[ |\psi_1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^t-1}|k\rangle\ \otimes|u\rangle \]

Step 2 — controlled powers of \(U\). The stack of controlled-\(U^{2^j}\) gates applies \(U^k\) to the eigenstate register when the counting register holds \(|k\rangle\). Because \(|u\rangle\) is an eigenstate,

\[ U^{k}|u\rangle = e^{2\pi i k\theta}|u\rangle , \]

so by generalised phase kick-back (L11 §3.2) the phase lands on the counting register:

\[ |\psi_2\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^t-1}e^{2\pi i k\theta}|k\rangle\ \otimes|u\rangle \]

The eigenstate register is unchanged and unentangled. All the information is now in the phase ramp of the counting register.

Step 3 — recognise the state. Compare with the QFT definition (L18):

\[ \mathrm{QFT}|j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_k e^{2\pi ijk/2^t}|k\rangle . \]

If \(\theta\) happens to equal \(j/2^t\) exactly for some integer \(j\), then \(|\psi_2\rangle\) is exactly \(\mathrm{QFT}|j\rangle\).

Step 4 — apply the inverse QFT.

\[ |\psi_3\rangle = \mathrm{QFT}^{-1}|\psi_2\rangle \]

Step 5 — measure the counting register, obtaining an integer \(m\). Output

\[ \tilde\theta = \frac{m}{2^t} . \]

docs.title: 19.5 The Exact Case
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(\theta = j/2^t\) for an integer \(0\le j < 2^t\) — equivalently, \(\theta\) has an exact \(t\)-bit binary expansion — then QPE returns \(m = j\) with probability 1.

Proof. By Step 3, \(|\psi_2\rangle = \mathrm{QFT}|j\rangle\) exactly. Applying the inverse:

\[ |\psi_3\rangle = \mathrm{QFT}^{-1}\mathrm{QFT}|j\rangle = |j\rangle . \]

Measurement returns \(j\) deterministically. \(\blacksquare\)

Interpretation. Writing \(\theta = 0.\theta_1\theta_2\cdots\theta_t\) in binary, the counting register ends up holding exactly those \(t\) bits.

docs.title: 19.6 The General Case and the Precision Theorem
docs.text:
When \(\theta\) is not an exact \(t\)-bit fraction, the output spreads around the nearest fraction. Let \(b\) be the integer such that \(b/2^t\) is the best \(t\)-bit approximation, and let \(\delta = \theta - b/2^t\) with \(|\delta| \le 2^{-(t+1)}\).

Amplitude of outcome \(m\).

\[ A_m = \frac{1}{2^t}\sum_{k=0}^{2^t-1}e^{2\pi ik(\theta - m/2^t)} = \frac{1}{2^t}\cdot\frac{1 - e^{2\pi i 2^t(\theta - m/2^t)}}{1 - e^{2\pi i(\theta - m/2^t)}} \]

(a finite geometric series), giving

\[ \Pr[m] = |A_m|^2 = \frac{1}{2^{2t}}\left|\frac{\sin\big(\pi 2^t(\theta - m/2^t)\big)} {\sin\big(\pi(\theta-m/2^t)\big)}\right|^2 . \]

This is the Fejér / Dirichlet kernel — a sharply peaked function centred at \(m = 2^t\theta\).

Theorem (Standard bound). \(\Pr[m = b] \ge \dfrac{4}{\pi^2} \approx 0.405\).

Theorem (Precision–probability). To obtain \(\theta\) accurate to \(n\) bits with success probability at least \(1-\epsilon\), use

\[ \boxed{\ t = n + \left\lceil \log_2\!\left(2 + \frac{1}{2\epsilon}\right)\right\rceil \ \text{counting qubits}\ } \]

Worked values.

Desired precision \(n\) Failure \(\epsilon\) Extra qubits Total \(t\) 4 0.25 2 6 8 0.10 3 11 10 0.01 6 16 20 0.01 6 26

Cost. The controlled-\(U^{2^j}\) gates require \(1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^{t-1} = 2^t - 1\) applications of \(U\), so the cost is \(O(2^t)\) applications — exponential in the number of bits of precision. This is why QPE gives high precision only when \(U\) itself can be exponentiated cheaply (as modular exponentiation can, by repeated squaring).

docs.title: 19.7 What If You Do Not Have the Eigenstate?
docs.text:
Usually you cannot prepare \(|u\rangle\) — that would often require knowing the answer. QPE handles this gracefully. Expand an arbitrary input in the eigenbasis:

\[ |\psi\rangle = \sum_u c_u |u\rangle . \]

By linearity, QPE produces

\[ \sum_u c_u\,|\tilde\theta_u\rangle\otimes|u\rangle . \]

Measuring the counting register returns \(\tilde\theta_u\) with probability \(|c_u|^2\), and collapses the eigenstate register to the corresponding \(|u\rangle\). You get a random eigenphase, sampled according to the overlap.

In Shor's algorithm the input \(|1\rangle\) is an equal superposition of all \(r\) relevant eigenstates of the modular-multiplication operator, so the measurement returns \(\approx s/r\) for a uniformly random \(s\in\{0,\dots,r-1\}\). That is precisely the output the continued-fractions step (L20) is designed to consume.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Exact phase estimation
docs.text:
\(U = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{2\pi i\cdot0.375}\end{pmatrix}\) with eigenstate \(|u\rangle = |1\rangle\). Use \(t=3\) counting qubits. What is measured?

Solution. \(\theta = 0.375 = \frac{3}{8}\). In binary:

\[ 0.375 = \frac{0}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} = 0.011_2 . \]

Since \(\theta = 3/2^3\) is an exact 3-bit fraction, the exact case applies:

\[ m = 3 = 011_2, \qquad \Pr[m=3] = 1 . \]

Output: \(\tilde\theta = 3/8 = 0.375\) ✓, exactly, in one run.

Check the state before the inverse QFT:

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt8}\sum_{k=0}^{7}e^{2\pi ik\cdot3/8}|k\rangle = \mathrm{QFT}_8|3\rangle \ \checkmark \]

docs.title: Problem 2 — Inexact phase, distribution of outcomes
docs.text:
Now \(\theta = 0.4\) with \(t = 3\). Compute \(\Pr[m]\) for all \(m\) and identify the most likely outcome.

Solution. \(2^t\theta = 8\times0.4 = 3.2\). The nearest integer is \(b = 3\), so \(\tilde\theta = 3/8 = 0.375\) with error \(0.025\).

Using \(\Pr[m] = \frac{1}{64}\left|\frac{\sin(8\pi(0.4 - m/8))}{\sin(\pi(0.4-m/8))}\right|^2\):

\(m\) \(0.4 - m/8\) \(\Pr[m]\) 0 \(0.400\) 0.006 1 \(0.275\) 0.009 2 \(0.150\) 0.026 3 \(0.025\) 0.877 4 \(-0.100\) 0.057 5 \(-0.225\) 0.013 6 \(-0.350\) 0.007 7 \(-0.475\) 0.005

Sum \(= 1.000\) ✓.

Most likely outcome: \(m = 3\) with probability 0.877, far above the guaranteed bound \(4/\pi^2 = 0.405\). Note the asymmetry: \(m=4\) (0.057) is more likely than \(m=2\) (0.026), because \(\theta = 0.4\) lies between \(3/8 = 0.375\) and \(4/8 = 0.5\) but nearer the former. The distribution is sharply concentrated, not spread out.

Practical procedure. Run QPE several times and take the mode. Two runs already give the correct answer with probability \(1 - (0.123)^2 \approx 98.5\%\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Choosing the number of counting qubits
docs.text:
You need \(\theta\) to 10 binary digits with failure probability at most 5 %. How many counting qubits, and how many applications of \(U\)?

Solution. Apply the formula with \(n = 10\), \(\epsilon = 0.05\):

\[ t = n + \left\lceil\log_2\!\left(2 + \frac{1}{2\times0.05}\right)\right\rceil = 10 + \lceil\log_2(2 + 10)\rceil = 10 + \lceil\log_2 12\rceil = 10 + \lceil3.585\rceil = 10 + 4 \] \[ \boxed{t = 14 \ \text{counting qubits}} \]

Applications of \(U\):

\[ 2^{14} - 1 = 16{,}383 . \]

Total qubits: 14 counting + however many \(|u\rangle\) requires.

Observation. Doubling the precision from 10 to 20 bits would need \(t = 24\) and \(2^{24}\approx1.7\times10^7\) applications of \(U\) — the exponential cost in precision. QPE buys precision at exponential cost in circuit depth, which is why NISQ devices cannot run it and why iterative QPE (one counting qubit reused \(t\) times, with classical feed-forward) was invented.

docs.title: Problem 4 — QPE applied to a Pauli
docs.text:
Apply QPE with \(t=2\) to \(U = Z\) with eigenstate \(|1\rangle\). Verify the output.

Solution. \(Z|1\rangle = -|1\rangle = e^{i\pi}|1\rangle = e^{2\pi i(1/2)}|1\rangle\), so \(\theta = \frac12\).

\(\theta = 1/2 = 2/4 = 2/2^t\) — exact for \(t=2\), with \(j = 2 = 10_2\).

Trace it. After Step 1: \(\frac12\sum_{k=0}^3|k\rangle|1\rangle\).

After Step 2 (phase \(e^{2\pi ik/2} = (-1)^k\)):

\[ \frac12\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle + |2\rangle - |3\rangle\big)\otimes|1\rangle \]

This is \(\mathrm{QFT}_4|2\rangle\) (computed in L18, Problem 1) ✓.

After \(\mathrm{QFT}_4^{-1}\): \(|2\rangle = |10\rangle\).

Measurement gives \(m=2\), so \(\tilde\theta = 2/4 = 0.5\) ✓, and the eigenvalue is \(e^{2\pi i(0.5)} = -1\) ✓.

Note. With \(t = 1\) this reduces to the Hadamard test of L11 Problem 4: one \(H\), one controlled-\(Z\), one \(H\), measure — giving 1 with certainty.

docs.title: Problem 5 — QPE for order finding (previewing Shor)
docs.text:
Let \(N=15\), \(a=7\). Define \(U_a|y\rangle = |ay \bmod 15\rangle\). Show that its eigenvalues have phases \(s/r\), and state what QPE would return.

Solution.

From L17, \(r = \mathrm{ord}_{15}(7) = 4\): the cycle is \(1 \to 7 \to 4 \to 13 \to 1\).

Eigenstates. For \(s = 0,1,\dots,r-1\) define

\[ |u_s\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k=0}^{r-1} e^{-2\pi i sk/r}\,\big|a^k \bmod N\big\rangle . \]

Verify the eigenvalue equation.

\[ U_a|u_s\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}e^{-2\pi isk/r}|a^{k+1}\rangle \]

Substitute \(k' = k+1\) (indices mod \(r\), using \(a^r \equiv 1\)):

\[ = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k'}e^{-2\pi is(k'-1)/r}|a^{k'}\rangle = e^{2\pi is/r}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{k'}e^{-2\pi isk'/r}|a^{k'}\rangle = e^{2\pi is/r}|u_s\rangle \ \checkmark \] \[ \boxed{\ \theta_s = \frac{s}{r} = \frac{s}{4} \in \left\{0,\ \tfrac14,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac34\right\}\ } \]

The problem of preparing \(|u_s\rangle\). Building \(|u_s\rangle\) requires knowing \(r\) — which is what we are trying to find. The resolution is the key identity

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}|u_s\rangle = |1\rangle . \]

Proof: the coefficient of \(|a^k\rangle\) in the sum is \(\frac{1}{r}\sum_s e^{-2\pi isk/r}\), which is 1 if \(k\equiv0\) and 0 otherwise — leaving only \(|a^0\rangle = |1\rangle\) ✓.

So we simply prepare \(|1\rangle\) — trivially easy — which is an equal superposition of all \(r\) eigenstates. By §6, QPE then returns \(\tilde\theta \approx s/4\) for a uniformly random \(s\in\{0,1,2,3\}\):

Measured \(\tilde\theta\) \(s\) Probability \(0.00\) 0 1/4 \(0.25\) 1 1/4 \(0.50\) 2 1/4 \(0.75\) 3 1/4

Recovering \(r\). From \(\tilde\theta = 0.25 = \frac14\) we read \(r = 4\) directly. From \(\tilde\theta = 0.5 = \frac12\) we get the reduced fraction \(\frac12\), giving \(r = 2\) — wrong, because \(s=2\) and \(r=4\) share the factor 2. From \(\tilde\theta = 0\) we learn nothing.

This is why Shor's algorithm needs continued fractions and a verification step \(a^r\stackrel{?}{\equiv}1\), and why it may need to be repeated. Useful outcomes here are \(s\in\{1,3\}\) (those coprime to \(r\)), occurring with probability \(\phi(r)/r = 2/4 = 1/2\).

docs.title: 19.9 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\theta = 0.625\) with \(t=3\): what is measured? [Ans: \(m=5\), exact]
  2. \(\theta = 1/3\) with \(t=4\): find \(b\) and the error. [Ans: \(b=5\), \(\tilde\theta = 5/16 = 0.3125\)]
  3. How many counting qubits for 6-bit precision with 1 % failure? [Ans: \(t=12\)]
  4. Apply QPE with \(t=2\) to \(U=S\) with eigenstate \(|1\rangle\). [Ans: \(\theta = 1/4\), \(m=1\), exact]
  5. Prove that the phases of \(U_a\) are exactly \(\{s/r\}\) for \(s = 0,\dots,r-1\).
  6. Show \(\Pr[b]\ge 4/\pi^2\) using \(|\sin x| \ge 2|x|/\pi\) for \(|x|\le\pi/2\).
  7. Why does the eigenstate register end up unentangled from the counting register in the exact case?

docs.title: 19.10 Summary
docs.text:
• QPE estimates \(\theta\) where \(U|u\rangle = e^{2\pi i\theta}|u\rangle\), using \(t\) counting qubits.
  • Circuit: Hadamards → controlled-\(U^{2^j}\) (phase kick-back writes the ramp \(e^{2\pi ik\theta}\)) → \(\mathrm{QFT}^{-1}\) → measure.
  • Exact case: if \(\theta\) has a \(t\)-bit binary expansion, the answer is deterministic.
  • General case: the outcome distribution is a Fejér kernel peaked at \(b\approx2^t\theta\), with \(\Pr[b]\ge 4/\pi^2\); use \(t = n + \lceil\log_2(2+\frac{1}{2\epsilon})\rceil\) qubits.
  • Cost is \(2^t-1\) applications of \(U\) — exponential in precision, so \(U\) must be cheaply exponentiable.
  • If you cannot prepare \(|u\rangle\), feed in any state: QPE returns a random eigenphase with probability \(|c_u|^2\). In Shor, the easily-prepared \(|1\rangle\) is an equal superposition of all \(r\) eigenstates.
  • QPE is the engine of Shor, HHL and quantum chemistry.

Next lesson: L20 — Shor's algorithm for integer factorization, assembled in full.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Phase Estimation tab: set \(\theta\) and \(t\), and see the Fejér-kernel probability distribution and the effect of adding counting qubits.

docs.title: Lesson 10: Quantum Teleportation, Superdense Coding and Quantum Error Correction
10.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Derive the quantum teleportation protocol step by step and state its resource requirements.
  2. Explain why teleportation does not violate no-cloning or no-signalling.
  3. Derive superdense coding and state the duality between it and teleportation.
  4. Explain why classical repetition codes fail and how stabiliser measurement solves the problem.
  5. Construct the 3-qubit bit-flip and phase-flip codes and describe the 9-qubit Shor code.
  6. State the quantum threshold theorem and interpret physical-vs-logical qubit overhead.

docs.title: 10.2 Quantum Teleportation
docs.text:
The task. Alice holds an unknown qubit \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\). She wants Bob to end up holding exactly \(|\psi\rangle\). They share one entangled pair and a classical channel. Alice may not send the qubit itself.

Resources: 1 shared ebit (\(|\Phi^+\rangle\)) + 2 classical bits + local operations.

docs.title: The circuit
docs.text:
Alice
              +-----------------------------+
 q0 |psi> ----------*--------[H]------[M]---------.
                    |                             |  m0
 q1 (EPR) ---------[X]----------------[M]------.  |
              +----------------------------+  |  |  m1
                                               |  |
 q2 (EPR) -------------------------------[X]--[Z]------> |psi>
                        Bob                ^    ^
                                           |    |
                                     controlled by m1, m0

Reading the diagram: * is a CNOT control, [X] its target, [M] a measurement, and the final [X]/[Z] on Bob's wire are applied only if the corresponding classical bit is 1.

Qubits 1 and 2 begin in the Bell state \(|\Phi^+\rangle\).

docs.title: Full derivation
docs.text:
Initial state (qubit 0 is Alice's unknown; qubits 1–2 are the shared pair):

\[ |\Psi_0\rangle = |\psi\rangle_0 \otimes |\Phi^+\rangle_{12} = \big(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\big)\otimes\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|00\rangle+|11\rangle\big) \] \[ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big[\alpha|000\rangle + \alpha|011\rangle + \beta|100\rangle + \beta|111\rangle\Big] \]

Step 1 — CNOT (control \(q_0\), target \(q_1\)). Flip \(q_1\) where \(q_0=1\):

\[ |\Psi_1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big[\alpha|000\rangle + \alpha|011\rangle + \beta|110\rangle + \beta|101\rangle\Big] \]

Step 2 — Hadamard on \(q_0\). Substitute \(|0\rangle \to \frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\) and \(|1\rangle\to\frac{|0\rangle-|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\):

\[ |\Psi_2\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\Big[ \alpha(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)|00\rangle + \alpha(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)|11\rangle + \beta(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)|10\rangle + \beta(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)|01\rangle\Big] \]

Step 3 — regroup by Alice's two qubits \(q_0q_1\):

\[ |\Psi_2\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\Big[ |00\rangle\big(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\big) + |01\rangle\big(\alpha|1\rangle + \beta|0\rangle\big) \] \[ + \;|10\rangle\big(\alpha|0\rangle - \beta|1\rangle\big) + |11\rangle\big(\alpha|1\rangle - \beta|0\rangle\big)\Big] \]

Read this carefully. Bob's qubit already carries \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) in all four branches — up to one of exactly four known corrections.

Step 4 — Alice measures \(q_0q_1\). Each outcome has probability \(\frac14\) (note \(|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1\)), and this is what makes the protocol non-signalling: Alice's statistics carry no information about \(|\psi\rangle\).

Step 5 — Bob's correction, determined by the two classical bits \(m_0m_1\):

Alice's bits \(m_0m_1\) Bob's state Correction Why \(00\) \(\alpha\lvert 0\rangle + \beta\lvert 1\rangle\) \(I\) already correct \(01\) \(\alpha\lvert 1\rangle + \beta\lvert 0\rangle\) \(X\) bit flipped \(10\) \(\alpha\lvert 0\rangle - \beta\lvert 1\rangle\) \(Z\) phase flipped \(11\) \(\alpha\lvert 1\rangle - \beta\lvert 0\rangle\) \(ZX\) both

General rule: apply \(X^{m_1}Z^{m_0}\). Bob then holds exactly \(|\psi\rangle\).

docs.title: Why no laws are broken
docs.text:
• No-cloning is respected. Alice's measurement destroys her copy. At the end exactly one copy of \(|\psi\rangle\) exists, in Bob's hands. Teleportation moves a state; it does not duplicate it.
  • No-signalling is respected. Without the two classical bits, Bob's qubit is in the maximally mixed state \(\rho_B = I/2\) — no information at all. The protocol is limited by the classical channel, hence by the speed of light.
  • \(|\psi\rangle\) is never learned. Neither party discovers \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\); measuring to find them would require infinitely many copies.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: Quantum repeaters (entanglement swapping), distributed quantum computing, and — importantly for fault tolerance — gate teleportation, the standard way to apply a \(T\) gate on encoded qubits using a pre-distilled magic state.

docs.title: 10.3 Superdense Coding
docs.text:
The task (the mirror image). Alice sends two classical bits to Bob by transmitting one qubit, using one pre-shared ebit.

Protocol.

  1. Alice and Bob share \(|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)\).
  2. To encode bits \(b_1b_0\), Alice applies \(Z^{b_1}X^{b_0}\) to her qubit only:
Bits \(b_1b_0\) Alice applies Resulting Bell state \(00\) \(I\) \(\lvert \Phi^+\rangle\) \(01\) \(X\) \(\lvert \Psi^+\rangle\) \(10\) \(Z\) \(\lvert \Phi^-\rangle\) \(11\) \(ZX\) \(\lvert \Psi^-\rangle\)
  1. Alice sends her single qubit to Bob.
  2. Bob, now holding both qubits, performs a Bell measurement (CNOT then \(H\), then measure both) and recovers \(b_1b_0\) with certainty, because the four Bell states are orthogonal.

Verification for \(b_1b_0 = 01\):

\[ (X\otimes I)\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|10\rangle+|01\rangle) = |\Psi^+\rangle \ \checkmark \]

The duality.

\[ \text{Teleportation: } 1 \text{ ebit} + 2 \text{ cbits} \Rightarrow 1 \text{ qubit sent} \] \[ \text{Superdense coding: } 1 \text{ ebit} + 1 \text{ qubit} \Rightarrow 2 \text{ cbits sent} \]

Holevo's bound (one qubit carries at most one classical bit) is not violated: the second bit was carried by the pre-shared entanglement, distributed earlier.

docs.title: Three obstacles that classical QEC does not face
docs.text:
1. No-cloning — you cannot make three copies of \(|\psi\rangle\).
  2. Measurement destroys — reading the qubit to check it collapses the superposition.
  3. Continuous errors — a qubit can suffer \(R_x(0.01)\), not just a discrete flip. There are uncountably many possible errors.

docs.title: The three ideas that solve them
docs.text:
1. Encode, don't copy. Spread one logical qubit across several physical qubits in an entangled state.
  2. Measure the syndrome, not the data. Measure operators that reveal which error occurred without revealing \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\).
  3. Error discretisation. A continuous error is a superposition of \(\{I, X, Y, Z\}\); the syndrome measurement projects it onto one of these. Correcting \(X\), \(Z\) and \(Y = iXZ\) therefore corrects everything. This is the theorem that makes QEC possible at all.

docs.title: The 3-qubit bit-flip code
docs.text:
Encoding.

\[ |0\rangle_L = |000\rangle, \qquad |1\rangle_L = |111\rangle \] \[ \alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle \ \longmapsto\ \alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle \]

Circuit: two CNOTs from \(q_0\) to \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). Note this is not cloning — the encoded state is entangled, not \(|\psi\rangle^{\otimes3}\).

Syndrome measurement. Measure the two stabilisers

\[ S_1 = Z_1Z_2, \qquad S_2 = Z_2Z_3 . \]

These are parity checks. They commute with each other and with the logical operators, so they reveal the error location without disturbing \(\alpha,\beta\).

\(S_1\) \(S_2\) Diagnosis Correction \(+1\) \(+1\) no error none \(-1\) \(+1\) flip on qubit 1 \(X_1\) \(-1\) \(-1\) flip on qubit 2 \(X_2\) \(+1\) \(-1\) flip on qubit 3 \(X_3\)

Corrects any single bit flip. Fails on two or more.

Failure probability. If each qubit flips independently with probability \(p\):

\[ P_{\text{fail}} = 3p^2(1-p) + p^3 = 3p^2 - 2p^3 \approx 3p^2 . \]

For \(p = 0.01\): \(P_{\text{fail}} \approx 2.98\times10^{-4}\) — a 34-fold improvement. The code helps whenever \(3p^2 < p\), i.e. \(p < 1/3\). This threshold behaviour is the seed of the full threshold theorem.

docs.title: The 3-qubit phase-flip code
docs.text:
A \(Z\) error is a bit flip in the Hadamard basis, because \(HZH = X\). So conjugate the whole bit-flip code by Hadamards:

\[ |0\rangle_L = |{+}{+}{+}\rangle, \qquad |1\rangle_L = |{-}{-}{-}\rangle \]

with stabilisers \(X_1X_2\) and \(X_2X_3\).

docs.title: The 9-qubit Shor code
docs.text:
Concatenate the two: encode with the phase-flip code, then encode each of its three qubits with the bit-flip code.

\[ |0\rangle_L = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\big(|000\rangle+|111\rangle\big)^{\otimes 3} \] \[ |1\rangle_L = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\big(|000\rangle-|111\rangle\big)^{\otimes 3} \]

This corrects an arbitrary single-qubit error — \(X\), \(Z\), \(Y\), or any continuous rotation — on any one of the nine qubits. It was the first QEC code (Peter Shor, 1995) and proved that fault-tolerant quantum computing is possible in principle.

Other important codes.

Code \([[n,k,d]]\) Note Shor \([[9,1,3]]\) first code Steane \([[7,1,3]]\) CSS code from the classical Hamming \([7,4,3]\) code Perfect / Laflamme \([[5,1,3]]\) smallest possible distance-3 code Surface code \([[d^2,1,d]]\) 2-D nearest-neighbour only; today's leading candidate

Notation \([[n,k,d]]\): \(n\) physical qubits, \(k\) logical qubits, distance \(d\), correcting \(t = \lfloor (d-1)/2\rfloor\) errors.

docs.title: The threshold theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Aharonov–Ben-Or; Knill–Laflamme–Zurek; Kitaev). If the physical error rate per gate is below a constant threshold \(p_{\text{th}}\), then arbitrarily long quantum computations can be performed reliably, with only polylogarithmic overhead in the number of qubits and gates.

For the surface code, \(p_{\text{th}} \approx 1\%\) — within reach of today's hardware. The price is overhead: roughly \(10^3\)–\(10^4\) physical qubits per logical qubit for cryptographically relevant computations. This is exactly why estimates for "breaking RSA-2048 with Shor" quote millions of physical qubits.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Teleporting a specific state
docs.text:
Alice teleports \(|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\big(|0\rangle + 2|1\rangle\big)\) and measures \(m_0m_1 = 10\). Write Bob's pre-correction state, the correction, and verify the final state.

Solution. Here \(\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\), \(\beta = \frac{2}{\sqrt5}\).

From the branch table, outcome \(10\) leaves Bob with

\[ \alpha|0\rangle - \beta|1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}|0\rangle - \frac{2}{\sqrt5}|1\rangle . \]

Correction: \(m_0 = 1\), \(m_1 = 0\), so apply \(X^{0}Z^{1} = Z\):

\[ Z\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt5}|0\rangle - \frac{2}{\sqrt5}|1\rangle\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}|0\rangle + \frac{2}{\sqrt5}|1\rangle = |\psi\rangle \ \checkmark \]

Note that the probability of this outcome is \(\frac14\) regardless of \(\alpha,\beta\) — Alice learns nothing about the state she teleported.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Superdense coding, full trace
docs.text:
Alice wants to send \(11\). Trace the protocol and verify Bob decodes correctly.

Solution.

Shared state: \(|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)\).

Encode: \(b_1b_0 = 11\), so Alice applies \(ZX\) to her qubit.

\[ (X\otimes I)|\Phi^+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|10\rangle + |01\rangle\big) \] \[ (Z\otimes I)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|10\rangle+|01\rangle\big) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(-|10\rangle + |01\rangle\big) = |\Psi^-\rangle \]

Decode (Bell measurement): apply CNOT\(_{0\to1}\) then \(H\) on \(q_0\).

\[ \mathrm{CNOT}\,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|01\rangle - |10\rangle\big) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|01\rangle - |11\rangle\big) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big)\otimes|1\rangle \] \[ (H\otimes I): \quad H\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle-|1\rangle) = H|-\rangle = |1\rangle \] \[ \Rightarrow\ |11\rangle . \]

Bob measures and reads \(b_1b_0 = 11\) ✓ with probability 1. Two classical bits delivered by one transmitted qubit.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Bit-flip code syndrome decoding
docs.text:
The state \(\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle\) suffers an \(X\) error on qubit 2. Compute the syndrome and show that correction restores the state exactly, without revealing \(\alpha,\beta\).

Solution.

Corrupted state: \(X_2\big(\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle\big) = \alpha|010\rangle + \beta|101\rangle\).

Measure \(S_1 = Z_1Z_2\) (parity of qubits 1 and 2):

  • \(|010\rangle\): bits \(0,1\) → parity odd → eigenvalue \(-1\)
  • \(|101\rangle\): bits \(1,0\) → parity odd → eigenvalue \(-1\)

Both branches give \(-1\), so the measurement returns \(S_1 = -1\) without collapsing the superposition — this is the key point.

Measure \(S_2 = Z_2Z_3\):

  • \(|010\rangle\): bits \(1,0\) → odd → \(-1\)
  • \(|101\rangle\): bits \(0,1\) → odd → \(-1\)

\(S_2 = -1\).

Syndrome \((-1,-1)\) ⟶ table says error on qubit 2 ⟶ apply \(X_2\):

\[ X_2\big(\alpha|010\rangle + \beta|101\rangle\big) = \alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle \ \checkmark \]

Why \(\alpha,\beta\) stay secret. The stabilisers act identically on \(|0\rangle_L\) and \(|1\rangle_L\), so their eigenvalues depend only on the error, never on the encoded amplitudes. This is the central design principle of stabiliser codes.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Error discretisation
docs.text:
A qubit in the bit-flip code suffers the continuous rotation \(R_x(\epsilon) = \cos\frac{\epsilon}{2}I - i\sin\frac{\epsilon}{2}X\) on qubit 1. Show that syndrome measurement corrects it exactly.

Solution. Write \(c = \cos\frac{\epsilon}{2}\), \(s = \sin\frac{\epsilon}{2}\). The corrupted state is

\[ |\psi'\rangle = \big(cI - is X_1\big)|\psi_L\rangle = c\,|\psi_L\rangle - is\,X_1|\psi_L\rangle . \]

This is a superposition of "no error" and "\(X_1\) error".

Measuring the syndrome \((S_1, S_2)\) projects onto one of the error subspaces:

  • With probability \(|c|^2 = \cos^2\frac{\epsilon}{2}\): syndrome \((+1,+1)\), state collapses to \(|\psi_L\rangle\). No error occurred.
  • With probability \(|s|^2 = \sin^2\frac{\epsilon}{2}\): syndrome \((-1,+1)\), state collapses to \(X_1|\psi_L\rangle\). Apply \(X_1\) to restore \(|\psi_L\rangle\).

In both cases the final state is exactly \(|\psi_L\rangle\) — the small continuous error has been digitised by the measurement and then removed. No approximation, no residual error.

Significance. This is why a code that corrects only the discrete set \(\{X,Y,Z\}\) corrects the continuum of all possible single-qubit errors. Without it, QEC would be impossible.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Logical error rate and the value of concatenation
docs.text:
Physical qubits have error rate \(p = 10^{-3}\). Compute the logical error rate for (a) the 3-qubit code, (b) one level of concatenation (\(9\) qubits), (c) two levels (\(27\) qubits). How many levels are needed for \(10^{-15}\)?

Solution. For a distance-3 code, \(p_L \approx 3p^2\) (fails only on 2 or more errors).

(a) \(p_L = 3(10^{-3})^2 = 3\times10^{-6}\).

(b) Concatenation applies the same formula to the previous level's rate:

\[ p_L^{(2)} = 3\left(3\times10^{-6}\right)^2 = 3 \times 9\times10^{-12} = 2.7\times10^{-11} . \]

(c) \(p_L^{(3)} = 3\left(2.7\times10^{-11}\right)^2 = 3\times 7.29\times10^{-22} = 2.19\times10^{-21}\).

So three levels already beat \(10^{-15}\) comfortably; two levels (\(2.7\times10^{-11}\)) do not.

Cost. Level \(k\) uses \(3^k\) physical qubits per logical qubit:

Level Physical qubits Logical error rate 1 3 \(3\times10^{-6}\) 2 9 \(2.7\times10^{-11}\) 3 27 \(2.2\times10^{-21}\)

Double-exponential suppression for exponential cost — the essence of the threshold theorem. Note that with \(p = 0.4 > 1/3\) the recursion diverges: concatenation makes things worse. This is the threshold in action.

docs.title: 10.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Alice teleports \(|+\rangle\) and measures \(11\). What is Bob's pre-correction state and what correction restores \(|+\rangle\)? [Ans: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|1\rangle-|0\rangle)\); apply \(ZX\)]
  2. Verify \((Z\otimes I)|\Phi^+\rangle = |\Phi^-\rangle\).
  3. Show that Bob's reduced density matrix before receiving Alice's bits is \(I/2\), proving no-signalling.
  4. Encode \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)\) in the phase-flip code and show a \(Z_2\) error is detected.
  5. For the 3-qubit code with \(p = 0.05\), compute the logical error rate and the improvement factor. [Ans: \(7.1\times10^{-3}\); ≈ 7×]
  6. Why is the surface code preferred over the Shor code on superconducting hardware?
  7. Explain why teleportation requires two classical bits and not one.

docs.title: 10.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Teleportation: 1 ebit + 2 cbits move an unknown qubit. Alice's Bell measurement leaves Bob's qubit correct up to one of four Pauli corrections \(X^{m_1}Z^{m_0}\). No cloning (Alice's copy is destroyed) and no signalling (Bob sees \(I/2\) until the bits arrive).
  • Superdense coding: the dual protocol — 1 ebit + 1 qubit send 2 classical bits, decoded by a Bell measurement.
  • QEC cannot copy. It encodes into entangled states and measures stabilisers, which reveal the error without revealing the data.
  • Error discretisation means correcting \(\{X,Y,Z\}\) corrects every continuous error.
  • 3-qubit codes fix bit flips or phase flips; the 9-qubit Shor code fixes both. \([[n,k,d]]\) notation; the surface code leads today.
  • Threshold theorem: below \(p_{\text{th}}\approx1\%\), arbitrarily long computation is possible with polylog overhead — but with \(10^3\)–\(10^4\) physical qubits per logical qubit in practice.

Unit I is now complete. You should be able to: manipulate states and gates algebraically, reason on the Bloch sphere, compute measurement statistics, detect entanglement, and explain why interference (not parallelism) is the source of quantum power.

Next lesson: L11 — Quantum oracles and phase kick-back (Unit II begins).

Practise now: unit1-qubit-lab.html → Teleportation tab runs the protocol shot by shot and shows Bob's state before and after correction; the QEC tab lets you inject errors and read syndromes.

docs.title: Lesson 5: Qubits, the Superposition Principle and the Bloch Sphere
5.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the superposition principle and give its precise mathematical content.
  2. Distinguish global phase (unobservable) from relative phase (observable).
  3. Derive the Bloch sphere parametrisation \(|\psi\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}|1\rangle\).
  4. Convert between state vectors and Bloch coordinates \((x,y,z)\) in both directions.
  5. Explain why a mixed state lies inside the Bloch ball and how it differs from a superposition.
  6. Name typical physical realisations of a qubit.

docs.title: 5.2 The Superposition Principle
docs.text:
Postulate 1 (State space). The state of an isolated quantum system is a unit vector in a complex Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\).

Superposition principle. If \(|\psi_1\rangle\) and \(|\psi_2\rangle\) are physically realisable states of a system, then so is every normalised linear combination

\[ |\psi\rangle = \alpha|\psi_1\rangle + \beta|\psi_2\rangle, \qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2 = 1 . \]

This is not a statement about ignorance. It is a statement that the state space is a vector space, and that nature realises all of it.

docs.title: Superposition versus classical probability — the key distinction
docs.text:
Consider two descriptions of a qubit:

Coherent superposition Classical mixture Description \(\lvert +\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lvert 0\rangle + \lvert 1\rangle)\) "It is \(\lvert 0\rangle\) or \(\lvert 1\rangle\), each w.p. ½" \(Z\)-measurement result 0 or 1, each w.p. ½ 0 or 1, each w.p. ½ \(X\)-measurement result \(+\) with probability 1 \(+\) or \(-\), each w.p. ½ Density matrix \(\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) \(\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\)

The two are experimentally distinguishable — just measure in the \(X\) basis. The off-diagonal entries of the density matrix are called coherences; a superposition has them, a mixture does not. Decoherence is precisely the process that destroys them.

This table is the single most important conceptual content of Unit I. A superposition is not "the system is secretly one of them and we don't know which."

docs.title: 5.3 Global versus Relative Phase
docs.text:
Definition (Global phase). States \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(e^{i\gamma}|\psi\rangle\) for real \(\gamma\) are called equal up to a global phase.

Theorem. A global phase is physically unobservable.

Proof. Measurement probabilities in any basis \(\{|e_j\rangle\}\) are \(|\langle e_j| e^{i\gamma}|\psi\rangle|^2 = |e^{i\gamma}|^2|\langle e_j|\psi\rangle|^2 = |\langle e_j|\psi\rangle|^2\), since \(|e^{i\gamma}|=1\). Expectation values of any observable are likewise unchanged: \(\langle\psi|e^{-i\gamma}Ae^{i\gamma}|\psi\rangle = \langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle\). \(\blacksquare\)

Definition (Relative phase). In \(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle\), the relative phase is \(\arg\beta - \arg\alpha\). It is observable.

Demonstration. Compare \(|+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)\) and \(|-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)\). Both give \(\Pr[0]=\Pr[1]=\frac12\) in the \(Z\) basis. But

\[ \langle +|-\rangle = 0, \]

so an \(X\)-basis measurement distinguishes them perfectly. The only difference between them is a relative phase of \(\pi\).

Rule of thumb. Global phase: throw it away. Relative phase: it is the algorithm. Every quantum algorithm in Unit II works by manipulating relative phases and then converting them into amplitudes via a Hadamard or a QFT.

docs.title: Derivation
docs.text:
Start from the general normalised qubit

\[ |\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle, \qquad \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C},\ |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1. \]

Four real parameters (\(\mathrm{Re}\,\alpha, \mathrm{Im}\,\alpha, \mathrm{Re}\,\beta, \mathrm{Im}\,\beta\)), minus one for normalisation, minus one for the unobservable global phase = two real parameters. A two-parameter family — a surface. Let us find it.

Write both amplitudes in polar form: \(\alpha = r_\alpha e^{i\gamma_\alpha}\), \(\beta = r_\beta e^{i\gamma_\beta}\). Discard the global phase \(e^{i\gamma_\alpha}\):

\[ |\psi\rangle \simeq r_\alpha|0\rangle + r_\beta e^{i\varphi}|1\rangle, \qquad \varphi = \gamma_\beta - \gamma_\alpha \in [0, 2\pi). \]

Normalisation \(r_\alpha^2 + r_\beta^2 = 1\) with \(r_\alpha, r_\beta \ge 0\) lets us set \(r_\alpha = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\), \(r_\beta = \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\) with \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\). Hence

\[ \boxed{\ |\psi\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,|1\rangle\ } \]

This is a point on the unit sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with polar angle \(\theta\) and azimuthal angle \(\varphi\) — the Bloch sphere.

Why the half-angle? Because \(\theta\) ranges over \([0,\pi]\) while the sphere needs a full \([0,\pi]\) polar sweep to go from north to south pole; the half-angle makes orthogonal states (\(\theta\) and \(\pi-\theta\) pairs) land at antipodal points. Specifically:

\[ \theta = 0 \Rightarrow |0\rangle \ \text{(north pole)}, \qquad \theta = \pi \Rightarrow |1\rangle \ \text{(south pole)} . \]

\(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) are orthogonal yet sit at opposite poles, separated by a Bloch-sphere angle of \(\pi\), not \(\pi/2\). Orthogonal in Hilbert space ⟷ antipodal on the Bloch sphere.

docs.title: Cartesian Bloch coordinates
docs.text:
\[ x = \sin\theta\cos\varphi, \qquad y = \sin\theta\sin\varphi, \qquad z = \cos\theta \]

Equivalently, as expectation values of the Paulis:

\[ \boxed{\ x = \langle\psi|X|\psi\rangle, \qquad y = \langle\psi|Y|\psi\rangle, \qquad z = \langle\psi|Z|\psi\rangle\ } \]

This is the practical way to compute Bloch coordinates and the way a real experiment measures them (quantum state tomography: estimate \(\langle X\rangle,\langle Y\rangle,\langle Z\rangle\) by repeated measurement in three bases).

docs.title: Gates as rotations
docs.text:
Every single-qubit unitary is (up to global phase) a rotation of the Bloch sphere:

Gate Bloch action \(X\) \(\pi\) rotation about the \(x\)-axis \(Y\) \(\pi\) rotation about the \(y\)-axis \(Z\) \(\pi\) rotation about the \(z\)-axis \(H\) \(\pi\) rotation about the axis \((\hat x + \hat z)/\sqrt2\) \(S\) \(\pi/2\) rotation about \(z\) \(T\) \(\pi/4\) rotation about \(z\) \(R_{\hat n}(\theta)\) \(\theta\) rotation about axis \(\hat n\) \[ R_{\hat n}(\theta) = e^{-i\theta(\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma)/2} = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2} I - i\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,(n_xX + n_yY + n_zZ) \]

Note the factor of 2: a \(2\pi\) rotation of the Bloch sphere corresponds to \(e^{-i\pi} = -1\) on the state vector — a global phase of \(-1\). You need \(4\pi\) to return the vector to itself. This is the famous spin-½ "spinor" property.

docs.title: Mixed states and the Bloch ball
docs.text:
A mixed state is described by a density matrix

\[ \rho = \frac{1}{2}\big(I + x X + y Y + z Z\big) = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 1+z & x-iy \\ x+iy & 1-z\end{pmatrix} \]

with \(r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \le 1\).

  • \(r = 1\): pure state, on the surface of the sphere. \(\mathrm{Tr}(\rho^2) = 1\).
  • \(r < 1\): mixed state, strictly inside the ball. \(\mathrm{Tr}(\rho^2) < 1\).
  • \(r = 0\): maximally mixed \(\rho = I/2\) — the centre; total ignorance.

Decoherence shrinks \(r\): the Bloch vector spirals toward the centre. Purity \(\mathrm{Tr}(\rho^2) = \frac{1+r^2}{2}\) is the standard quality measure.

docs.title: 5.5 Physical Realisations of a Qubit
docs.text:
Physical system \(\lvert 0\rangle\) \(\lvert 1\rangle\) Photon polarisation Horizontal Vertical Electron / nuclear spin Spin up Spin down Superconducting transmon Ground state First excited state Trapped ion Two hyperfine levels Neutral atom Ground state Rydberg state

In each case the "two-level system" is an approximation: real systems have more levels, and leakage out of the computational subspace is a genuine error channel on hardware.

docs.title: Problem 1 — State to Bloch coordinates (algebraic route)
docs.text:
Find the Bloch coordinates of \(|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle + \frac{1+i}{2}|1\rangle\).

Solution. First check normalisation: \(\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^2 + \left|\frac{1+i}{2}\right|^2 = \frac12 + \frac{1^2+1^2}{4} = \frac12+\frac12 = 1\) ✓.

Write \(\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), \(\beta = \frac{1+i}{2}\).

\[ z = |\alpha|^2 - |\beta|^2 = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0 \] \[ x = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta), \qquad y = 2\,\mathrm{Im}(\alpha^*\beta) \] \[ \alpha^*\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1+i}{2} = \frac{1+i}{2\sqrt2} \] \[ x = 2\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.7071, \qquad y = 2\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.7071 \] \[ (x,y,z) = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\ 0\right) \]

Check: \(x^2+y^2+z^2 = \frac12+\frac12+0 = 1\) ✓ (pure state, on the surface).

Angles: \(\theta = \arccos(0) = \pi/2\) (equator); \(\varphi = \arctan(y/x) = \arctan 1 = \pi/4\).

(Useful identities used above: \(x = 2\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta)\), \(y = 2\mathrm{Im}(\alpha^*\beta)\), \(z = |\alpha|^2-|\beta|^2\).)

docs.title: Problem 2 — Bloch coordinates to state
docs.text:
A qubit has Bloch vector \((x,y,z) = \left(\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\). Find \(\theta\), \(\varphi\) and the state vector.

Solution. Check purity: \(\frac14 + \frac14 + \frac12 = 1\) ✓ — pure.

\[ \theta = \arccos z = \arccos\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{4} = 45^\circ \] \[ \varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) = \operatorname{atan2}(-\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = -\frac{\pi}{4} \ \ \big(\text{i.e. } 7\pi/4\big) \]

Amplitudes:

\[ \cos\frac{\theta}{2} = \cos\frac{\pi}{8} = 0.9239, \qquad \sin\frac{\theta}{2} = \sin\frac{\pi}{8} = 0.3827 \] \[ |\psi\rangle = 0.9239\,|0\rangle + 0.3827\,e^{-i\pi/4}\,|1\rangle \] \[ = 0.9239|0\rangle + 0.3827\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} - \tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\right)|1\rangle = 0.9239|0\rangle + (0.2706 - 0.2706i)|1\rangle . \]

Verification: \(0.9239^2 + (0.2706^2+0.2706^2) = 0.8536 + 0.1464 = 1\) ✓.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Relative phase is observable, global phase is not
docs.text:
