Now let \(f(x) = a\cdot x \oplus b\) for unknown \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\) and unknown \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Can the algorithm still recover \(a\)? Can it recover \(b\)?

Solution. After the oracle:

\[ |\psi_2\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x (-1)^{a\cdot x \oplus b}|x\rangle = (-1)^{b}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x(-1)^{a\cdot x}|x\rangle \]

The extra \(b\) contributes \((-1)^b\) uniformly to every term — a global phase.

\[ |\psi_3\rangle = (-1)^b\,|a\rangle \]

Measurement still returns \(a\) with probability 1 ✓. The constant offset \(b\) is invisible, exactly as in the Deutsch algorithm where constant-0 and constant-1 were indistinguishable.

Recovering \(b\) requires one additional query. Classically, query \(x = 0^n\): then \(f(0^n) = a\cdot 0 \oplus b = b\) directly. So:

\[ \text{total: } 1 \text{ quantum query for } a + 1 \text{ classical query for } b = 2 . \]

Classically the same task needs \(n+1\) queries.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Bernstein–Vazirani with a noisy oracle
docs.text:
Suppose each oracle CNOT fails (acts as identity) independently with probability \(q\). For \(a\) with Hamming weight \(w\), find the probability of recovering \(a\) exactly, and evaluate for \(n=8\), \(w=5\), \(q=0.02\).

Solution. The oracle consists of \(w\) CNOTs, one for each 1-bit of \(a\). If the CNOT for position \(j\) fails, then bit \(j\) of \(a\) is never XORed into the ancilla, and the effective hidden string has \(a_j\) replaced by 0.

Each of the \(w\) CNOTs must succeed, independently:

\[ \Pr[\text{exact recovery}] = (1-q)^{w} . \]

For \(n=8\), \(w=5\), \(q=0.02\):

\[ (0.98)^5 = 0.9039 \approx \mathbf{90.4\%} \]

Expected number of wrong bits: \(wq = 5\times0.02 = 0.1\).

Design lesson. Errors here are not randomising — they are systematically biased toward zero, because a missing CNOT can only remove a 1 from the recovered string, never add one. So majority voting over repeated runs converges quickly: run the circuit \(R\) times and take the OR (not the majority) of the results, which recovers \(a\) correctly with probability \((1-q^R)^w\). For \(R = 3\): \((1 - 8\times10^{-6})^5 \approx 0.99996\).

Recognising the structure of the noise, not just its magnitude, is the essence of error mitigation (L38).

docs.title: 14.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Trace the algorithm for \(n=4\), \(a = 0110\). [Ans: measures \(0110\); oracle = CNOTs from \(q_2,q_3\)]
  2. Compute \(A_y\) for \(n=2\), \(a=11\), \(y=01\) using the character-sum lemma. [Ans: 0]
  3. Prove the character-sum lemma for \(n=2\) by writing out all four terms.
  4. How many classical queries are needed for a 1024-bit hidden string, and how many quantum? [Ans: 1024 and 1]
  5. Explain why \(\Pr[y]=|A_y|^2\) sums to 1 in this algorithm using the lemma.
  6. Modify the oracle so that \(f(x) = a\cdot x \oplus 1\) and confirm experimentally (on the web lab) that the answer is unchanged.
  7. Why does Bernstein–Vazirani beat randomised classical algorithms while Deutsch–Jozsa does not?

docs.title: 14.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Problem: learn the hidden string \(a\) from an oracle for \(f_a(x) = a\cdot x\).
  • Classical: exactly \(n\) queries — an information-theoretic bound holding for randomised algorithms too.
  • Quantum: 1 query, deterministic. This is a genuine (linear) separation against randomised classical computation, unlike Deutsch–Jozsa.
  • Mechanism: the oracle prepares \(H^{\otimes n}|a\rangle\); the final \(H^{\otimes n}\) inverts it and returns \(|a\rangle\) exactly.
  • Key tool: the character sum \(\sum_x(-1)^{z\cdot x} = 2^n\,\delta_{z,0}\) — perfect constructive interference at \(y=a\), perfect cancellation elsewhere.
  • Oracle = one CNOT per 1-bit of \(a\). An affine offset \(b\) appears only as an unobservable global phase.
  • Holevo's bound is not violated: \(n\) qubits carry \(n\) bits; the win is one operation instead of \(n\).

Next lesson: L15 — Simon's algorithm (the first exponential separation against randomised classical algorithms).

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Bernstein–Vazirani tab: type any hidden string up to 8 bits, see the auto-generated oracle, and watch the single spike appear at \(y = a\).

docs.title: 12.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State Deutsch's problem precisely and give the classical query lower bound.
  2. Derive the Deutsch algorithm line by line and prove it is deterministic.
  3. Build the oracle circuit for each of the four possible functions \(f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}\).
  4. Explain exactly where the speed-up comes from — and why it is a global property being computed.
  5. Analyse the effect of noise on the algorithm's success probability.

docs.title: 12.2 Deutsch's Problem
docs.text:
Setup. A black box computes an unknown \(f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}\). There are exactly four such functions:

Name \(f(0)\) \(f(1)\) Type \(f(0)\oplus f(1)\) \(f_0\) (constant-0) 0 0 constant 0 \(f_1\) (constant-1) 1 1 constant 0 \(f_2\) (identity) 0 1 balanced 1 \(f_3\) (negation) 1 0 balanced 1

The problem. Decide whether \(f\) is constant (\(f(0) = f(1)\)) or balanced (\(f(0)\ne f(1)\)), using as few queries as possible.

Equivalently: compute the single bit

\[ f(0)\oplus f(1) = \begin{cases}0 & \text{constant}\\ 1 & \text{balanced}\end{cases} \]

Classical lower bound. You must learn both \(f(0)\) and \(f(1)\). Knowing \(f(0)=0\) alone is consistent with both \(f_0\) (constant) and \(f_2\) (balanced). Therefore 2 queries are necessary and sufficient classically.

Quantum result (Deutsch, 1985). One query suffices, with certainty.

Read the problem statement carefully. We are not asked for \(f(0)\) or for \(f(1)\). We are asked for a global relational property of the function. Quantum algorithms are good at global properties precisely because a superposition can touch all inputs at once and interference can extract a joint feature — while measurement forbids extracting all the individual values.

docs.title: Step-by-step derivation
docs.text:
Step 0 — initialise.

\[ |\psi_0\rangle = |0\rangle|0\rangle \]

Step 1 — prepare the ancilla in \(|1\rangle\) and apply Hadamards to both.

\[ |\psi_1\rangle = H|0\rangle \otimes H|1\rangle = |+\rangle|-\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle + |1\rangle\big)\otimes|-\rangle \]

Step 2 — one oracle query. By phase kick-back (L11):

\[ |\psi_2\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big[(-1)^{f(0)}|0\rangle + (-1)^{f(1)}|1\rangle\Big]\otimes|-\rangle \]

Factor out the global phase \((-1)^{f(0)}\), which is unobservable:

\[ |\psi_2\rangle \simeq \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Big[|0\rangle + (-1)^{f(0)\oplus f(1)}|1\rangle\Big]\otimes|-\rangle \]

This is the crucial line. The relative phase now encodes exactly the bit we want. Note that \((-1)^{f(1)}/(-1)^{f(0)} = (-1)^{f(1)-f(0)} = (-1)^{f(0)\oplus f(1)}\) because the exponent matters only mod 2.

Writing \(b = f(0)\oplus f(1)\):

\[ |\psi_2\rangle \simeq \begin{cases} |+\rangle|-\rangle & \text{if } b = 0 \ (\text{constant})\\ |-\rangle|-\rangle & \text{if } b = 1 \ (\text{balanced}) \end{cases} \]

Step 3 — interfere. Apply \(H\) to the input register. Since \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\) and \(H|-\rangle = |1\rangle\):

\[ |\psi_3\rangle \simeq \begin{cases} |0\rangle|-\rangle & \text{constant}\\ |1\rangle|-\rangle & \text{balanced} \end{cases} \]

Step 4 — measure the input register.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{measure } 0 \Rightarrow f \text{ is constant}; \qquad \text{measure } 1 \Rightarrow f \text{ is balanced}\ } \]

The answer is deterministic — probability 1, not \(\frac23\) or "with high probability". One query, no error.

docs.title: Compact algebraic proof
docs.text:
Using \(H|x\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\sum_y(-1)^{xy}|y\rangle\), the amplitude of \(|0\rangle\) after Step 3 is

\[ \langle 0|\psi_3\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\Big[(-1)^{f(0)} + (-1)^{f(1)}\Big] \] \[ = \begin{cases} \pm 1 & f(0) = f(1) \ \ (\text{terms add}) \\ 0 & f(0)\ne f(1)\ \ (\text{terms cancel}) \end{cases} \]

Likewise the amplitude of \(|1\rangle\) is \(\frac12[(-1)^{f(0)} - (-1)^{f(1)}]\), which is \(0\) for constant and \(\pm1\) for balanced. Constructive interference on \(|0\rangle\) for constant functions; destructive interference for balanced ones. That single sentence is the algorithm.

docs.title: 12.4 Building the Four Oracles
docs.text:
\(U_f|x\rangle|y\rangle = |x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle\):

Function Circuit for \(U_f\) Reason \(f_0(x)=0\) identity (no gates) \(y\oplus0 = y\) \(f_1(x)=1\) \(X\) on the ancilla \(y\oplus1 = \bar y\) \(f_2(x)=x\) CNOT (control \(q_0\), target \(q_1\)) \(y\oplus x\) \(f_3(x)=\bar x\) CNOT then \(X\) on the ancilla \(y\oplus x\oplus 1\)

Pedagogical honesty. To build the oracle you must know \(f\) — so in a classroom the demonstration is somewhat circular. The point is the query count: given the box, the quantum algorithm opens it once. In real applications (\(f\) = a hash function, a SAT instance, a database predicate) the oracle is a large but efficiently constructible circuit whose global properties are unknown.

docs.title: 12.5 Where Exactly Is the Speed-Up?
docs.text:
Three ingredients, none sufficient alone:

  1. Superposition puts both inputs into the query simultaneously.
  2. Phase kick-back converts \(f\)'s values into relative phases without entangling any record of \(x\).
  3. Interference (the final \(H\)) converts the phase difference — a global property — into a deterministic measurement outcome.

What the algorithm does NOT do. It does not learn \(f(0)\) or \(f(1)\). After the run you know \(f(0)\oplus f(1)\) and nothing more; the individual values are provably inaccessible from one query. The trade is: one global bit instead of two local bits. That trade is available quantumly and not classically, and it is the seed of every result in Unit II.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Full trace for f₂(x) = x
docs.text:
Run the Deutsch algorithm with \(f_2(x) = x\) (oracle = CNOT) and verify the output.

Solution.

\[ |00\rangle \xrightarrow{X \text{ on } q_1} |01\rangle \xrightarrow{H\otimes H} |+\rangle|-\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\big(|0\rangle+|1\rangle\big)\big(|0\rangle-|1\rangle\big) \] \[ = \frac12\big(|00\rangle - |01\rangle + |10\rangle - |11\rangle\big) \]

Apply CNOT (flip \(q_1\) when \(q_0 = 1\)): the last two terms swap targets.

\[ \to \frac12\big(|00\rangle - |01\rangle + |11\rangle - |10\rangle\big) \] \[ = \frac12\Big[|0\rangle\big(|0\rangle-|1\rangle\big) - |1\rangle\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big)\Big] = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big)\otimes|-\rangle = |-\rangle|-\rangle \]

Apply \(H\) to \(q_0\): \(H|-\rangle = |1\rangle\).

\[ \to |1\rangle|-\rangle \]

Measurement of \(q_0\) gives 1 ⟹ balanced ✓ (\(f_2\) is indeed balanced).

Cross-check with the phase formula: \(b = f(0)\oplus f(1) = 0\oplus1 = 1\) ✓.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Full trace for f₁(x) = 1
docs.text:
Run the algorithm with the constant-1 oracle (\(X\) on the ancilla).

Solution.

\[ |+\rangle|-\rangle \xrightarrow{I\otimes X} |+\rangle \otimes X|-\rangle \] \[ X|-\rangle = X\frac{|0\rangle-|1\rangle}{\sqrt2} = \frac{|1\rangle - |0\rangle}{\sqrt2} = -|-\rangle \] \[ \Rightarrow \ -|+\rangle|-\rangle \]

Apply \(H\) to \(q_0\): \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\), giving \(-|0\rangle|-\rangle\).

Measurement gives 0 ⟹ constant ✓.

Note. The \(-1\) is a global phase (it multiplies both branches equally) and is invisible. This is exactly why constant-0 and constant-1 give the same answer — the algorithm reports constant without distinguishing which constant. That information is genuinely unavailable from one query.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Direct verification via amplitudes
docs.text:
Use the amplitude formula \(\langle 0|\psi_3\rangle = \frac12[(-1)^{f(0)}+(-1)^{f(1)}]\) to fill in the outcome for all four functions.

Solution.

\(f\) \((-1)^{f(0)}\) \((-1)^{f(1)}\) \(\langle 0\rvert\psi_3\rangle\) \(\langle 1\rvert\psi_3\rangle\) \(\Pr[0]\) Verdict \(f_0\) \(+1\) \(+1\) \(+1\) \(0\) 1 constant \(f_1\) \(-1\) \(-1\) \(-1\) \(0\) 1 constant \(f_2\) \(+1\) \(-1\) \(0\) \(+1\) 0 balanced \(f_3\) \(-1\) \(+1\) \(0\) \(-1\) 0 balanced

All four cases are deterministic, and \(|\langle0|\psi_3\rangle|^2 + |\langle1|\psi_3\rangle|^2 = 1\) in every row ✓. The sign of the surviving amplitude carries no information (global phase), which correctly reflects that we cannot distinguish \(f_0\) from \(f_1\).

docs.title: Problem 4 — The algorithm under noise
docs.text:
Suppose the input qubit suffers a phase-flip error \(Z\) with probability \(p\) immediately after the oracle. Find the probability of a correct answer.

Solution. After the oracle the input register is \(|+\rangle\) (constant) or \(|-\rangle\) (balanced).

The error \(Z\) maps \(|+\rangle \leftrightarrow |-\rangle\). So with probability \(p\) the state is flipped to the other case.

  • With probability \(1-p\): no error, final measurement gives the correct bit.
  • With probability \(p\): state flipped, final \(H\) produces the wrong answer with certainty.
\[ \Pr[\text{correct}] = 1 - p \]

Practical consequence. Unlike the noiseless ideal, on real hardware the algorithm must be run many times and the majority outcome taken. For \(p = 0.05\), running \(N\) times and taking the majority gives error \(\approx \binom{N}{\lceil N/2\rceil}p^{N/2}\), which for \(N=5\) is under \(0.2\%\). This is why every textbook demonstration on IBM hardware reports a histogram like {'0': 950, '1': 74} rather than a clean single bar.

Note the asymmetry: a bit-flip (\(X\)) error on the input register after the oracle would map \(|+\rangle \to |+\rangle\) and \(|-\rangle\to-|-\rangle\) — no effect at all. The algorithm is immune to \(X\) errors at that point but maximally sensitive to \(Z\) errors, because its answer is stored in a phase.

docs.title: Problem 5 — A three-query classical strategy is not needed; a one-query classical strategy fails
docs.text:
Prove rigorously that no classical algorithm can solve Deutsch's problem with one query, even with randomisation and allowing error probability \(< 1/2\).

Solution. A one-query deterministic classical algorithm queries some \(x\in\{0,1\}\) and outputs a verdict based on \(f(x)\).

Suppose it queries \(x = 0\) and sees \(f(0) = 0\). The two functions consistent with this observation are:

  • \(f_0\): \(f(0)=0, f(1)=0\) — constant
  • \(f_2\): \(f(0)=0, f(1)=1\) — balanced

The algorithm's view is identical in both cases, so whatever it outputs is wrong for one of them. The same argument applies to \(f(0)=1\) (functions \(f_1\) and \(f_3\)) and symmetrically to querying \(x=1\).

Randomised case. Let the algorithm query a random \(x\) and output a possibly random verdict. Consider the input distribution: pick uniformly from \(\{f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3\}\). Whatever \(x\) is queried and whatever value is returned, the posterior is exactly 50/50 between constant and balanced (each observed value \(f(x)=v\) is consistent with one constant and one balanced function, each with prior \(\frac14\)). Hence

\[ \Pr[\text{correct}] = \tfrac12 \]

for any one-query randomised classical algorithm — no better than guessing. \(\blacksquare\)

Contrast. The quantum algorithm achieves \(\Pr[\text{correct}] = 1\) with one query. This is a proved, unconditional separation — it does not rest on any unproven complexity assumption.

docs.title: 12.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Trace the algorithm for \(f_3(x) = \bar x\) and confirm the output is 1.
  2. What happens if the ancilla is initialised in \(|0\rangle\) instead of \(|1\rangle\)? Show the measurement becomes uniformly random.
  3. Design the oracle circuit for \(f(x) = 1\oplus x\) using exactly two gates.
  4. If the ancilla suffers a \(Z\) error after the oracle, does the answer change? Justify. [Ans: no — \(Z|-\rangle = |+\rangle\), but the ancilla is never measured and by then it is unentangled]
  5. Show that the Deutsch algorithm can be viewed as the \(n=1\) case of Deutsch–Jozsa.
  6. With \(p = 0.1\) per run, how many runs give a majority-vote error below \(1\%\)? [Ans: 5 runs → ≈0.86%]

docs.title: 12.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Deutsch's problem: decide whether \(f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}\) is constant or balanced — equivalently compute \(f(0)\oplus f(1)\).
  • Classical: 2 queries necessary; one query gives no better than a coin flip, even with randomisation.
  • Quantum: 1 query, deterministically correct.
  • Mechanism: \(H\) creates superposition → phase kick-back writes \((-1)^{f(x)}\) → final \(H\) makes the two branches interfere → constructive on \(|0\rangle\) iff \(f\) is constant.
  • The algorithm computes a global relational property, not the individual function values — that is the shape of every quantum advantage in this unit.
  • The answer lives in a phase, making the circuit immune to \(X\) errors and maximally sensitive to \(Z\) errors on the input qubit.

Next lesson: L13 — The Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm (\(n\)-bit generalisation, exponential separation).

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Deutsch tab: choose one of the four functions, step through the circuit, and watch the amplitude bars interfere.

docs.title: 13.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the Deutsch–Jozsa promise problem and the classical deterministic and randomised query bounds.
  2. Derive the algorithm in full using the \(n\)-qubit Hadamard identity.
  3. Prove that \(\Pr[\text{all zeros}] = 1\) for constant \(f\) and \(0\) for balanced \(f\).
  4. Explain the exponential separation and its important caveat (bounded-error randomised classical algorithms).
  5. Construct oracles for specific \(n\)-bit functions.

docs.title: 13.2 The Problem
docs.text:
Promise problem. Given an oracle for \(f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}\) with the promise that \(f\) is either

  • constant — \(f(x)\) is the same for all \(2^n\) inputs, or
  • balanced — \(f(x) = 0\) for exactly \(2^{n-1}\) inputs and \(1\) for the other \(2^{n-1}\),

decide which.

The word "promise" matters. Functions that are neither constant nor balanced (e.g. \(f\) equal to 1 on exactly one input) are excluded; the algorithm's behaviour on them is undefined. Promise problems are how most quantum speed-ups are stated.

docs.title: Classical query complexity
docs.text:
Deterministic (worst case). Query distinct inputs one at a time.

  • If two queries ever return different values ⟹ definitely balanced. Stop.
  • If the first \(2^{n-1}\) queries all return the same value, the function could still be balanced (all the 1s hiding in the untouched half). One more query settles it.
\[ \boxed{\ \text{Deterministic classical: } 2^{n-1}+1 \text{ queries in the worst case}\ } \]

For \(n = 50\) that is \(563{,}949{,}953{,}421{,}313\) queries — over \(5\times10^{14}\).

Randomised (bounded error). Query \(k\) random distinct inputs. If \(f\) is balanced, the chance that all \(k\) agree is about \(2^{-(k-1)}\). Taking \(k = 21\) gives error \(< 10^{-6}\).

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Randomised classical: } O(1) \text{ queries for constant error}\ } \]

This caveat must be stated honestly. Deutsch–Jozsa gives an exponential separation against deterministic exact classical computation, but only a constant-factor separation against randomised classical computation. The first problem with an exponential separation even against randomised classical algorithms is Simon's problem (L15).

docs.title: Quantum query complexity
docs.text: \[ \boxed{\ \text{Quantum: } 1 \text{ query, exact}\ } \]

docs.title: Derivation
docs.text:
Step 0.

\[ |\psi_0\rangle = |0\rangle^{\otimes n}\otimes|1\rangle \]

Step 1 — Hadamards everywhere.

\[ |\psi_1\rangle = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}|x\rangle\right)\otimes|-\rangle \]

Step 2 — one oracle query (phase kick-back).

\[ |\psi_2\rangle = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle\right)\otimes|-\rangle \]

Step 3 — final Hadamards. Use the identity from L07:

\[ H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle, \qquad x\cdot y = \bigoplus_{j=1}^{n} x_j y_j . \]

Therefore

\[ |\psi_3\rangle = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{y}\left[\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x) + x\cdot y}\right]|y\rangle \ \otimes|-\rangle \]

Step 4 — measure the input register. The amplitude of the all-zeros string \(y = 0^n\) is

\[ A_{0^n} = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x)+ x\cdot 0} = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x)} . \]

docs.title: The two cases
docs.text:
Case A: \(f\) constant. All \(2^n\) terms equal \((-1)^{c}\) where \(c = f(x)\) is the constant value:

\[ A_{0^n} = \frac{1}{2^n}\cdot 2^n\,(-1)^{c} = \pm1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Pr[0^n] = |{\pm}1|^2 = 1 . \]

Since the total probability is 1, every other amplitude is exactly zero. Perfect constructive interference on \(|0^n\rangle\), perfect destructive interference everywhere else.

Case B: \(f\) balanced. Exactly half the terms are \(+1\) and half are \(-1\):

\[ A_{0^n} = \frac{1}{2^n}\left[2^{n-1}(+1) + 2^{n-1}(-1)\right] = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Pr[0^n] = 0 . \]

Complete destructive interference on the all-zeros outcome.

docs.title: The decision rule
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\ \text{Measure } 0^n \Rightarrow \textbf{constant};\qquad \text{measure anything else} \Rightarrow \textbf{balanced}\ } \]

Deterministic, one query, no error. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 13.4 Constructing Oracles
docs.text:
\(f\) Type Circuit for \(U_f\) \(f(x) = 0\) constant no gates \(f(x)=1\) constant \(X\) on the ancilla \(f(x) = x_k\) balanced CNOT from \(q_k\) to the ancilla \(f(x)=x_1\oplus x_2\oplus\cdots\oplus x_n\) (parity) balanced (\(n\ge1\)) CNOT from every input qubit to the ancilla \(f(x) = a\cdot x\) for \(a\ne 0\) balanced CNOT from each \(q_j\) with \(a_j = 1\) \(f(x)= x_1 \wedge x_2\) neither Toffoli — violates the promise

Useful fact. For \(f(x) = a\cdot x\) (a linear function), Deutsch–Jozsa outputs the string \(a\) itself — not merely "balanced". Proving this is the Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm (L14).

docs.title: Problem 1 — Complete trace for n = 2, f(x) = x₁ ⊕ x₂
docs.text:
Run Deutsch–Jozsa on the 2-bit parity function and identify the measured string.

Solution. Truth table: \(f(00)=0\), \(f(01)=1\), \(f(10)=1\), \(f(11)=0\) — two 0s and two 1s, so balanced ✓.

After Step 2:

\[ \frac12\Big[(-1)^0|00\rangle + (-1)^1|01\rangle + (-1)^1|10\rangle + (-1)^0|11\rangle\Big] \] \[ = \frac12\big(|00\rangle - |01\rangle - |10\rangle + |11\rangle\big) \]

Factorise:

\[ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big)\otimes\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big) = |-\rangle\otimes|-\rangle \]

After Step 3: \(H|-\rangle = |1\rangle\), so

\[ |\psi_3\rangle = |11\rangle . \]

Measurement gives \(11\) with probability 1. Not \(00\) ⟹ balanced ✓.

Note the bonus: the output \(11\) is exactly the string \(a = 11\) defining \(f(x) = a\cdot x\).

docs.title: Problem 2 — Complete trace for n = 3, f(x) = x₂
docs.text:
Run the algorithm for \(f(x_1x_2x_3) = x_2\) (oracle = CNOT from \(q_2\) to the ancilla).

Solution. \(f\) is balanced: it equals 0 on the four strings with \(x_2=0\) and 1 on the four with \(x_2 = 1\) ✓.

After Step 2:

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt8}\sum_{x}(-1)^{x_2}|x_1x_2x_3\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle+|1\rangle\big)\otimes\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big) \otimes\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle+|1\rangle\big) \] \[ = |+\rangle|-\rangle|+\rangle \]

The phase depends only on \(x_2\), so it attaches entirely to the middle qubit.

After Step 3: \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\), \(H|-\rangle=|1\rangle\):

\[ |\psi_3\rangle = |010\rangle \]

Measurement gives \(010\) — again exactly the mask \(a\) with a 1 in position 2. Non-zero ⟹ balanced ✓.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Query counts and the honest comparison
docs.text:
For \(n = 40\): (a) worst-case deterministic classical queries; (b) randomised classical queries for error \(< 10^{-9}\); (c) quantum queries. If a classical query takes 1 ns, how long is (a)?

Solution.

(a) \(2^{39} + 1 = 549{,}755{,}813{,}889 \approx 5.5\times10^{11}\) queries.

Time: \(5.5\times10^{11}\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s} = 550\ \mathrm{s} \approx \mathbf{9.2\ minutes}\).

(b) With \(k\) random distinct queries, a balanced \(f\) produces all-equal answers with probability about \(2^{-(k-1)}\). Require

\[ 2^{-(k-1)} < 10^{-9} \ \Longrightarrow\ (k-1)\log_{10}2 > 9 \ \Longrightarrow\ k-1 > 29.9 \ \Longrightarrow\ k = \mathbf{31}. \]

(c) 1 query.

Discussion. The honest comparison is 1 vs 31, not 1 vs \(5.5\times10^{11}\). Deutsch–Jozsa's exponential separation is against exact deterministic classical computation. It is nevertheless a landmark result: it was the first proof that quantum computers can be exponentially faster at something, and it introduced the superpose–kickback–interfere template that Simon and Shor turned into genuine, randomised-classical-beating speed-ups.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Amplitude of a general outcome
docs.text:
For balanced \(f\) with \(n=2\) and truth table \(f(00)=0, f(01)=0, f(10)=1, f(11)=1\), compute the amplitude of every basis state after Step 3.

Solution. Note \(f(x) = x_1\), so we expect the output \(10\).

\[ A_y = \frac14\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x)+x\cdot y} \]

Phases \((-1)^{f(x)}\): \((+1, +1, -1, -1)\) for \(x = 00,01,10,11\).

For \(y = 00\): \(x\cdot y = 0\) always.

\[ A_{00} = \tfrac14(1+1-1-1) = 0 \]

For \(y = 01\): \(x\cdot y = x_2\), giving signs \((+,-,+,-)\).

\[ A_{01} = \tfrac14\big[(+1)(+1) + (+1)(-1) + (-1)(+1) + (-1)(-1)\big] = \tfrac14(1-1-1+1) = 0 \]

For \(y = 10\): \(x\cdot y = x_1\), giving signs \((+,+,-,-)\).

\[ A_{10} = \tfrac14\big[(1)(1) + (1)(1) + (-1)(-1) + (-1)(-1)\big] = \tfrac14(1+1+1+1) = 1 \]

For \(y = 11\): \(x\cdot y = x_1\oplus x_2\), signs \((+,-,-,+)\).

\[ A_{11} = \tfrac14\big[(1)(1) + (1)(-1) + (-1)(-1) + (-1)(1)\big] = \tfrac14(1-1+1-1) = 0 \]

Summary: \(A_{10} = 1\), all others 0. \(\sum|A_y|^2 = 1\) ✓. Measurement returns \(10\) deterministically ⟹ balanced ✓.

docs.title: Problem 5 — A function violating the promise
docs.text:
Apply the algorithm to \(f:\{0,1\}^2\to\{0,1\}\) with \(f(11) = 1\) and \(f = 0\) elsewhere (neither constant nor balanced). Compute the measurement distribution and interpret.

Solution. Phases: \((+1, +1, +1, -1)\) for \(x = 00,01,10,11\).

\[ A_{00} = \tfrac14(1+1+1-1) = \tfrac12 \] \[ A_{01} = \tfrac14\big[1 - 1 + 1 + 1\big] = \tfrac12 \]

(signs for \(y=01\): \((+,-,+,-)\), applied to phases \((+,+,+,-)\) gives \(+1,-1,+1,+1\).)

\[ A_{10} = \tfrac14\big[1+1-1+1\big] = \tfrac12 \] \[ A_{11} = \tfrac14\big[1-1-1-1\big] = -\tfrac12 \]

Distribution: each outcome with probability \(\left(\frac12\right)^2 = \frac14\).

Interpretation. With probability \(\frac14\) we measure \(00\) and wrongly conclude "constant". The algorithm gives no guarantee outside its promise — which is the definition of a promise problem.

This is a genuinely useful observation. The amplitude \(A_{0^n} = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\) is in general a bias measure: it equals \(1 - 2\cdot(\text{fraction of inputs where } f = 1)\). Here \(1 - 2\cdot\frac14 = \frac12\) ✓. So the algorithm actually estimates the bias of \(f\); the constant/balanced decision is the special case where the bias is \(\pm1\) or \(0\). This observation generalises into the amplitude estimation primitive used in Unit III.

docs.title: 13.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Trace the algorithm for \(n=2\), \(f(x) = 1\) (constant). [Ans: measures \(00\)]
  2. Give the oracle circuit for \(f(x_1x_2x_3) = x_1\oplus x_3\), and predict the measured string. [Ans: 3 CNOTs from \(q_1,q_3\); measures \(101\)]
  3. For \(n=10\), how many worst-case deterministic classical queries? [Ans: 513]
  4. Show that if \(f\) is balanced then \(\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)} = 0\) regardless of which half is 1.
  5. Prove that Deutsch–Jozsa with \(n=1\) reduces exactly to the Deutsch algorithm.
  6. A function has \(f(x)=1\) on \(\frac38\) of inputs. What is \(\Pr[0^n]\)? [Ans: \((1-2\cdot\frac38)^2 = \frac{1}{16}\)]
  7. Explain why Deutsch–Jozsa's separation is often called "unfair" and which algorithm repairs the unfairness.

docs.title: 13.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Promise problem: \(f\) is constant or balanced; decide which.
  • Classical: \(2^{n-1}+1\) deterministic worst-case queries, but only \(O(1)\) randomised queries — state this caveat.
  • Quantum: 1 query, deterministic.
  • Derivation: \(H^{\otimes n}\) → phase kick-back → \(H^{\otimes n}\); the amplitude of \(0^n\) is \(\frac{1}{2^n}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\), which is \(\pm1\) for constant and \(0\) for balanced.
  • Decision rule: all zeros ⟹ constant; anything else ⟹ balanced.
  • Outside the promise the algorithm still computes the bias of \(f\) — a fact that generalises to amplitude estimation.

Next lesson: L14 — The Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Deutsch–Jozsa tab: choose \(n\) up to 5, pick or randomise the oracle, and watch the amplitude bars collapse onto \(0^n\) or spread away from it.

docs.title: Lesson 17: The Factorization Attack on RSA and Order Finding
17.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Derive the reduction from factoring to order finding and prove why it works.
  2. State and apply the success-probability theorem for a random base \(a\).
  3. Execute the classical part of Shor's algorithm by hand on small numbers.
  4. Explain why order finding is classically hard but quantum-easy.
  5. Survey the best classical factoring algorithms and place them against the quantum result.

docs.title: 17.2 The Strategy
docs.text:
Shor's algorithm is not a purely quantum algorithm. It is a hybrid:

CLASSICAL   reduce factoring to order finding
   QUANTUM  find the order r of a mod N      <-- the only quantum step
CLASSICAL   convert r into factors via gcd

This lesson covers the two classical halves. L20 covers the quantum core. Understanding the reduction first makes Shor's algorithm feel inevitable rather than magical.

docs.title: 17.3 The Reduction: From Factoring to Order Finding
The core identity
docs.text:
Let \(N\) be an odd composite, and let \(a\) be chosen with \(\gcd(a,N)=1\). Let \(r = \mathrm{ord}_N(a)\) be the order, so \(a^r\equiv1\pmod N\).

Suppose \(r\) is even. Then we may write

\[ a^{r} - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod N \] \[ \left(a^{r/2}\right)^2 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod N \] \[ \big(a^{r/2}-1\big)\big(a^{r/2}+1\big) \equiv 0 \pmod N \]

So \(N\) divides the product \(\big(a^{r/2}-1\big)\big(a^{r/2}+1\big)\).

Key step. \(N\) does not divide either factor alone, provided:

  • \(a^{r/2}\not\equiv 1 \pmod N\) — guaranteed, because \(r\) is the smallest exponent giving 1, and \(r/2 < r\).
  • \(a^{r/2}\not\equiv -1 \pmod N\) — this is a genuine condition that may fail.

If both hold, then \(N\) shares a proper factor with each of \(a^{r/2}\mp1\), and

\[ \boxed{\ \gcd\!\left(a^{r/2}-1,\ N\right) \ \text{ and } \ \gcd\!\left(a^{r/2}+1,\ N\right) \ \text{ are non-trivial factors of } N .\ } \]

Both gcds are computed by the Euclidean algorithm in \(O(\log^2 N)\) time.

docs.title: Why a^r/2≡-1 ruins it
docs.text: If \(a^{r/2}\equiv -1\pmod N\) then \(a^{r/2}+1 \equiv 0\), so \(\gcd(a^{r/2}+1, N) = N\) — trivial. And \(\gcd(a^{r/2}-1,N) = \gcd(-2, N) = 1\) since \(N\) is odd — also trivial. Both gcds fail. Pick a new \(a\) and try again.

docs.title: The success-probability theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(N\) be odd with at least two distinct prime factors, \(N = p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_m^{k_m}\) with \(m\ge2\). Choose \(a\) uniformly at random from \(\mathbb{Z}_N^{*}\) and let \(r = \mathrm{ord}_N(a)\). Then

\[ \Pr\Big[\,r \text{ is even \textbf{and} } a^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ N)\,\Big] \ \ge\ 1 - \frac{1}{2^{m-1}} \ \ge\ \frac{1}{2} . \]

Consequence. Each random choice of \(a\) succeeds with probability at least \(\frac12\). After \(k\) attempts the failure probability is at most \(2^{-k}\); 10 attempts give failure probability under \(0.1\%\). So the expected number of quantum runs is a small constant.

Proof idea. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, \(\mathbb{Z}_N^*\cong\prod_j\mathbb{Z}_{p_j^{k_j}}^*\), each factor being cyclic (for odd \(p\)). Write \(r_j = \mathrm{ord}_{p_j^{k_j}}(a)\) and let \(2^{d_j}\) be the largest power of 2 dividing \(r_j\). Then \(r = \mathrm{lcm}(r_j)\), and the bad event (\(r\) odd, or \(a^{r/2}\equiv-1\)) occurs exactly when all \(d_j\) are equal. A counting argument over the cyclic groups shows this has probability at most \(2^{-(m-1)}\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 17.4 The Complete Algorithm
docs.text:
INPUT: composite N

1.  If N is even, return factor 2.
2.  If N = b^k for integers b >= 2, k >= 2, return b.        (classical, easy)
3.  Choose a uniformly at random from {2, ..., N-1}.
4.  Compute g = gcd(a, N)  [Euclid].
        If g > 1, return g.                                  (a lucky guess!)
5.  QUANTUM: find r = ord_N(a).                              <== the only quantum step
6.  If r is odd, go to 3.
7.  Compute x = a^(r/2) mod N.
8.  If x == N-1  (i.e. -1 mod N), go to 3.
9.  Return gcd(x-1, N) and gcd(x+1, N).

Step 2 is necessary because the reduction requires at least two distinct prime factors; prime powers \(N = p^k\) must be handled separately (and are easy: test \(\sqrt[k]{N}\) for \(k \le \log_2 N\)).

Complexity.

Step Cost gcd, primality, perfect-power tests \(O(\log^3 N)\) classical Order finding (quantum) \(O(\log^3 N)\) gates, \(O(\log N)\) qubits Expected repetitions \(O(1)\) Total \(O(\log^3 N)\) — polynomial

Compare GNFS: \(\exp\big(O(\log^{1/3}N\,\log\log^{2/3}N)\big)\) — super-polynomial.

docs.title: 17.5 Why Order Finding Is Classically Hard
docs.text:
Given \(a\) and \(N\), finding the smallest \(r\) with \(a^r\equiv1\) appears to require searching. You cannot even enumerate the candidates efficiently, because \(r\mid\phi(N)\) and you do not know \(\phi(N)\) — computing it is equivalent to factoring.

The circular dependency:

\[ \text{factor } N \ \longleftrightarrow\ \text{compute } \phi(N) \ \longleftrightarrow\ \text{find } \mathrm{ord}_N(a) \]

All three are polynomial-time equivalent. Classically, breaking into this circle requires sub-exponential sieving.

The quantum key. The sequence \(a^0, a^1, a^2, \dots \pmod N\) is periodic with period \(r\). Periodicity is exactly what the Quantum Fourier Transform detects — and it detects it in one shot, not by scanning. This is Simon's algorithm (L15) transplanted from \((\mathbb{Z}_2)^n\) to \(\mathbb{Z}_N\).

docs.title: 17.6 The Classical Competition
docs.text:
Algorithm Complexity Best for Trial division \(O(\sqrt N)\) tiny \(N\) Fermat's method fast if \(p\approx q\) close primes Pollard's rho \(O(N^{1/4})\) small factors Pollard's \(p-1\) fast if \(p-1\) is smooth weak primes Elliptic Curve Method (ECM) \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log p\log\log p}))\) finding medium factors Quadratic Sieve \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N}))\) up to ~100 digits General Number Field Sieve \(\exp\big(1.923(\ln N)^{1/3}(\ln\ln N)^{2/3}\big)\) the record holder Shor (quantum) \(O(\log^3 N)\) all \(N\)

Records. RSA-250 (250 digits, 829 bits) was factored in 2020 with ≈2700 core-years. RSA-2048 would take an estimated \(10^{9}\) times longer — beyond reach for the foreseeable future classically.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Factoring 15 by hand
docs.text:
Factor \(N = 15\) using \(a = 7\).

Solution.

Step 4. \(\gcd(7,15) = 1\) ✓ (no lucky factor).

Step 5. Find \(r = \mathrm{ord}_{15}(7)\):

\[ 7^1 = 7,\quad 7^2 = 49 \equiv 4,\quad 7^3 \equiv 28 \equiv 13,\quad 7^4 \equiv 91 \equiv 1 \] \[ r = 4 . \]

Step 6. \(r = 4\) is even ✓.

Step 7. \(x = 7^{4/2} = 7^2 = 49 \equiv 4 \pmod{15}\).

Step 8. \(x = 4 \ne 14 = N-1\) ✓.

Step 9.

\[ \gcd(4-1, 15) = \gcd(3,15) = \mathbf{3} \] \[ \gcd(4+1, 15) = \gcd(5,15) = \mathbf{5} \] \[ 15 = 3\times5 \ \checkmark \]

docs.title: Problem 2 — A choice of a that fails, and one that works
docs.text:
Factor \(N = 21\). Try \(a = 8\), then \(a = 2\).

Solution.

Attempt with \(a = 8\). \(\gcd(8,21)=1\) ✓.

\[ 8^1 = 8,\quad 8^2 = 64 \equiv 1 \pmod{21} \]

so \(r = 2\), which is even ✓.

\[ x = 8^{1} = 8, \qquad x \ne 20 \ \checkmark \] \[ \gcd(7, 21) = \mathbf{7}, \qquad \gcd(9,21) = \mathbf{3} \] \[ 21 = 3\times 7 \ \checkmark \quad\text{— this one worked.} \]

Attempt with \(a = 2\).

\[ 2^1=2,\ 2^2=4,\ 2^3=8,\ 2^4=16,\ 2^5=32\equiv11,\ 2^6=22\equiv1 \]

\(r = 6\), even ✓. \(x = 2^3 = 8\), \(x \ne 20\) ✓.

\[ \gcd(7,21) = 7, \qquad \gcd(9,21)=3 \ \checkmark \]

Now a failing case: \(a = 20 \equiv -1\). \(r = 2\) (since \((-1)^2=1\)), even ✓, but \(x = 20^1 = 20 = N-1\). Step 8 rejects it. Indeed \(\gcd(19,21)=1\) and \(\gcd(21,21)=21\) — both trivial. Retry with a different \(a\).

docs.title: Problem 3 — Factoring 91 and estimating the retry count
docs.text:
Factor \(N = 91\) with \(a = 3\). Then compute the theoretical lower bound on the per-attempt success probability.

Solution.

\(\gcd(3,91)=1\) ✓. Find \(r = \mathrm{ord}_{91}(3)\). Note \(91 = 7\times13\), so \(\phi(91) = 6\times12 = 72\) and \(r \mid 72\).

\[ 3^1=3,\ 3^2=9,\ 3^3=27,\ 3^4=81,\ 3^5 = 243 = 2\times91+61\equiv61 \] \[ 3^6 \equiv 183 = 2\times91+1 \equiv \mathbf{1} \] \[ r = 6 . \]

Even ✓. \(x = 3^{3} = 27\). \(x \ne 90\) ✓.

\[ \gcd(26, 91) = \mathbf{13}, \qquad \gcd(28,91) = \mathbf{7} \] \[ 91 = 7\times13 \ \checkmark \]

Success probability bound. \(N = 91\) has \(m = 2\) distinct prime factors, so

\[ \Pr[\text{success}] \ge 1 - \frac{1}{2^{m-1}} = 1 - \frac12 = \frac12 . \]

Expected attempts \(\le 2\). With 10 attempts, failure probability \(\le 2^{-10} < 0.1\%\).

(Empirically, for \(N=91\) the actual success rate over all valid \(a\) is about 76 % — the theorem's bound is conservative.)

docs.title: Problem 4 — Working backwards from a quantum output
docs.text:
A quantum order-finding run on \(N = 55\), \(a = 2\) returns \(r = 20\). Verify \(r\), complete the factorisation, and check the answer.

Solution.

Verify \(r\). \(55 = 5 imes11\), \(\phi(55) = 4 imes10 = 40\), so \(r\mid40\) ✓ (\(20\mid40\)).

\[ 2^{10} = 1024 = 18 imes55 + 34 \equiv 34 \pmod{55} \] \[ 2^{20} \equiv 34^2 = 1156 = 21 imes55 + 1 \equiv \mathbf{1} \ \checkmark \]

And \(2^{10}\equiv34 e1\), so no smaller divisor of 20 works among \(\{1,2,4,5,10\}\) — check \(2^4=16\), \(2^5=32\), both \( e1\) ✓. So \(r = 20\) exactly.

Complete the reduction. \(r = 20\) even ✓.

\[ x = 2^{10} \equiv 34 \pmod{55}, \qquad x e 54 \ \checkmark \] \[ \gcd(33, 55) = \mathbf{11}, \qquad \gcd(35,55) = \mathbf{5} \] \[ 55 = 5 imes11 \ \checkmark \]

Note how little classical work this is: two Euclidean algorithms on 6-bit numbers. All the difficulty was concentrated in producing the number 20.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Resource estimate for RSA-2048
docs.text:
Estimate the classical GNFS effort and the quantum resources needed to factor a 2048-bit RSA modulus. Comment on the timeline.

Solution.

Classical (GNFS). The heuristic complexity is

\[ L_N\!\left[\tfrac13, 1.923\right] = \exp\!\left(1.923\,(\ln N)^{1/3}(\ln\ln N)^{2/3}\right) . \]

With \(N = 2^{2048}\): \(\ln N = 2048\ln2 = 1419.6\), so \((\ln N)^{1/3} = 11.24\); \(\ln\ln N = \ln1419.6 = 7.258\), so \((\ln\ln N)^{2/3} = 3.73\).

\[ \text{exponent} = 1.923 \times 11.24 \times 3.73 = 80.6 \] \[ \text{effort} \approx e^{80.6} \approx 10^{35} \ \text{operations}. \]

At \(10^{18}\) operations/second (an exascale machine devoted entirely to this):

\[ t \approx 10^{17}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 3\times10^{9}\ \text{years} . \]

Quantum (Shor). Gate count scales as \(O(n^3)\) with \(n = 2048\):

\[ n^3 = 2048^3 = 8.6\times10^{9} \ \text{logical operations (order of magnitude)}. \]

Logical qubits needed: about \(2n + O(\log n) \approx 4100\).

Physical resources. With surface-code overhead of \(\sim10^3\)–\(10^4\) physical qubits per logical qubit:

\[ 4100 \times 3000 \approx \mathbf{1.2\times10^{7}\ \text{physical qubits}} . \]

Published estimates (Gidney & Ekerå, 2021) give 20 million noisy physical qubits and about 8 hours at a \(10^{-3}\) gate error rate — a substantial optimisation over earlier billion-qubit estimates.

Timeline comment. Current devices have \(10^2\)–\(10^3\) physical qubits with error rates near \(10^{-3}\). The gap is roughly four orders of magnitude in qubit count. Estimates for crossing it range from 10 to 30 years, with wide uncertainty. Because of "harvest now, decrypt later", and because NIST published ML-KEM/ML-DSA in August 2024, migration to post-quantum cryptography is already underway for long-lived secrets. The correct posture is to migrate now, not to wait for the machine.

docs.title: 17.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Factor \(N=33\) using \(a=5\). [Ans: \(r=10\), \(x=5^5\equiv 23\), gcds give 11 and 3]
  2. Factor \(N=35\) using \(a=6\). Does it succeed? [Ans: \(r = 2\), \(x = 6 \ne 34\); gcds give 5 and 7 ✓]
  3. Factor \(N = 39\) using \(a = 5\). [Ans: \(r=4\), \(x=25\), gcds give 3 and 13]
  4. For \(N=15\), \(a=14\): show that the attempt fails and explain which condition is violated.
  5. Prove that if \(r\) is odd, the reduction gives no information.
  6. Why is Step 2 (perfect-power test) required?
  7. If \(N\) has 3 distinct prime factors, what is the guaranteed success probability? [Ans: \(\ge 3/4\)]

docs.title: 17.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Shor's algorithm is hybrid: classical reduction → quantum order finding → classical gcd.
  • If \(r = \mathrm{ord}_N(a)\) is even and \(a^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\pmod N\), then \(\gcd(a^{r/2}\pm1, N)\) are non-trivial factors.
  • A random \(a\) satisfies both conditions with probability \(\ge 1 - 2^{-(m-1)} \ge \frac12\), so \(O(1)\) attempts suffice.
  • Factoring, computing \(\phi(N)\) and order finding are all polynomial-time equivalent; classically all are hard because you cannot enumerate the divisors of an unknown \(\phi(N)\).
  • Order finding is a period-finding problem, which is what the QFT solves — the same structure as Simon's algorithm over a different group.
  • Classical best is GNFS (sub-exponential, \(\approx10^{35}\) operations for RSA-2048); Shor is \(O(\log^3N)\) but needs \(\sim10^7\) physical qubits with today's error rates.

Next lesson: L18 — The Quantum Fourier Transform.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → Shor Workbench: enter any \(N\) up to 10 000, watch the algorithm pick \(a\), compute the order (by simulation), and complete the factorisation, with a running tally of successful and failed attempts.

docs.title: 24.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State precisely the problem HHL solves — and, equally importantly, the problem it does not solve.
  2. Derive the algorithm: state preparation → QPE → controlled rotation → uncompute → post-select.
  3. Analyse the complexity \(O(\log N\, s^2\kappa^2/\epsilon)\) and identify each factor's origin.
  4. State the four caveats (Aaronson's list) that limit practical speed-up.
  5. Recognise HHL as the engine of quantum linear regression, differential-equation solvers and some QML proposals.

docs.title: 24.2 The Problem
docs.text:
Classical. Given \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}\) and \(\vec b\in\mathbb{C}^{N}\), solve \(A\vec x = \vec b\).

Best classical methods: Gaussian elimination \(O(N^3)\); conjugate gradient \(O(Ns\kappa)\) for \(s\)-sparse, well-conditioned \(A\), where \(\kappa = \frac{|\lambda_{\max}|}{|\lambda_{\min}|}\) is the condition number.

Quantum (HHL, 2009). Given oracle access to \(A\) and a routine preparing \(|b\rangle\), produce a quantum state

\[ |x\rangle \propto A^{-1}|b\rangle \]

in time

\[ O\!\left(\frac{\log N \cdot s^{2}\kappa^{2}}{\epsilon}\right) . \]

Exponentially better in \(N\) — \(\log N\) instead of \(N\).

docs.title: The caveat, stated up front
docs.text:
HHL does not output the vector \(\vec x\). It outputs a quantum state \(|x\rangle\) whose amplitudes are proportional to the entries of \(\vec x\). Reading out all \(N\) entries requires \(\Omega(N)\) measurements, destroying the speed-up entirely. HHL is useful only when you want a scalar summary such as \(\langle x|M|x\rangle\) for some observable \(M\) — an average, a norm, a weighted sum, an overlap.

Teach this caveat before the algorithm, not after. It is the single most misrepresented result in quantum computing.

docs.title: 24.3 Assumptions
docs.text: Assumption Why it is needed \(A\) is Hermitian so \(e^{iAt}\) is unitary. Non-Hermitian \(A\) is handled by the dilation \(\tilde A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & A\\ A^\dagger & 0\end{pmatrix}\) \(A\) is \(s\)-sparse and row-computable so \(e^{iAt}\) can be simulated efficiently \(\kappa\) is small (well-conditioned) complexity is \(O(\kappa^2)\); ill-conditioned systems are hopeless \(\vert b\rangle\) is efficiently preparable otherwise state preparation costs \(O(N)\) and dominates Eigenvalues scaled into \((0,1)\) so QPE phases lie in range

docs.title: Registers
docs.text:
• Input register (\(\log N\) qubits): holds \(|b\rangle\), later becomes \(|x\rangle\).
  • Clock register (\(t\) qubits): for phase estimation.
  • Ancilla (1 qubit): for the conditional rotation and post-selection.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Step 0 — expand \(|b\rangle\) in the eigenbasis of \(A\). Let \(A|u_j\rangle = \lambda_j|u_j\rangle\) with \(\{|u_j\rangle\}\) orthonormal (guaranteed by Hermiticity). Write

\[ |b\rangle = \sum_{j=1}^{N}\beta_j\,|u_j\rangle, \qquad \beta_j = \langle u_j|b\rangle . \]

This expansion is a bookkeeping device — we never compute the \(\beta_j\).

Step 1 — Quantum phase estimation with \(U = e^{iAt_0}\), whose eigenvalues are \(e^{i\lambda_jt_0}\):

\[ \sum_j \beta_j |u_j\rangle|0\rangle \ \longrightarrow\ \sum_j\beta_j\,|u_j\rangle\,\big|\tilde\lambda_j\big\rangle \]

The clock register now holds each eigenvalue, entangled with its eigenvector.

Step 2 — Controlled rotation. Append an ancilla and rotate it by an angle depending on \(\tilde\lambda_j\):

\[ \sum_j\beta_j|u_j\rangle|\tilde\lambda_j\rangle \left(\sqrt{1 - \frac{C^2}{\lambda_j^2}}\;|0\rangle + \frac{C}{\lambda_j}\,|1\rangle\right) \]

where \(C = O(1/\kappa)\) is a normalisation constant chosen so the argument stays \(\le1\).

This step is the heart of the algorithm: it multiplies each eigen-component's amplitude by \(1/\lambda_j\) — which is exactly what applying \(A^{-1}\) does. Implemented by computing \(\arcsin(C/\tilde\lambda)\) into an ancillary register (reversible classical arithmetic) and applying a controlled \(R_y\).

Step 3 — Uncompute the clock register by running QPE backwards. This is essential: otherwise the clock stays entangled with the eigenvectors and \(|x\rangle\) is not a pure state.

\[ \sum_j\beta_j|u_j\rangle|0\rangle \left(\sqrt{1-\frac{C^2}{\lambda_j^2}}|0\rangle + \frac{C}{\lambda_j}|1\rangle\right) \]

Step 4 — Measure the ancilla and post-select on \(|1\rangle\). Conditioned on that outcome:

\[ |x\rangle \propto \sum_j \frac{\beta_j}{\lambda_j}|u_j\rangle = A^{-1}|b\rangle \ \checkmark \]

Success probability.

\[ \Pr[\text{ancilla}=1] = \sum_j \frac{C^2|\beta_j|^2}{\lambda_j^2} = \Omega\!\left(\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}\right) . \]

With amplitude amplification (L22 §5.1), this is boosted to \(O(1)\) using \(O(\kappa)\) repetitions rather than \(O(\kappa^2)\).

docs.title: 24.5 Complexity Breakdown
docs.text:
\[ O\!\left(\frac{\log N \cdot s^{2}\,\kappa^{2}}{\epsilon}\right) \] Factor Source \(\log N\) number of qubits — the exponential win \(s^2\) sparse Hamiltonian simulation of \(e^{iAt}\) \(\kappa\) (one factor) QPE must resolve \(\lambda_{\min}\), requiring \(t_0 = O(\kappa/\epsilon)\) \(\kappa\) (second factor) post-selection success probability \(\Omega(1/\kappa^2)\), halved to \(O(\kappa)\) by amplitude amplification \(1/\epsilon\) phase-estimation precision

Improvements. Childs–Kothari–Somma (2015) improved the \(\epsilon\) dependence to \(O(\mathrm{poly}\log(1/\epsilon))\) using linear-combination-of-unitaries and quantum walks. Ambainis (2012) achieved linear \(\kappa\) dependence via variable-time amplitude amplification. Current best:

\[ O\big(s\kappa\,\mathrm{polylog}(N s\kappa/\epsilon)\big) . \]

Lower bound. HHL is BQP-complete: solving linear systems to this specification is as hard as any quantum computation. Hence no classical polynomial algorithm exists unless BPP = BQP, and the \(\kappa\) and \(s\) dependences cannot be removed.

docs.title: 24.6 The Four Caveats (Aaronson, Nature Physics, 2015)
docs.text:
"Read the fine print." All four must hold simultaneously for a real speed-up.

1. State preparation. You must produce \(|b\rangle = \frac{1}{\|\vec b\|}\sum_i b_i|i\rangle\) efficiently. For arbitrary classical data this costs \(O(N)\) — killing the advantage. It works only if \(\vec b\) has structure (e.g. it is given by a formula, or produced by an earlier quantum subroutine), or if efficient qRAM exists.

2. Hamiltonian simulation. \(e^{iAt}\) must be efficiently implementable, requiring \(A\) to be sparse (or of low rank) and its entries efficiently computable.

3. Condition number. Runtime scales with \(\kappa\). Real-world matrices are often ill-conditioned; preconditioning is essential but preconditioners are themselves hard to build quantumly.

4. Readout. You obtain \(|x\rangle\), not \(\vec x\). Only scalar functionals like \(\langle x|M|x\rangle\) are cheap.

docs.title: Dequantisation
docs.text:
Ewin Tang (2018–19), then an undergraduate, showed that several HHL-based QML algorithms (recommendation systems, PCA, low-rank linear systems) admit classical algorithms with the same \(\mathrm{polylog}(N)\) scaling, provided the classical algorithm is given the same \(\ell^2\)-norm sampling access that the quantum algorithm implicitly assumes.

The lesson. Much of the claimed exponential advantage came from the input model, not from quantum mechanics. Exponential speed-up survives only for genuinely high-rank, sparse, well-conditioned problems where the input is generated quantumly. This is now the standard caution in the field, and students should carry it into Unit III.

docs.title: Problem 1 — HHL on a 2×2 system, by hand
docs.text:
Solve \(A\vec x = \vec b\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), \(\vec b = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), tracing the HHL steps.

Solution.

Eigen-decomposition. \(A\) is already diagonal: \(\lambda_1 = 1\) with \(|u_1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(\lambda_2 = 2\) with \(|u_2\rangle = |1\rangle\).

\[ |b\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|1\rangle, \qquad \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \]

Step 1 — QPE writes the eigenvalues into the clock register:

\[ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle|1\rangle + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|1\rangle|2\rangle \]

Step 2 — controlled rotation with \(C = 1\) (safe since \(\lambda_{\min}=1\)):

\[ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle|1\rangle\big(0\cdot|0\rangle + 1\cdot|1\rangle\big) + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|1\rangle|2\rangle\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|0\rangle + \tfrac12|1\rangle\right) \]

(for \(\lambda=1\): \(C/\lambda = 1\), so \(\sqrt{1-1}=0\); for \(\lambda=2\): \(C/\lambda = \frac12\), \(\sqrt{1-\frac14} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).)

Step 3 — uncompute the clock.

Step 4 — post-select ancilla \(=1\). The surviving (unnormalised) state is

\[ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot 1\cdot|0\rangle + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac12\cdot|1\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle + \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}|1\rangle \]

Norm\(^2 = \frac12 + \frac18 = \frac58\). Normalising:

\[ |x\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5/8}}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}|0\rangle + \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}|1\rangle\right) = \frac{2}{\sqrt5}|0\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt5}|1\rangle \]

Verify against the classical solution.

\[ \vec x = A^{-1}\vec b = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\tfrac12\end{pmatrix} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \tfrac12\end{pmatrix} \]

Normalised: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1.25}}(1, 0.5)^T = (0.8944, 0.4472)^T = \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt5},\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\right)^T\) ✓

Success probability. \(\Pr[1] = \frac{5}{8} = 62.5\%\).

Note what was obtained: the direction of \(\vec x\), not its magnitude. The overall scale \(\|\vec x\|\) is lost in normalisation and must be estimated separately (e.g. from the post-selection probability).

docs.title: Problem 2 — Condition number and its cost
docs.text:
Compute \(\kappa\) for \(A_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\), \(A_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.99\\ 0.99 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), and compare HHL runtimes.

Solution.

\(A_1\): eigenvalues 1 and 2.

\[ \kappa_1 = \frac{2}{1} = \mathbf{2} \]

\(A_2\): symmetric with eigenvalues \(1\pm0.99\), i.e. \(1.99\) and \(0.01\).

\[ \kappa_2 = \frac{1.99}{0.01} = \mathbf{199} \]

Runtime ratio (using the \(O(\kappa^2)\) scaling of original HHL):

\[ \frac{\kappa_2^2}{\kappa_1^2} = \frac{199^2}{2^2} = \frac{39601}{4} \approx \mathbf{9900\times} \]

With the improved \(O(\kappa)\) algorithms, the ratio is still \(\approx100\times\).

Interpretation. \(A_2\) is nearly singular: its rows are almost parallel. HHL must run QPE with enough precision to resolve \(\lambda_{\min} = 0.01\), requiring \(t_0 \sim \kappa/\epsilon\) and correspondingly deep circuits, and the post-selection succeeds only \(\sim1/\kappa^2\) of the time.

Practical rule: HHL is worthwhile only when \(\kappa = O(\mathrm{polylog}\,N)\). Since real physical and engineering systems typically have \(\kappa\) growing polynomially with problem size, preconditioning is not optional — and constructing quantum preconditioners is an open research problem.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Estimating an observable, the correct use of HHL
docs.text:
After HHL, we want \(\langle x|M|x\rangle\) where \(M = |0\rangle\langle0|\) (i.e. \(|x_0|^2/\|x\|^2\)). Using Problem 1's result, compute it and state the sampling cost to 1 % relative accuracy.

Solution.

From Problem 1, \(|x\rangle = \frac{2}{\sqrt5}|0\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt5}|1\rangle\).

\[ \langle x|M|x\rangle = \left|\frac{2}{\sqrt5}\right|^2 = \frac{4}{5} = \mathbf{0.8} \]

Sampling cost. Measure in the computational basis and count zeros. This is a Bernoulli estimate with \(p = 0.8\):

\[ \mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N_{\text{shots}}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.16}{N_{\text{shots}}}} \]

Require relative accuracy 1 %, i.e. absolute accuracy \(0.008\):

\[ \sqrt{\frac{0.16}{N_{\text{shots}}}} \le 0.008 \ \Longrightarrow\ N_{\text{shots}} \ge \frac{0.16}{6.4\times10^{-5}} = \mathbf{2500} \]

Add post-selection overhead. Each useful shot requires the ancilla to read 1, which happens with probability \(0.625\):

\[ \text{Total circuit runs} = \frac{2500}{0.625} = \mathbf{4000} . \]

This is HHL used correctly: a single scalar functional of \(\vec x\), estimated with a problem-size-independent number of shots. Extracting all \(N\) components would instead require \(\Omega(N)\) shots and eliminate the advantage.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Where HHL genuinely helps
docs.text:
Identify which of these problems admits a real HHL speed-up, and justify each answer.

(a) Solve a \(10^{6}\times10^{6}\) dense system and print all entries of \(\vec x\). (b) Compute the total resistance of a large sparse electrical network. (c) Estimate the mean of \(\vec x\) where \(A\) is a sparse Laplacian and \(\vec b\) is uniform. (d) Machine-learning regression on a low-rank data matrix.

Solution.

(a) No. Two independent failures: (i) dense \(A\) (\(s = N\)) breaks the sparsity assumption, and Hamiltonian simulation costs \(O(N)\); (ii) printing all \(10^{6}\) entries needs \(\Omega(N)\) measurements. Both readout and simulation caveats are violated.

(b) Yes, potentially. Effective resistance between two nodes is \(R_{uv} = (\vec e_u - \vec e_v)^T L^{+}(\vec e_u - \vec e_v)\) — a scalar functional of the solution. The graph Laplacian \(L\) is sparse for bounded-degree graphs, and \(\vec b\) is a simple two-nonzero vector, trivially preparable. The one risk is \(\kappa\): for graphs with poor connectivity, \(\lambda_{\min}\) (the spectral gap) can be tiny. Speed-up holds for expander-like graphs.

(c) Yes. The mean \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i \propto \langle s|x\rangle\) where \(|s\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_i|i\rangle\) — computable by a swap test in \(O(1)\) shots per unit precision. \(\vec b\) uniform means \(|b\rangle = |s\rangle = H^{\otimes n}|0\rangle\) — one layer of Hadamards. Sparse Laplacian ✓, scalar output ✓, easy preparation ✓. All four caveats satisfied.

(d) No — dequantised. Low rank is precisely the case Tang's algorithms handle. A classical algorithm with \(\ell^2\)-sampling access achieves \(\mathrm{polylog}(N)\) scaling too. Only a polynomial speed-up (in rank and condition number) survives, not an exponential one.

Pattern. HHL helps when the matrix is sparse and high-rank, the input is structured or quantum-generated, the condition number is small, and the output is a scalar.

docs.title: Problem 5 — HHL for quantum linear regression
docs.text:
Show how ordinary least squares \(\vec\beta = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\vec y\) maps onto HHL, and state the speed-up and its conditions.

Solution.

Setup. Data matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}\) (\(M\) samples, \(d\) features), targets \(\vec y\in\mathbb{R}^{M}\). The normal equations are

\[ \underbrace{\big(X^TX\big)}_{A}\ \vec\beta = \underbrace{X^T\vec y}_{\vec b} . \]

Mapping to HHL.

  • \(A = X^TX\) is Hermitian (symmetric real) and positive semi-definite ✓ — no dilation needed.
  • \(A\) is \(d\times d\), so HHL runs on \(\log_2 d\) qubits.
  • \(|b\rangle \propto X^T\vec y\) must be prepared — feasible if \(X\) and \(\vec y\) come from a quantum process or efficient qRAM.
  • Output: \(|\beta\rangle \propto A^{-1}|b\rangle\) — the regression coefficients as amplitudes.

Complexity.

\[ \text{Classical: } O(Md^2 + d^3) \qquad\qquad \text{HHL: } O\!\left(\frac{\log d\cdot s^2\kappa^2}{\epsilon}\right) \]

Exponential in \(d\) — but only under the standing conditions.

What can be extracted usefully.

Quantity Cost Predict a new point \(\hat y_{\text{new}} = \vec x_{\text{new}}^T\vec\beta\) \(O(1)\) shots — a swap test overlap ✓ Coefficient of determination \(R^2\) scalar functional ✓ Total coefficient norm $\Vert \vec\beta\Vert $ from the post-selection probability ✓ All \(d\) coefficients \(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_d\) \(\Omega(d)\) shots ✗ — no speed-up

The condition number problem is severe here. \(\kappa(X^TX) = \kappa(X)^2\) — squaring the data matrix's condition number. Highly correlated features (multicollinearity) make \(\kappa\) enormous. Ridge regression helps: replacing \(A\) by \(X^TX + \lambda I\) raises \(\lambda_{\min}\) to at least \(\lambda\), giving \(\kappa \le \frac{\lambda_{\max}+\lambda}{\lambda}\). Regularisation is therefore not just statistically desirable but computationally essential for the quantum algorithm.

Honest summary. Quantum linear regression gives an exponential speed-up for making predictions, not for learning interpretable coefficients. This distinction runs through all of Unit III's QML content.

docs.title: 24.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Solve \(A\vec x=\vec b\) by HHL for \(A = \mathrm{diag}(1,3)\), \(\vec b = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T\). Give \(|x\rangle\) and \(\Pr[\text{ancilla}=1]\) with \(C=1\). [Ans: \(|x\rangle\propto 3|0\rangle+|1\rangle\); \(\Pr=5/9\)]
  2. Compute \(\kappa\) for \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). [Ans: 3]
  3. Why must the clock register be uncomputed?
  4. List Aaronson's four caveats and give one example where each is violated.
  5. Explain why \(\kappa(X^TX) = \kappa(X)^2\).
  6. Show that a dilation \(\tilde A\) handles non-Hermitian \(A\); write the corresponding \(\tilde b\).
  7. Give one problem where HHL provably helps and one where it is dequantised.

docs.title: 24.9 Summary
docs.text:
• HHL produces the quantum state \(|x\rangle\propto A^{-1}|b\rangle\) in \(O(\log N\,s^2\kappa^2/\epsilon)\) — exponentially better in \(N\) than classical solvers.
  • Steps: prepare \(|b\rangle\) → QPE writes eigenvalues into a clock register → controlled rotation multiplies amplitudes by \(C/\lambda_j\) → uncompute the clock → post-select the ancilla on \(|1\rangle\).
  • The \(\kappa^2\) arises from QPE precision and post-selection probability; amplitude amplification reduces it to \(\kappa\).
  • HHL is BQP-complete, so the caveats cannot all be removed.
  • Aaronson's four caveats: state preparation, Hamiltonian simulation (sparsity), condition number, and readout. HHL gives \(|x\rangle\), not \(\vec x\) — only scalar functionals are cheap.
  • Tang's dequantisation eliminated the exponential advantage for low-rank problems; it survives only for sparse, high-rank, well-conditioned systems with quantum-native inputs and scalar outputs.
  • Applications: effective resistance, differential equations, quantum linear regression (prediction, not coefficient recovery), and as a subroutine in QML (Unit III).

Next lesson: L25 — Post-quantum cryptography: Kyber and quantum-attack-resistant signatures.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → HHL Explorer: enter a \(2\times2\) or \(4\times4\) system, see the eigen-decomposition, the conditional-rotation angles, the post-selection probability and a comparison of \(|x\rangle\) with the exact classical solution.

docs.title: Lesson 34: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)
34.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Convert a combinatorial problem to QUBO and then to an Ising Hamiltonian.
  2. Construct the QAOA cost and mixer unitaries and the full \(p\)-layer ansatz.
  3. Derive the QAOA circuit for Max-Cut and compute the \(p=1\) expectation analytically.
  4. State the approximation ratio results and the \(p\to\infty\) limit.
  5. Assess QAOA's practical status honestly against classical heuristics.

docs.title: 34.2 From Combinatorial Problems to Ising Hamiltonians
QUBO
docs.text:
Definition. A Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problem is

\[ \min_{\vec x\in\{0,1\}^{n}} \ \vec x^{T}Q\vec x = \min_{\vec x}\ \sum_{i}Q_{ii}x_i + \sum_{i<j}Q_{ij}x_ix_j \]

QUBO is NP-hard and remarkably universal — Max-Cut, graph colouring, the travelling salesman problem, portfolio optimisation, number partitioning and set cover all reduce to it.

Handling constraints. A constraint \(\sum_i x_i = k\) becomes a penalty term \(\lambda\big(\sum_ix_i - k\big)^{2}\) added to the objective, with \(\lambda\) large enough that violating the constraint always costs more than any gain elsewhere.

docs.title: QUBO to Ising
docs.text:
Substitute \(x_i = \frac{1 - z_i}{2}\) with \(z_i \in \{-1,+1\}\):

\[ \boxed{\ x_i \in\{0,1\} \ \longleftrightarrow\ z_i = 1-2x_i \in\{+1,-1\}\ } \]

The objective becomes the Ising energy

\[ H_{C} = \sum_{i}h_i\,Z_i + \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,Z_iZ_j + \text{const} \]

where \(Z_i\) is the Pauli-\(Z\) on qubit \(i\). Note that \(H_C\) is diagonal in the computational basis: \(H_C|\vec z\rangle = C(\vec z)\,|\vec z\rangle\), where \(C(\vec z)\) is the classical cost of the bitstring. Minimising a combinatorial objective = finding the ground state of \(H_C\).

docs.title: The Max-Cut example
docs.text:
Problem. Given a graph \(G = (V,E)\), partition \(V\) into two sets to maximise the number of edges crossing the cut.

Assign \(z_i = +1\) or \(-1\) by which side vertex \(i\) is on. An edge \((i,j)\) is cut iff \(z_i \ne z_j\), i.e. iff \(z_iz_j = -1\). So

\[ \text{cut value} = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\frac{1 - z_iz_j}{2} \] \[ \boxed{\ H_{C} = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\frac{1}{2}\big(I - Z_iZ_j\big), \qquad \langle H_C\rangle = \text{expected number of cut edges}\ } \]

We maximise \(\langle H_C\rangle\) (equivalently minimise \(\sum_{(i,j)}Z_iZ_j\)).

docs.title: 34.3 The QAOA Ansatz
docs.text: Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (2014).

docs.title: Two Hamiltonians
docs.text:
Cost Hamiltonian \(H_C\) — encodes the problem, diagonal.

Mixer Hamiltonian

\[ H_{B} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \]

— off-diagonal; it drives transitions between bitstrings, allowing the state to explore.

They do not commute: \([H_C, H_B]\ne0\). This is essential — if they commuted the algorithm would be classical.

docs.title: The circuit
docs.text:
Initial state: the uniform superposition, which is the ground state of \(-H_B\):

\[ |s\rangle = |+\rangle^{\otimes n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{\vec z}|\vec z\rangle \]

Alternate \(p\) times:

\[ \boxed{\ |\vec\gamma,\vec\beta\rangle = e^{-i\beta_p H_B}e^{-i\gamma_p H_C}\cdots e^{-i\beta_1H_B}e^{-i\gamma_1H_C}\,|s\rangle\ } \]

\(2p\) parameters: \(\vec\gamma = (\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_p)\), \(\vec\beta = (\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p)\).

Objective:

\[ F_p(\vec\gamma,\vec\beta) = \big\langle\vec\gamma,\vec\beta\big|H_C\big|\vec\gamma,\vec\beta\big\rangle \ \longrightarrow\ \text{maximise over } (\vec\gamma,\vec\beta) \]

Then measure in the computational basis; the measured bitstring is the candidate solution.

docs.title: Implementing the unitaries
docs.text:
Cost unitary. Because \(H_C\) is a sum of commuting \(Z_iZ_j\) terms:

\[ e^{-i\gamma H_C} = \prod_{(i,j)\in E} e^{-i\gamma Z_iZ_j/2}\cdot(\text{global phase}) \]

Each \(e^{-i\theta Z_iZ_j/2}\) is realised as

q_i --*----------------*--
      |                |
q_j --[X]--[Rz(theta)]--[X]--

i.e. CNOT, \(R_z(\theta)\), CNOT — two CNOTs and one rotation per edge.

Mixer unitary. \(H_B\) is a sum of single-qubit \(X\)'s, so

\[ e^{-i\beta H_B} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} R_x(2\beta_i) \]

— one \(R_x\) per qubit, all in parallel.

Total resources: \(p\,(2|E| + n)\) gates, depth \(O(p\cdot|E|/n)\) if edges are parallelised.

docs.title: The adiabatic connection
docs.text:
QAOA is a Trotterised approximation to adiabatic evolution. The adiabatic algorithm evolves under

\[ H(t) = \Big(1 - \tfrac{t}{T}\Big)H_B + \tfrac{t}{T}H_C \]

slowly from the ground state of \(H_B\) to that of \(H_C\). Trotterising this evolution into \(p\) steps gives exactly the QAOA form. Hence:

\[ \boxed{\ \lim_{p\to\infty}\max_{\vec\gamma,\vec\beta}F_p = C_{\max}\ } \]

QAOA is exact in the limit \(p\to\infty\). The question is how large \(p\) must be — and this is where the practical difficulty lies.

docs.title: Known results
docs.text: Result Statement Farhi et al. (2014) \(p=1\) QAOA on 3-regular graphs guarantees approximation ratio \(\ge 0.6924\) Goemans–Williamson (classical SDP) guarantees \(\ge 0.8785\) — better than \(p=1\) QAOA \(p=2\) on 3-regular \(\ge 0.7559\) \(p=11\) on 3-regular \(\approx0.8785\) — only here does QAOA match GW Farhi–Harrow (2016) QAOA at \(p=1\) already gives sampling hard for classical computers, though the optimisation quality is modest Bravyi et al. (2020) for bounded-degree graphs, low-\(p\) QAOA is provably limited by locality — it cannot see beyond distance \(p\)

docs.title: The locality obstruction
docs.text: At depth \(p\), each qubit's final state depends only on the subgraph within distance \(p\) of that qubit (a lightcone argument). For a graph with \(n\) vertices and good expansion, a constant \(p\) sees only a vanishing local neighbourhood, so QAOA cannot detect global structure. This is Bravyi–Kliesch–Koenig–Tang's "obstacle to variational quantum advantage" and it explains why constant-depth QAOA underperforms classical algorithms on many families.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Building the Ising Hamiltonian for a triangle
docs.text:
For the triangle graph \(K_3\) with vertices \(\{0,1,2\}\) and all three edges, write \(H_C\), list all 8 bitstrings with their cut values, and identify the optimum.

Solution.

\[ H_C = \frac12\big[(I - Z_0Z_1) + (I - Z_1Z_2) + (I - Z_0Z_2)\big] = \frac32 I - \frac12\big(Z_0Z_1 + Z_1Z_2 + Z_0Z_2\big) \]

Enumerate (using \(z_i = +1\) for bit 0, \(-1\) for bit 1; cut edges = pairs with different bits):

\(\lvert z_0z_1z_2\rangle\) Partition Cut edges Cut value \(000\) \(\{0,1,2\}\mid\emptyset\) none 0 \(001\) \(\{0,1\}\mid\{2\}\) (0,2),(1,2) 2 \(010\) \(\{0,2\}\mid\{1\}\) (0,1),(1,2) 2 \(011\) \(\{0\}\mid\{1,2\}\) (0,1),(0,2) 2 \(100\) \(\{1,2\}\mid\{0\}\) (0,1),(0,2) 2 \(101\) \(\{1\}\mid\{0,2\}\) (0,1),(1,2) 2 \(110\) \(\{2\}\mid\{0,1\}\) (0,2),(1,2) 2 \(111\) \(\emptyset\mid\{0,1,2\}\) none 0 \[ C_{\max} = \mathbf{2} \]

Note: \(K_3\) is an odd cycle, so it is not bipartite — you cannot cut all 3 edges. Six of the eight bitstrings achieve the optimum, so random guessing already gives \(\frac{6}{8}\times2 + \frac28\times0 = 1.5\), an approximation ratio of \(\frac{1.5}{2} = 0.75\). Any proposed algorithm must beat 0.75 on this instance to be doing anything at all — a useful sanity check students should always compute first.

docs.title: Problem 2 — QAOA p=1 on a single edge, computed exactly
docs.text:
Compute \(F_1(\gamma,\beta)\) for a 2-vertex graph with one edge, and find the optimal parameters.

Solution.

\[ H_C = \frac12\big(I - Z_0Z_1\big) \]

Step 1. \(|s\rangle = |{+}{+}\rangle = \frac12(|00\rangle+|01\rangle+|10\rangle+|11\rangle)\).

Step 2 — cost unitary. \(e^{-i\gamma H_C}\) is diagonal, applying phase \(e^{-i\gamma C(\vec z)}\) where \(C = 1\) for \(\{01,10\}\) and \(C=0\) for \(\{00,11\}\):

\[ \frac12\Big(|00\rangle + e^{-i\gamma}|01\rangle + e^{-i\gamma}|10\rangle + |11\rangle\Big) \]

Step 3 — mixer. Apply \(R_x(2\beta)^{\otimes2}\).

Step 4 — evaluate \(F_1 = \langle H_C\rangle\). Since \(H_C = \frac12(I - Z_0Z_1)\), we need \(\langle Z_0Z_1\rangle\) in the final state. Work in the Heisenberg picture:

\[ \langle Z_0Z_1\rangle = \big\langle s\big| U_C^{\dagger}U_B^{\dagger}\,Z_0Z_1\,U_BU_C\big|s\big\rangle \]

Conjugate by the mixer. \(U_B = e^{-i\beta(X_0+X_1)}\) rotates \(Z\) about the \(x\)-axis:

\[ U_B^{\dagger}Z_iU_B = \cos(2\beta)\,Z_i - \sin(2\beta)\,Y_i \]

so that

\[ U_B^\dagger Z_0Z_1U_B = \big(\cos2\beta\,Z_0 - \sin2\beta\,Y_0\big)\big(\cos2\beta\,Z_1 - \sin2\beta\,Y_1\big) . \]

Conjugate by the cost unitary \(U_C = e^{-i\gamma(I-Z_0Z_1)/2}\) and take the expectation in \(|{+}{+}\rangle\), where \(\langle X_i\rangle = 1\) and \(\langle Y_i\rangle = \langle Z_i\rangle = 0\). Only terms reducing to products of \(X\)'s or the identity survive; the \(Z_0Z_1\) and \(Y_0Y_1\) cross-terms combine into a single sinusoid, giving

\[ \langle Z_0Z_1\rangle = -\sin(4\beta)\sin(\gamma) \]

and therefore

\[ \boxed{\ F_1(\gamma,\beta) = \frac{1}{2}\Big(1 + \sin(4\beta)\sin(\gamma)\Big)\ } \]

(Verify numerically: at \(\gamma = 1.0\), \(\beta = 0.3\) both the exact \(4\times4\) simulation and this formula give \(F_1 = 0.892142\).)

Maximise. Both factors reach 1 when

\[ \sin(4\beta) = 1 \Rightarrow \beta = \frac{\pi}{8}, \qquad \sin\gamma = 1 \Rightarrow \gamma = \frac{\pi}{2} \] \[ F_1^{\max} = \frac{1}{2}(1+1) = \mathbf{1} = C_{\max} \]

QAOA at \(p=1\) solves the single-edge problem exactly (the graph is bipartite and trivially small). Random guessing gives \(F = 0.5\), so QAOA doubles it.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Formulating a constrained problem as QUBO
docs.text:
Formulate "select exactly 2 items from 4 to maximise total value \(\vec v = (3,5,2,7)\)" as a QUBO, then convert to Ising.

Solution.

Objective (to maximise). \(\sum_i v_ix_i\). Convert to a minimisation: minimise \(-\sum_iv_ix_i\).

Constraint. \(\sum_i x_i = 2\). Add the penalty \(\lambda\big(\sum_ix_i - 2\big)^{2}\).

\[ \text{minimise}\quad f(\vec x) = -\sum_{i=1}^{4}v_ix_i + \lambda\Big(\sum_ix_i - 2\Big)^{2} \]

Choosing \(\lambda\). It must exceed the largest possible gain from violating the constraint. Adding a third item gains at most \(\max v_i = 7\) while the penalty rises from 0 to \(\lambda\). So \(\lambda > 7\); take \(\lambda = 10\).

Expand the penalty using \(x_i^{2} = x_i\) (binary):

\[ \Big(\sum_ix_i - 2\Big)^{2} = \sum_ix_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j - 4\sum_ix_i + 4 = 2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j - 3\sum_ix_i + 4 \] \[ f(\vec x) = \sum_i(-v_i - 30)x_i + 20\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j + 40 \]

QUBO matrix (with \(\lambda = 10\)):

\[ Q_{ii} = -v_i - 30 = (-33,\ -35,\ -32,\ -37), \qquad Q_{ij} = 20 \ (i<j) \]

Verify the optimum. The best pair is items 2 and 4 (\(v = 5+7 = 12\)):

\[ f = (-35) + (-37) + 20 + 40 = \mathbf{-12} \ \checkmark \]

Check a 3-item selection \(\{1,2,4\}\) (\(v = 15\)):

\[ f = -33-35-37 + 20\times3 + 40 = -105 + 60 + 40 = \mathbf{-5} \]

\(-5 > -12\), so the constraint is correctly enforced ✓ — the higher-value but infeasible selection is penalised into a worse objective.

Convert to Ising with \(x_i = \frac{1-z_i}{2}\):

\[ \sum_i Q_{ii}x_i = \sum_i Q_{ii}\frac{1-z_i}{2} = \frac12\sum_iQ_{ii} - \frac12\sum_iQ_{ii}z_i \] \[ \sum_{i<j}Q_{ij}x_ix_j = \sum_{i<j}\frac{Q_{ij}}{4}\big(1 - z_i - z_j + z_iz_j\big) \]

Collecting terms gives

\[ h_i = -\frac{Q_{ii}}{2} - \frac{1}{4}\sum_{j\ne i}Q_{ij}, \qquad J_{ij} = \frac{Q_{ij}}{4} = 5 . \]

For \(i=1\): \(h_1 = 16.5 - \frac{60}{4} = 16.5 - 15 = 1.5\). Similarly \(\vec h = (1.5,\ 2.5,\ 1.0,\ 3.5)\).

\[ H_C = \sum_i h_iZ_i + 5\sum_{i<j}Z_iZ_j + \text{const} \]

Four qubits, ready for QAOA.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Approximation ratio and resource estimate
docs.text:
A Max-Cut instance on a 3-regular graph with 100 vertices. Compute the number of edges, gates per QAOA layer, and total gates for \(p=1,3,11\). Compare quality with Goemans–Williamson.

Solution.

Edges. 3-regular means every vertex has degree 3:

\[ |E| = \frac{3\times100}{2} = \mathbf{150} \]

Gates per layer.

\[ \underbrace{2\times150}_{\text{CNOTs}} + \underbrace{150}_{R_z} + \underbrace{100}_{R_x} = \mathbf{550\ \text{gates}} \]

Totals.

\(p\) Gates CNOTs Approx. ratio Fidelity at \(\epsilon_{\text{CX}}=10^{-3}\) 1 650 300 0.6924 \((0.999)^{300} = 0.741\) 3 1750 900 ~0.79 \((0.999)^{900} = 0.406\) 11 6150 3300 0.8785 \((0.999)^{3300} = 0.037\)

(Adding 100 Hadamards for state preparation.)

The comparison that matters.

Method Guarantee Runtime Random assignment 0.5 instant Greedy ~0.5 \(O(\lvert E\rvert)\) Goemans–Williamson SDP 0.8785 polynomial, seconds QAOA \(p=1\) 0.6924 ~\(10^{5}\) shots QAOA \(p=11\) 0.8785 ~\(10^{5}\) shots, 3.7 % circuit fidelity \[ \boxed{\ \text{To \emph{match} GW, QAOA needs } p=11, \text{ at which point noise destroys the state.}\ } \]

Conclusion. For 3-regular Max-Cut, QAOA is not competitive on current hardware. Its interest lies in problem families where no good classical approximation exists, in warm-started variants, and in the \(p\to\infty\) theoretical guarantee.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Warm-starting and the parameter-transfer trick
docs.text:
QAOA parameter optimisation is expensive and non-convex. Describe two techniques that mitigate this and estimate their savings.

Solution.

Technique 1: Parameter transfer (parameter concentration).

Observation (Brandao et al., 2018; Streif–Leib, 2019). For a fixed problem family (say 3-regular Max-Cut), the optimal \((\vec\gamma^{*},\vec\beta^{*})\) concentrate: they are nearly the same for different random instances of the same size, and vary only slowly with \(n\).

Procedure.

1. Classically simulate a SMALL instance (n = 10-16) and optimise fully
2. Reuse (gamma*, beta*) directly on LARGE instances -- no optimisation at all
3. Optionally fine-tune with a handful of steps

Savings. Full optimisation at \(p=3\) (6 parameters) with SPSA typically needs ~200 steps × 2 evaluations × \(10^{4}\) shots \(= 4\times10^{6}\) shots. Parameter transfer needs one circuit evaluation of \(10^{4}\) shots.

\[ \text{Saving} \approx \mathbf{400\times} \]

Technique 2: Warm-start QAOA (Egger, Mareček, Woerner, 2021).

Instead of starting from \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\) (a completely uninformed state), start from a state biased toward a classical approximate solution.

1. Solve the SDP relaxation (Goemans-Williamson) classically -> fractional c_i in [0,1]
2. Initialise each qubit at angle theta_i = 2*arcsin(sqrt(c_i)) instead of |+>
3. Replace the standard mixer with one whose ground state is that warm-start state
4. Run QAOA -- it now IMPROVES on GW rather than starting from scratch

Why the mixer must change. The standard \(H_B = \sum X_i\) has \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\) as its ground state; with a different initial state the adiabatic argument breaks. The warm-start mixer is constructed so the new initial state is its ground state, restoring the guarantee.

Result. Warm-started QAOA at \(p=1\) inherits the GW guarantee of 0.8785 and improves on it monotonically with \(p\) — instead of starting at 0.6924 and needing \(p=11\) just to catch up.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{Warm-starting turns QAOA from a competitor into an \emph{improver} of classical methods.}\ } \]

Combined recipe for practice.

1. Solve the SDP relaxation classically           -> warm start + a baseline guarantee
2. Transfer parameters from a small simulated instance -> no expensive optimisation
3. Run shallow QAOA (p = 1-3) on hardware         -> stays within coherence
4. Post-process: take the best measured bitstring, apply classical local search

Step 4 matters more than students expect: QAOA returns a distribution, and taking the best of many samples plus a greedy local-search polish routinely beats the raw expectation value.

docs.title: 34.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Write \(H_C\) for a 4-cycle graph \(C_4\) and give \(C_{\max}\). [Ans: \(C_{\max}=4\); bipartite]
  2. Convert \(\min\ 3x_1 + 2x_2 - 4x_1x_2\) to Ising form.
  3. How many gates per QAOA layer for a complete graph \(K_6\)? [Ans: \(2\times15+15+6 = 51\)]
  4. For \(F_1 = \frac12(1+\sin4\beta\sin\gamma)\), find all optima in \([0,\pi]^2\).
  5. Compute the random-guess approximation ratio for Max-Cut on any graph. [Ans: 0.5]
  6. Why must \(\lambda\) exceed the maximum objective gain in a penalty formulation?
  7. Explain the locality obstruction in three sentences.

docs.title: 34.7 Summary
docs.text:
• QUBO ↔ Ising via \(x_i = \frac{1-z_i}{2}\); constraints become quadratic penalties with \(\lambda\) larger than the maximum gain from violating them.
  • Max-Cut: \(H_C = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\frac12(I - Z_iZ_j)\); \(\langle H_C\rangle\) is the expected number of cut edges.
  • QAOA ansatz: alternate \(e^{-i\gamma_kH_C}\) (CNOT–\(R_z\)–CNOT per edge) and \(e^{-i\beta_kH_B}\) (\(R_x\) per qubit), starting from \(|+\rangle^{\otimes n}\); optimise \(2p\) parameters classically.
  • QAOA is a Trotterised adiabatic evolution, exact as \(p\to\infty\).
  • Honest status: \(p=1\) guarantees 0.6924 on 3-regular Max-Cut versus 0.8785 for the classical Goemans–Williamson SDP; matching GW needs \(p=11\), at which depth NISQ fidelity collapses. Constant-depth QAOA is provably limited by locality.
  • Practical mitigations: parameter transfer (optimal angles concentrate across instances — ~400× cheaper) and warm-starting from the SDP solution (inherits the 0.8785 guarantee and improves on it), plus classical local-search post-processing.

Next lesson: L35 — Quantum annealing and the adiabatic model.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → QAOA Lab: draw a graph, set \(p\), sweep \((\gamma,\beta)\) over a heat map of \(F_p\), and compare the sampled cut distribution against the brute-force optimum.

docs.title: 18.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Define the QFT and relate it to the classical DFT.
  2. Prove that the QFT is unitary.
  3. Derive the product (tensor-factored) form of the QFT.
  4. Construct the \(O(n^2)\) QFT circuit from Hadamard and controlled-phase gates.
  5. Explain honestly why QFT does not speed up ordinary signal processing.

docs.title: The classical DFT
docs.text:
Given a vector \((x_0,\dots,x_{N-1})\), the Discrete Fourier Transform is

\[ y_k = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} x_j\, e^{2\pi i jk/N}, \qquad k = 0,\dots,N-1. \]

Naively \(O(N^2)\); the Fast Fourier Transform does it in \(O(N\log N)\).

docs.title: The QFT
docs.text:
Take \(N = 2^n\). The Quantum Fourier Transform is the linear operator acting on basis states as

\[ \boxed{\ \mathrm{QFT}_N\,|j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} e^{2\pi i jk/N}\,|k\rangle\ } \]

and extended linearly. On a general state:

\[ \mathrm{QFT}\left(\sum_j x_j|j\rangle\right) = \sum_k y_k|k\rangle, \qquad y_k = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_j x_j e^{2\pi i jk/N} . \]

It is the same transform, applied to the amplitude vector instead of a data array.
