docs.title: Matrix form
docs.text:
Let \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}\) (a primitive \(N\)-th root of unity). Then

\[ \mathrm{QFT}_N = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1\\ 1 & \omega & \omega^2 & \cdots & \omega^{N-1}\\ 1 & \omega^2 & \omega^4 & \cdots & \omega^{2(N-1)}\\ \vdots & & & \ddots & \vdots\\ 1 & \omega^{N-1} & \omega^{2(N-1)} & \cdots & \omega^{(N-1)^2}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad (\mathrm{QFT})_{kj} = \frac{\omega^{jk}}{\sqrt N} . \]

Special case \(N = 2\): \(\omega = e^{i\pi} = -1\), so

\[ \mathrm{QFT}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} = H . \]

The Hadamard gate is the single-qubit QFT. This is why \(H^{\otimes n}\) served as the "Fourier transform" in Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani and Simon — those algorithms work over \((\mathbb{Z}_2)^n\), whose Fourier transform is exactly \(H^{\otimes n}\).

docs.title: Unitarity
docs.text:
\[ \big(\mathrm{QFT}^\dagger \mathrm{QFT}\big)_{jl} = \sum_k \overline{(\mathrm{QFT})_{kj}}\,(\mathrm{QFT})_{kl} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\omega^{-jk}\omega^{kl} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\omega^{k(l-j)} \]

This is a geometric series. If \(l = j\) every term is 1, giving \(\frac{N}{N} = 1\). If \(l\ne j\), put \(d = l-j \not\equiv 0 \pmod N\):

\[ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\omega^{kd} = \frac{\omega^{Nd}-1}{\omega^{d}-1} = \frac{1-1}{\omega^d-1} = 0 \]

since \(\omega^N = 1\). Hence \(\mathrm{QFT}^\dagger\mathrm{QFT} = I\): the QFT is unitary and can be implemented as a quantum circuit. \(\blacksquare\)

The inverse is

\[ \mathrm{QFT}^{-1}|j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_k e^{-2\pi ijk/N}|k\rangle . \]

docs.title: 18.3 The Product Form
docs.text:
This is the derivation that turns an \(N\times N\) matrix into an \(O(n^2)\)-gate circuit.

Binary notation. Write \(k = k_1k_2\cdots k_n\) in binary, so \(k = \sum_{l=1}^{n}k_l\,2^{n-l}\). Define the binary fraction

\[ 0.k_lk_{l+1}\cdots k_n \;=\; \frac{k_l}{2} + \frac{k_{l+1}}{4} + \cdots + \frac{k_n}{2^{n-l+1}} . \]

Derivation. Start from the definition with \(N = 2^n\):

\[ \mathrm{QFT}|j\rangle = \frac{1}{2^{n/2}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^n-1} e^{2\pi i jk/2^n}|k\rangle \]

Substitute \(k/2^n = \sum_{l=1}^n k_l 2^{-l}\):

\[ = \frac{1}{2^{n/2}}\sum_{k_1=0}^{1}\cdots\sum_{k_n=0}^{1} \ \bigotimes_{l=1}^{n} e^{2\pi i j k_l 2^{-l}}|k_l\rangle \]

The sum over each \(k_l\) is independent, so the whole thing factorises:

\[ = \frac{1}{2^{n/2}}\bigotimes_{l=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{k_l\in\{0,1\}} e^{2\pi ijk_l2^{-l}}|k_l\rangle\right) = \bigotimes_{l=1}^{n}\ \frac{|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i j/2^{l}}|1\rangle}{\sqrt2} \]

Finally, \(e^{2\pi ij/2^l}\) depends only on the fractional part of \(j/2^l\), which is \(0.j_{n-l+1}\cdots j_n\). Writing it out:

\[ \boxed{\ \mathrm{QFT}|j_1j_2\cdots j_n\rangle = \frac{\big(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\,0.j_n}|1\rangle\big) \big(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\,0.j_{n-1}j_n}|1\rangle\big)\cdots \big(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\,0.j_1j_2\cdots j_n}|1\rangle\big)}{2^{n/2}}\ } \]

Read this carefully — it is remarkable. The QFT of any computational basis state is a product state: no entanglement is created. Each output qubit is on the equator of the Bloch sphere, at an azimuthal angle given by successively finer binary fractions of \(j\).

Note also that qubit 1 of the output depends on \(j_n\) alone, while qubit \(n\) depends on all of \(j\) — so the output emerges in reversed order, which is why the circuit ends with SWAPs.

docs.title: Gates required
docs.text:
• Hadamard \(H\).
  • Controlled phase \(CR_m\), where
\[ R_m = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & e^{2\pi i/2^{m}}\end{pmatrix} . \]

Note \(R_1 = Z\), \(R_2 = S\), \(R_3 = T\).

docs.title: The construction
docs.text:
j1 --[H]--[R2]--[R3]-- ... --[Rn]------------------------------ x
            |     |            |
j2 ---------*-----|------------|----[H]--[R2]-- ... --[R(n-1)]-- x
                  |            |          |               |
j3 ---------------*------------|----------*---------------|-----
                               |                          |
jn ----------------------------*--------------------------*-----
                                                            then SWAPs

Algorithm.

for l = 1 to n:
    apply H to qubit l
    for m = 2 to n-l+1:
        apply controlled-R_m  (control = qubit l+m-1, target = qubit l)
reverse the qubit order with floor(n/2) SWAP gates

Why it works. \(H\) on qubit \(l\) produces \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\,0.j_l}|1\rangle)\) — it writes the first binary digit into the phase. Each subsequent controlled-\(R_m\) adds the next digit \(j_{l+m-1}/2^m\), building up the binary fraction \(0.j_lj_{l+1}\cdots j_n\) one bit at a time.

docs.title: Gate count
docs.text:
\[ n + (n-1) + \cdots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = O(n^2) \ \text{gates}, \ \ \text{plus } \lfloor n/2\rfloor \text{ SWAPs.} \] Classical FFT QFT Input size \(N = 2^n\) numbers \(n\) qubits Operations \(O(N\log N) = O(2^n n)\) \(O(n^2)\) Output all \(N\) coefficients, readable a quantum state; one sample only

The QFT is exponentially faster than the FFT — \(O(n^2)\) versus \(O(2^nn)\).

docs.title: The honest caveat
docs.text:
The QFT does not speed up signal processing. Two reasons:

  1. You cannot read the output. Measuring gives one \(k\) sampled from \(|y_k|^2\). Extracting all \(N\) coefficients needs \(\Omega(N)\) repetitions, wiping out the advantage.
  2. You cannot load the input efficiently. Preparing \(\sum_j x_j|j\rangle\) from classical data generally costs \(O(N)\) operations.

The QFT is useful precisely when the answer is a single global feature of the spectrum — such as the period — that can be read from one sample. That is exactly the situation in phase estimation and Shor's algorithm.

docs.title: Approximate QFT
docs.text: Phases \(e^{2\pi i/2^m}\) for large \(m\) are exponentially small rotations, indistinguishable from identity on noisy hardware. Dropping all \(R_m\) with \(m > \log_2(n/\epsilon)\) gives the approximate QFT with error \(\epsilon\), using only \(O(n\log n)\) gates. In practice this is what is implemented, and it also improves accuracy on NISQ devices by removing gates that contribute more noise than signal.

docs.title: Problem 1 — QFT on 2 qubits, matrix and action
docs.text:
Write \(\mathrm{QFT}_4\) explicitly and compute \(\mathrm{QFT}_4|2\rangle\).

Solution. \(N = 4\), \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/4} = i\).

\[ \mathrm{QFT}_4 = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & i & -1 & -i\\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1\\ 1 & -i & -1 & i\end{pmatrix} \]

(using \(i^2=-1\), \(i^3=-i\), \(i^4=1\), \(i^6 = -1\), \(i^9 = i\)).

\(\mathrm{QFT}_4|2\rangle\) is the third column:

\[ \mathrm{QFT}_4|2\rangle = \frac12\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle + |2\rangle - |3\rangle\big) \]

Verify with the product form. \(j = 2 = 10_2\), so \(j_1 = 1, j_2 = 0\).

\[ \mathrm{QFT}|10\rangle = \frac{\big(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\,0.j_2}|1\rangle\big) \big(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\,0.j_1j_2}|1\rangle\big)}{2} \]

\(0.j_2 = 0.0 = 0\), so the first factor is \(|0\rangle + |1\rangle\). \(0.j_1j_2 = 0.10_2 = \frac12\), so \(e^{2\pi i\cdot\frac12} = e^{i\pi} = -1\), and the second factor is \(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\).

\[ = \frac12\big(|0\rangle+|1\rangle\big)\big(|0\rangle - |1\rangle\big) = \frac12\big(|00\rangle - |01\rangle + |10\rangle - |11\rangle\big) \ \checkmark \]

which matches (with \(|00\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(|01\rangle=|1\rangle\), etc.).

docs.title: Problem 2 — The QFT of a periodic state
docs.text:
Let \(N = 8\) and \(|\psi\rangle = \frac12\big(|0\rangle+|2\rangle+|4\rangle+|6\rangle\big)\) (period 2). Compute \(\mathrm{QFT}_8|\psi\rangle\) and interpret.

Solution. \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/8} = e^{i\pi/4}\).

\[ \mathrm{QFT}_8|\psi\rangle = \frac12\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt8}\sum_{k=0}^{7} \left[\sum_{j\in\{0,2,4,6\}}\omega^{jk}\right]|k\rangle \]

Inner sum, with \(\omega^{2k} = e^{i\pi k/2} = i^{k}\):

\[ S_k = \sum_{m=0}^{3} \left(i^{k}\right)^{m} = 1 + i^k + i^{2k} + i^{3k} \]

This geometric series equals \(4\) when \(i^k = 1\) (i.e. \(k \equiv 0 \bmod 4\)) and \(0\) otherwise:

\(k\) \(i^k\) \(S_k\) 0 1 4 1 \(i\) 0 2 \(-1\) 0 3 \(-i\) 0 4 1 4 5,6,7 — 0 \[ \mathrm{QFT}_8|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{2\sqrt8}\big(4|0\rangle + 4|4\rangle\big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|0\rangle + |4\rangle\big) \]

Interpretation. The input had period \(p = 2\) in the "time" domain; the output is supported on multiples of \(N/p = 8/2 = 4\). Measuring returns \(0\) or \(4\), each with probability \(\frac12\), and \(4 = N/p\) reveals \(p = 8/4 = 2\).

This is the entire mechanism of Shor's algorithm: period in → multiples of \(N/p\) out.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Building the 3-qubit QFT circuit
docs.text:
List the exact gate sequence for \(\mathrm{QFT}_8\) and count the gates.

Solution.

qubit 1: H, then CR2 (control q2), then CR3 (control q3)
qubit 2: H, then CR2 (control q3)
qubit 3: H
finally: SWAP(q1, q3)

Explicitly, in order:

# Gate Target Control Phase applied 1 \(H\) \(q_1\) — — 2 \(CR_2\) \(q_1\) \(q_2\) \(e^{2\pi i/4} = i\) 3 \(CR_3\) \(q_1\) \(q_3\) \(e^{2\pi i/8}\) 4 \(H\) \(q_2\) — — 5 \(CR_2\) \(q_2\) \(q_3\) \(i\) 6 \(H\) \(q_3\) — — 7 SWAP \(q_1, q_3\) — —

Count: \(3 + 3 = 6\) gates (3 Hadamards + 3 controlled-phases) plus 1 SWAP.

Check against the formula: \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{3\times4}{2} = 6\) ✓, and \(\lfloor 3/2 \rfloor = 1\) SWAP ✓.

Compare: the classical FFT on 8 points needs \(8\log_2 8 = 24\) complex operations. The QFT needs 6 gates. The gap grows explosively: for \(n = 20\) (\(N = 10^6\)), the FFT needs \(2\times10^{7}\) operations while the QFT needs 210 gates.

docs.title: Problem 4 — QFT of a shifted state (the shift theorem)
docs.text:
Show that \(\mathrm{QFT}_N|j_0\rangle\) and \(\mathrm{QFT}_N|j_0 + s\rangle\) (mod \(N\)) differ only by phases, so that measurement statistics are identical. Explain the consequence for Shor's algorithm.

Solution.

\[ \mathrm{QFT}|j_0+s\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_k e^{2\pi i(j_0+s)k/N}|k\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_k e^{2\pi ij_0k/N}\,e^{2\pi isk/N}|k\rangle \]

Each amplitude is multiplied by \(e^{2\pi isk/N}\), which has modulus 1. Therefore

\[ \big|\langle k|\mathrm{QFT}|j_0+s\rangle\big|^2 = \frac{1}{N} = \big|\langle k|\mathrm{QFT}|j_0\rangle\big|^2 . \]

Statistics are identical. A shift in the input becomes a phase ramp in the output, invisible to measurement.

Consequence for Shor. After measuring the output register in Shor's algorithm, the input register is in a state like

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt m}\sum_{t=0}^{m-1}|x_0 + tr\rangle \]

— a periodic comb with period \(r\) but an unknown random offset \(x_0\). This theorem shows that \(x_0\) affects only phases, never probabilities. That is exactly why Shor's algorithm can afford to throw away the measurement of the output register. (It is also the same mechanism that let Simon's algorithm work despite the random \(x_0\) — see L15 §3.2.)

docs.title: Problem 5 — QFT of a single basis state versus a superposition
docs.text:
Compute \(\mathrm{QFT}_4|0\rangle\) and \(\mathrm{QFT}_4\big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_j|j\rangle\big)\), and explain the duality.

Solution.

(a) From the first column of the matrix:

\[ \mathrm{QFT}_4|0\rangle = \frac12\big(|0\rangle+|1\rangle+|2\rangle+|3\rangle\big) \]

A perfectly localised input gives a perfectly uniform output.

(b) Now the uniform input \(|\psi\rangle = \frac12\sum_{j=0}^{3}|j\rangle\):

\[ \mathrm{QFT}|\psi\rangle = \frac12\cdot\frac12\sum_k\left[\sum_{j=0}^{3}i^{jk}\right]|k\rangle \]

The bracket is \(\sum_{j}i^{jk}\), a geometric series equal to 4 when \(k = 0\) and 0 otherwise (same argument as in §1.4):

\[ \mathrm{QFT}|\psi\rangle = \frac{4}{4}|0\rangle = |0\rangle \]

Duality. Delta function ↔ uniform; uniform ↔ delta function. This is the discrete uncertainty principle: a state cannot be sharply localised in both the computational basis and the Fourier basis. The product of the two "widths" is bounded below.

Connection to earlier lessons. For \(n=1\) this is just \(H|0\rangle = |+\rangle\) and \(H|+\rangle = |0\rangle\) — the QFT generalises the Hadamard's amplitude↔phase exchange to \(\mathbb{Z}_N\).

docs.title: 18.6 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Write out \(\mathrm{QFT}_8\)'s first two rows explicitly using \(\omega = e^{i\pi/4}\).
  2. Compute \(\mathrm{QFT}_4|1\rangle\) using both the matrix and the product form.
  3. Compute the QFT of \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle + |4\rangle)\) for \(N=8\). [Ans: supported on even \(k\)]
  4. How many gates does \(\mathrm{QFT}_{1024}\) need? [Ans: \(n=10\), so 55 gates + 5 SWAPs]
  5. Verify that \(R_2 = S\) and \(R_3 = T\).
  6. Prove that \(\mathrm{QFT}^4 = I\) up to a permutation (the classical DFT has period 4).
  7. Explain in two sentences why the QFT cannot accelerate JPEG compression.

docs.title: 18.7 Summary
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{QFT}_N|j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_k e^{2\pi ijk/N}|k\rangle\); it is the DFT applied to amplitudes, and it is unitary (proved by the geometric-series/root-of-unity argument).
  • \(\mathrm{QFT}_2 = H\), which is why \(H^{\otimes n}\) served as the Fourier transform in Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani and Simon.
  • Product form: the QFT of any basis state factorises into \(n\) single-qubit states with phases given by binary fractions of \(j\) — no entanglement, and output in reversed qubit order.
  • Circuit: \(H\) + controlled-\(R_m\) in a triangular pattern, \(O(n^2)\) gates versus the FFT's \(O(2^nn)\); the approximate QFT needs only \(O(n\log n)\).
  • QFT does not accelerate signal processing — you cannot read all outputs or load all inputs. It is useful only when a single global feature (the period) is wanted.
  • Period \(p\) in ⟶ support on multiples of \(N/p\) out. A shift in the input becomes a phase ramp, invisible to measurement — this is what makes Shor robust to the unknown offset.

Next lesson: L19 — Quantum phase estimation.

Practise now: unit2-algorithms-lab.html → QFT Explorer: enter any amplitude vector or set a period, apply the QFT, and see the magnitude and phase spectra side by side.

docs.title: 36.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Describe the layers of the quantum software stack and what each is responsible for.
  2. Compare simulator types (statevector, density matrix, stabiliser, tensor network, MPS) and their scaling.
  3. Explain transpilation and why it is unavoidable.
  4. Read and write basic OpenQASM.
  5. Choose an appropriate framework for a given task.

docs.title: 36.2 The Quantum Software Stack
docs.text:
+--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  APPLICATION      chemistry, finance, ML, optimisation  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  ALGORITHM        VQE, QAOA, Shor, Grover, QPE          |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  CIRCUIT / SDK    Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane, Q#           |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  INTERMEDIATE     OpenQASM 3, QIR, Quil                 |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  COMPILER         transpiler: routing, mapping, opt.    |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  CONTROL          pulse-level: Qiskit Pulse, OpenPulse  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+
  |  HARDWARE / SIM   QPU, statevector, tensor network      |
  +--------------------------------------------------------+

The analogy with classical computing: the SDK is the high-level language, OpenQASM is the assembly language, the transpiler is the compiler back end, and the pulse layer is the microcode.

docs.title: 36.3 Simulator Types
docs.text:
The most consequential practical choice a student makes.

Simulator Memory Time Max qubits Handles noise? Statevector \(O(2^{n})\) \(O(2^{n})\) per gate ~30–40 no (pure states only) Density matrix \(O(4^{n})\) \(O(4^{n})\) ~15–20 yes Stabiliser (CHP) \(O(n^{2})\) \(O(n^{2})\) thousands Clifford + Pauli noise only Matrix product state (MPS) \(O(n\chi^{2})\) \(O(n\chi^{3})\) 100s (low entanglement) with care Tensor network depends on contraction width varies 100s (shallow) limited Extended stabiliser \(O(\chi\,\mathrm{poly}(n))\), \(\chi = 2^{O(t)}\) — 100s with few \(T\) gates limited

docs.title: Statevector — the default
docs.text:
Stores all \(2^{n}\) complex amplitudes.

\(n\) Memory (complex128) 20 16 MB 30 16 GB 34 256 GB 40 17.6 TB

A laptop handles ~28 qubits; a workstation ~34; a supercomputer ~45–49. Every additional qubit doubles the requirement — the wall is hard and unavoidable.

docs.title: Stabiliser — the surprising one
docs.text:
Gottesman–Knill theorem (L08). Circuits of Clifford gates (\(H\), \(S\), CNOT) with computational-basis measurement are simulable in \(O(n^2)\) classical time.

So a 10 000-qubit Clifford circuit simulates instantly, while a 40-qubit circuit with \(T\) gates does not. What makes simulation hard is not qubit count but non-Cliffordness. Stabiliser simulators are essential for quantum error correction research, where circuits are large but almost entirely Clifford.

docs.title: MPS / tensor network — the entanglement-aware one
docs.text:
An MPS represents the state as a chain of tensors with bond dimension \(\chi\), which bounds the entanglement across any cut:

\[ S_{\max} = \log_2\chi \]

Low-entanglement states are cheap. A product state has \(\chi = 1\); a shallow 1-D circuit has small \(\chi\). Cost grows as \(O(n\chi^3)\), so an MPS simulator can handle hundreds of qubits if the circuit does not generate much entanglement — but blows up for deep, highly entangling circuits.

This is how "quantum supremacy" claims get contested. Google's 2019 Sycamore result was later partially reproduced classically with improved tensor-network contraction, and the argument continues.

docs.title: 36.4 Transpilation
docs.text: Definition. Transpilation (or compilation) rewrites an abstract circuit into one executable on specific hardware.

docs.title: The four tasks
docs.text:
1. Gate translation (basis change). Hardware supports only a fixed basis gate set, e.g. IBM's \(\{\)ECR or CZ, \(R_z\), \(S_x\), \(X\}\). Every abstract gate must be decomposed into it.

\[ H \ \longrightarrow\ R_z(\pi)\,S_x\,R_z(\pi/2) \quad(\text{up to phase}) \]

2. Qubit mapping (layout). Assign logical qubits to physical qubits, preferring those with the best coherence and gate fidelity.

3. Routing (SWAP insertion). Real devices allow two-qubit gates only between connected qubits. A CNOT between distant qubits requires SWAPs to bring them together.

Suppose the device connectivity is a line:  q0 - q1 - q2 - q3
Requested: CNOT(q0, q3)

Compiled:  SWAP(q0,q1)  SWAP(q1,q2)  CNOT(q2,q3)  SWAP(q1,q2)  SWAP(q0,q1)

Each SWAP costs 3 CNOTs, so this one logical gate becomes \(4\times3 + 1 = 13\) CNOTs. Routing is often the dominant cost on real hardware, and finding the optimal routing is NP-hard.

4. Optimisation. Cancel adjacent inverse gates, merge consecutive rotations (\(R_z(a)R_z(b) = R_z(a+b)\)), commute gates past each other, resynthesise blocks.

docs.title: Optimisation levels (Qiskit convention)
docs.text:
Level Behaviour Use 0 mapping only, no optimisation debugging 1 light — adjacent-gate cancellation quick runs 2 medium — commutation analysis default 3 heavy — resynthesis, noise-adaptive layout production

Level 3 typically reduces CNOT count by 30–60 % over level 0 — a decisive difference on NISQ hardware, where CNOT error (\(\sim10^{-2}\)) dominates.

docs.title: Why transpilation is not optional
docs.text: Requested Delivered on hardware Any two-qubit pair only physically coupled pairs Any gate only the basis set Ideal gates gates with \(10^{-3}\)–\(10^{-2}\) error Arbitrary depth depth limited by \(T_2/t_{\text{gate}}\)

docs.title: 36.5 OpenQASM
docs.text: The assembly language of quantum computing, and the interchange format between frameworks.

docs.title: A Bell state in OpenQASM 3
docs.text:
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";

qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;

h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];

c = measure q;

docs.title: OpenQASM 2 versus 3
docs.text:
Feature QASM 2 QASM 3 Classical control flow none if, for, while Real-time computation no yes Timing / delay no yes Typed classical variables no yes (int, float, bit) Mid-circuit measurement + feed-forward limited full support

QASM 3's classical control matters because error correction and teleportation both require measuring, computing on the result, and applying a conditional gate — all within coherence time.

docs.title: QASM 3 with feed-forward (teleportation correction)
docs.text:
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";

qubit[3] q;
bit m0;
bit m1;

// ... prepare and entangle ...

m0 = measure q[0];
m1 = measure q[1];

if (m1 == 1) { x q[2]; }
if (m0 == 1) { z q[2]; }

docs.title: Problem 1 — Choosing a simulator
docs.text:
Which simulator would you use, and why, for each task?

(a) Verify a 25-qubit Grover circuit. (b) Simulate a 500-qubit surface-code round. (c) Study depolarising noise on a 12-qubit VQE. (d) Simulate a 100-qubit shallow QAOA circuit.

Solution.

(a) Statevector. 25 qubits needs \(2^{25}\times16 = 537\) MB — fits in RAM. Grover contains multi-controlled gates (non-Clifford), so stabiliser simulation is unavailable. Statevector gives exact amplitudes, which is what verification requires.

(b) Stabiliser (CHP / Aaronson–Gottesman). Surface-code syndrome extraction is entirely Clifford (CNOTs, Hadamards, measurements). \(O(n^2)\) scaling makes 500 qubits trivial — statevector would need \(2^{500}\) amplitudes, more than there are atoms in the universe.

(c) Density matrix. Noise turns a pure state into a mixed one, which a statevector cannot represent. \(4^{12} = 1.7\times10^{7}\) entries × 16 bytes \(= 268\) MB — comfortable. (Alternative: statevector + Monte Carlo trajectory sampling, cheaper but needs many runs.)

(d) MPS or tensor network. \(2^{100}\) is impossible for statevector. A shallow QAOA circuit generates limited entanglement, so the bond dimension \(\chi\) stays modest and MPS cost \(O(n\chi^{3})\) is manageable. Caveat: if \(p\) is large, \(\chi\) grows exponentially and MPS fails too.

The general rule.

\[ \text{Clifford? } \to \text{stabiliser}; \quad \text{noisy \& small? } \to \text{density matrix}; \quad \text{low entanglement? } \to \text{MPS}; \quad \text{otherwise } \to \text{statevector, } n \le 30. \]

docs.title: Problem 2 — Statevector memory and the wall
docs.text:
Compute memory for statevector simulation at \(n = 26, 30, 34, 38\) using complex128 (16 bytes). What is the largest \(n\) on (a) a 16 GB laptop, (b) a 1 TB server, (c) a 1 PB supercomputer?

Solution.

\[ M = 2^{n}\times16 \ \text{bytes} \] \(n\) Amplitudes Memory 26 \(6.7\times10^{7}\) 1.07 GB 30 \(1.07\times10^{9}\) 17.2 GB 34 \(1.72\times10^{10}\) 275 GB 38 \(2.75\times10^{11}\) 4.4 TB

Maximum \(n\) per platform (allowing ~half the memory for the state, since gate application often needs a working copy):

(a) 16 GB laptop: \(2^{n}\times16 \le 8\times10^{9} \Rightarrow 2^{n}\le5\times10^{8} \Rightarrow n \le \mathbf{28}\).

(b) 1 TB server: \(2^{n}\le 3.1\times10^{10} \Rightarrow n\le\mathbf{34}\).

(c) 1 PB supercomputer: \(2^{n}\le3.1\times10^{13} \Rightarrow n\le\mathbf{44}\).

The brutal arithmetic. Going from a laptop to a petascale supercomputer — a \(10^{5}\)-fold memory increase — buys only 16 more qubits. Each qubit costs a factor of 2, so a factor of \(10^{5}\) is \(\log_2 10^{5} \approx 16.6\) qubits.

\[ \boxed{\ \text{This is precisely why quantum computers are interesting: } 50 \text{ qubits already exceeds all classical memory.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 3 — Transpilation cost of routing
docs.text:
A circuit needs CNOT(\(q_0\), \(q_7\)) on a device with linear connectivity \(q_0 - q_1 - \cdots - q_7\). Count the physical CNOTs, and compute the circuit fidelity at CNOT error \(10^{-2}\).

Solution.

Distance. \(q_0\) to \(q_7\) is 7 hops apart, so 6 SWAPs are needed to bring them adjacent (moving \(q_0\) next to \(q_7\)).

Naive routing.

SWAP(0,1) SWAP(1,2) SWAP(2,3) SWAP(3,4) SWAP(4,5) SWAP(5,6)   -- 6 SWAPs in
CNOT(6,7)                                                      -- 1 CNOT
SWAP(5,6) SWAP(4,5) SWAP(3,4) SWAP(2,3) SWAP(1,2) SWAP(0,1)   -- 6 SWAPs out
\[ \text{CNOTs} = 12\ \text{SWAPs}\times3 + 1 = \mathbf{37} \]

Optimised (no swap-back). If subsequent gates can use the permuted layout, the return SWAPs are unnecessary and a final classical relabelling of the measurement bits suffices:

\[ 6\times3 + 1 = \mathbf{19}\ \text{CNOTs} \]

Fidelity.

\[ F_{\text{naive}} = (1 - 10^{-2})^{37} = 0.99^{37} = \mathbf{0.689} \] \[ F_{\text{opt}} = 0.99^{19} = \mathbf{0.826} \]

One logical CNOT costs 17–31 % of the circuit's fidelity.

Design implications.

  1. Design circuits for the hardware topology. Nearest-neighbour circuits transpile for free.
  2. Use optimization_level=3, which uses SABRE routing and avoids unnecessary swap-backs.
  3. Prefer devices with better connectivity. Trapped-ion machines have all-to-all coupling and need zero SWAPs — often outperforming faster superconducting devices on connectivity-heavy circuits despite slower gates.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Writing and reading OpenQASM
docs.text:
Write OpenQASM 3 for a 3-qubit GHZ state with measurement. Then hand-simulate this QASM and state the output distribution:

qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
h q[1];
cz q[0], q[1];
h q[1];
c = measure q;

Solution.

Part 1 — GHZ.

OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";

qubit[3] q;
bit[3] c;

h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
cx q[0], q[2];

c = measure q;

Expected output: 000 and 111, each with probability \(\frac12\).

Part 2 — hand-simulate the given circuit.

Recall from L08 that \(\mathrm{CNOT}_{0\to1} = (I\otimes H)\,CZ\,(I\otimes H)\). The circuit is \(H_0, H_1, CZ, H_1\), which is

\[ (I\otimes H)\,CZ\,(H\otimes H) = (I\otimes H)\,CZ\,(I\otimes H)\,(H\otimes I) = \mathrm{CNOT}_{0\to1}\,(H\otimes I) \]

So the circuit is exactly \(H\) on \(q_0\) then CNOT — the Bell-state circuit.

\[ |00\rangle \ \longrightarrow\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|00\rangle + |11\rangle\big) \]

Output distribution: 00 and 11 with probability 0.5 each; 01 and 10 never occur.

Verification by direct computation:

\[ |00\rangle \xrightarrow{H\otimes H} \tfrac12\big(|00\rangle+|01\rangle+|10\rangle+|11\rangle\big) \] \[ \xrightarrow{CZ} \tfrac12\big(|00\rangle+|01\rangle+|10\rangle-|11\rangle\big) \] \[ \xrightarrow{I\otimes H} \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\Big[(|00\rangle+|01\rangle) + (|00\rangle-|01\rangle) + (|10\rangle+|11\rangle) - (|10\rangle - |11\rangle)\Big] \] \[ = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\big[2|00\rangle + 2|11\rangle\big] = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|00\rangle+|11\rangle\big) \ \checkmark \]

docs.title: Problem 5 — Framework selection for a research project
docs.text:
Recommend a framework for each project, with reasoning.

(a) Train a 6-qubit VQC with PyTorch integration. (b) Estimate the physical qubits needed to factor RSA-2048. (c) Minimise the CNOT count of a 20-qubit chemistry circuit. (d) Compare the same circuit on superconducting, trapped-ion and neutral-atom hardware. (e) Simulate 200 qubits of a surface code.

Solution.

(a) PennyLane. It is the only framework with first-class automatic differentiation that interoperates natively with PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX. A QNode is a differentiable PyTorch module, so quantum layers drop straight into an existing classical network, and gradients flow through by parameter-shift automatically. (TensorFlow Quantum is the Keras-only alternative.)

(b) Q# / Azure Quantum Resource Estimator. Microsoft's tool is purpose-built for this: it takes a Q# program, applies a chosen QEC scheme (surface code, Hastings–Haah), a physical error rate and a gate-time model, and outputs physical qubit counts and runtime. No other framework does fault-tolerant resource estimation as a first-class feature.

(c) pytket (Quantinuum). Independent benchmarks consistently show TKET producing 10–30 % fewer two-qubit gates than other transpilers, thanks to its Clifford-resynthesis and phase-polynomial passes. It also accepts circuits from Qiskit and Cirq, so you can write in Qiskit and compile with pytket.

(d) Amazon Braket. It provides a single SDK and a single billing account across IonQ (trapped ion), Rigetti and IQM (superconducting), and QuEra (neutral atom). Writing the comparison in any vendor SDK would mean maintaining three separate code paths and three accounts.

(e) Stim (Craig Gidney's stabiliser simulator), accessible from Python. Surface-code circuits are Clifford, and Stim simulates millions of Clifford gates per second — orders of magnitude faster than Qiskit's or Cirq's stabiliser back ends. It is the standard tool in the QEC community, paired with PyMatching for decoding.

The meta-lesson. There is no single best framework. Frameworks are interoperable via OpenQASM 3, so the professional workflow is to use each where it is strongest: prototype in Qiskit, differentiate in PennyLane, compile with pytket, estimate resources in Q#, and benchmark on Braket.

docs.title: 36.8 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Memory for a 22-qubit statevector at complex64 (8 bytes)? [Ans: 33.6 MB]
  2. Why can a 1000-qubit Clifford circuit be simulated but not a 50-qubit universal one?
  3. How many CNOTs to route CNOT(\(q_0,q_4\)) on a line, with swap-back? [Ans: \(8\times3+1 = 25\)]
  4. Write OpenQASM 3 for the Deutsch algorithm with \(f(x)=x\).
  5. What bond dimension does a 2-qubit maximally entangled state need? [Ans: \(\chi = 2\)]
  6. Which framework for benchmarking three vendors' hardware, and why?
  7. Compare optimisation levels 0 and 3 in terms of CNOT count and fidelity.

docs.title: 36.9 Summary
docs.text:
• The stack runs application → algorithm → SDK → intermediate representation (OpenQASM/QIR) → transpiler → pulse → hardware.
  • Simulator choice is the key practical decision: statevector (\(O(2^n)\), ≤30–40 qubits), density matrix (\(O(4^n)\), noisy, ≤20), stabiliser (\(O(n^2)\), thousands of qubits but Clifford only), MPS/tensor network (hundreds of qubits at low entanglement).
  • What makes simulation hard is non-Cliffordness and entanglement, not qubit count.
  • Transpilation performs gate translation, layout, routing (SWAP insertion — often the dominant cost) and optimisation. Level 3 typically saves 30–60 % of CNOTs.
  • OpenQASM 3 is the interchange standard and adds classical control flow, enabling mid-circuit measurement with feed-forward.
  • Framework choice follows the task: Qiskit (general/teaching), PennyLane (QML/autodiff), pytket (compilation), Q# (resource estimation), Braket (multi-vendor), Stim (QEC).

Next lesson: L37 — IBM Qiskit I: circuits, simulation and primitives.

Practise now: unit4-platforms-lab.html → Circuit Builder: build a circuit visually and see the equivalent Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane, Q# and OpenQASM 3 code emitted side by side.

docs.title: 28.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. State the variational principle and explain why it underpins all hybrid algorithms.
  2. Define the VQC model, its ansatz, its measurement and its loss function.
  3. Design an ansatz and count its parameters and depth.
  4. Choose a classical optimiser appropriate to shot noise.
  5. Compare the VQC with the QSVM and with a classical neural network.

docs.title: 28.2 The Variational Principle
docs.text:
Theorem. For any Hamiltonian \(H\) with ground-state energy \(E_0\) and any normalised state \(|\psi\rangle\),

\[ \langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle \ \ge\ E_0 , \]

with equality iff \(|\psi\rangle\) is a ground state.

Proof. Expand \(|\psi\rangle = \sum_j c_j|E_j\rangle\) in the eigenbasis of \(H\):

\[ \langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle = \sum_j |c_j|^2 E_j \ \ge\ E_0\sum_j|c_j|^2 = E_0 . \qquad\blacksquare \]

Consequence. Minimising \(\langle\psi(\vec\theta)|H|\psi(\vec\theta)\rangle\) over a parameterised family gives an upper bound on \(E_0\) that improves monotonically. This is the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and the template for QAOA (L34) and the VQC.

Why it suits NISQ hardware.

Property Benefit Shallow circuits fits within coherence time Classical optimiser in the loop absorbs systematic errors Variational bound a noisy result is still an upper bound No QPE, no long coherent evolution orders of magnitude cheaper than Shor-style algorithms

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
|0>^n --[ U_phi(x) ]--[ W(theta) ]--[ measure Z_0 ]--> <Z_0> --> class
        \___________/  \__________/
          encoding      trainable
        (fixed, L26)      ansatz
\[ f_{\vec\theta}(\vec x) = \big\langle 0\big| U_{\phi}^{\dagger}(\vec x)\,W^{\dagger}(\vec\theta)\, M\,W(\vec\theta)\,U_{\phi}(\vec x)\big|0\big\rangle \]

with \(M\) typically \(Z_0\) (measure the first qubit) or \(Z^{\otimes n}\) (parity of all qubits).

docs.title: From expectation value to a class label
docs.text:
For binary classification with \(\langle Z\rangle\in[-1,+1]\):

Approach Formula Sign readout \(\hat y = \mathrm{sign}\big(f_{\vec\theta}(\vec x) + b\big)\) Probability readout \(p(y=1) = \frac{1 + f_{\vec\theta}(\vec x)}{2}\) Sigmoid readout \(p(y=1) = \sigma\big(a f_{\vec\theta}(\vec x)+b\big)\) with trainable \(a,b\)

For \(C\) classes, measure \(C\) different observables (or \(\lceil\log_2 C\rceil\) qubits' bitstrings) and apply a softmax.

docs.title: Loss functions
docs.text:
Mean squared error (labels \(\pm1\)):

\[ L(\vec\theta) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\big(f_{\vec\theta}(\vec x_i) - y_i\big)^{2} \]

Binary cross-entropy (labels \(0/1\), probability readout):

\[ L(\vec\theta) = -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\Big[y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\Big] \]

Cross-entropy generally trains faster because its gradient does not vanish when predictions are confidently wrong.

docs.title: The hardware-efficient ansatz
docs.text:
one layer, n qubits:
    Ry(theta_1) Ry(theta_2) ... Ry(theta_n)      <- rotations
    Rz(theta_{n+1}) ... Rz(theta_{2n})
    CNOT(0,1) CNOT(1,2) ... CNOT(n-2,n-1) CNOT(n-1,0)   <- entangling ring

Parameter count for \(L\) layers with two rotations per qubit:

\[ P = 2nL \quad(\text{plus } 2n \text{ if a final rotation layer is added}) \]

Depth: \(O(L\cdot n)\) if the CNOTs are sequential, \(O(L)\) if they are parallelised.

Pros: uses native gates and native connectivity, so it transpiles with little overhead. Cons: carries no problem structure and is highly prone to barren plateaus (L29).

docs.title: Expressivity versus trainability
docs.text:
Ansatz depth Expressivity Trainability Too shallow cannot represent the target function easy to train, underfits Just right matches the problem trainable Too deep approaches a random unitary (2-design) barren plateau — untrainable

The central tension of variational QML. Deeper circuits can represent more functions, but the gradient variance decays as \(O(2^{-n})\) once the ansatz approaches a unitary 2-design. More expressive does not mean better. This is the exact analogue of the kernel-concentration problem in L27, and the same \(2^{-n}\) factor is responsible.

docs.title: Design guidelines
docs.text:
1. Start shallow (2–4 layers) and add layers only if the model underfits.
  2. Prefer problem-inspired ansätze when domain structure is known (UCCSD for chemistry, QAOA for optimisation, QCNN for spatially local data).
  3. Use local cost functions (e.g. \(\langle Z_0\rangle\)) rather than global ones (\(\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle\)) — Cerezo et al. (2021) proved local costs have gradients that vanish only polynomially for shallow circuits, not exponentially.
  4. Initialise smartly: identity-block initialisation or layer-by-layer growth avoids starting in a plateau.

docs.title: 28.5 Classical Optimisers
docs.text:
Optimiser Circuit evaluations per step Gradient Noise robustness Verdict SPSA 2 (independent of \(P\)) stochastic approximation excellent best default on hardware Adam + parameter shift \(2P\) exact analytic good best on simulators COBYLA ~1 none (direct search) fair good for few parameters Nelder–Mead ~1 none poor avoid for \(P > 10\) L-BFGS-B \(2P\) + line search numerical poor fails with shot noise

Why SPSA dominates on real hardware. It perturbs all parameters simultaneously with a random \(\pm1\) vector \(\vec\Delta\):

\[ \hat g_k = \frac{L(\vec\theta_k + c_k\vec\Delta_k) - L(\vec\theta_k - c_k\vec\Delta_k)}{2c_k} \ \vec\Delta_k^{-1} \]

Two circuit evaluations give a noisy but unbiased descent direction, regardless of whether \(P\) is 10 or 1000. Compare Adam with parameter shift, which needs \(2P\) evaluations per step. For \(P=100\): 2 versus 200 circuit runs.

Never use gradient-free methods that assume a smooth deterministic objective (L-BFGS-B, Nelder–Mead) with finite shots — shot noise makes the objective non-deterministic, and these methods interpret the noise as curvature.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Counting parameters and depth
docs.text:
Design a VQC for a 4-feature binary classification problem with a 3-layer hardware-efficient ansatz. Count parameters, gates and depth.

Solution.

Qubits: \(n = 4\) (angle encoding, one feature per qubit).

Encoding layer: 4 \(R_y\) gates, depth 1, 0 trainable parameters.

Ansatz, per layer: 4 \(R_y\) + 4 \(R_z\) + 4 CNOTs (ring \(0{\to}1{\to}2{\to}3{\to}0\)).

Parameters:

\[ P = 3\ \text{layers}\times 4\ \text{qubits}\times 2\ \text{rotations} = \mathbf{24} \]

Gate count:

\[ \underbrace{4}_{\text{encoding}} + 3\times(\underbrace{8}_{\text{rotations}} + \underbrace{4}_{\text{CNOT}}) = 4 + 36 = \mathbf{40\ \text{gates}} \]

Depth (rotations on distinct qubits run in parallel; the CNOT ring needs 2 time steps with nearest-neighbour coupling plus 1 for the wrap-around):

\[ 1 + 3\times(1 + 1 + 3) \approx \mathbf{16} \]

Feasibility. With gate error \(10^{-3}\) and 40 gates, circuit fidelity \(\approx(0.999)^{40} = 0.96\) — comfortably runnable on NISQ hardware.

Shot cost per training epoch. With 120 training samples and SPSA:

\[ 2\ \text{evaluations}\times120\ \text{samples}\times1024\ \text{shots} = 245{,}760 \ \text{shots/step} \]

At 100 steps: \(2.5\times10^{7}\) shots ≈ 1.4 hours at 5 kHz.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Forward pass by hand
docs.text:
A single-qubit VQC encodes \(x\) via \(R_y(x)\) and applies \(W(\theta) = R_y(\theta)\), measuring \(\langle Z\rangle\). Derive \(f_\theta(x)\) and find \(\theta\) that classifies \(x=0\) as \(+1\) and \(x = \pi\) as \(-1\).

Solution.

\(R_y\) rotations about the same axis compose additively:

\[ R_y(\theta)R_y(x)|0\rangle = R_y(\theta+x)|0\rangle = \cos\frac{\theta+x}{2}|0\rangle + \sin\frac{\theta+x}{2}|1\rangle \] \[ \langle Z\rangle = \cos^{2}\frac{\theta+x}{2} - \sin^{2}\frac{\theta+x}{2} = \cos(\theta+x) \] \[ \boxed{\ f_\theta(x) = \cos(\theta + x)\ } \]

Requirements.

  • \(f_\theta(0) = \cos\theta = +1 \Rightarrow \theta = 0\)
  • \(f_\theta(\pi) = \cos(\theta+\pi) = -\cos\theta = -1 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 0\) ✓
\[ \theta^{*} = 0 \]

What this model can and cannot do. \(f_\theta(x) = \cos(\theta+x)\) is a single Fourier mode — consistent with L26 Problem 4, since \(x\) is encoded exactly once. It can separate \(x\)-values that differ by roughly \(\pi\), but it cannot learn a function with two humps (e.g. classify \(x=0\) and \(x=\pi\) as \(+1\) but \(x=\pi/2\) as \(-1\)).

To fix it, re-upload the data: \(R_y(x)\,R_y(\theta_1)\,R_y(x)\dots\) — but note that consecutive \(R_y\)s just add, so the re-uploading must be interleaved with a different-axis rotation, e.g. \(R_y(x)R_z(\theta_1)R_y(x)\), to generate the second harmonic. This is why practical data-re-uploading circuits alternate rotation axes.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Training curve and overfitting
docs.text:
A VQC with 24 parameters trains on 120 samples. Training accuracy reaches 98 % but test accuracy is 72 %. Diagnose and give three fixes.

Solution.

Diagnosis: overfitting. The 26-point gap between training and test accuracy is the signature.

Why it happens here. Effective capacity is set not only by \(P=24\) but by the feature-space dimension \(2^n = 16\) and by the number of accessible Fourier frequencies. With 120 samples and an expressive entangling ansatz, the model has enough freedom to memorise.

Three fixes.

1. Reduce ansatz depth. Drop from 3 layers to 2, giving \(P = 16\). Fewer parameters and fewer accessible frequencies ⟶ a smoother decision boundary. (Directly analogous to reducing the width of a neural network.)

2. Regularise. Add an \(L_2\) penalty to the loss:

\[ L'(\vec\theta) = L(\vec\theta) + \lambda\|\vec\theta\|^{2} \]

Small \(\|\vec\theta\|\) keeps rotations near identity, biasing toward simpler functions. Typical \(\lambda\in[10^{-4},10^{-2}]\), chosen by cross-validation.

3. Use fewer data re-uploads. Each re-upload adds a Fourier frequency (L26). Reducing from 2 re-uploads to 1 halves the model's maximum frequency, forcing a smoother fit.

Also worth trying.

  • More training data — the most reliable fix if available.
  • Shot noise as regularisation. Reducing shots from 8192 to 1024 injects noise into gradients, which acts like dropout. This is a genuine and somewhat counter-intuitive benefit of NISQ hardware.
  • Early stopping on a validation set.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Optimiser comparison, quantified
docs.text:
A VQC has 40 parameters and 200 training samples, using 1024 shots per expectation value. Compare the circuit executions per optimisation step for SPSA, Adam+parameter-shift, and COBYLA. Which finishes 200 steps fastest at 5000 shots/second?

Solution.

SPSA. Two loss evaluations per step; each loss evaluation requires one circuit per training sample:

\[ 2\times200 = 400 \ \text{circuits} \Rightarrow 400\times1024 = 409{,}600 \ \text{shots/step} \]

Adam + parameter shift. The parameter-shift rule (L29) needs 2 circuits per parameter per sample:

\[ 2\times40\times200 = 16{,}000\ \text{circuits} \Rightarrow 1.64\times10^{7}\ \text{shots/step} \]

COBYLA. Approximately 1 loss evaluation per step:

\[ 200 \ \text{circuits} \Rightarrow 204{,}800\ \text{shots/step} \]

Time for 200 steps at 5000 shots/s.

Optimiser Shots/step Total shots Time SPSA \(4.1\times10^{5}\) \(8.2\times10^{7}\) 4.6 hours Adam + PS \(1.64\times10^{7}\) \(3.3\times10^{9}\) 182 hours (7.6 days) COBYLA \(2.0\times10^{5}\) \(4.1\times10^{7}\) 2.3 hours

Recommendation: SPSA. COBYLA is cheaper per step but converges poorly with 40 parameters and is badly affected by shot noise (it builds a linear model of a noisy objective). Adam with exact gradients converges in fewer steps, but each step is 40× more expensive — a net loss unless running on a fast simulator.

Practical hybrid strategy. Pre-train on a noiseless simulator with Adam + parameter shift (where circuits are cheap), then fine-tune on hardware with SPSA. This is standard practice.

docs.title: Problem 5 — VQC versus QSVM versus classical: a decision framework
docs.text:
For each scenario, recommend VQC, QSVM or a classical model, with reasoning.

(a) 50 samples, 4 features, NISQ device available. (b) 10 000 samples, 20 features. (c) Data generated by a quantum experiment (measurement outcomes from a spin chain). (d) 500 samples, 8 features, need interpretable feature importances.

Solution.

(a) 50 samples, 4 features → QSVM. The kernel matrix is only \(\frac{50\times49}{2} = 1225\) entries — perfectly affordable. QSVM's optimisation is convex, so it needs no hyperparameter search over ansatz depth, no random initialisation, no barren-plateau risk. With so little data, a VQC would overfit and its non-convex training would be unreliable. (Also run a classical RBF SVM as the honest baseline.)

(b) 10 000 samples, 20 features → classical. QSVM needs \(5\times10^{7}\) kernel entries — utterly infeasible (\(O(M^2)\) wall). A VQC on 20 qubits with a deep ansatz would hit barren plateaus. And the shot cost of 10 000 forward passes per epoch is prohibitive. Gradient boosting or a neural network will win decisively and run in seconds.

(c) Quantum data → VQC (or a quantum autoencoder). This is the QQ quadrant — the one place a real advantage is expected. The data is already a quantum state, so there is no encoding bottleneck at all: feed the state directly into the ansatz. Classical methods would first need full tomography, which costs exponentially many measurements. This is the scenario where QML is genuinely the right tool.

(d) 500 samples, interpretability required → classical. Neither VQC nor QSVM offers interpretable feature attributions: the model output is \(\langle\psi|M|\psi\rangle\) after an entangling circuit, from which per-feature importance cannot be read off. Use logistic regression with coefficients, or a tree ensemble with SHAP values. (This is a serious, under-discussed limitation of QML for regulated domains such as credit scoring and medical diagnosis, where explainability is a legal requirement.)

The decision table.

Situation Choose Small dataset, classical data, want reliability QSVM Medium dataset, want a trainable flexible model VQC (shallow ansatz, local cost) Large dataset classical Quantum-native data VQC / quantum autoencoder — the real opportunity Interpretability required classical

docs.title: 28.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Count parameters for a 5-layer hardware-efficient ansatz on 6 qubits with \(R_y,R_z\) per qubit. [Ans: 60]
  2. Derive \(f_\theta(x)\) for encoding \(R_y(x)\), ansatz \(R_x(\theta)\), measuring \(\langle Z\rangle\).
  3. Why does SPSA need only 2 evaluations regardless of \(P\)?
  4. Compute the shots per Adam step for \(P=100\), \(M=50\), 2048 shots. [Ans: \(2.05\times10^{7}\)]
  5. Explain why a global cost \(\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle\) is worse than a local one \(\langle Z_0\rangle\).
  6. Give two reasons QSVM cannot suffer barren plateaus.
  7. A VQC gets 100 % training and 50 % test accuracy on a balanced binary task. What is happening?

docs.title: 28.8 Summary
docs.text:
• The variational principle guarantees \(\langle\psi(\vec\theta)|H|\psi(\vec\theta)\rangle \ge E_0\), making variational algorithms robust to noise and suitable for NISQ hardware.
  • VQC: encode \(\vec x\), apply a trainable \(W(\vec\theta)\), measure an observable, map to a class label; train with a classical optimiser in a hybrid loop.
  • Ansatz design is a trade-off: too shallow underfits, too deep hits barren plateaus. Prefer shallow, problem-inspired ansätze and local cost functions.
  • SPSA is the practical optimiser on hardware (2 evaluations per step regardless of parameter count); parameter-shift + Adam is best on simulators; avoid L-BFGS/Nelder–Mead with shot noise.
  • VQC vs QSVM: QSVM is convex and plateau-free but costs \(O(M^2)\); VQC scales better in \(M\) but is non-convex and can be untrainable.
  • The honest use case for both is quantum-native data (QQ quadrant); on classical tabular data, classical models remain the baseline to beat and usually win.

Next lesson: L29 — Quantum neural networks, the parameter-shift rule and barren plateaus.

Practise now: unit3-qml-lab.html → VQC Trainer: choose a dataset, set ansatz depth and optimiser, and watch the loss curve and decision boundary evolve in real time.

docs.title: Lesson 44: TKET / pytket, XACC and ProjectQ
44.1 Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this hour a student will be able to:

  1. Explain the compiler-first design philosophy behind TKET.
  2. Use pytket passes to optimise circuits and interoperate with other SDKs.
  3. Describe XACC's service-oriented architecture and its HPC role.
  4. Describe ProjectQ's compiler-engine pipeline and its pedagogical value.
  5. Choose a compilation toolchain and quantify the benefit.

docs.title: 44.2 TKET / pytket — Compilation as the Product
docs.text:
Quantinuum's TKET is written in C++ with a Python interface (pytket). Its premise is that on NISQ hardware, two-qubit gate count is the binding constraint, so the compiler — not the SDK — is where the value lies.

TKET is retargetable and SDK-agnostic: you can write a circuit in Qiskit, optimise it with TKET, and run it on IonQ.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install pytket
pip install pytket-qiskit pytket-cirq pytket-braket pytket-quantinuum

docs.title: Basic use
docs.text:
from pytket import Circuit
from pytket.extensions.qiskit import AerBackend

c = Circuit(2, 2)
c.H(0).CX(0, 1).measure_all()

backend = AerBackend()
compiled = backend.get_compiled_circuit(c)
result = backend.run_circuit(compiled, n_shots=1000)
print(result.get_counts())

docs.title: Interoperability — TKET's practical superpower
docs.text:
from pytket.extensions.qiskit import qiskit_to_tk, tk_to_qiskit
from pytket.extensions.cirq  import cirq_to_tk, tk_to_cirq
from pytket.qasm import circuit_from_qasm, circuit_to_qasm

tk_circ = qiskit_to_tk(qiskit_circuit)      # import from Qiskit
# ... optimise with TKET ...
qiskit_circ = tk_to_qiskit(tk_circ)         # export back
\[ \boxed{\ \text{Write in your favourite SDK} \ \to\ \text{optimise with TKET} \ \to\ \text{run anywhere.}\ } \]

docs.title: Optimisation passes
docs.text:
from pytket.passes import (FullPeepholeOptimise, CliffordSimp, RemoveRedundancies,
                           SequencePass, DecomposeBoxes, PauliSimp,
                           SynthesiseTket, KAKDecomposition)

FullPeepholeOptimise().apply(c)     # the general-purpose workhorse
CliffordSimp().apply(c)             # resynthesise Clifford subcircuits
PauliSimp().apply(c)                # exponentiated-Pauli resynthesis (chemistry, QAOA)
RemoveRedundancies().apply(c)       # cancel adjacent inverses
KAKDecomposition().apply(c)         # optimal 2-qubit resynthesis (<= 3 CNOTs)

custom = SequencePass([DecomposeBoxes(), FullPeepholeOptimise(), CliffordSimp()])
custom.apply(c)

The most important passes.

Pass What it does Typical CX saving RemoveRedundancies cancels \(GG^\dagger\) pairs 5–15 % KAKDecomposition any 2-qubit unitary → at most 3 CNOTs (provably optimal) 10–30 % CliffordSimp resynthesises Clifford blocks 15–40 % PauliSimp reorders and merges \(e^{i\theta P}\) terms 30–60 % on chemistry/QAOA FullPeepholeOptimise applies a curated sequence of the above 20–50 %

PauliSimp deserves special mention. Chemistry (UCCSD, Trotterised Hamiltonians) and QAOA circuits consist almost entirely of exponentiated Pauli strings \(e^{i\theta P}\). PauliSimp reorders commuting terms and merges their CNOT ladders, which is why TKET's advantage is largest exactly where circuits matter most.

docs.title: Architecture-aware routing
docs.text:
from pytket.architecture import Architecture
from pytket.passes import DefaultMappingPass, RoutingPass
from pytket.placement import GraphPlacement

arch = Architecture([(0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,4)])      # a line
DefaultMappingPass(arch).apply(c)

TKET's routing consistently inserts fewer SWAPs than competitors in published benchmarks — the main source of its measured advantage.

docs.title: 44.3 XACC — Quantum Computing for HPC
docs.text: Oak Ridge National Laboratory's XACC (eXtreme-scale ACCelerator) treats a QPU as an accelerator attached to a classical supercomputer, exactly as XACC's designers treat GPUs.

docs.title: The service-oriented architecture
docs.text:
Application  (C++ / Python)
        |
   XACC Framework
    /   |     |    \
Compilers  IRTransformations  Accelerators  Observables
    |         |                   |
 XASM      optimisation      IBM, Rigetti,
 Quil,                       IonQ, TNQVM,
 OpenQASM                    simulators

Every component is a plugin discovered at runtime, so a new backend is added without touching application code.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import xacc

qpu = xacc.getAccelerator('aer', {'shots': 1024})
buf = xacc.qalloc(2)

xacc.qasm('''
.compiler xasm
.circuit bell
.qbit q
H(q[0]);
CX(q[0], q[1]);
Measure(q[0]);
Measure(q[1]);
''')

bell = xacc.getCompiled('bell')
qpu.execute(buf, bell)
print(buf.getMeasurementCounts())

docs.title: Where XACC matters
docs.text:
• C++ first, so it links directly into existing HPC simulation codes (NWChem, LAMMPS).
  • MPI-aware, so quantum tasks can be distributed across a cluster.
  • TNQVM — a tensor-network simulator that scales to hundreds of qubits on supercomputers.
  • Embedded QPU calls inside classical simulations — for example, a molecular-dynamics code calling a VQE for the electronic-structure step.

XACC's users are national laboratories, not individual researchers. It is the right answer when the quantum computation is one step inside a large classical HPC workflow.

docs.title: 44.4 ProjectQ — The Teaching Compiler
docs.text: ETH Zürich's ProjectQ (Steiger, Häner, Troyer, 2018) is small, readable and beautifully structured. Its lasting contribution is the compiler-engine pipeline.

docs.title: The engine list
docs.text:
from projectq import MainEngine
from projectq.ops import H, CNOT, Measure, All
from projectq.backends import Simulator
from projectq.setups import restrictedgateset

eng = MainEngine(backend=Simulator(),
                 engine_list=[TagRemover(), LocalOptimizer(5),
                              AutoReplacer(rule_set), InstructionFilter(...)])

q = eng.allocate_qureg(2)
H | q[0]
CNOT | (q[0], q[1])
All(Measure) | q
eng.flush()
print(int(q[0]), int(q[1]))

The | operator for gate application (H | qubit) is ProjectQ's distinctive syntax, echoing Dirac notation.

docs.title: The pipeline concept
docs.text:
User code -> Engine1 -> Engine2 -> ... -> Backend
              (tag)    (optimise)         (simulator/hardware)

Each engine receives a stream of commands, transforms it, and forwards it. Compilation happens while you write, not as a separate step — which makes the compilation process unusually visible and is exactly why ProjectQ is such a good teaching tool.

Its historical significance. ProjectQ demonstrated the modular compiler-engine architecture that Qiskit's PassManager and TKET's pass system both later adopted. Development has slowed, so it is now recommended for understanding how compilers work, not for production.

docs.title: 44.5 Comparative Summary
docs.text: Framework Origin Language Killer feature Use when pytket / TKET Quantinuum C++/Python best-in-class optimisation you need every CNOT saved XACC ORNL C++/Python HPC integration quantum inside a classical HPC workflow ProjectQ ETH Zürich Python readable compiler pipeline teaching compiler internals Qiskit IBM Python ecosystem general use Cirq Google Python hardware transparency device research

docs.title: Problem 1 — Measuring TKET's optimisation benefit
docs.text:
A 6-qubit UCCSD chemistry circuit has 320 CNOTs after naive compilation. Estimate the CNOT count after TKET's FullPeepholeOptimise and PauliSimp, and compute the fidelity improvement at \(\epsilon_{\text{CX}} = 8\times10^{-3}\).

Solution.

Baseline.

\[ F_{\text{naive}} = (1 - 0.008)^{320} = 0.992^{320} = e^{320\ln0.992} = e^{-2.5697} = \mathbf{0.0766} \]

7.7 % fidelity — the circuit is unusable.

After FullPeepholeOptimise (typical 35 % CNOT reduction):

\[ 320\times0.65 = 208\ \text{CNOTs} \] \[ F = 0.992^{208} = e^{-1.670} = \mathbf{0.1882} \]

After PauliSimp as well (UCCSD is entirely exponentiated Paulis — typical 50 % total reduction):

\[ 320\times0.50 = 160\ \text{CNOTs} \] \[ F = 0.992^{160} = e^{-1.285} = \mathbf{0.2767} \]

Summary.

Compilation CNOTs Fidelity Improvement Naive 320 0.0766 1.0× FullPeepholeOptimise 208 0.1882 2.5× + PauliSimp 160 0.2767 3.6×

Why a 3.6× fidelity gain matters so much. Estimating an observable to precision \(\epsilon\) requires shots scaling as \(1/(F^2\epsilon^2)\) — the signal is attenuated by \(F\), so the variance penalty goes as \(F^{-2}\):

\[ \frac{S_{\text{naive}}}{S_{\text{optimised}}} = \left(\frac{0.2767}{0.0766}\right)^{2} = 3.61^{2} = \mathbf{13\times} \] \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{A 50 \% CNOT reduction cuts the shot budget — and the cost — by }13\times.\ } \]

On Braket's IonQ pricing (L41), a $13 000 experiment becomes a $1 000 experiment. The compiler pays for itself immediately.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Cross-framework workflow
docs.text:
Write a workflow that builds a circuit in Qiskit, optimises it with TKET, and runs it on IonQ via Braket. Explain each step's rationale.

Solution.

# ---------- 1. BUILD in Qiskit (best ecosystem, familiar syntax) ----------
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
import numpy as np

qc = QuantumCircuit(4)
qc.h(range(4))
for i in range(3):
    qc.cx(i, i+1)
    qc.rz(np.pi/4, i+1)
    qc.cx(i, i+1)
qc.measure_all()
print("Qiskit CX count:", qc.count_ops().get('cx', 0))     # 6

# ---------- 2. OPTIMISE with TKET (best compiler) ----------
from pytket.extensions.qiskit import qiskit_to_tk, tk_to_qiskit
from pytket.passes import FullPeepholeOptimise, PauliSimp, SequencePass

tk = qiskit_to_tk(qc)
print("TKET CX before:", tk.n_gates_of_type(OpType.CX))
SequencePass([PauliSimp(), FullPeepholeOptimise()]).apply(tk)
print("TKET CX after :", tk.n_gates_of_type(OpType.CX))

# ---------- 3. RUN on IonQ via Braket (best fidelity + all-to-all) ----------
from pytket.extensions.braket import BraketBackend

backend = BraketBackend(device="Aria-1", region="us-east-1",
                        s3_bucket="my-bucket", s3_folder="results")
compiled = backend.get_compiled_circuit(tk)      # final device-specific compilation
handle = backend.process_circuit(compiled, n_shots=1000)
print(backend.get_result(handle).get_counts())

Rationale for each step.

Step Tool Why Build Qiskit largest ecosystem, most familiar to students, best documentation Optimise TKET independently benchmarked as the strongest optimiser; PauliSimp targets exactly this circuit's \(e^{i\theta ZZ}\) structure Run IonQ via Braket all-to-all connectivity means zero SWAPs; IonQ's native \(ZZ\) gate matches the circuit

Expected result on this circuit. The pattern CX, Rz, CX is exactly \(e^{-i\theta Z\otimes Z/2}\) (L34 §2.3). PauliSimp recognises the three such blocks, notes that adjacent ones share a qubit and their CNOT ladders can be merged, and reduces the CNOT count from 6 to 4.

\[ F: (0.996)^{6} = 0.976 \ \longrightarrow\ (0.996)^{4} = 0.984 \]

Modest here because the circuit is tiny; on a full 20-qubit UCCSD circuit the same pass saves hundreds of CNOTs.

The general principle.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{The frameworks are interoperable. Use each where it is strongest — that is the professional workflow.}\ } \]

docs.title: Problem 3 — Understanding the KAK decomposition bound
docs.text:
Explain why any two-qubit unitary needs at most 3 CNOTs, and compute the saving when a naive compilation used 6.

Solution.

The parameter-counting argument.

\(SU(4)\) — the group of two-qubit unitaries up to global phase — has dimension

\[ \dim SU(4) = 4^{2} - 1 = \mathbf{15\ \text{real parameters}} . \]

A circuit of \(k\) CNOTs interleaved with arbitrary single-qubit gates provides:

  • Single-qubit gates: \(2(k+1)\) of them (a layer before each CNOT and one after), each contributing 3 parameters — but global phases and commuting phases reduce the independent count.
  • The standard counting gives: with \(k\) CNOTs you can reach at most \(3\times2(k+1) - (\text{redundancies})\) parameters.

The precise result (Vidal–Dawson, Vatan–Williams, 2004):

CNOTs Parameters reachable Covers \(SU(4)\)? 0 6 no (product unitaries only) 1 9 no 2 12 no 3 15 yes — exactly enough \[ \boxed{\ \textbf{Any two-qubit unitary decomposes into at most 3 CNOTs, and this is tight.}\ } \]

The constructive form (KAK / Cartan decomposition).

\[ U = (A_1\otimes A_2)\,\exp\!\big(i(c_1 XX + c_2 YY + c_3 ZZ)\big)\,(B_1\otimes B_2) \]

where \(A_i, B_i \in SU(2)\) and the central "canonical" part needs exactly 3 CNOTs in general — and fewer in special cases: 2 CNOTs if one \(c_i = 0\), 1 CNOT if two vanish, 0 if all three do.

The saving from 6 to 3.

\[ \text{CNOT reduction} = 50\% \]

At \(\epsilon_{\text{CX}} = 10^{-2}\):

\[ F_{6} = 0.99^{6} = 0.9415, \qquad F_{3} = 0.99^{3} = 0.9703 \] \[ \text{error reduction} = \frac{1 - 0.9415}{1 - 0.9703} = \frac{0.0585}{0.0297} = \mathbf{1.97\times} \]

Where this arises in practice. Any circuit containing arbitrary two-qubit blocks — a variational ansatz with cirq.MatrixGate on pairs, a compiled Hamiltonian evolution, a decomposed Toffoli. TKET's KAKDecomposition pass finds the optimal form automatically. A naive decomposition routinely uses 6–9 CNOTs where 3 suffice.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Designing an HPC-integrated workflow with XACC
docs.text:
A materials-science group runs classical DFT on a supercomputer and wants to replace the strongly-correlated part with a VQE. Design the XACC workflow.

Solution.

The scientific setup. Density functional theory handles most of a material's electrons well but fails for strongly correlated orbitals (transition-metal \(d\)-electrons). The DFT + embedding approach treats a small active space with a higher-accuracy method — here, a VQE.

Why XACC rather than Qiskit.

  1. The DFT code is C++/Fortran running under MPI on thousands of cores. XACC is a C++ library that links directly; calling Python from an MPI Fortran code is painful.
  2. The VQE is called inside the self-consistency loop, thousands of times — the overhead of process boundaries matters.
  3. XACC's TNQVM tensor-network simulator runs on the same supercomputer, so the "quantum" step can be simulated at scale until real hardware is ready.

The workflow.

[ MPI rank 0..N: classical DFT ]
            |
            |  active-space Hamiltonian (a few orbitals)
            v
[ XACC: build Observable from the fermionic Hamiltonian ]
            |
            |  Jordan-Wigner / Bravyi-Kitaev mapping
            v
[ XACC: VQE with UCCSD ansatz ]
            |
     +------+-------+
     |              |
 [ TNQVM sim ]  [ real QPU via IBM/IonQ plugin ]
     |              |
     +------+-------+
            |
            v
   ground-state energy -> back into the DFT self-consistency loop

#include "xacc.hpp"
#include "xacc_observable.hpp"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    xacc::Initialize(argc, argv);

    // Hamiltonian produced by the classical DFT code
    auto H = xacc::quantum::getObservable("pauli", hamiltonian_string);

    auto accelerator = xacc::getAccelerator("tnqvm", {{"tnqvm-visitor","exatn"}});
    auto optimizer   = xacc::getOptimizer("nlopt", {{"algorithm","cobyla"}});
    auto ansatz      = xacc::getService<xacc::Instruction>("uccsd");

    auto vqe = xacc::getAlgorithm("vqe", {{"ansatz", ansatz},
                                          {"observable", H},
                                          {"accelerator", accelerator},
                                          {"optimizer", optimizer}});
    auto buffer = xacc::qalloc(n_qubits);
    vqe->execute(buffer);

    double energy = (*buffer)["opt-val"].as<double>();
    xacc::Finalize();
    return 0;
}

The key architectural benefit. Switching from the TNQVM simulator to real hardware is a one-line change:

auto accelerator = xacc::getAccelerator("ibm:ibmq_kolkata");

No application code changes. That plugin architecture is precisely what a long-lived HPC codebase needs: the quantum backend will change many times over the code's lifetime, but the science code should not.

Honest assessment. Today the TNQVM simulator gives better results than any available QPU for active spaces of practical size, so the "quantum" step is currently classical. The value of the workflow now is readiness — when hardware improves, the pipeline already exists.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Choosing a compilation toolchain
docs.text:
Recommend a toolchain for each scenario, quantifying the benefit where possible.

(a) A 50-qubit QAOA circuit on IBM hardware, minimising CNOTs. (b) A teaching demonstration of how compilers insert SWAPs. (c) A VQE embedded in a Fortran molecular-dynamics code. (d) Rapid prototyping of a QML idea. (e) Publishing a benchmark comparing compiler quality.

Solution.

(a) 50-qubit QAOA on IBM → Qiskit for construction, TKET for compilation.

QAOA circuits are exponentiated Pauli strings, so PauliSimp is directly applicable. Published benchmarks put TKET 10–30 % below Qiskit's transpiler on two-qubit count for such circuits.

Quantified. Suppose Qiskit level 3 yields 400 CNOTs and TKET yields 320. At \(\epsilon_{\text{CX}} = 8\times10^{-3}\):

\[ F_{\text{Qiskit}} = 0.992^{400} = 0.0403, \qquad F_{\text{TKET}} = 0.992^{320} = 0.0766 \] \[ \text{shot budget ratio} = \left(\frac{0.0766}{0.0403}\right)^{2} = 3.62^{2} = \mathbf{13\times \text{fewer shots}} \]

Use pytket-qiskit to submit directly to IBM after TKET compilation.

(b) Teaching how compilers insert SWAPs → ProjectQ, or Qiskit with visualisation.

ProjectQ's engine pipeline is small enough to read end to end — a student can literally follow a command through each engine. Alternatively, Qiskit's transpile(..., optimization_level=0) with circuit.draw() before and after makes SWAP insertion visible. TKET is the wrong choice here: it is a C++ black box, excellent at its job but opaque.

(c) VQE inside Fortran MD code → XACC.

The only framework designed for this. C++ API, MPI-aware, links into existing HPC codes, and swaps backends without touching application code (Problem 4).

(d) Rapid QML prototyping → PennyLane.

Autodiff, PyTorch/JAX integration, extensive templates, excellent documentation. Compilation quality is irrelevant at prototype stage — you are running on a simulator where CNOT count does not affect correctness.

(e) Publishing a compiler benchmark → all of them, on a standard benchmark suite.

Use QASMBench or MQT Bench for the circuits, compile with Qiskit (levels 0–3), TKET (several pass sequences), Cirq and pytket-tket, and report:

  • two-qubit gate count,
  • circuit depth,
  • compilation wall-clock time,
  • and — critically — verified circuit equivalence (unitary comparison on small instances), since an "optimiser" that silently changes the circuit is worse than useless.

Report all four metrics. A compiler that halves the CNOT count but takes an hour to run is unusable for variational algorithms that recompile every iteration; a compiler that is fast but occasionally incorrect is unusable full stop.

The summary rule.

\[ \boxed{\ \textbf{SDK for building, TKET for compiling, XACC for HPC embedding, ProjectQ for understanding.}\ } \]

docs.title: 44.7 Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Compute the fidelity gain from reducing 500 CNOTs to 300 at \(\epsilon = 10^{-2}\). [Ans: 0.0066 → 0.0490, 7.4×]
  2. Why can any two-qubit unitary use at most 3 CNOTs?
  3. Which TKET pass suits a Trotterised chemistry circuit, and why? [Ans: PauliSimp]
  4. Write pytket code converting a Qiskit circuit, optimising it and converting back.
  5. What makes XACC suitable for HPC and Qiskit unsuitable?
  6. Explain ProjectQ's engine pipeline in three sentences.
  7. If CNOT count falls 40 %, by what factor does the shot budget fall at \(\epsilon = 10^{-2}\) and 300 initial CNOTs? [Ans: \(F: 0.0490 \to 0.1638\), shots fall \(11.2\times\)]

docs.title: 44.8 Summary
docs.text:
• TKET/pytket is compiler-first and SDK-agnostic: import from Qiskit or Cirq, optimise, export anywhere. Its passes (FullPeepholeOptimise, CliffordSimp, PauliSimp, KAKDecomposition) typically cut two-qubit counts by 20–50 %.
  • A 50 % CNOT reduction cuts the required shot budget by ~13×, because signal attenuation enters the variance as \(F^{-2}\) — the compiler pays for itself in hardware cost immediately.
  • KAK decomposition: \(\dim SU(4) = 15\) and 3 CNOTs provide exactly 15 parameters, so any two-qubit unitary needs at most 3 CNOTs — and naive compilations routinely use 6–9.
  • XACC treats the QPU as an HPC accelerator: C++ API, MPI-aware, plugin architecture so backends swap without application changes, TNQVM for large tensor-network simulation. Built for national-laboratory workflows.
  • ProjectQ pioneered the compiler-engine pipeline later adopted by Qiskit's PassManager and TKET. Its value today is pedagogical — it is small enough to read.
  • The professional workflow is polyglot: SDK for building, TKET for compiling, XACC for HPC embedding, ProjectQ for understanding.

Next lesson: L45 — Comparative study, benchmarking and the capstone project.
